# Birko.Framework — Full Codebase Code-Review Audit

_Generated 2026-06-17 — project-by-project multi-agent review of all 172 non-test `Birko.*` projects, with adversarial verification of every critical & high finding._

## Status

- **Coverage: 172 / 172 projects reviewed** (complete).
- **Verification: complete for crit/high.** All 24 criticals and 147 highs were adversarially re-checked (a second agent re-opened the cited file). **7 findings were rejected as false positives and removed.** Medium/low are reviewer claims, not individually verified.
- **Findings: 864** — 24 critical, 147 high, 275 medium, 418 low.

## How to turn this into tasks

Every finding below has a **stable ID** (`CR-C01` … criticals, `CR-H001` … highs, `CR-M001` … medium, `CR-L001` … low) and a uniform field block, so each `###` entry maps **1:1 to a task**. To create a task from a finding, copy:
- **ID / Title** → task title (e.g. `CR-C01 — Ollama streaming POSTs to the base URL`)
- **Path** → the absolute file:line to open (already resolved against the project root)
- **Detail** → task Context
- **Fix** → suggested approach
- **Acceptance** → derive from Fix + add a regression test
- **Status** → `open` initially; flip to `done` / `wontfix` as you triage

Paths are absolute as of 2026-06-17; line numbers may drift as fixes land — re-grep the symbol if a line looks off.

## Critical findings (24)

### CR-C01 · 🔴 critical · Birko.AI.Providers
- **Title:** Ollama streaming POSTs to the base URL instead of /api/chat
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI.Providers\Providers\OllamaProvider.cs:156`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: streaming now posts to `var url = $"{_baseUrl}/api/chat";` (matching the non-streaming path) and adds `num_predict = -1` to the streaming payload. New `Birko.AI.Providers.Tests` (also closes CR-H006) verifies the streaming + non-streaming requests hit `/api/chat` via an injected fake `HttpMessageHandler` (new constructor test seam).
- **Detail:** In SendMessageStreamingAsync, the request is built with `new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, _baseUrl)` — posting to e.g. http://localhost:11434 (the root), not the chat endpoint. The non-streaming path (line 41) correctly uses `var url = $"{_baseUrl}/api/chat";`. Every streaming call to Ollama will hit the wrong path and fail (404 / not a valid endpoint), so streaming is completely broken for this provider.
- **Fix:** Build the URL the same way as the non-streaming path: `var url = $"{_baseUrl}/api/chat";` and pass `url` to the HttpRequestMessage. Also consider passing `num_predict` in the streaming payload to match the non-streaming request.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI.Providers\Providers\OllamaProvider.cs. At line 156, SendMessageStreamingAsync builds the request as `new HttpRequestMessage(HttpMethod.Post, _baseUrl)`, posting to the root URL (e.g. http://localhost:11434) with no endpoint path. In contrast, the non-streaming SendMessageAsync at line 41 correctly composes `var url = $"{_baseUrl}/api/chat";` and uses it at line 48. The streaming response parser (ParseOllamaStreamChunksWithToolCapture) expects Ollama's /api/chat NDJSON shape (message.content, message.tool_calls, done at lines 263-308), confirming /api/chat is the intended target. Posting the chat payload to the Ollama root does not hit the chat endpoint, so streaming will not work. This is a genuine, critical, actionable bug; the fix is to use `$"{_baseUrl}/api/chat"` as the non-streaming path does. _baseUrl is normalized with TrimEnd('/') at line 19, so simple suffix concatenation is correct.

### CR-C02 · 🔴 critical · Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis
- **Title:** Scheduled/delayed jobs are dequeued immediately — score scale mismatch with dequeue threshold
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis\RedisJobQueue.cs:100,103-107,351-354`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: the score is now **time-dominant** — `scheduledAt.Ticks / 1e4` with a **bounded priority tiebreaker** (`< 1` time-unit, so it can never pull a future-scheduled job across the eligibility threshold) — and the dequeue threshold uses the SAME encoding via `GetDequeueThreshold(now) = now.Ticks / 1e4`. So future/delayed jobs (incl. FailAsync retry backoff) correctly wait until their time, while priority still orders ready jobs. Deliberate semantics change: priority is now a within-ready tiebreaker rather than globally dominant (the two can't coexist with a single score+threshold — see the design note). New `Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis.Tests` (closes CR-H010) reflection-tests the invariants (due eligible / future+high-priority not eligible / priority orders ready); the Lua dequeue path needs a live Redis (infra gap).
- **Detail:** GetQueueScore stores the time component as scheduledAt.Ticks / 1e4 (and subtracts priority*1e13), but DequeueScript compares ZRANGEBYSCORE -inf <now> where now = DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks (full ticks, no /1e4 scaling, no priority term). A job scheduled for the current time has a score of ~6.4e13 (priority 0) while the dequeue threshold is ~6.4e17 — over four orders of magnitude larger. Therefore EVERY future-scheduled job (FailAsync retries with backoff at lines 188-195, and any descriptor with ScheduledAt/Delay set) is already <= now and is dequeued immediately. The retry backoff delay and the README's 'Failed jobs re-scheduled with configurable delay' / 'Higher priority jobs dequeued first' guarantees are both broken: a retried job is picked up instantly instead of after RetryPolicy.GetDelay, and a high-priority job (negative score) is the only thing reliably ordered.
- **Fix:** Make the dequeue threshold use the same encoding as the stored score. Compute now in the C# caller as GetQueueScore(int.MaxValue, DateTime.UtcNow) (so any priority's time-eligible jobs qualify) or, more simply, store the time component unscaled and pass DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks consistently, OR have the Lua script receive the pre-encoded threshold ARGV[1] = scheduledAt.Ticks/1e4 for the lowest acceptable priority. The two scoring conventions must be identical on both write and read paths. Add a test that enqueues a job with ScheduledAt in the future and asserts DequeueAsync returns null until that time.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis\RedisJobQueue.cs. The score function GetQueueScore (line 351-354) computes the time component as scheduledAt.Ticks / 1e4, while the dequeue threshold (line 100) uses raw DateTime.UtcNow.Ticks with no scaling, passed into DequeueScript's ZRANGEBYSCORE key -inf now (line 33). For the current date, now.Ticks is ~6.39e17, but a priority-0 job's score (now or future-scheduled) is ~6.39e13 — about 4 orders of magnitude below the threshold. So ZRANGEBYSCORE -inf now matches every such job immediately, regardless of ScheduledAt. I verified the math numerically: a job scheduled 30s in the future still has score 6.39e13 <= threshold 6.39e17, so it is dequeued instantly. This breaks the FailAsync retry backoff (lines 188-195: ScheduledAt = UtcNow + delay, re-added via GetQueueScore at line 194) and any ScheduledAt/Delay job — the README's 'Failed jobs re-scheduled with configurable delay' guarantee is violated. There is only one dequeue path and no compensating scaling elsewhere (confirmed via grep). The fix is to make the score's time term and the threshold use the same scale (either drop /1e4 from the score or divide now by 1e4). One minor correction to the finding: the priority-ordering guarantee is mostly intact (lower score still sorts first among eligible jobs); the genuinely broken guarantee is the scheduling/delay one. But the cited critical defect — future-scheduled jobs dequeued immediately due to the score/threshold scale mismatch — is real and accurate.

### CR-C03 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Communication.Hardware
- **Title:** LPT.Write/Read pass the LPT number as the hardware I/O address
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Hardware\Ports/LPT.cs:42 (and Read at :51)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: added `LPT.ResolvePortAddress(int)` mapping the logical LPT number 1/2/3 → base I/O address 0x378/0x278/0x3BC (raw addresses ≥ 0x100 pass through; ambiguous small values throw); Write/Read now use the resolved address. Comment typo (623→632) fixed. New `Birko.Communication.Hardware.Tests` covers the mapping (the P/Invoke itself needs real hardware).
- **Detail:** Output(portnumber, d) and Input(portnumber) pass portnumber (the logical LPT number, e.g. 1 or 2 from LPTSettings.Number) as the first argument, which inpout32 Out32/Inp32 interpret as the absolute port ADDRESS. The class's own comment (lines 22-23) documents that LPT1 = 0x378 (888) and LPT2 = 0x278 (632), so passing 1/2 writes to I/O ports 1/2 instead of the parallel port data register. Hardware writes/reads will go to the wrong address.
- **Fix:** Map Number -> base address (e.g. 1 => 0x378, 2 => 0x278) and pass that address to Output/Input, or store the address directly in settings instead of a port number.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Hardware\Ports\LPT.cs.

The inpout32 P/Invoke declarations make the bug unambiguous: line 25-26 declares Output(int adress, int value) mapped to EntryPoint "Out32", and line 28-29 declares Input(int adress) mapped to "Inp32". The first parameter of inpout32's Out32/Inp32 is the absolute I/O port ADDRESS.

Line 34: portnumber = settings.Number — stores the logical LPT index (LPTSettings.Number, e.g. 1 or 2).
Line 42: Output(portnumber, d) passes that logical index (1/2) as the address.
Line 51: Input(portnumber) does the same for reads.

The class's own comment (lines 22-24) documents that LPT1 = 0x378 (888) and LPT2 = 0x278 (the comment misprints the decimal as 623; 0x278 is actually 632), so a real driver should write to 888/632, not 1/2. Passing 1/2 targets I/O ports 1/2, which are not the parallel-port data register — hardware writes/reads go to the wrong address exactly as described.

The finding is REAL and actionable: the code should map the logical LPT number to its hardware base address (e.g. 1 -> 0x378, 2 -> 0x278) before calling Out32/Inp32. The only flaw in the finding text is repeating the comment's typo (632 vs 623), which does not affect the validity of the issue.

### CR-C04 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.CosmosDB
- **Title:** AbstractModel has no Cosmos 'id' property — point reads/writes by Guid cannot work
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB\Stores/AsyncCosmosDBStore.cs:176,187 (and CosmosDBStore.cs:158,171; container created with /id at AsyncCosmosDBStore.cs:458 / CosmosDBStore.cs:365)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (Cosmos-local, no change to the shared AbstractModel): new `CosmosGuidIdSerializer : CosmosSerializer` (wired via `Settings.GetCosmosClientOptions().Serializer`) injects a string `id` == the model's `Guid` on write, so documents match the `/id` partition key and point reads/writes by `guid.ToString()` resolve; the model's own `Guid` is still emitted for round-trip and the extra `id` is ignored on read. Non-model types (query/account responses) serialize normally. Unit-tested in `Birko.Data.CosmosDB.Tests/CosmosGuidIdSerializerTests` (id-injection + round-trip + non-model); the point-operation behavior needs the Cosmos emulator (infra gap).
- **Detail:** Documents are created with `new PartitionKey(data.Guid.Value.ToString())` and the container's partition key path is '/id'. The Cosmos SDK requires every document to carry a string 'id' field, and with path '/id' the partition-key value must equal that 'id'. But AbstractModel (Birko.Data.Core/Models/AbstractModel.cs) only exposes a `Guid? Guid` property — it serializes to "Guid" (PascalCase), never "id". No custom CosmosSerializer or JSON mapping is configured (Settings.GetCosmosClientOptions only sets RequestTimeout/AllowBulkExecution). So either CreateItemAsync fails (the supplied PartitionKey won't match the doc's '/id', which the SDK auto-fills with a random GUID), or the doc is stored under a random id and `ReadItemAsync<T>(guid.ToString(), new PartitionKey(guid.ToString()))` / ReplaceItem / DeleteItem by `guid.ToString()` can never locate it. The unit tests only exercise null/empty guards with mocks, so this is never caught.
- **Fix:** Add an 'id' mapping that mirrors Guid (e.g. a partial AbstractModel with a [JsonPropertyName("id")] string projection of Guid, or a custom CosmosSerializer that maps Guid<->id), or set PartitionKeyPath to a real serialized property and use the actual 'id' value for point reads. Add an integration test (Cosmos emulator) that round-trips Create then Read(Guid).
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified against actual code. AbstractModel (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Core\Models\AbstractModel.cs:9) exposes only `public virtual Guid? Guid` — it serializes to the JSON property "Guid" (PascalCase), never "id". There is no [JsonProperty("id")] attribute, no second partial with an Id member, and no custom CosmosSerializer: Settings.GetCosmosClientOptions() (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB\Stores\Settings.cs:39-46) sets only RequestTimeout and AllowBulkExecution, so the SDK's default serializer is used and serializes property names as declared.

Meanwhile the container is created with partition key path "/id" (AsyncCosmosDBStore.cs:458 via Settings.PartitionKeyPath default "/id" at Settings.cs:19; identical in CosmosDBStore.cs). Writes pass `new PartitionKey(data.Guid.Value.ToString())` (AsyncCosmosDBStore.cs:176, 231, 245, 289, 381, 409, 435) and point reads/replaces/deletes use `guid.ToString()` as the document id plus the matching PartitionKey (e.g. ReadItemAsync<T>(guid.ToString(), new PartitionKey(guid.ToString())) at line 187). The synchronous CosmosDBStore.cs mirrors the same pattern at the cited lines.

The Cosmos SDK requires every document to carry a string 'id'; with partition key path '/id' the supplied partition-key value must equal the document's 'id'. Since AbstractModel never emits an 'id' that equals data.Guid.ToString(), CreateItemAsync will fail with a PartitionKey/document mismatch, or the SDK auto-fills 'id' with a random GUID and the point read/replace/delete by guid.ToString() can never locate the stored document. Either way Guid-keyed point operations cannot work. The unit tests only exercise null/empty guards with mocks, so this is uncaught. This is a genuine critical bug. The only minor uncertainty is the exact SDK runtime failure mode (throw vs silent random-id), but both outcomes leave point operations broken, so isReal=true with high confidence.

### CR-C05 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.EventSourcing
- **Title:** Created event's AggregateId does not match the Guid the inner store assigns
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.EventSourcing\Stores/EventSourcingStoreWrapper.cs:59-63`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (`item.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid();` assigned before building the event, then `item.Guid.Value` used for GetVersion + AggregateId + inner store); new test project `Birko.Data.EventSourcing.Tests`, test `EventSourcingStoreWrapperTests.Create_RecordsEventUnderThePersistedGuid`
- **Detail:** In Create, GetVersion is queried with `item.Guid ?? Guid.Empty`, but the DomainEvent's AggregateId is built from `item.Guid ?? Guid.NewGuid()` — a fresh, throwaway Guid generated inside the wrapper. The wrapper never assigns this Guid back to `item.Guid`. The inner store (e.g. AbstractInMemoryStore.CreateCore: `data.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid()`) then independently assigns yet another Guid to the entity. So for the normal create case (entity Guid is null before insert), the event is recorded under one random AggregateId while the row is persisted under a different one. Replay(aggregateId)/GetHistory(aggregateId) called with the entity's real Guid will never find the Created event, which defeats the core purpose of the library. Also GetVersion(Guid.Empty) effectively pools the version counter of all unsaved aggregates under Guid.Empty.
- **Fix:** Assign the Guid before recording the event and before delegating: `item.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid();` then use `item.Guid.Value` for both GetVersion and the DomainEvent AggregateId, and pass that same item to the inner store (whose `??=` will then be a no-op).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. In EventSourcingStoreWrapper.Create (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.EventSourcing\Stores\EventSourcingStoreWrapper.cs:54-79) for the normal create case where item.Guid is null:

- Line 59: GetVersion(item.Guid ?? Guid.Empty) queries the version counter under Guid.Empty.
- Line 63: the DomainEvent's AggregateId is built from item.Guid ?? Guid.NewGuid() — a fresh throwaway Guid (call it X) that is never assigned back to item.Guid.
- Line 72: the Created event is appended under AggregateId X.
- Line 78: _innerStore.Create(item, null) is called. The inner store assigns a DIFFERENT Guid (confirmed in C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.InMemory\Stores\AbstractInMemoryStore.cs:61, data.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid()) — call it Y. The row is persisted under Y and item.Guid becomes Y.

So the event is recorded under X while the entity persists under Y, and X is lost (never read back). Replay(Y)/GetHistory(Y) call _eventStore.Read(Y) (lines 247-268), which never finds the Created event recorded under X. This defeats the core purpose of the event-sourcing library.

The secondary point is also valid: GetVersion(Guid.Empty) pools the version counter of all unsaved aggregates under Guid.Empty.

The same flawed pattern is replicated in the three sibling wrappers (AsyncEventSourcingStoreWrapper.cs:61, EventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.cs:49, AsyncEventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.cs:51), all using item.Guid ?? Guid.Empty for GetVersion. The fix is to assign item.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid() before building the event so the same Guid drives GetVersion, the event AggregateId, and the inner-store row.

### CR-C06 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.EventSourcing
- **Title:** Same Guid-mismatch on bulk Create (sync + async)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.EventSourcing\Stores/EventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.cs:49-62`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (same `item.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid();` up-front assignment in `EventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.Create`, `AsyncEventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.CreateAsync`, and `AsyncEventSourcingStoreWrapper.CreateAsync`); tests `EventSourcingStoreWrapperTests.BulkCreate_RecordsEventsUnderEachPersistedGuid` (+ async)
- **Detail:** EventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.Create and AsyncEventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.CreateAsync (AsyncEventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.cs:51-64) repeat the single-store create bug: GetVersion uses `item.Guid ?? Guid.Empty`, the event AggregateId uses `item.Guid ?? Guid.NewGuid()`, item.Version is set, but item.Guid is left null so the inner bulk store assigns its own Guid. Every Created event recorded for a newly-inserted batch is orphaned from its persisted row. AsyncEventSourcingStoreWrapper.CreateAsync (AsyncEventSourcingStoreWrapper.cs:61-66) has the identical defect.
- **Fix:** Same fix as the single-store case: `item.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid();` up front, then use item.Guid.Value consistently for GetVersion, the event, and the inner write.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. In EventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.Create (Stores/EventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.cs:45-69) the loop computes GetVersion(item.Guid ?? Guid.Empty), builds a DomainEvent with AggregateId = item.Guid ?? Guid.NewGuid() (line 53), sets item.Version (line 62), but never assigns item.Guid. The item is then handed to the inner bulk store at line 69. AsyncEventSourcingBulkStoreWrapper.CreateAsync (lines 47-71) is identical (line 55 / line 71), and AsyncEventSourcingStoreWrapper.CreateAsync (lines 56-81) has the same defect (event AggregateId line 66, item.Guid left null before _innerStore.CreateAsync at line 81).

I verified the orphaning claim against the inner store: AbstractModel.Guid defaults to null (Birko.Data.Core/Models/AbstractModel.cs:9), and the canonical bulk CreateCore assigns its own Guid when null — AbstractInMemoryStore.CreateCore does `item.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid()` (Stores/AbstractInMemoryStore.cs:158). So for any newly-inserted item with a null Guid: the event's AggregateId is a fresh Guid.NewGuid() generated inside the wrapper, while the persisted row gets a *different* Guid.NewGuid() generated inside the inner store. The two never match, so the Created event is orphaned from its row and replay/history lookups by the persisted Guid return nothing.

Notably the Update/Delete paths in the same files correctly guard `if (item?.Guid == null) continue;` and use item.Guid.Value, so only the Create paths exhibit this. The finding is accurate in description, line references, and the three cited call sites. Severity (critical) is justified for an event-sourcing store whose core invariant is event-to-aggregate linkage.

### CR-C07 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.JSON
- **Title:** JsonStore.SaveData writes a Dictionary but LoadData reads a List — round-trip is broken
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.JSON\Stores\JsonStore.cs:213`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (`JsonStore.SaveData` now writes `_items.Values`); regression test `Birko.Data.JSON.Tests/JsonPersistenceTests.JsonStore_CreateThenReloadInNewInstance_RoundTrips`
- **Detail:** SaveData() calls WriteToStream(fileStream, _items) where _items is Dictionary<Guid,T>. System.Text.Json serializes a dictionary as a JSON object ({"guid": {...}}). But LoadData() (line 193) deserializes List<T> from the same file, which expects a JSON array. Deserializing the object as a List<T> throws a JsonException (or yields no items). The async AsyncJsonStore.SaveDataAsync (AsyncJsonStore.cs:239) correctly writes _items.Values (a JSON array), proving .Values is the intended shape. So the single-file sync store cannot reload anything it saved.
- **Fix:** Change line 213 to WriteToStream(fileStream, _items.Values) to match LoadData's List<T> expectation, mirroring the async store.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. In Birko.Data.JSON:

- `_items` is declared `protected Dictionary<Guid, T> _items` (AbstractJsonStore.cs:26).
- `JsonStore.SaveData()` (JsonStore.cs:205-214) deletes the file then calls `WriteToStream(fileStream, _items)` at line 213, passing the whole Dictionary. The serializer is plain System.Text.Json (SystemJsonSerializer, JsonSerializer.Serialize), which serializes a `Dictionary<Guid,T>` as a JSON OBJECT keyed by guid: `{"<guid>": {...}, ...}`.
- `JsonStore.LoadData()` (JsonStore.cs:185-202) deserializes `ReadFromStream<List<T>>(fileStream)` at line 193 — i.e. it expects a JSON ARRAY. Deserializing a JSON object into `List<T>` throws JsonException ("The JSON value could not be converted to ... List`1").

So the single-file sync JsonStore cannot reload data it previously saved: after the first SaveData (which overwrites the initial "[]" from InitCore with an object), any new store instance calling SetSettings->LoadData on that file throws.

The async counterpart confirms the intended shape: AsyncJsonStore.SaveDataAsync (AsyncJsonStore.cs:239) writes `_items.Values` (array shape) and reads `List<T>` (line 205) — a consistent round-trip. The sync store's use of `_items` instead of `_items.Values` is the defect.

The fix is a one-line change: `WriteToStream(fileStream, _items.Values)` at JsonStore.cs:213.

Caveat on impact (not on existence): the mismatch is invisible within a single live session because reads go through the in-memory dictionary; it only surfaces on a fresh load of a previously-saved file — but that is the entire point of a persistent file-backed store, so the severity is justified.

### CR-C08 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.JSON
- **Title:** JsonSeparateStore/JsonSeparateBulkStore.SaveData throw KeyNotFoundException and never persist new items
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.JSON\Stores\JsonSeparateStore.cs:132`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (guard inverted to `if (!_files.ContainsKey)` + register path via `_files.Add`, write unconditionally, mirroring the async store); regression test `Birko.Data.JSON.Tests/JsonPersistenceTests.JsonSeparateStore_CreateNewEntity_WritesFileWithoutThrowing`
- **Detail:** In SaveData the per-item file write is guarded by `if (_files.ContainsKey(item.Key))`. Newly created entities are never in _files (the base CreateCore only populates _items, not _files), so they are silently skipped and never written to disk. Worse, immediately after the guarded block, line 145 (JsonSeparateStore) / line 144 (JsonSeparateBulkStore.cs) reads `_files[item.Key]` UNCONDITIONALLY for every item, throwing KeyNotFoundException for any item not already mapped — i.e. on the very first Create/Save of any new entity. The async counterpart AsyncJsonSeparateStore.SaveDataAsync (lines 149-161) does the opposite and correct thing: `if (!_files.ContainsKey(item.Key)) { ... _files.Add(...); }` then writes unconditionally. The two sync separate stores are buggy clones of that logic with the condition inverted/misplaced.
- **Fix:** Mirror AsyncJsonSeparateStore.SaveDataAsync: when _files does NOT contain item.Key, compute the path and add it to _files; then write the file and remove from removedFiles unconditionally. Same fix in both JsonSeparateStore.cs and JsonSeparateBulkStore.cs.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.JSON\Stores\JsonSeparateStore.cs the SaveData method (lines 132-149) wraps the per-item file write in `if (_files.ContainsKey(item.Key))` (line 134), then on line 145 unconditionally accesses `_files[item.Key]` in `if (removedFiles.ContainsKey(_files[item.Key]))`. JsonSeparateBulkStore.cs has the identical defect (guard line 133, unconditional access line 144).

The base AbstractJsonStore.CreateCore (line 73-80) does `_items.Add(...)` then `SaveData()` and never populates `_files`; the bulk CreateCore (line 175-189) likewise only touches `_items`. So a brand-new entity's Guid is present in `_items` but absent from `_files` when SaveData runs.

Consequences, both as described:
1. Write skipped: line 134's guard is false for any new key, so the WriteToStream block never executes — the new entity is never persisted to disk.
2. Exception: line 145/144 then evaluates `_files[item.Key]` (the C# indexer) for a key not present, throwing KeyNotFoundException on the very first Create/Save of any new entity.

The async counterpart AsyncJsonSeparateStore.SaveDataAsync (lines 147-161) does the correct thing: `if (!_files.ContainsKey(item.Key)) { ... _files.Add(item.Key, path); }` then deletes/writes unconditionally — proving the sync stores have the condition inverted and the write misplaced. The path is guarded only by Path/Name null checks, not by anything that would prevent reaching this code in normal use. Cited file/line (JsonSeparateStore.cs:132) and the bulk line (144) match the source.

### CR-C09 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.Migrations.MongoDB
- **Title:** Transactions wrap no operations — commit/abort are no-ops, "rolled back" claim is false
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.MongoDB\MongoMigrationRunner.cs:60-87`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: the `IClientSessionHandle` is now threaded from the runner → `MongoMigrationContext(db, session)` → `MongoSchemaBuilder`/`MongoDataMigrator`, and every driver call uses the session overload when present (`UpdateMany`/`DeleteMany`/`InsertMany`/`Aggregate`/`CreateCollection`/`DropCollection`/`RenameField`/`Indexes.CreateOne`/`DropOne`). So operations now actually participate in the transaction and abort rolls them back — the "Changes rolled back if session was used" message is finally accurate. Bonus: `MongoIndexBuilder.Build()` made `public` (overrides the CR-C14 terminal), fixing the latent CR-H062 where it was never reachable. Verified to compile against the real MongoDB.Driver overloads by the new `Birko.Data.Migrations.MongoDB.Tests`; transactional behavior needs a live replica set (infra gap). RESIDUAL: the version-record write (`store.RecordMigration`/`RemoveMigration`) still runs outside the session — a smaller follow-up to make version tracking fully atomic with the DDL.
- **Detail:** When UseSession is true and the cluster is a replica set, the runner calls session.StartTransaction() (line 63) and later session?.CommitTransaction() (line 87) / session?.AbortTransaction() (line 95). However each migration runs against `new Context.MongoMigrationContext(_database)` (line 68), and that context only holds the bare IMongoDatabase — the IClientSessionHandle is never threaded into MongoMigrationContext, MongoDataMigrator, or MongoSchemaBuilder. In the MongoDB driver an operation only participates in a transaction if the session handle is passed to it (e.g. coll.UpdateMany(session, ...)). Because every UpdateMany/DeleteMany/InsertMany/Indexes.CreateOne call here is issued WITHOUT the session, the transaction encloses nothing: every data change is committed immediately and independently. CommitTransaction/AbortTransaction operate on an empty transaction. The MigrationException message "Changes rolled back if session was used" (line 100) is therefore misleading — partial migrations are NOT rolled back, leaving the database in an inconsistent half-migrated state with no record written.
- **Fix:** Thread the IClientSessionHandle through MongoMigrationContext -> MongoDataMigrator / MongoSchemaBuilder and pass it to every collection operation (UpdateMany(session, ...), InsertMany(session, ...), Indexes.CreateOne(session, ...), etc.). Also write the store record (RecordMigration/RemoveMigration) inside the same session. If session plumbing is out of scope, drop the transaction code and the rollback claim so callers are not misled.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading all four cited files. MongoMigrationRunner.cs:62-63 starts a session/transaction, but each migration runs against `new Context.MongoMigrationContext(_database)` (line 68) which is constructed with ONLY the IMongoDatabase — the IClientSessionHandle is never threaded in. MongoMigrationContext.cs:16-21 confirms the constructor takes only IMongoDatabase and builds MongoSchemaBuilder/MongoDataMigrator from it. MongoDataMigrator.cs issues every operation without the session overload: UpdateMany (line 27), DeleteMany (line 34), Aggregate (line 54), InsertMany (line 68). MongoSchemaBuilder.cs likewise: CreateCollection (22), DropCollection (28), UpdateMany for RenameField (61), Indexes.CreateOne (132), DropOne (44) — none take a session. In the MongoDB driver an operation only participates in a transaction when the IClientSessionHandle is passed as the first argument, so the transaction here encloses zero operations: every data change commits immediately and independently. CommitTransaction (line 87) / AbortTransaction (line 95) therefore operate on an empty transaction, and the MigrationException message "Changes rolled back if session was used" (line 100) is false — partial migrations are NOT rolled back. Additionally, store.RecordMigration/RemoveMigration (lines 77/81) also run outside any session, so the version-tracking record itself is non-transactional, reinforcing the inconsistent half-migrated-state risk. The classes don't even accept a session parameter, so the atomicity guarantee implied by the code is entirely absent. Genuine, critical, actionable bug; fix requires plumbing the session handle through the context/migrator/schema-builder and passing it to every driver call (and the store writes).

The project is a shared project (Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB.shproj + .projitems), which has no ImplicitUsings and no GlobalUsings file, and the framework convention is explicit usings — so the import must be present in the file itself. Cross-checking siblings: every other migration Context file that uses LINQ (CosmosDB, ElasticSearch, InfluxDB, MongoDB DataMigrators + several SchemaBuilders) explicitly imports System.Linq; RavenDBDataMigrator.cs is the only LINQ-using file in that set missing it. Fix is to add 'using System.Linq;' to the RavenDB file.

Any() is a System.Linq extension method, but the file's usings (lines 1-4) are only Raven.Client.Documents, System, System.Collections.Generic, and Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB.Settings — no System.Linq. This yields compile error CS1061.

The project is a shared project (.shproj/.projitems) with no ImplicitUsings and no global usings file (grep for ImplicitUsings/global using returned nothing), and the codebase follows the explicit-using convention: the two sibling files that legitimately use LINQ both explicitly import System.Linq (RavenMigrationStore.cs:6 uses .Any()/.Select()/.Max(); RavenDBSchemaBuilder.cs uses .ToList()). The indexer access migrations[...] on line 73 is fine (interface member, not LINQ), so only the Any() call is broken.

Additionally corroborated: the cited sibling Context\RavenDBDataMigrator.cs has the identical defect — it uses .Select() (line 24) and .ToList() (lines 67,79) but its usings (lines 1-7) also omit System.Linq. Fix: add `using System.Linq;` to RavenMigrationRunner.cs (and to RavenDBDataMigrator.cs).

### CR-C12 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB
- **Title:** CountDocuments ignores its own built query and counts the entire database
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB\Context/RavenDBDataMigrator.cs:54-69`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (executes the built `query.Statistics(out var queryStats).Take(0).ToList()` so collection scope + filter are honored, instead of a separate unscoped query). Behavioral test needs a live RavenDB server (infra gap noted in the test project).
- **Detail:** The method builds 'query' from the collection and applies the filter via ApplyFilterToQuery(query, ...), then never executes that query. Instead it runs a completely separate session.Query<dynamic>().Take(0) with no collection scoping and no WHERE clause, and returns queryStats.TotalResults — i.e. the total count of ALL documents in the database, regardless of collection or filter. Both the collection argument and the filterJson are effectively ignored. The 'query' local and 'stats'/queryStats wiring is misassembled.
- **Fix:** Execute the DocumentQuery that was actually built (e.g. query.Statistics(out var s).Take(0).ToList(); return s.TotalResults;) so the collection scope and filter are honored.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB\Context\RavenDBDataMigrator.cs lines 54-69. CountDocuments builds `query = session.Advanced.DocumentQuery<dynamic>(collection)` (collection-scoped) and conditionally applies the filter to it via ApplyFilterToQuery(query, filterJson). However, that `query` local is never executed. Instead it runs a separate, unscoped `session.Query<dynamic>().Statistics(out var queryStats).Take(0).ToList()` and returns `queryStats.TotalResults`. The separate query has no collection scoping and no WHERE clause, so its TotalResults reflects all documents the empty query matches (effectively the whole database / default index), regardless of the `collection` and `filterJson` arguments. The `stats` local (the empty Take(0) list) and the misassigned statistics confirm the wiring is broken: both arguments are ignored in the returned count. This is a genuine, actionable critical correctness bug — the fix is to execute the built `query` (e.g. via `query.Statistics(out var queryStats).Take(0).ToList()` on the DocumentQuery, then return queryStats.TotalResults) instead of the separate session.Query call.

### CR-C13 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB
- **Title:** CopyData ignores targetCollection and transformJson; copies source onto itself
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB\Context/RavenDBDataMigrator.cs:72-87`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done (fail-fast) — fixed 2026-07-06: `CopyData` now throws `NotSupportedException` instead of silently re-saving source onto itself. A correct cross-collection copy (re-key into target + apply transform, via server-side PatchByQueryOperation) is a tracked follow-up. Regression test `RavenDBDataMigratorTests.CopyData_IsNotSupported_AndThrowsBeforeTouchingTheServer`.
- **Detail:** The method loads documents from sourceCollection and re-stores them, but never references targetCollection or transformJson. Since the loaded docs retain their existing ids/metadata, session.Store + SaveChanges just re-saves them into the source collection — nothing is copied to the target. The public contract (CopyData(source, target, transform)) is unfulfilled. Take(int.MaxValue) also loads the entire collection into memory in one session, a scalability hazard for a migration tool.
- **Fix:** Either implement an actual copy (project each doc into targetCollection with new ids / @collection metadata, applying transformJson), or use a server-side PatchByQueryOperation. If copy-across-collections is genuinely unsupported, throw NotSupportedException rather than silently doing nothing.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading Context/RavenDBDataMigrator.cs:72-87. CopyData(sourceCollection, targetCollection, transformJson) loads docs from sourceCollection (session.Query<dynamic>(sourceCollection)) and re-stores them via session.Store(doc) + SaveChanges(). Neither targetCollection nor transformJson is referenced anywhere in the method body. Because RavenDB documents loaded via session retain their existing ids and collection metadata, Store re-attaches them to their original ids, so SaveChanges re-saves into the source collection — nothing is copied to the target. The interface IDataMigrator (Birko.Data.Migrations/Context/IDataMigrator.cs:10) declares all three parameters as meaningful, and the MongoDB sibling (MongoDataMigrator.cs:44-55) correctly implements cross-collection copy via $merge into targetCollection, confirming the intended contract that the RavenDB implementation fails to honor. The secondary claim is also valid: .Take(int.MaxValue).ToList() (line 78-79) loads the entire collection into one session in memory, a real scalability hazard for a migration tool (also fragile given RavenDB's default page-size caps). Both the core bug and the scalability concern are genuine and actionable.

### CR-C14 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.Migrations.SQL
- **Title:** Schema builder never emits CREATE TABLE / CREATE INDEX — Build() is dead code
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.SQL\Context/SqlSchemaBuilder.cs:208,297`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: added a terminal `Build()` to `ICollectionBuilder`/`IIndexBuilder` (Birko.Data.Patterns) as a C# **default interface method** (empty no-op — so every other migration provider keeps compiling unchanged and eager providers need no override); `SqlCollectionBuilder.Build()`/`SqlIndexBuilder.Build()` changed from `internal` to `public` to override it and emit the CREATE TABLE / CREATE INDEX. Migrations now end a `CreateCollection(...).WithField(...)` / `CreateIndex(...)` chain with `.Build()`. No in-repo migration used the fluent path (nothing to migrate). Verified with real in-memory SQLite in `Birko.Data.Migrations.SQL.Tests/SqlSchemaBuilderTests` (table created on Build, nothing without Build, index created). Chosen over "eager-incremental ALTERs" (fragile for composite PKs across dialects) and a required interface member (would break all providers).
- **Detail:** ISchemaBuilder.CreateCollection(name) returns a SqlCollectionBuilder, and CreateIndex returns a SqlIndexBuilder, that accumulate fields via WithField(...) and only execute the actual CREATE TABLE / CREATE INDEX SQL inside an internal void Build() method. Build() is internal and is never called anywhere in this project (nor can ICollectionBuilder/IIndexBuilder callers trigger it — the interfaces in Birko.Data.Patterns have no Build()). Unlike the MongoDB provider, where CreateCollection does the work eagerly (MongoSchemaBuilder.cs:22 calls _database.CreateCollection(name) immediately), the SQL builder defers everything to Build(). Net effect: a migration that does context.Schema.CreateCollection("Foo").WithField(...) silently creates nothing — the builder is GC'd without ever running its SQL. Same for CreateIndex(...).WithField(...).Unique(). AddField/DropField/DropCollection/RenameField work (they execute eagerly), but table and index creation through the fluent builder is a no-op.
- **Fix:** Make CreateCollection/CreateIndex execute eagerly (mirror the MongoDB provider), or have the builders implement IDisposable/an explicit terminal call that the interface exposes, and call Build() from there. At minimum the WithField/Unique terminal needs a reachable trigger.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual code at C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.SQL\Context\SqlSchemaBuilder.cs.

CreateCollection(name) (line 24) returns a private SqlCollectionBuilder whose WithField overloads (lines 175-206) only accumulate into _fields/_primaryKeyFields and return this; the only code that actually issues CREATE TABLE is internal void Build() (line 208). Likewise CreateIndex(...) (line 54) returns SqlIndexBuilder whose WithField/Unique only accumulate, and the CREATE INDEX runs only in internal void Build() (line 297).

A project-wide grep for "Build" returns ONLY the two definition sites (208, 297) plus unrelated .gitignore comments — Build() is never invoked anywhere. There is no reflection/Invoke, no IDisposable/disposer dispatch, no runner hook that calls it.

The interfaces in Birko.Data.Patterns confirm callers cannot trigger it: ICollectionBuilder exposes only two WithField overloads; IIndexBuilder exposes WithField/Unique/Sparse/WithProperty. Neither has a Build()/finalize method, so an ISchemaBuilder-typed caller (a migration) has no way to execute the accumulated SQL.

The MongoDB comparison is accurate: MongoSchemaBuilder.CreateCollection executes _database.CreateCollection(name) eagerly (line 22), establishing that the platform-agnostic contract expects CreateCollection to do the work itself. By contrast the eager SQL methods (AddField/DropField/DropCollection/RenameField/DropIndex) do execute and work.

Net effect exactly as described: context.Schema.CreateCollection("Foo").WithField(...) and CreateIndex(...).WithField(...).Unique() silently create nothing. This is a genuine, actionable critical bug (table/index creation via the fluent builder is a no-op). 

Minor note (does not change the verdict): the same dead internal Build() pattern also exists in MongoDB's index builder (MongoIndexBuilder.Build, line 121), so the "Unlike the MongoDB provider..." framing is only fully true for collection creation — Mongo creates the collection eagerly but its custom-index Build() is also never called. For the SQL project under review, however, both CreateCollection and CreateIndex are genuinely no-ops as claimed.

### CR-C15 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.MongoDB.Views
- **Title:** Persistent-view query re-runs the full base pipeline on top of an already-projected view
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.MongoDB.Views\MongoViewStore.cs:44, 71-137`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: `BuildPipeline` was renamed to `BuildQueryStages` and no longer seeds with `_basePipeline` — it returns only the query-time stages ($match/$sort/$skip/$limit over the view's field shape). `ExecutePipelineAsync` prepends `_basePipeline` ONLY on the on-the-fly (source-collection) branch; the Persistent/Auto branch queries the MongoDB view (which already has the base pipeline applied) with the query stages alone, so the base is no longer re-run over already-projected documents. Behavioral test needs a live MongoDB server (MongoDB.Views has no `.Tests` sibling — CR-H073); the fix is a structural pipeline correction.
- **Detail:** MongoViewManager.EnsureAsync creates the MongoDB view with pipeline = TranslatePipeline(definition) (the $lookup/$unwind/$group/$project base pipeline). The view collection therefore already exposes documents in the final view shape (view-property-named, _id:0). But BuildPipeline starts every query with `new List<BsonDocument>(_basePipeline)` (line 77) and ExecutePipelineAsync passes that whole list — base stages plus filter/sort/skip/limit — to AggregateAsync against the persistent view collection (lines 127-130). So for Persistent/Auto modes the base pipeline is applied twice: the second pass runs $lookup/$group/$project that reference SOURCE-entity field names against documents that only have VIEW field names, producing wrong or empty results. Only OnTheFly mode (which queries the source collection) is correct.
- **Fix:** When querying the persistent view collection, pass only the query-time stages (filter $match, $sort, $skip, $limit) — not _basePipeline. Split BuildPipeline into a base portion (for OnTheFly against the source collection) and a query-only portion (for the persistent view). E.g. BuildQueryStages(filter, orderBy, offset, limit) returns just the $match/$sort/$skip/$limit, and ExecutePipelineAsync prepends _basePipeline only in the on-the-fly branch.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading all three source files. MongoViewManager.EnsureAsync (MongoViewManager.cs:50) creates the persistent MongoDB view using pipeline = TranslatePipeline(definition) — the full $lookup/$unwind/$group/$project base pipeline — so the view collection already exposes documents in final view shape (TranslatePipeline emits $project with _id:0 and ViewProperty-named fields, MongoViewTranslator.cs:78-102). In MongoViewStore, _basePipeline is ALSO TranslatePipeline(definition) (line 29), and BuildPipeline starts every query with `new List<BsonDocument>(_basePipeline)` (line 77), appending filter/sort/skip/limit. For Persistent/Auto modes, ExecutePipelineAsync passes that entire stages list to AggregateAsync against the persistent VIEW collection (lines 127-130). The re-run base stages reference SOURCE field names (e.g. $project reads "$"+field.SourceProperty / ResolveFieldPath at MongoViewTranslator.cs:85,89; $lookup/$group use source paths), but the view documents only carry ViewProperty names with _id:0. The second pass therefore reads non-existent source fields, producing null/missing fields, broken grouping, or empty results. Only OnTheFly mode (lines 140-143, querying the source collection) is correct. The comment at MongoViewStore.cs:79 ("after $project, so it works on view fields") confirms the design intended the base pipeline to run once against the source, not be re-applied over the already-projected view. No tests exist that contradict this (no MongoView test files found). The fix is to send only the tail stages to the view collection in Persistent/Auto mode. This is a genuine, actionable, severe correctness bug.

### CR-C16 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.SQL.Caching
- **Title:** Filter-based PropertyUpdate and Delete bypass cache invalidation (stale reads)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.Caching\Stores/CachedAsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs:101-146`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: `CachedAsyncDataBaseBulkStore` now overrides the two filter-based native writes — `UpdateAsync(filter, PropertyUpdate<T>)` and `DeleteAsync(filter)` — calling `base` then `InvalidateCacheAsync`, so filter writes no longer leave stale cached reads. (The `UpdateAsync(filter, Action<T>)` overload was already safe — it loops per-item through `UpdateCoreAsync`.) New `Birko.Data.SQL.Caching.Tests` (also closes CR-H085) compile-guards the overrides and proves the invalidation invariant (every per-query key starts with the table prefix; `MemoryCache.RemoveByPrefixAsync` drops exactly that table's queries). End-to-end filter-write-clears-cache needs a live SQL backend + model mapping (infra gap).
- **Detail:** The base AsyncDataBaseBulkStore exposes two public virtual filter-based write methods that execute the write DIRECTLY against the connector without routing through any *Core method: UpdateAsync(Expression filter, PropertyUpdate<T> updates, ct) (AsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs:155-179, native AsyncConnector.UpdateAsync) and DeleteAsync(Expression filter, ct) (AsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs:204-214, native AsyncConnector.DeleteAsync). The cached store only overrides the *Core methods (Create/Update/DeleteCoreAsync), so these two native bulk operations mutate the table without ever calling InvalidateCacheAsync. After a filter-based update or delete, ReadCoreAsync continues to serve stale cached results for that table until the TTL expires. This is the framework-documented native bulk path (Update(filter, PropertyUpdate<T>) / Delete(filter)), so it is a primary code path, not an edge case. Note UpdateAsync(filter, Action<T>) is safe because it loops through per-item UpdateAsync which does hit UpdateCoreAsync.
- **Fix:** Override public virtual Task UpdateAsync(Expression<Func<T,bool>> filter, PropertyUpdate<T> updates, ct) and DeleteAsync(Expression<Func<T,bool>> filter, ct) (and consider the Action<T> overload for consistency), calling base then InvalidateCacheAsync(ct).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading both files. In the base class C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL\Stores\AsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs, two public virtual filter-based write methods bypass the *Core template pattern entirely: UpdateAsync(Expression filter, PropertyUpdate<T> updates, ct) (lines 155-179) writes directly via AsyncConnector.UpdateAsync / Connector.Update, and DeleteAsync(Expression filter, ct) (lines 204-214) writes directly via AsyncConnector.DeleteAsync / Connector.Delete. Neither calls any *Core method. The cached store C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.Caching\Stores\CachedAsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs overrides only the *Core methods (Read/Create/Update/Delete CoreAsync, lines 44-144) and never overrides those two filter-based public methods, so InvalidateCacheAsync (lines 150-156) is never invoked for them. InvalidateCacheAsync removes by per-table prefix, and ReadCoreAsync caches under the same per-table prefix (key built from _tableName), so after a filter-based update/delete the cached ReadCoreAsync results for that table remain stale until TTL expiry. The finding's nuance is also correct: UpdateAsync(filter, Action<T>) (lines 141-152) loops through per-item UpdateAsync(item) which does route through UpdateCoreAsync and therefore invalidates correctly. This is the framework-documented native bulk path (Update(filter, PropertyUpdate<T>) / Delete(filter)), a primary code path. The finding is real and actionable: the cached store should override both filter-based methods to call InvalidateCacheAsync after the write. Line citations in the finding (CachedAsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs:101-146 for the write region; AsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs:155-179 and 204-214 for the base methods) all match.

### CR-C17 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.SQL.ViewModel
- **Title:** AsyncDataBaseRepository hard-codes AbstractConnector, so its store type-check rejects every real concrete store
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.ViewModel\Repositories\AsyncDataBaseRepository.cs:24-25,36`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: `AsyncDataBaseRepository` is now generic over `TConnector` (`where TConnector : AbstractConnector`), mirroring the sync `DataBaseRepository<TConnector, TViewModel, TModel>`; the store guard + `DataBaseStore` accessor use `AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<TConnector, TModel>` (+ added a `Connector` accessor and a parameterless ctor for parity). New `Birko.Data.SQL.ViewModel.Tests` proves a concrete `AsyncSQLiteStore` is accepted and resolved (both failed before) and an unrelated store is rejected. Consumer `BardStudio` (its `MusicTrackRepository`/`PlaylistViewModelRepository`, the only users found) updated to the 3-param form with `SqLiteConnector`.
- **Detail:** Both the DataBaseStore property (lines 24-25) and the constructor guard (line 36) reference the closed generic Stores.AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<SQL.Connectors.AbstractConnector, TModel>. C# generic types are invariant. Concrete async SQL stores derive from AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<MSSqlConnector,T>, AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<PostgreSQLConnector,T>, AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<SqLiteConnector,T> etc. (verified: AsyncMSSqlStore<T> : AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<MSSqlConnector,T> in Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql/Stores/AsyncMSSqlStore.cs:19). None of those IS-A AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<AbstractConnector,T>. Consequences: (1) store.IsStoreOfType<TModel, AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<AbstractConnector,TModel>>() returns false for any real store, so the only constructor throws ArgumentException when given a working store; (2) the DataBaseStore property's GetUnwrappedStore<TModel, AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<AbstractConnector,TModel>>() always returns null. The class is abstract with no default constructor, so a subclass can only supply a store the base will reject — it is effectively dead/unusable. Note the concrete async repos (e.g. AsyncMSSqlRepository) deliberately do NOT use this base; they extend AbstractAsyncBulkViewModelRepository directly with the correctly-typed AsyncMSSqlStore<TModel>, which is why this defect has gone unnoticed.
- **Fix:** Make the class generic over the connector type to mirror the sync DataBaseRepository<TConnector,...>: add a TConnector type parameter (where TConnector : AbstractConnector) and use AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<TConnector, TModel> in both the property and the guard. Alternatively, if a single non-generic async repo is intended, relax the check (e.g. unwrap and test against the open generic AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<,> via reflection) so concrete connector closures match.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified directly against the cited code and the surrounding type hierarchy.

CITED FILE (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.ViewModel\Repositories\AsyncDataBaseRepository.cs):
- Lines 24-25: `DataBaseStore` => `Store?.GetUnwrappedStore<TModel, Stores.AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<SQL.Connectors.AbstractConnector, TModel>>()` — matches finding.
- Line 36: constructor guard `!store.IsStoreOfType<TModel, Stores.AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<SQL.Connectors.AbstractConnector, TModel>>()` throwing ArgumentException — matches finding.

TYPE HIERARCHY:
- AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<DB,T> has `where DB : AbstractConnector` (Birko.Data.SQL/Stores/AsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs:20-22).
- Concrete stores close the connector arg: AsyncMSSqlStore<T> : AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<MSSqlConnector,T> (verified Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql/Stores/AsyncMSSqlStore.cs:19); AsyncSQLiteStore<T> : AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<SqLiteConnector,T> (verified Birko.Data.SQL.SqLite/Stores/AsyncSQLiteStore.cs:18).

MECHANISM CONFIRMED:
- IsStoreOfType<T,TStore> and GetUnwrappedStore<T,TStore> both rely on runtime `store is TStore` / `unwrapped is TStore` (Birko.Data.Stores/StoreExtensions.cs:73,86,126,139,159,172,192,205). The `is` operator honors generic invariance exactly like compile-time assignment, so a store of type AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<SqLiteConnector,T> is NOT an AsyncDataBaseBulkStore<AbstractConnector,T>. Therefore the guard's `is` check is false for every real store -> constructor throws; and the property's `as` cast yields null. The class is abstract with only this rejecting constructor, so it is effectively unusable with any real store.

REAL CONSUMERS EXIST (strengthens the finding): BardStudio sibling repo has ViewModels/MusicTrackRepository and ViewModels/PlaylistViewModelRepository that genuinely subclass AsyncDataBaseRepository and are constructed with IAsyncBulkStore<T>; the only stores available (e.g. MusicTrackStore : AsyncSQLiteStore<MusicTrack>) would be rejected at runtime. (Note: BardStudio's DI in App.axaml.cs imports BardStudio.Data.Repositories, so it resolves a different same-named non-buggy MusicTrackRepository, which is why the broken path isn't actually exercised in that app's runtime — but the buggy subclasses still compile and would throw if instantiated.)

The finding's only slightly-overstated claim is "gone unnoticed because no concrete async repos use this base" — concrete framework repos (AsyncMSSqlRepository) do extend AbstractAsyncBulkViewModelRepository directly, as claimed, but consumer subclasses do exist. This does not change the conclusion. The defect is genuine, critical, and actionable: the hard-coded AbstractConnector generic argument must be made open (e.g. add a TConnector type parameter, or check against a non-generic base/interface).

### CR-C18 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.Sync
- **Title:** Sync knowledge is never persisted (Update on records with null PK)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync\SyncProvider.cs:170 / AsyncSyncProvider.cs:171`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (sync + async providers): knowledge is no longer persisted via `Update` on null-PK records (a no-op). The persistence step now splits `knowledgeUpdates` into inserts (no existing row → `Create`, which assigns a PK) and updates (existing row → reuse its PK via the scope-keyed `knowledge` map), so knowledge is durably upserted without duplicates. Regression tests `KnowledgePersistenceTests` (persist-then-readable + run-twice-no-duplicate) in `Birko.Data.Sync.Tests`.
- **Detail:** Each batch builds knowledgeUpdates via _knowledgeStore.CreateKnowledgeItem(...) (SyncProvider.cs:305 / AsyncSyncProvider.cs:306). That factory sets EntityGuid but leaves the store primary key AbstractModel.Guid null (AbstractModel.cs:9 defaults Guid to null; the test store factory at TestSyncKnowledgeItemStore.cs:31 never sets Guid either). These knowledge items are then written with _knowledgeStore.Update(knowledgeUpdates, null) / UpdateAsync(...) — never Create. On a real bulk store, Update of records that do not yet exist (and have null PK) is a no-op or throws, so sync-knowledge rows are never inserted on the first run. The provider's entire delta/conflict story (IsRemoteDeleted/IsLocalDeleted, version hashes, lastSyncTime-based isInitialSync) depends on this knowledge being readable on the next run; if it is never persisted, every run after the first still has empty knowledge and delete-detection and conflict-vs-delete logic never fire. Use Save (upsert) or assign Guid and Create new items / Update existing ones.
- **Fix:** Have CreateKnowledgeItem assign a Guid (or look up existing knowledge by EntityGuid+Scope and reuse its Guid), and persist via an upsert (Save) rather than Update so first-run knowledge is actually inserted.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. Every link in the finding's chain holds:

1. SyncProvider.cs:170 calls `_knowledgeStore.Update(knowledgeUpdates, null)` (async equivalent AsyncSyncProvider.cs:171 `UpdateAsync(...)`). It is Update, never Create/Save.
2. The knowledge items in `knowledgeUpdates` are built exclusively via `_knowledgeStore.CreateKnowledgeItem(...)` at SyncProvider.cs:305 / AsyncSyncProvider.cs:306.
3. AbstractModel.cs:9 defaults the store PK to null: `public virtual Guid? Guid { get; set; } = null;`.
4. The factory (TestSyncKnowledgeItemStore.cs:29-41) sets `EntityGuid`, `Scope`, versions, and delete flags but never sets `Guid`, so the PK stays null.
5. Smoking gun — the backing InMemory store's bulk `UpdateCore` (Birko.Data.InMemory AbstractInMemoryStore.cs:171 sync / AbstractAsyncInMemoryStore.cs:182 async) filters `x.Guid.HasValue && _items.ContainsKey(x.Guid.Value)`. Null-PK records fail `Guid.HasValue` and are silently skipped — never inserted. This is exactly the "Update of records that don't yet exist is a no-op" behavior the finding predicts, and it also matches how real SQL/Mongo bulk stores treat Update-by-PK of nonexistent rows.
6. Knowledge is read back keyed by EntityGuid (SyncProvider.cs:48/111 via GetGuid(ISyncKnowledgeItem) which returns EntityGuid) and the delta/conflict logic in SyncProviderBase.DetermineSyncAction depends on knowledgeItem?.IsRemoteDeleted / IsLocalDeleted (lines 66, 78, 106, 129). If knowledge is never persisted, every run after the first still sees empty knowledge, so delete-detection and conflict-vs-delete branches never fire — the impact described is accurate.
7. The suggested fix is valid: Save (upsert) exists on AbstractStore.cs:133 / AbstractAsyncStore.cs:146; alternatively assign Guid and Create.
8. The bug is unguarded by tests: the only knowledge-persistence test (SyncProviderTests.cs:167 Sync_UpdatesSyncKnowledge) asserts only GetLastSyncTime, which is backed by a separate _syncTimes dictionary set via SetLastSyncTime — it never reads back a knowledge item or checks knowledge.Items.Count, so the failing insert is masked.

This is a genuine, critical, actionable correctness bug affecting both the sync and async providers. Line numbers cited in the finding are accurate.

- **Title:** Tenant filter can never match — uses random record Guid as a tenant-id prefix
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.RavenDB\Stores\AsyncRavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:55 (also lines 118, 158) and RavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:53 (also 116, 156)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
