The idiomatic fix is to let the tenant travel on the item via `ITenant` / `ITenantSyncKnowledgeItem`, which is exactly the abstraction the framework already provides.
- **Detail:** All tenant-scoped queries filter with `x.Guid!.Value.ToString().StartsWith(tenantId.Value.ToString())`. `Guid` is the record's own identity, populated with a fresh `Guid.NewGuid()` in `ConvertToRavenItem` (line 182), completely unrelated to any tenant. A random GUID string will essentially never start with the tenant GUID string, so every call to GetKnowledge/DeleteKnowledge/SetLastSyncTime with a non-null tenantId silently returns/affects zero documents. There is also no TenantGuid/tenant column on the model to filter on. The `Guid!` non-null assertion is a second hazard (CS8602 suppression on a Guid? that can be null).
- **Fix:** Persist the tenant explicitly (add a TenantGuid property to RavenSyncKnowledgeItem and ConvertToRavenItem, filter `x => x.TenantGuid == tenantId`), or scope by document-id prefix / collection. Drop the StartsWith-on-record-Guid logic entirely.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual source (in Stores/ subfolder; the cited bare-filename paths and exact line numbers are slightly off, but every cited line content matches). All six sites use `query.Where(x => x.Guid!.Value.ToString().StartsWith(tenantId.Value.ToString()))`: AsyncRavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs lines 55, 118, 158 and RavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs lines 53, 116, 156. `Guid` is the record's own identity from AbstractModel (`public virtual Guid? Guid { get; set; } = null;` — IGuidEntity), populated with a fresh `Guid.NewGuid()` in ConvertToRavenItem (line 182/180), completely unrelated to any tenant. A random GUID string will essentially never start with the tenant GUID string, so tenant-scoped GetKnowledge/DeleteKnowledge/SetLastSyncTime/GetLastSyncTime calls return or affect zero documents. RavenSyncKnowledgeItem has no TenantGuid/tenant field at all, confirming there is nothing correct to filter on — the code comments even admit tenant filtering is a placeholder ("could use collection prefix/suffix or document ID filtering"). The `Guid!` non-null assertion is a genuine second hazard: Guid is Guid? defaulting to null, so `.Value` can throw NRE and `!` suppresses a real CS8602. Genuine, critical, actionable bug.

### CR-C20 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.Sync.RavenDB
- **Title:** Async DeleteKnowledgeAsync deletes by Guid? instead of the entity — wrong overload, runtime failure
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.RavenDB\Stores\AsyncRavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:124`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06 (`session.Delete(item)` — the tracked entity — matching the sync sibling; compile-guarded by `Birko.Data.Sync.RavenDB.Tests`)
- **Detail:** `session.Delete(item.Guid)` passes a `Guid?` to IAsyncDocumentSession.Delete, which has no `Guid`/`Guid?` overload — it binds to the generic `Delete<T>(T entity)` and tries to delete a boxed Guid value as a tracked entity (it is not session-tracked), so nothing is deleted / it throws. The sync sibling correctly calls `session.Delete(item)` (RavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:122). The two implementations diverge.
- **Fix:** Use `session.Delete(item)` (the loaded entity) as the sync store does, matching base DeleteCore which deletes by string id `data.Guid.Value.ToString()`.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual files at C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.RavenDB\Stores\.

AsyncRavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:124 reads `session.Delete(item.Guid);` inside DeleteKnowledgeAsync's loop over query results. The sync sibling RavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:122 correctly reads `session.Delete(item);`. The two implementations diverge exactly as the finding states.

Type check: `item` is a RavenSyncKnowledgeItem (from `await query.ToListAsync(...)`, so session-tracked). `item.Guid` comes from AbstractModel and is `Guid?` (nullable value type) — confirmed because the same file uses `x.Guid!.Value` at lines 55, 118, 158 (the `!` and `.Value` are only valid on a nullable).

Overload analysis of RavenDB's IAsyncDocumentSession.Delete: the available overloads are `Delete<T>(T entity)`, `Delete(string id)`, and `Delete(string id, string expectedChangeVector)`. There is no Guid/Guid? overload. `Delete(string)` is not a match (no implicit Guid?->string conversion), so the call binds to the generic `Delete<Guid?>(Guid? entity)`. It therefore compiles, but at runtime RavenDB treats the boxed Guid? as an entity instance and looks it up in the session's identity/tracking map; the Guid was never loaded or stored through this session, so it is not tracked and RavenDB throws InvalidOperationException ("... is not associated with the session, cannot delete unknown entity instance"). Net effect: deletion never happens / throws — exactly the described runtime failure.

Corroboration from the sibling Birko.Data.RavenDB store (RavenDBStore.cs / AsyncRavenDBStore.cs): it deletes either by passing the tracked entity OR by `session.Delete(item.Guid.Value.ToString())` (string ID) — never by passing a raw Guid, confirming the correct usages and that passing a Guid is not a supported pattern.

The finding is genuine, actionable, and accurately diagnosed. Fix: change line 124 to `session.Delete(item);` to match the sync sibling (the entity is already tracked from the query). Severity-wise this makes async DeleteKnowledgeAsync non-functional, so 'critical' is justified.

### CR-C21 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.XML
- **Title:** Batch stores write single-entity files but read List<T> — all data lost on reload
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.XML\Stores\XmlBatchStore.cs:72 (and AsyncXmlBatchStore.cs, XmlBatchBulkStore.cs, AsyncXmlBatchBulkStore.cs)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: `XmlBatchStore`/`AsyncXmlBatchStore` now implement real batched persistence — `SaveData(Async)` writes `_items` in chunks of `_batchSize` as `List<T>` files (`{Name}-{index}.xml`) matching the `List<T>` read, and all CRUD Core methods (single + bulk) rewrite the batches. `XmlBatchBulkStore`/`AsyncXmlBatchBulkStore` were rebased onto the batch stores (bare subclasses) so they inherit it. Also fixed a pre-existing stack-overflow: the batch stores redeclared `SetSettings(ISettings)` with `new`, which hid the `SetSettings(Settings)` override from member lookup so every `SetSettings` call recursed into `SetSettings(ISettings)` forever (batch stores were never configurable) — the redundant overload was removed. Regression tests in `Birko.Data.XML.Tests/XmlPersistenceTests` (batch round-trip across multiple files, batch-bulk, async batch).
- **Detail:** XmlBatchStore/XmlBatchBulkStore inherit their write path from XmlSeparateStore, whose CreateCore/UpdateCore serialize a single T per file (XmlSeparateStore.cs:147 `WriteToStream(fileStream, data)` where data is T). But the batch stores' LoadData deserializes each file as `List<T>` (XmlBatchStore.cs:92 `ReadFromStream<List<T>>(fileStream)`). The on-disk shape (a single `<TestModel>` root) does not match `ArrayOfTestModel`/`List<T>`, so deserialization fails, the per-file try/catch swallows it (lines 104-108), and every entity is silently dropped on reload. A batch store round-trip (write, dispose, reload) loses all data.
- **Fix:** Implement a real batch write path in the batch stores (group _items into chunks of _batchSize and serialize each chunk as List<T> to one {Name}-batchN.xml file), overriding CreateCore/UpdateCore/DeleteCore + SaveData instead of inheriting the per-entity writes from XmlSeparateStore. The _batchSize field is currently never read (see separate finding).
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual code. The four batch stores genuinely have a write/read shape mismatch that causes silent total data loss on reload.

Write path (single T per file): XmlBatchStore and XmlBatchBulkStore both extend the separate-store hierarchy (XmlBatchStore -> XmlSeparateStore; XmlBatchBulkStore -> XmlSeparateBulkStore, which is an empty subclass of XmlSeparateStore). Neither batch store overrides CreateCore/UpdateCore, so they inherit XmlSeparateStore.CreateCore (line 147: WriteToStream(fileStream, data) where data is a single T) writing one entity per file named {Name}-{Guid}.xml. Same for the async pair via AsyncXmlSeparateStore (line 160/181 WriteToStream(fileStream, data)). The _batchSize field is stored but never used to actually batch-write multiple entities into one file.

Read path (List<T> per file): XmlBatchStore.LoadData line 92 and XmlBatchBulkStore.LoadData line 93 call ReadFromStream<List<T>>(fileStream); the async variants (AsyncXmlBatchStore line 101, AsyncXmlBatchBulkStore line 102) call ReadFromStreamAsync<List<T>>. The load glob is _settings.Name + "-*.xml", which matches the {Name}-{Guid}.xml files written by CreateCore.

Serialization: confirmed the store uses System.Xml.Serialization.XmlSerializer (SystemXmlSerializer). XmlSerializer serializes a single T with a type-named root (e.g. <TestModel>) but deserializing as List<T> expects <ArrayOfTestModel>; the root-name mismatch makes Deserialize throw InvalidOperationException.

Silent swallow: each batch LoadData wraps the read in try { ... } catch { continue; } (XmlBatchStore lines 104-108, etc.), so the deserialization failure is swallowed per file and every entity is dropped. A write/dispose/reload round-trip on any batch store loses all data with no error surfaced.

All cited file/line references are accurate and the bug applies to all four named files. This is a real, critical, actionable defect.

### CR-C22 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Data.XML
- **Title:** Bulk Create/Update/Delete on Separate/Batch stores never write files
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.XML\Stores\XmlSeparateStore.cs:128`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: `XmlSeparateStore` and `AsyncXmlSeparateStore` now override the bulk `CreateCore`/`UpdateCore`/`DeleteCore` (`*CoreAsync`) overloads to route through the per-file single-item Core methods, so bulk operations persist to disk instead of mutating memory and calling the no-op `SaveData`. `XmlSeparateBulkStore`/`AsyncXmlSeparateBulkStore` (bare subclasses) inherit the fix. Regression test `Birko.Data.XML.Tests/XmlPersistenceTests.SeparateBulkStore_BulkCreate_PersistsAndReloads`.
- **Detail:** XmlSeparateStore overrides only the *single-item* CreateCore/UpdateCore/DeleteCore to do per-file I/O, and makes SaveData() a no-op (lines 128-132). The *bulk* CreateCore(IEnumerable<T>)/UpdateCore/DeleteCore are inherited from AbstractXmlStore, which only mutate the in-memory _items dictionary and then call SaveData() — which is the no-op. So calling the bulk APIs (e.g. via XmlSeparateBulkStore / XmlBatchBulkStore, the very classes meant for bulk use) mutates memory but writes nothing to disk; the changes vanish on reload. Same defect in AsyncXmlSeparateStore (SaveDataAsync is Task.CompletedTask, async bulk Core methods inherited from AbstractAsyncXmlStore only touch _items).
- **Fix:** Override the bulk CreateCore(IEnumerable<T>)/UpdateCore/DeleteCore (sync and async) in XmlSeparateStore to perform the per-file writes/deletes, or route them through the single-item Core methods.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. The defect is real and present in all four file-per-entity / batch stores.

Mechanism (sync):
- AbstractXmlStore<T> defines the bulk Core methods CreateCore(IEnumerable<T>) / UpdateCore / DeleteCore (lines 174-225). Each only mutates the in-memory _items dictionary and then calls SaveData().
- XmlSeparateStore<T> (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.XML\Stores\XmlSeparateStore.cs:128) overrides SaveData() to be an empty no-op ("handled in CreateCore/UpdateCore/DeleteCore"), and does per-file I/O only in the SINGLE-item CreateCore/UpdateCore/DeleteCore (lines 135-184). It does NOT override any of the bulk Core overloads.
- XmlStore<T> (the intermediate base) does not override the bulk Core methods either, and its SaveData() does write — but XmlSeparateStore's no-op override is the one that runs for Separate/Batch instances.
- Therefore XmlSeparateBulkStore<T> (a bare subclass, no overrides) and XmlBatchBulkStore<T> inherit the bulk Core methods that mutate memory then call the no-op SaveData() → nothing is written to disk; changes vanish on reload.

Batch store is worse: XmlBatchStore<T> extends XmlSeparateStore<T> and overrides only LoadData(), inheriting both the no-op SaveData() and the inherited bulk Core methods → bulk ops write nothing.

Async mirror confirmed:
- AbstractAsyncXmlStore<T>.CreateCoreAsync(IEnumerable<T>) (line 232) and the Update/Delete bulk overloads only mutate _items then call SaveDataAsync(ct).
- AsyncXmlSeparateStore<T> (AsyncXmlSeparateStore.cs:138-143) overrides SaveDataAsync to Task.CompletedTask (no-op) and does per-file I/O only in the single-item *CoreAsync methods; it does not override the bulk *CoreAsync methods. AsyncXmlBatchStore<T> extends it and overrides only LoadDataAsync.

Net result exactly as the finding states: bulk Create/Update/Delete on the Separate and Batch XML stores (the very classes intended for bulk use, e.g. XmlSeparateBulkStore / XmlBatchBulkStore) mutate memory but persist nothing. The single-item CRUD path is fine. The cited file/line and the description are accurate. The fix is to override the bulk Core / CoreAsync methods in the Separate (and Batch) stores to perform per-file (or per-batch) I/O, rather than relying on the inherited memory-only + no-op-Save path.

Severity "critical" is justified for a persistence store whose documented purpose is durable storage, since silent data loss on bulk paths is a correctness bug, not merely a performance/edge concern.

### CR-C23 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Security.AspNetCore
- **Title:** Role/permission separator mismatch breaks permission checks on the real JWT path
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.AspNetCore\Authentication/TokenServiceAdapter.cs:62 and User/ClaimsCurrentUser.cs:60`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — already resolved by the 2026-06-25 delimiter fix (postdates this audit): both `ClaimsCurrentUser` and `ResolvedPermissionsCurrentUser` now split role/permission claim values on `[',', ';']` (matching the `;` `TokenServiceAdapter` joins with), so multi-value permissions surface correctly on the production JWT path. Covered by `ClaimsCurrentUserTests` (both-delimiter cases) + `ResolvedPermissionsCurrentUserTests`. No further change required.
- **Detail:** TokenServiceAdapter.GenerateAccessToken joins Roles/Permissions with ';' into a SINGLE dictionary value (lines 62, 65). JwtTokenProvider.GenerateToken (Birko.Security.Jwt/JwtTokenProvider.cs:38) creates exactly one Claim per dictionary key, so the JWT ends up with one 'permission' claim whose value is 'a;b;c' — it does NOT expand to multiple claims as the comment on TokenServiceAdapter.cs:58-60 asserts. At request time ClaimsCurrentUser.Permissions (and .Roles) splits the claim value on ',' (comma), not ';'. Result: a token generated by TokenServiceAdapter yields a single un-split permission entry 'a;b;c', so ICurrentUser.Permissions.Contains("a") is false. ClaimsPermissionChecker, PermissionEndpointFilter, and any [Authorize]-style check that relies on these claims silently deny access (and roles never match). The adapter's own ValidateToken happens to split on ';' so the unit-test roundtrip passes and masks the bug, but the production middleware path (token -> JWT bearer -> ClaimsCurrentUser) is broken whenever a user has more than one role or permission.
- **Fix:** Pick one separator end-to-end. Either emit multiple claims (loop and add one dictionary-incompatible claim per value — would require an ITokenProvider overload accepting multi-valued claims), or join and split on the SAME delimiter. Simplest fix: have ClaimsCurrentUser/ResolvedPermissionsCurrentUser split on both ',' and ';', AND make TokenServiceAdapter.ValidateToken consistent. Add a test that runs a generated token through the actual JwtBearer/ClaimsCurrentUser path with 2+ permissions.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified the full chain by reading all cited files plus the JWT bearer wiring.

1. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.AspNetCore\Authentication\TokenServiceAdapter.cs:62 and :65 — Roles/Permissions are joined with string.Join(";", ...) into a SINGLE dictionary value, exactly as the finding states.

2. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.Jwt\JwtTokenProvider.cs:38 — GenerateToken does `claims.Select(c => new Claim(c.Key, c.Value))`, creating exactly ONE Claim per dictionary key with the value passed verbatim. There is NO logic to split a ";"-joined value into multiple claims. Therefore the comment at TokenServiceAdapter.cs:59-60 ("JwtTokenProvider expands these to multiple JWT claims internally") is factually wrong — a token for permissions ["a","b","c"] yields a single 'permission' claim with value "a;b;c".

3. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.AspNetCore\Authentication\JwtBearerExtensions.cs — the JWT bearer setup adds no claim-splitting or comma translation; the standard JwtSecurityTokenHandler surfaces the claim value verbatim into ClaimsPrincipal.

4. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.AspNetCore\User\ClaimsCurrentUser.cs:50 and :60 — Roles and Permissions split each claim value on ',' (comma). Splitting "a;b;c" on ',' yields a single element "a;b;c", so Permissions.Contains("a") is false.

5. Consumers confirm the impact: ClaimsPermissionChecker.cs:29-30 and PermissionEndpointFilter.cs:28 gate access via _currentUser.Permissions.Contains(...) and Contains("*"). Both silently deny when the user has more than one permission, and Roles never match either.

6. The bug is masked in unit tests because TokenServiceAdapter.ValidateToken (lines 107, 111) splits on ';', making the adapter's own generate/validate roundtrip self-consistent — but that path is NOT the production request path (JWT bearer -> ClaimsPrincipal -> ClaimsCurrentUser), which is the one that breaks.

Separator mismatch (';' produced vs ',' consumed on the production path) is unambiguous and confirmed by direct reading. The single-value case happens to work (no separator present), so the break only manifests with 2+ roles/permissions — consistent with the finding. Genuine, actionable, critical.

### CR-C24 · 🔴 critical · Birko.Security.BCrypt
- **Title:** Hand-rolled BCrypt is not validated against any reference vector; key-expansion deviates from the spec
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.BCrypt\Hashing/BCryptPasswordHasher.cs:330-398`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — fixed 2026-07-06: rewrote `EksBlowfishSetup` to the canonical Provos–Mazières/OpenBSD schedule via a proper `ExpandKey(state, data, key)` (continuous cyclic 32-bit data stream, running (l,r) across P then S) — `ExpandKey(salt,key)` once then `2^cost ×` `ExpandKey(0,key)`+`ExpandKey(0,salt)`; and replaced `BlowfishEncrypt` with the exact jBCrypt 16-round encipher (`l^=P[0]`; 8× `r^=F(l)^P[++i]; l^=F(r)^P[++i]`; result `(r^P[17], l)`). Base64 encode/decode + the Orphean-Beholder loop were already correct. **Validated against published `$2a$06$` reference vectors** (empty / "a" / "abc" / special-chars) in the new `BCryptReferenceVectorTests` — 27 tests green. Confirmed unused by any consumer (Symbio + DraCode both use `Pbkdf2PasswordHasher`), so no stored hashes were invalidated. README carries a maintenance note recommending `BCrypt.Net-Next` if a NuGet dep later becomes acceptable.
- **Detail:** EksBlowfishSetup does not match the canonical BCrypt EksBlowfish key schedule. The standard schedule is: ExpandKey(state, salt, key) once, then 2^cost times { ExpandKey(state, 0, key); ExpandKey(state, 0, salt) }, where ExpandKey XORs the running (l,r) with the data (salt) in 64-bit blocks cyclically while filling P then S. Here the initial salt-expansion (lines 345-366) instead XORs the salt into l/r TWICE per P slot via two different mechanisms (StreamToWord at 349-350 AND GetSaltWord at 352-353), with a keyOffset reset wedged between them at line 351, and then the S-box fill (359-366) recomputes salt words by ABSOLUTE index (GetSaltWord(salt, i) -> (i*4)%len) instead of continuing the running salt cycle. The expensive-loop salt re-key (388-396) XORs salt into P only and never XORs salt into the (l,r) data stream during the S/P regeneration. The net effect is a deterministic hash that is internally self-consistent (so Hash->Verify round-trips) but is NOT the BCrypt algorithm: a '$2a$'-tagged value produced here will not verify under BCrypt.Net, libbcrypt, OpenBSD crypt, PHP password_hash, etc., and vice versa. Emitting the '$2a$' identifier on a non-standard hash is actively misleading for any system expecting interoperability or future migration off this library.
- **Fix:** Replace this with a vetted implementation (e.g. the BCrypt.Net-Next NuGet package) rather than maintaining bespoke crypto, OR — at minimum — add known-answer tests against published OpenBSD/BCrypt reference vectors (e.g. bcrypt of a known password+salt must equal the documented '$2a$..' string) and fix EksBlowfishSetup until they pass. Do not ship custom password hashing without reference-vector coverage.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.BCrypt\Hashing\BCryptPasswordHasher.cs (only source file; no .Tests project, no reference vectors exist anywhere in the repo).

The EksBlowfishSetup (lines 330-398) does NOT implement the canonical bcrypt EksBlowfish key schedule (Provos & Mazieres / OpenBSD), where the initial step is ExpandKey(state, salt, key) — P[i] ^= key (cyclic 32-bit), then for each of the 9 P slots and 512 S slots: (l,r) ^= one 64-bit salt block (continuous cyclic stream), encrypt, store.

Confirmed deviations in the INITIAL expand step:
- Lines 349-353 XOR the salt into (l,r) TWICE per P slot via two different mechanisms (StreamToWord at 349-350 AND GetSaltWord at 352-353), with a keyOffset reset wedged in at line 351. Canonical XORs the salt block exactly once.
- Line 349 passes keyOffset (which was left tracking a position in the KEY array after the key-XOR loop) into StreamToWord(salt, ...) to index the SALT array — cross-wired offset. Because the two XORed values differ they do not cancel, producing a genuinely scrambled schedule.
- S-box fill (lines 359-366) uses GetSaltWord(salt, i) by ABSOLUTE index ((i*4)%len) and only one XOR, structurally inconsistent with the double-XOR P fill and with the canonical continuous salt stream.

Net effect is exactly as the finding states: a deterministic, internally self-consistent hash (Hash->Verify round-trips because the same broken schedule runs on both sides) that is NOT the bcrypt algorithm. A $2a$-tagged value produced here will not verify under BCrypt.Net/libbcrypt/OpenBSD crypt/PHP password_hash, and vice versa. README line 8 explicitly advertises "$2a$XX$ modular crypt format, compatible with other BCrypt implementations," so emitting $2a$ here is actively misleading for interop/migration. No known-answer/reference-vector tests exist to catch this.

One sub-claim is imprecise but does not change the verdict: the finding says the expensive-loop salt re-key (lines 388-396) "never XORs salt into the (l,r) data stream" is a deviation. In canonical bcrypt the expensive loop is ExpandKey(state,0,key) then ExpandKey(state,0,salt), and in ExpandKey(state,0,salt) the salt plays the KEY role (P ^= salt) with a ZERO data block, so NOT XORing salt into (l,r) there is actually correct. So lines 388-396 are closer to canonical than claimed. However the decisive errors are in the initial ExpandKey (lines 345-366), which are unambiguously wrong and fully justify the finding. Critical severity is appropriate: a hand-rolled, unvalidated crypto primitive that mislabels its non-standard output as standard bcrypt.

## High findings (147)

### CR-H001 · 🟠 high · Birko.AI
- **Title:** RunCommandTool deadlocks / loses output on large stdout+stderr
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI\Tools/RunCommandTool.cs:50-57`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done
- **Detail:** Both StandardOutput and StandardError are redirected, but the code calls proc.WaitForExit(timeout) FIRST and only reads StandardOutput/StandardError.ReadToEnd() afterwards. This is the classic .NET process deadlock: if the child process fills the OS pipe buffer (~4KB) for either stream while the parent is blocked in WaitForExit, the child blocks on write and never exits, so WaitForExit hits the timeout and the output is lost (process gets killed). Any command producing more than a few KB of output before exiting can hang until timeout.
- **Fix:** Read the streams asynchronously while waiting. Use proc.OutputDataReceived/ErrorDataReceived + BeginOutputReadLine/BeginErrorReadLine, or start both ReadToEndAsync() tasks before WaitForExitAsync(), then await all. e.g. var outTask = proc.StandardOutput.ReadToEndAsync(); var errTask = proc.StandardError.ReadToEndAsync(); if (!proc.WaitForExit(timeout)) {...}; await Task.WhenAll(outTask, errTask).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI\Tools\RunCommandTool.cs. Both streams are redirected (lines 40-41: RedirectStandardOutput=true, RedirectStandardError=true). The code calls proc.WaitForExit(timeoutSeconds*1000) at line 50 BEFORE reading either stream, and only calls StandardOutput.ReadToEnd()/StandardError.ReadToEnd() afterward at lines 56-57. This is the classic .NET synchronous-read deadlock documented in Microsoft's Process.StandardOutput remarks: with both streams redirected and read synchronously after WaitForExit, a child that fills the OS pipe buffer for either stream blocks on write and never exits. WaitForExit then hits the timeout, the process is killed (line 52) and the early return at line 53 ("Error: Process timed out") fires before the read calls, so all output is lost. For a command-runner tool intended to run builds/tests (which routinely emit more than a pipe buffer's worth of output before exiting), this is a real, high-severity, actionable bug. Correct fix: start async reads (ReadToEndAsync on both, or BeginOutputReadLine/BeginErrorReadLine) before WaitForExit and await them. Minor caveat: the exact pipe buffer size is OS-dependent (commonly 4KB-64KB on Windows, not strictly ~4KB), but this does not change the failure mode or its validity.

### CR-H003 · 🟠 high · Birko.AI.Orchestration
- **Title:** SuggestOptimalOrder returns dependencies in reverse (dependents before dependencies)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI.Orchestration\Services\StepDependencyAnalyzer.cs:97`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done
- **Detail:** Visit() is a standard post-order DFS: it recurses into dependencies[step] FIRST and only appends the step itself afterward (line 117). After the full DFS, `sorted` is already in correct dependencies-first order (a step that depends on `other` appears AFTER `other`). The subsequent `sorted.Reverse()` at line 97 then inverts this into dependents-first order — the exact opposite of a valid execution order. Concretely: if step B modifies a file that step A creates, `dependencies[B]` contains A, post-order yields [A, B], and Reverse() yields [B, A] — so the consumer would run B (which edits the file) before A (which creates it). The doc comment promises 'optimal execution order based on file dependencies' but delivers the reverse. Fix: remove the `sorted.Reverse()` call (post-order DFS over a depends-on graph already produces a valid topological order).
- **Fix:** Delete line 97 (`sorted.Reverse();`). Post-order DFS where edges point from a step to the steps it depends on already yields dependencies-first ordering with no reversal needed. Add a test asserting that a creator step precedes its modifier step.

The graph at line 82 is a depends-on graph: dependencies[step].Add(other) fires when step.FilesToModify contains a file other.FilesToCreate creates, i.e. step must run AFTER other. Visit() (lines 101-118) is a standard post-order DFS — it recurses into dependencies[step] first (lines 112-113) then appends step itself (line 117). Post-order over a depends-on graph already produces a valid topological execution order with dependencies appearing before dependents. The sorted.Reverse() at line 97 then inverts this into dependents-first order, directly contradicting the doc comment (lines 71-72) promising "optimal execution order based on file dependencies." The finding's worked example is exact: B depends on A → dependencies[B]=[A] → post-order [A,B] → Reverse() → [B,A], running B (edits file) before A (creates file). The proposed fix (remove the Reverse() call) is correct. ### CR-H007 · 🟠 high · Birko.AI.Resilience
- **Title:** Cost tracking hard-codes empty model name, defeating per-model pricing
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI.Resilience\Services\TrackedLlmProvider.cs:144`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — TokenUsage now carries Model (populated from the provider response by LlmProviderBase + Claude/Gemini/ZAi); TrackedLlmProvider passes usage.Model through so per-model pricing resolves.
- **Detail:** RecordUsageFromResponse builds the UsageRecord with Model: "". CostTrackingService.FindPricing first tries the exact key "{provider}:{model}" then falls back to "{provider}:*". With model always empty, the exact lookup key is "{provider}:" which can never match a configured ProviderPricing (whose Model defaults to "*"), so only the wildcard price is ever used. Any consumer that configures distinct per-model prices (e.g. claude-opus vs claude-haiku) silently gets the wildcard price or $0. The persisted UsageRecordEntity.Model is also always empty, so usage reports can't break down by model. ILlmProvider/LlmResponse/TokenUsage expose no model name, so the model isn't available here — this needs a model surfaced from the provider (e.g. add Model to TokenUsage or LlmResponse, or a Model property on the provider) before per-model pricing can work.
- **Fix:** Surface the model on the response/provider and pass it through, or document that only provider-level (provider:*) pricing is supported and drop the exact-model lookup path so the limitation is explicit.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. TrackedLlmProvider.cs:144 hardcodes Model: "" when building the UsageRecord. CostTrackingService.FindPricing (lines 133-140) first tries the exact key "{provider}:{model}" then falls back to "{provider}:*". With model always empty, the exact key is "{provider}:". ProviderPricing.Model defaults to "*" (CostTrackingConfiguration.cs:13), so a configured per-model entry keys as "{provider}:claude-opus" and can NEVER match "{provider}:" — only a wildcard "{provider}:*" entry is reachable, otherwise FindPricing returns null and CalculateCost returns 0. So any consumer configuring distinct per-model prices silently gets the wildcard price or $0. UsageRecordEntity.Model (line 48) is also always persisted empty, breaking per-model usage reporting. The model name truly is unavailable at the call site: TokenUsage exposes only PromptTokens/CompletionTokens/TotalTokens, LlmResponse exposes StopReason/Content/Usage/ErrorMessage, and ILlmProvider exposes only Name (provider name) — none carry a model name. The proposed fix (surface a Model on TokenUsage/LlmResponse or the provider) is therefore the correct prerequisite. Minor caveat (does not change the verdict): a single wildcard pricing config still resolves correctly, so the bug bites specifically when distinct per-model prices are configured — exactly as the finding states. Genuine, actionable, high severity for any cost-sensitive multi-model deployment.

### CR-H008 · 🟠 high · Birko.BackgroundJobs.CosmosDB
- **Title:** FailAsync sets Failed instead of Dead on retry exhaustion and ignores retry backoff
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.CosmosDB\CosmosDBJobQueue.cs:87-104`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done
- **Detail:** On exhaustion (AttemptCount >= MaxRetries) the job is set to JobStatus.Failed. Per JobStatus.cs, Failed = "failed but will be retried" and Dead = "failed after exhausting all retry attempts". The exhausted job should be Dead. Additionally, when retries remain it is set to Pending with no delay, whereas the IJobQueue.FailAsync contract states "If retries remain, re-enqueues it with a delay" and the MongoDB backend reschedules with JobStatus.Scheduled + ScheduledAt = now + RetryPolicy.GetDelay(AttemptCount). This Cosmos implementation has no RetryPolicy at all, so failed jobs are retried immediately with no backoff, and dead jobs are mislabeled.
- **Fix:** Mirror MongoDBJobQueue: accept an optional RetryPolicy in the constructor; on retry set Status=Scheduled with ScheduledAt = DateTime.UtcNow + retryPolicy.GetDelay(model.AttemptCount); on exhaustion set Status=(int)JobStatus.Dead, not Failed.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual sources. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.CosmosDB\CosmosDBJobQueue.cs FailAsync (lines 87-104): on exhaustion (AttemptCount >= MaxRetries) it sets model.Status = (int)JobStatus.Failed (line 95); when retries remain it sets JobStatus.Pending (line 100) with no scheduling/delay. JobStatus.cs documents Failed=4 as "failed but will be retried" (line 30) and Dead=5 as "failed after exhausting all retry attempts" (line 35) — so the exhausted job is mislabeled Failed instead of Dead. IJobQueue.cs FailAsync doc (lines 29-32) states "If retries remain, re-enqueues it with a delay." The MongoDB reference (MongoDBJobQueue.cs lines 107-127) implements this correctly: retries-remain -> JobStatus.Scheduled + ScheduledAt = UtcNow + _retryPolicy.GetDelay(AttemptCount) (lines 116-118); exhausted -> JobStatus.Dead (line 122). MongoDB injects a RetryPolicy (field line 20, ctors lines 25/35); the Cosmos class has NO RetryPolicy field and its constructors (lines 27-39) accept none, so there is no backoff mechanism at all — retried jobs go straight to Pending and are immediately re-dequeued. All three sub-claims (wrong Dead vs Failed label, missing delay/backoff, no RetryPolicy) are accurate; cited line range is exact. Minor note: the finding doesn't mention that Cosmos PurgeAsync (line 144) purges Failed (not Dead), which coincidentally aligns with the mislabeling so purge still works — but this does not undermine the finding; the contract-label mismatch and missing backoff are genuine, actionable defects.

### CR-H009 · 🟠 high · Birko.BackgroundJobs.CosmosDB
- **Title:** PurgeAsync purges the wrong statuses (Failed instead of Dead)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.CosmosDB\CosmosDBJobQueue.cs:140-159`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done
- **Detail:** PurgeAsync filters on Completed | Failed | Cancelled. Failed is a retryable/intermediate status, so a transiently-failed job that happens to be old could be purged while it still has retries pending; meanwhile genuinely terminal Dead jobs are never purged. The IJobQueue.PurgeAsync doc says "Removes completed and dead jobs", and MongoDBJobQueue purges Completed | Dead | Cancelled. This bug is paired with the FailAsync status bug — they are internally consistent with each other but both wrong vs. the contract.
- **Fix:** Change the filter to (Completed || Dead || Cancelled). Fix together with the FailAsync terminal-status change.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. CosmosDBJobQueue.PurgeAsync (CosmosDBJobQueue.cs:143-148) filters on Completed | Failed | Cancelled. The JobStatus enum (Birko.BackgroundJobs/Core/JobStatus.cs) documents Failed=4 as "Job failed but will be retried" (non-terminal) and Dead=5 as "Job failed after exhausting all retry attempts" (terminal). The IJobQueue contract (Core/IJobQueue.cs:50-51) explicitly states PurgeAsync "Removes completed and dead jobs older than the specified age." So Cosmos purges the wrong status (Failed, an intermediate status) and never purges the genuinely-terminal Dead status. The sibling MongoDBJobQueue.PurgeAsync (lines 171-173) correctly uses Completed | Dead | Cancelled, proving the intended behavior. The pairing with the FailAsync bug is also confirmed: Cosmos FailAsync sets JobStatus.Failed on retry exhaustion (line 95) where MongoDB sets JobStatus.Dead (line 122) — so Cosmos never produces a Dead job and never purges it. Concrete harm: terminal Dead jobs accumulate forever and are never purged, contradicting the documented contract. Fix: change failedStatus to (int)JobStatus.Dead in the purge filter to match MongoDB and the contract.

### CR-H011 · 🟠 high · Birko.BackgroundJobs.SQL
- **Title:** DequeueAsync is a non-atomic read-then-update — two workers can dequeue the same job
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.SQL\SqlJobQueue.cs:60-104`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — DequeueAsync now claims atomically via a conditional native UPDATE (WHERE Status==eligible) + a ClaimToken re-read to confirm the winner; regression test runs 6 concurrent workers over SQLite with zero double-claims.
- **Detail:** DequeueAsync reads the top candidate (ReadAsync with limit 1) and then, in a separate UpdateAsync, flips Status to Processing and bumps AttemptCount. There is no row lock, optimistic-concurrency check, or conditional UPDATE...WHERE Status=Pending guarding the gap between read and write. Two workers polling concurrently will both read the same Pending/Scheduled row and both mark it Processing, so the same job is executed twice. The class XML doc explicitly advertises 'support distributed processing' and the README lists 'distributed' use, so this is a correctness defect, not a non-goal. The SqlJobLockProvider exists but is a separate opt-in class the caller must wire around the whole processor — DequeueAsync itself does nothing to serialize claims.
- **Fix:** Make the claim atomic: issue a conditional native update (Update(filter, PropertyUpdate<T>) with a filter that includes Status==Pending/eligible, setting Status=Processing) and treat 'rows affected == 0' as 'lost the race, pick another'; or wrap read+update in a transaction with SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED via the SqlTransactionContext the README already references. Failing that, document loudly that DequeueAsync is not safe for concurrent workers without an external lock.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.SQL\SqlJobQueue.cs:60-104. DequeueAsync performs a read-then-update with no atomicity guard:
- Lines 71-87: ReadAsync(limit:1) selects the top eligible (Pending or due Scheduled) job, ordered by Priority/EnqueuedAt.
- Lines 97-99: mutates the in-memory candidate (Status=Processing, AttemptCount++, LastAttemptAt).
- Line 101: UpdateAsync(candidate) — an unconditional update by primary key (Guid). There is no row lock, no optimistic-concurrency/version check, and no conditional UPDATE...WHERE Status=Pending between the read and the write.

Two workers polling concurrently will both read the same top row and both flip it to Processing, so the job executes twice. This is a classic non-atomic dequeue race.

The finding's supporting claims also check out: the class XML doc (SqlJobQueue.cs:16) advertises "support distributed processing", and README.md:7 lists persistent storage as a feature, so concurrent/distributed use is an explicit goal, not a non-goal. SqlJobLockProvider is indeed a separate, opt-in class the caller must wrap around the processor (README.md:79-87), and it only actually locks on PostgreSQL via pg_try_advisory_lock (SqlJobLockProvider.cs:56) — on any non-Postgres provider TryAcquireAsync returns true without locking (lines 68-73). So DequeueAsync itself does nothing to serialize claims, exactly as stated.

The defect is actionable: the framework's bulk-store contract provides Update(filter, PropertyUpdate<T>) for native conditional updates (SQL SET ... WHERE), which would let DequeueAsync issue an atomic conditional claim (UPDATE ... SET Status=Processing WHERE Id=@id AND Status IN (Pending,Scheduled)) and check the affected-row count, or use a row lock / SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED. The high severity is justified for a job queue: double-execution of jobs is a real correctness hazard.

### CR-H013 · 🟠 high · Birko.Caching.Hybrid
- **Title:** Per-key SemaphoreSlim locks in _locks are never cleaned up (unbounded leak)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Caching.Hybrid\HybridCache.cs:156`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — per-key locks are now reference-counted and removed once the last caller releases (race-free under a gate); regression test asserts the lock map returns to empty after 500 distinct keys and a 20-way stampede.
- **Detail:** GetOrSetAsync does _locks.GetOrAdd(key, _ => new SemaphoreSlim(1,1)) for every distinct key, but nothing ever removes entries from _locks until Dispose(). The sibling MemoryCache (Memory/MemoryCache.cs:119-124) prunes unused locks on each cleanup-timer tick precisely to avoid this; HybridCache copied the lock pattern but not the eviction. A long-running process that calls GetOrSetAsync with many distinct keys (e.g. per-entity keys) will accumulate one SemaphoreSlim per key forever, an unbounded memory leak.
- **Fix:** After releasing keyLock in the finally, attempt to prune the lock when it is uncontended (e.g. if keyLock.CurrentCount == 1 then _locks.TryRemove with a value check), or run a periodic cleanup like MemoryCache.EvictExpired does. Be careful to avoid a race where a waiter holds a reference to a removed semaphore.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading both files. HybridCache.cs:156 does `_locks.GetOrAdd(key, _ => new SemaphoreSlim(1,1))` for every distinct key in GetOrSetAsync, and entries are removed only in Dispose() (lines 245-247). HybridCache has no cleanup timer at all (no Timer field). The sibling MemoryCache (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Caching\Memory\MemoryCache.cs:119-124) prunes unused locks on each cleanup-timer tick (EvictExpired removes locks whose key is gone from _entries and whose CurrentCount==1, timer wired at line 24). So HybridCache genuinely copied the per-key lock pattern (identical GetOrAdd at MemoryCache.cs:78) without the eviction. A long-running process calling GetOrSetAsync with many distinct keys accumulates one SemaphoreSlim per key forever = unbounded leak. The only inaccuracy in the finding is the sibling path: it says Memory/MemoryCache.cs relative to Birko.Caching.Hybrid, but the file actually lives in the Birko.Caching project. The cited line numbers (119-124) and described behavior are exactly correct, and the primary cited location (HybridCache.cs:156) and the leak itself are fully accurate and actionable.

- **Title:** Sliding expiration never enforces the absolute-expiration cap
- **Path:** `C:/Source/Birko/Framework/Birko.Caching.Redis/RedisCache.cs:191-201`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the meta hash now stores an absolute DEADLINE (unix seconds); refresh computes min(sliding, deadline-now) via a pure ComputeRefreshedTtl helper and expires the entry once the deadline passes. New Birko.Caching.Redis.Tests covers the shrinking-budget + past-deadline cases.
- **Detail:** When an entry is set with both SlidingExpiration and AbsoluteExpiration (CacheEntryOptions.AbsoluteAndSliding), the meta hash stores 'absolute' as the ORIGINAL absolute window in seconds (SetAsync line 81), not an absolute deadline timestamp. On every cache hit, RefreshSlidingExpirationAsync recomputes the new TTL as min(slidingSpan, absoluteSeconds) where absoluteSeconds is that constant original window — it never decreases. So an entry that is accessed within the sliding window is re-extended to min(sliding, absolute) forever and can live indefinitely, defeating the absolute cap entirely (the entire point of AbsoluteAndSliding). To actually cap, the code must persist the creation/deadline time and compute the remaining absolute TTL.
- **Fix:** Store an absolute DEADLINE (e.g. creation UtcNow + AbsoluteExpiration as unix seconds) in the meta hash. On refresh, compute remainingAbsolute = deadline - now; set newExpiry = min(slidingSpan, remainingAbsolute) and clamp to >= 0 (delete/expire-now if past deadline).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code at C:/Source/Birko/Framework/Birko.Caching.Redis/RedisCache.cs and the contract/reference implementation.

Semantics: Birko.Caching/Core/CacheEntryOptions.cs documents AbsoluteExpiration as "Entry expires after this duration from creation, regardless of access." The reference Birko.Caching/Memory/MemoryCacheEntry.cs enforces this correctly: IsExpired() returns true once `now - CreatedAt > AbsoluteExpiration`, independent of sliding access. So AbsoluteAndSliding is supposed to be a hard cap relative to creation time.

The bug in RedisCache:
- SetAsync line 81 stores the meta hash field 'absolute' = opts.AbsoluteExpiration?.TotalSeconds — the ORIGINAL window length (a constant, e.g. 3600s), not a deadline timestamp.
- RefreshSlidingExpirationAsync (lines 192-200) runs on every GetAsync hit (called at line 60). It reads that constant absoluteSeconds and computes newExpiry = min(slidingSpan, absoluteSeconds) (line 198), then re-sets the key TTL via KeyExpireAsync.

For a typical AbsoluteAndSliding(ttl=1h, sliding=5m): sliding(5m) < absolute-window(1h), so newExpiry = 5m on EVERY hit. absoluteSeconds is a fixed window that never decreases, so an entry touched within each sliding window is re-extended forever — the 1h absolute cap is never enforced. This exactly matches the finding and diverges from the MemoryCache reference contract.

Additional corroboration: line 197 reads the current TTL into `ttl` but never uses it — dead code consistent with an abandoned attempt to compute the remaining deadline, reinforcing that the deadline logic is missing. The suggested fix (persist creation/deadline time and compute remaining absolute TTL) is the correct remedy.

Genuine, actionable, high-severity correctness bug.

### CR-H016 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Bluetooth
- **Title:** RemoveReadData(-1) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports/BluetoothLE.cs:462-473`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — RemoveReadData now removes exactly what Read returned (whole buffer for size<0), and HasReadData(size<0) returns Count>0; new Birko.Communication.Bluetooth.Tests covers the drain-all/empty/partial/boundary cases offline.
- **Detail:** Read(int) documents size=-1 as 'read all available', and Read(-1) works. But RemoveReadData(-1) calls Read(-1) (returns all data), then HasReadData(-1) returns true (ReadData.Count >= -1 is always true), then executes ReadData.RemoveRange(0, -1), which throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. So the documented 'drain all' path is broken for the remove variant, and HasReadData(-1) is also semantically wrong (always true even on an empty buffer).
- **Fix:** Handle size < 0 in RemoveReadData by removing ReadData.Count instead of size, and special-case size < 0 in HasReadData (e.g. return ReadData.Count > 0 or always treat negative as 'all available').
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports\BluetoothLE.cs.

Read(int) (lines 400-417) documents size=-1 as "all available" and handles it explicitly: when size < 0 it returns ReadData.GetRange(0, ReadData.Count). So Read(-1) works as documented.

RemoveReadData(int) (lines 462-473) does NOT replicate that special-casing:
- Line 464: Read(-1) returns all data (works).
- Line 465: HasReadData(-1) returns ReadData.Count >= -1, which is always true.
- Line 469: ReadData.RemoveRange(0, size) executes as ReadData.RemoveRange(0, -1). List<T>.RemoveRange requires count >= 0 and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for a negative count.

Both sub-claims hold:
1. The documented "drain all" path is broken for the remove variant — RemoveReadData(-1) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.
2. HasReadData(-1) is semantically wrong: ReadData.Count >= -1 is always true, even on an empty buffer (Count == 0 >= -1).

The asymmetry between Read (handles size < 0) and RemoveReadData/HasReadData (do not) is genuine and actionable. A fix would special-case size < 0 in RemoveReadData (remove all / use result.Length) and guard HasReadData against negative size.

### CR-H017 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Bluetooth
- **Title:** Class owns IDisposable WinRT device but implements only a finalizer, not IDisposable
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports/BluetoothLE.cs:14,574-580`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — implements IDisposable (Dispose→Close, SuppressFinalize); the finalizer now runs Dispose(false) which releases only the unmanaged Linux socket fd and never Thread.Join / disposes the managed WinRT device.
- **Detail:** On Windows _device (BluetoothLEDevice) is IDisposable and is only released via CleanupWindows() called from Close() or the finalizer. The class has no IDisposable implementation, so deterministic cleanup depends on callers explicitly calling Close(). Relying on the finalizer (~BluetoothLE) to call Close() is unreliable and dangerous: the finalizer calls Close(), which does Thread.Join(1000), acquires locks (Clear -> ReadData), and disposes WinRT objects from the finalizer thread. This can deadlock or touch already-finalized objects. Resource-holding ports should implement IDisposable.
- **Fix:** Implement IDisposable (Dispose calls Close), keep the finalizer minimal or remove it, and have Dispose/Close guard against being run on the finalizer thread (avoid Thread.Join / managed-object disposal from the finalizer).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code at C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports\BluetoothLE.cs and its base types.

Verified claims:
- Line 14: `_device` is `Windows.Devices.Bluetooth.BluetoothLEDevice`, which is IDisposable; it is owned by the class and disposed via `CleanupWindows()` (lines 196-210, `_device.Dispose()` at 205).
- The class implements NO IDisposable: `BluetoothLE : AbstractPort` declares only a finalizer `~BluetoothLE()` (lines 574-580). The base `AbstractPort` (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication\Ports\AbstractPort.cs) is `: IPort` only, and `IPort` (IPort.cs) does NOT extend IDisposable. So there is no `Dispose()` and `using` cannot work.
- Deterministic cleanup depends on a caller explicitly calling `Close()` — `CleanupWindows()` is reachable only from `Close()` (line 438), the connect-failure path (line 191), and the finalizer (line 578).
- The finalizer calls `Close()` (line 578), which does `_readThread.Join(1000)` (line 431), then `CleanupWindows()` (WinRT `_device.Dispose()`), then `Clear()` (line 444) which mutates the shared `ReadData` list that other methods lock on. Running thread joins, lock-touching cleanup, and WinRT object disposal from the finalizer thread is genuinely unsafe (deadlock / touching already-finalized objects) and violates the standard dispose pattern.

This is a real, actionable, high-severity design defect. The proper fix is to implement IDisposable (and ideally the full Dispose(bool disposing) pattern so the finalizer only releases unmanaged/WinRT handles without joining threads or taking locks), and to make IPort/AbstractPort IDisposable so callers can use `using`. The only minor caveat is that the finalizer's reentry into Close() is partly self-mitigating in the common case where Close() was already called (IsOpen() returns false, finalizer no-ops), but the absence of IDisposable and the heavyweight/unsafe finalizer body remain a legitimate issue.

### CR-H018 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Bluetooth
- **Title:** Cancellation deadlocks Windows discovery (continuation gated on the cancellation token never completes the TCS)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports/BluetoothLEDevices.cs:163-179,236-251`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the timeout ContinueWith is no longer bound to cancellationToken (always stops the watcher + completes), and a cancellationToken.Register now stops the watcher and TrySetCanceled's the awaited task, so cancellation unblocks the await instead of hanging. (WinRT discovery is #if WINDOWS; fix verified by reasoning.)
- **Detail:** In both Windows discovery methods, EnumerationCompleted schedules Task.Delay(timeout).ContinueWith(t => { watcher.Stop(); completionSource.TrySetResult(true); }, cancellationToken). The continuation is itself bound to cancellationToken, so when the token is cancelled the continuation is cancelled and never runs — watcher.Stop() is never called and completionSource never completes, so 'await completionSource.Task' hangs forever. Cancellation should complete (cancel) the awaited task, not silently drop the only code path that completes it.
- **Fix:** Do not pass cancellationToken to ContinueWith (let it always stop/complete), and register cancellationToken to call watcher.Stop()/completionSource.TrySetCanceled() directly so cancellation actually unblocks the await.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports\BluetoothLEDevices.cs. Both Windows discovery methods (DiscoverDevicesWindowsAsync, lines 163-179; DiscoverDevicesWithServiceWindowsAsync, lines 236-251) use the exact pattern the finding describes:

  watcher.EnumerationCompleted += (sender, args) => {
      Task.Delay(timeout).ContinueWith(t => { watcher.Stop(); completionSource.TrySetResult(true); }, cancellationToken);
  };
  watcher.Stopped += (sender, args) => { completionSource.TrySetResult(true); };
  watcher.Start();
  await completionSource.Task;

The continuation is bound to cancellationToken. Per TPL semantics, when the token is cancelled the continuation transitions to the Canceled state and its delegate body never executes — so neither watcher.Stop() nor completionSource.TrySetResult(true) runs. The watcher.Stopped handler (the other completion path) only fires as a consequence of watcher.Stop(), which is inside that same skipped continuation, so it never fires either. I verified there is no cancellationToken.Register callback, no .WaitAsync(cancellationToken) on the awaited task, and no other code path that completes or cancels completionSource. Therefore on cancellation 'await completionSource.Task' never completes and the method hangs indefinitely instead of returning or throwing OperationCanceledException — the inverse of the intended behavior. The bug is genuine and actionable (e.g., omit the token from ContinueWith so it always stops, or register a cancellation callback that stops the watcher / cancels the TCS).

Minor caveats that do not negate the finding: the code is under an #if WINDOWS guard (only affects Windows builds), and the methods carry an intrinsic timeout, so a caller who never cancels is unaffected — but any caller that does cancel hits a permanent hang, justifying the high severity.

### CR-H019 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Camera
- **Title:** Unread RedirectStandardError pipe can deadlock the capture
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Camera\Cameras/FfmpegCameraSource.cs:59-74`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — stderr is now drained to Stream.Null concurrently with stdout before WaitForExit; Camera.Tests gained a no-deadlock regression (a real chatty process completes within a timeout). Same concurrent-drain pattern proven in CR-H001.
- **Detail:** ProcessStartInfo sets both RedirectStandardOutput=true and RedirectStandardError=true, but the code only drains stdout (CopyToAsync on StandardOutput.BaseStream) and never reads StandardError. ffmpeg is extremely verbose on stderr (banner, stream info, encoding progress). When ffmpeg's stderr output exceeds the OS pipe buffer (~4KB on most platforms — easily reached), ffmpeg blocks writing to stderr while this method blocks reading stdout, producing a classic redirected-process deadlock. It only unblocks when the CancellationToken fires (if one was passed) or hangs indefinitely otherwise. Either redirect and concurrently drain stderr (e.g. start a Task reading StandardError.BaseStream before awaiting stdout), or set RedirectStandardError=false if stderr content is unwanted.
- **Fix:** Read both streams concurrently: var errTask = process.StandardError.BaseStream.CopyToAsync(Stream.Null, ct); await stdout copy; await errTask; then WaitForExitAsync. Or set RedirectStandardError=false.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Camera\Cameras\FfmpegCameraSource.cs. The ProcessStartInfo sets RedirectStandardOutput=true (line 59) AND RedirectStandardError=true (line 60), but the capture path only drains stdout via `await process.StandardOutput.BaseStream.CopyToAsync(ms, ct)` (line 72) and never reads StandardError anywhere. This is a genuine redirected-process pipe deadlock: ffmpeg writes copious diagnostics to stderr by default (banner, build config, input/output stream info, per-frame progress). If stderr output fills the OS pipe buffer before ffmpeg finishes writing the JPEG to stdout, ffmpeg blocks on its stderr write while the C# code blocks in CopyToAsync on stdout — neither side progresses. WaitForExitAsync (line 74) is never reached because execution is stuck on line 72. The only escape is the CancellationToken firing (catch at line 85); with no token (the default `ct = default`) the method hangs indefinitely. The risk is real on the platforms this code explicitly targets (Linux/v4l2 defaults, ~4KB pipe buffer), where the ffmpeg banner alone can exceed the buffer. The proposed fixes (concurrently drain StandardError on a separate Task before awaiting stdout, or set RedirectStandardError=false) are correct and standard. Minor caveat: the "~4KB on most platforms" claim understates Windows pipe buffer sizes, but that does not invalidate the bug — it is the classic .NET Process documentation warning about redirecting both streams and reading only one synchronously. Actionable and high severity.

### CR-H020 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.GraphQL
- **Title:** WebSocket subprotocol mismatch: graphql-transport-ws negotiated but legacy start/stop messages sent
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.GraphQL\GraphQLClient.cs:219,247 (+ GraphQLSubscription.cs:61)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — start/stop replaced with subscribe/complete to match the negotiated graphql-transport-ws subprotocol.
- **Detail:** ConnectAsync negotiates the subprotocol 'graphql-transport-ws' (the modern graphql-ws protocol, whose client->server operation message type is 'subscribe' and termination is 'complete'). But SubscribeAsync sends type="start" (line 247) and UnsubscribeAsync sends type="stop" (GraphQLSubscription.cs:61) — those are the message types of the OLDER subscriptions-transport-ws protocol (whose subprotocol token is 'graphql-ws'). A conformant graphql-transport-ws server will reject the 'start' frame (close code 4400 'invalid message'), so subscriptions break against modern servers. The receive loop accepts both 'data' and 'next' (line 122) which masks the inbound side, but the outbound start/stop are still wrong for the negotiated protocol.
- **Fix:** Pick one protocol consistently: for 'graphql-transport-ws' send type="subscribe" to start and type="complete" to stop; for the legacy protocol negotiate subprotocol "graphql-ws" and keep start/stop. Ideally honor GraphQLSettings.SubscriptionProtocol / a protocol setting.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. GraphQLClient.cs:219 hard-codes webSocket.Options.AddSubProtocol("graphql-transport-ws") — the modern graphql-ws protocol. But GraphQLClient.cs:247 starts the subscription with type="start" (with id+payload), and GraphQLSubscription.cs:61 terminates with type="stop". Those start/stop message types belong to the OLDER subscriptions-transport-ws protocol (subprotocol token "graphql-ws"); the negotiated graphql-transport-ws protocol uses type="subscribe" to start and type="complete" to stop. The protocol facts in the finding are accurate: a conformant graphql-transport-ws server rejects the unknown "start" frame (close code 4400 "invalid message"), so subscriptions break against modern servers. The receive loop (GraphQLSubscription.cs:122) does accept both "data" and "next", which papers over the inbound side, but the outbound start/stop frames are genuinely wrong for the negotiated subprotocol — confirming the finding's own qualification. This is a real, actionable, high-severity correctness bug: the chosen subprotocol token and the message vocabulary disagree. Fix is to either send subscribe/complete (matching the negotiated token) or negotiate "graphql-ws" and keep start/stop; ideally driven by a protocol setting (GraphQLSettings has a SubscriptionProtocol enum, though it currently only distinguishes WebSocket/SSE, not the two ws variants).

### CR-H021 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.GraphQL
- **Title:** WebSocket receive assumes one frame <= 8192 bytes; fragmented or larger messages throw and silently kill the subscription
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.GraphQL\GraphQLClient.cs:232-235; GraphQLSubscription.cs:95-112`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — both receive sites use a new WebSocketMessageReader that accumulates fragments until EndOfMessage; the ack wait tolerates ping (pong reply) / ka frames. Regression test drives fragmented + >8KB + close frames via a scripted WebSocket.
- **Detail:** Both the connection_ack read (GraphQLClient.cs:233-235) and the subscription receive loop (GraphQLSubscription.cs:101-112) do a single ReceiveAsync into a fixed 8192-byte buffer and immediately JsonDocument.Parse(buffer, 0, result.Count) without checking result.EndOfMessage. Any GraphQL data payload larger than 8KB, or any frame the server fragments, is parsed as truncated JSON -> JsonException. In the receive loop that exception is swallowed by the broad catch (lines 193-200/finally), so the subscription just completes with no error surfaced to the observer; for connection_ack it throws out of SubscribeAsync. Also a server 'ping'/'ka' frame arriving before connection_ack would fail the ackType check at line 237.
- **Fix:** Loop ReceiveAsync into a growable buffer (MemoryStream / ArrayBufferWriter) until EndOfMessage before parsing; tolerate ping/keep-alive frames while waiting for connection_ack.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. `EndOfMessage` is never referenced anywhere in the project (grep returned zero hits). Both receive sites use a single `ReceiveAsync` into a fixed 8192-byte buffer and immediately parse `result.Count` bytes:

1) GraphQLClient.cs:232-235 — `var buffer = new byte[8192]; var ackResult = await webSocket.ReceiveAsync(...); var ackJson = Encoding.UTF8.GetString(buffer, 0, ackResult.Count); JsonDocument.Parse(ackJson)`. No EndOfMessage check. A connection_ack frame >8KB or fragmented yields truncated JSON → JsonException, which is thrown out of SubscribeAsync (no surrounding catch for it in that scope).

2) GraphQLSubscription.cs:95-112 — same pattern in the background receive loop: `var buffer = new byte[8192]; ... var result = await _webSocket.ReceiveAsync(...); var json = Encoding.UTF8.GetString(buffer, 0, result.Count); JsonDocument.Parse(json)`. Any data payload >8KB or server-fragmented frame → JsonException.

Silent kill is confirmed (with a minor attribution nuance): the loop's catch clauses are specifically `catch (OperationCanceledException)` (line 189) and `catch (WebSocketException)` (line 193) — NEITHER catches JsonException. So a JsonException is not "swallowed by the broad catch" as worded; instead it propagates past those, the `finally` (197-200) runs `Complete()` which calls `observer.OnCompleted()` (subscription completes normally, no error surfaced), and the exception then escapes StartReceivingAsync and is swallowed by the bare `catch { }` in the `Task.Run` fire-and-forget wrapper at GraphQLClient.cs:270-273. Net effect is exactly what the finding describes: the subscription silently completes with no error reaching the observer.

The ping/ka claim is also real: the ack read accepts exactly one frame and requires `ackType == "connection_ack"` (line 237), with no loop to skip control frames. A keep-alive (`ka`) or `ping` frame arriving before the ack (both permitted by subscriptions-transport-ws / graphql-ws) fails the check and throws `GraphQLException`.

The only inaccuracy in the finding is the description of which catch swallows the JsonException (it's the finally+Task.Run bare catch, not the WebSocketException catch), but the severity, root cause (no EndOfMessage / fixed buffer / immediate parse), and observable consequences are all accurate and actionable. The fix is to loop ReceiveAsync until EndOfMessage (and grow/accumulate the buffer) at both sites, and to loop over non-ack control frames during the ack handshake.

### CR-H022 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Hardware
- **Title:** LPT.RemoveReadData throws ArgumentException for any size > 0
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Hardware\Ports/LPT.cs:71-79`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — LPT is stateless; RemoveReadData now just returns Read(size) with no RemoveRange on the always-empty ReadData. (size>0 P/Invokes inpout32; size 0 tested offline.)
- **Detail:** HasReadData(int) is hard-coded to return true (line 67), so RemoveReadData always executes ReadData.RemoveRange(0, size). But LPT.Read(size) builds and returns a *local* List<byte> and never appends to the inherited ReadData buffer, so ReadData is always empty. RemoveRange(0, size) with size > ReadData.Count throws ArgumentException. RemoveReadData is therefore broken for any non-zero size.
- **Fix:** For the stateless LPT (Input reads directly from the port), RemoveReadData should just return Read(size) without touching ReadData; or have Read append to ReadData so the RemoveRange is valid.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Hardware\Ports\LPT.cs. The cited line numbers are accurate:

- Line 66-69: `HasReadData(int size)` is hard-coded to `return true`, ignoring its argument.
- Lines 46-54: `LPT.Read(int size)` builds a purely local `List<byte> o`, populates it from the hardware via `Input(portnumber)`, returns `o.ToArray()`, and NEVER appends to the inherited `ReadData` buffer.
- Lines 71-79: `RemoveReadData(int size)` calls `Read(size)` (which does not touch `ReadData`), then because `HasReadData(size)` always returns true, unconditionally executes `ReadData.RemoveRange(0, size)`.

Since LPT.Read never populates ReadData, the inherited ReadData list is always empty. `List<T>.RemoveRange(0, size)` throws ArgumentException when `index + count > Count` — i.e. whenever `size > 0` and `ReadData.Count == 0`. So RemoveReadData is broken for any non-zero size; only `size == 0` (RemoveRange(0,0)) is safe.

The contrast is clear against the sibling Serial.cs in the same folder: Serial.ReadSerial does `ReadData.AddRange(buffer)` and Serial.Read returns slices of ReadData, so Serial.HasReadData correctly checks `ReadData.Count >= size` and its identical RemoveReadData pattern works. LPT copied the same RemoveReadData/HasReadData shape but its Read implementation diverges (reads straight from hardware into a local list), leaving ReadData perpetually empty and HasReadData stubbed to true — exactly the mismatch the finding describes.

Caveat (does not change correctness): the AbstractPort base class lives in the sibling Birko.Communication.Ports project which is not checked out locally, so I confirmed ReadData's List<byte> semantics indirectly from its usage (AddRange/GetRange/RemoveRange/Count) across LPT.cs and Serial.cs rather than from the type declaration. LPT is also Windows/inpout32.dll P/Invoke hardware-specific, so the path may be rarely exercised, but the bug is genuine and actionable.
