### CR-H024 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.IR
- **Title:** RC5 encode/decode cannot round-trip (leading zero-duration entry)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.IR\Protocols/Rc5Protocol.cs:42-52,133-149,68-80`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — Decode now tolerates the leading 0µs mark Encode emits (RC5 S1=1 starts space-then-mark); added a Theory round-trip test asserting address/command/toggle survive.
- **Detail:** The RC5 frame always starts with S1=1 (bit 13 is set: `frame = (1 << 13) | ...`). For a '1' bit, RC5 Manchester is space-then-mark, so the first half-bit emitted is a space (newLevel=false). In AddTransition, the `durations.Count == 0` branch handles a leading space by adding a zero-length mark first: `durations.Add(0)`. So Encode() always produces `Durations[0] == 0`. Decode() iterates durations computing `slots = Math.Round(duration / HalfBit)`; for the 0 entry slots = 0, which hits `if (slots < 1 || slots > 3) return null;`. Result: a freshly-encoded RC5 timing always decodes to null — the protocol cannot decode its own output. (NEC and Samsung both have passing round-trip tests; RC5 has none, so this is uncaught.)
- **Fix:** Either strip a leading zero-duration mark before returning from Encode (real IR transmitters can't emit a 0µs mark anyway), or have Decode skip/tolerate a leading 0-duration entry. Add an Encode→Decode round-trip test (and a toggle/address/command preservation assertion) mirroring the NEC/Samsung tests.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed REAL and empirically reproduced by compiling/running the actual Rc5Protocol.cs (net10.0).

Root cause as described:
- Encode() builds the frame as `(1<<13)|(1<<12)|...`, so bit 13 (S1) is always 1. For a '1' bit the first half is a space (firstHalf = !bit = false).
- The very first AddTransition call hits the `durations.Count == 0` branch with newLevel=false, which executes `durations.Add(0); durations.Add(period);` — so Encode() always emits `Durations[0] == 0`.
- Decode() loops over durations computing `slots = Math.Round(duration / HalfBit)`; for the leading 0 entry slots = 0, hitting `if (slots < 1 || slots > 3) return null;`.

Empirical run for Address=0x05, Command=0x0C, Toggle=0:
  Durations = 0,889,889,889,1778,889,889,889,889,1778,1778,1778,1778,889,889,1778,889,889,1778,889,889,889
  Decode(timing) == null  ->  True
So a freshly encoded RC5 frame decodes to null; the protocol cannot round-trip its own output. The cited line ranges (Encode 42-52, AddTransition 133-149, Decode slot check 68-80) are accurate.

Why it's uncaught: NEC (NecProtocolTests.cs:55,70) and Samsung (SamsungProtocolTests.cs:38,81,95) both have Encode_Then_Decode_RoundTrip tests; Rc5ProtocolTests.cs has only encode-validity and decode-rejection tests and never chains Encode->Decode, so the regression is unguarded.

Minor inaccuracy in the finding's wording: it says "RC5 has none" implying no test file exists, but Rc5ProtocolTests.cs does exist — it just lacks any round-trip test. This does not affect the validity of the core bug; if anything it strengthens it (a test file exists yet still misses the defect). Actionable fix would be to make Decode tolerate/skip a leading zero-duration entry (or have Encode not emit one) and add an RC5 round-trip test.

### CR-H025 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Modbus
- **Title:** Partial/truncated frame parsed when full response does not arrive within timeout
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Modbus\Protocols/ModbusClient.cs:203-220`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — after the poll, a frame shorter than expectedMinResponse is only parsed when it is a COMPLETE Modbus error response (high-bit func code + full short frame); otherwise it is treated as a timeout. Tests cover truncated-normal->timeout and short-error->ModbusException.
- **Detail:** WaitAndParseResponse polls until HasReadData(expectedMinResponse) OR the timeout elapses. After the loop it only verifies HasReadData(5) (the absolute minimum), then reads RemoveReadData(_port.GetData().Length) — i.e. whatever happens to be buffered at that instant. On a slow or byte-streaming transport (RTU over real serial is the canonical case) a device can deliver >=5 but fewer than expectedMinResponse bytes before the deadline; the code then parses a truncated frame. For RTU this surfaces as a spurious 'CRC mismatch' (ParseRtuResponse:76) or short-frame ModbusException; for TCP it can mis-frame the response. The expectedMinResponse wait is therefore only advisory, not enforced. The in-memory MockPort delivers the whole response atomically, so no test exercises this path.
- **Fix:** After the poll loop, treat 'not enough bytes for expectedMinResponse' as a timeout (unless an error response — high-bit function code — is detectable in the first 2/8 bytes, which is shorter). Distinguish 'error response arrived (short)' from 'genuine partial frame' before reading; do not parse on a frame shorter than expectedMinResponse for a non-error response.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code at C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Modbus\Protocols\ModbusClient.cs:203-220 and the supporting files.

WaitAndParseResponse polls `while (!_port.HasReadData(expectedMinResponse) && elapsed < ResponseTimeoutMs)`. The loop exits on EITHER condition without distinguishing them. After the loop it only validates `HasReadData(5)` (the absolute minimum, line 212), not `expectedMinResponse`. It then reads `RemoveReadData(_port.GetData().Length)` (line 215) — whatever is buffered at that instant. So if a device delivers >=5 but fewer than expectedMinResponse bytes before the deadline, the timeout guard passes and a truncated frame is parsed. The expectedMinResponse wait is therefore advisory, not enforced — exactly as the finding states.

Downstream consequences verified in ModbusFrame.cs:
- RTU: ParseRtuResponse (line 68) computes CRC over data.Length-2; a truncated frame produces `receivedCrc != calculatedCrc` -> InvalidOperationException("Modbus RTU CRC mismatch") at lines 76-77 (finding cited line 76 — accurate). A short frame can also overrun via `byteCount = data[2]` + Array.Copy(data, 3, ...).
- TCP: ParseTcpResponse requires data.Length >= 9; 5-8 bytes throws ModbusException(0), and a partial payload mis-frames (byteCount = data[8]).

The 'no test exercises this' claim is also confirmed: MockPort.cs:25-28 sets the entire _readBuffer atomically via the ResponseData setter, and HasReadData returns true once the full buffer is present. There is no mechanism to stage partial/streaming delivery, so the truncated-frame path is never tested.

This is a genuine, actionable correctness bug. The fix is to re-check HasReadData(expectedMinResponse) (not just 5) after the loop and throw TimeoutException on a partial frame. Severity 'high' is reasonable for the RTU-over-serial case where byte-streaming is the norm.

### CR-H026 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Network
- **Title:** ReadData mutated/read without lock in Read, HasReadData, and RemoveReadData (race with background reader thread)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Network\Ports/TcpIp.cs:44-59,141-154 (same in Ports/Udp.cs:45-59,131-144)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — Read/HasReadData/RemoveReadData now take lock (ReadData) in both TcpIp and Udp, matching the WebSocketPort reference; RemoveReadData reads+removes atomically under one lock.
- **Detail:** The background ReadWorker thread mutates ReadData under `lock (ReadData)` (TcpIp.cs:122, Udp.cs:116), but the consumer-facing methods Read(size), HasReadData(size), and the RemoveRange call inside RemoveReadData all touch ReadData with no lock. List<byte> is not thread-safe: a concurrent AddRange from the worker thread while the caller is in GetRange/RemoveRange can throw (e.g. 'Destination array was not long enough' / index out of range) or return torn data. The reference implementation WebSocketPort.RemoveReadData (WebSocketPort.cs:176) explicitly wraps RemoveRange in `lock (ReadData)`; these two ports do not. The inline comment at TcpIp.cs:122 ('AbstractPort doesn't lock ReadData, but we should be safe') acknowledges the issue but the read side was left unguarded.
- **Fix:** Wrap every access to ReadData (the GetRange in Read, the Count check in HasReadData, and the RemoveRange in RemoveReadData) in `lock (ReadData)`, matching WebSocketPort. Ideally compute snapshot + removal under a single lock so the HasReadData/Read/RemoveRange sequence is atomic.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. `ReadData` is a shared `List<byte>` on AbstractPort (AbstractPort.cs:28) mutated by the background ReadWorker thread under `lock (ReadData)` in both TcpIp.cs:122-125 and Udp.cs:116-119. The consumer-facing methods touch it WITHOUT a lock: TcpIp.Read (lines 44-59, GetRange), HasReadData (141-144, Count), RemoveReadData (146-154, RemoveRange at line 151); Udp identically at Read (45-59), HasReadData (131-134), RemoveReadData (RemoveRange at 141). List<byte> is not thread-safe; a concurrent AddRange (can reallocate the backing array) racing with GetRange/RemoveRange can throw ArgumentException/IndexOutOfRangeException or return torn data — a genuine crash/corruption race on the primary read API. The cited reference WebSocketPort.cs is the correct contrast: its Read wraps GetRange in lock (ReadData) (57-67) and RemoveReadData wraps RemoveRange in lock (ReadData) (176-179), by the same author — demonstrating the inconsistency is an oversight, not intentional. The inline comment at TcpIp.cs:122 explicitly acknowledges the locking concern yet the read side was left unguarded. All cited line numbers match exactly. Minor caveat: WebSocketPort's own HasReadData (166-168) is also unlocked, so the reference isn't perfectly synchronized, but this does not weaken the finding since the load-bearing GetRange/RemoveRange operations are guarded in the reference and unguarded in TcpIp/Udp. The fix is straightforward: wrap the GetRange/RemoveRange operations in lock (ReadData), mirroring WebSocketPort.

### CR-H027 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.Network
- **Title:** RemoveReadData(-1) throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Network\Ports/TcpIp.cs:146-154 (same in Ports/Udp.cs:136-144)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — RemoveReadData now removes exactly what Read returned (whole buffer for size<0) and HasReadData(size<0) returns Count>0; concurrent append/drain + drain-all tests added (new Birko.Communication.Network.Tests).
- **Detail:** Read(size) supports a negative size as 'read everything' (TcpIp.cs:49-52). But RemoveReadData does not: with size = -1, `result = Read(-1)` returns the whole buffer, `HasReadData(-1)` evaluates `Count >= -1` which is always true, then `ReadData.RemoveRange(0, -1)` is called — List<T>.RemoveRange throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException for a negative count. So the documented 'read all' convention works for Read but crashes for RemoveReadData.
- **Fix:** Handle the negative-size case explicitly: when size < 0, remove ReadData.Count items (or call ReadData.Clear()) instead of RemoveRange(0, size).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code in both cited files (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Network\Ports\TcpIp.cs lines 44-154 and Ports\Udp.cs lines 45-144).

Read(int) explicitly supports a negative size as "read all": HasReadData(-1) returns ReadData.Count >= -1 (always true), and the `if (size < 0)` branch (TcpIp.cs:49-52, Udp.cs:49-52) returns the whole buffer. RemoveReadData lacks the symmetric negative-size handling:
- result = Read(-1) succeeds (returns whole buffer).
- HasReadData(-1) is always true (Count >= -1).
- ReadData.RemoveRange(0, -1) is then called unconditionally. List<T>.RemoveRange requires count >= 0, so a negative count throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException.

Thus the documented "read all" convention works for Read but crashes for RemoveReadData. The defect is identical in both TcpIp.cs (146-154) and Udp.cs (136-144), exactly as the finding states. The line numbers are accurate and the bug is genuine and actionable (fix: branch on size < 0 in RemoveReadData and remove ReadData.Count, and special-case negative size in HasReadData).

One minor caveat: "high" severity is somewhat generous since the crash only manifests on the -1 "drain all" path, which the framework's own example call sites (NetworkExamples.cs) never use (they pass data.Length). But the finding's correctness, location, and reasoning are all accurate, so it is a real, actionable issue.

### CR-H028 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.NFC
- **Title:** NfcReaderPort never disposes its owned IDisposable transport (resource leak)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.NFC\Ports/NfcReaderPort.cs:16`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — NfcReaderPort implements IDisposable: unsubscribes TagDetected/TagRemoved and disposes the owned transport. Test verifies dispose + unsubscribe + idempotency.
- **Detail:** NfcReaderPort wraps an INfcTransport (which is IDisposable and owns a SerialPort / HttpClient / CancellationTokenSource), but the port itself does not implement IDisposable and never calls _transport.Dispose(). AbstractPort.Close() only calls DisconnectAsync, which for SerialNfcTransport disposes the port but leaves the _pollCts undisposed, and for HttpNfcTransport leaves the owned HttpClient and _pollCts undisposed. A consumer that constructs and discards NfcReaderPort instances leaks serial handles, HttpClients, and CancellationTokenSources. The port also subscribes to transport.TagDetected/TagRemoved in the constructor and never unsubscribes, keeping the port alive via the transport.
- **Fix:** Implement IDisposable on NfcReaderPort: unsubscribe the two event handlers and call _transport.Dispose(). Alternatively dispose the transport (or at least _pollCts) in Close().
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified every claim against the actual source.

1. INfcTransport IS IDisposable (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.NFC\Transports\INfcTransport.cs:12 — `public interface INfcTransport : IDisposable`).

2. NfcReaderPort (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.NFC\Ports\NfcReaderPort.cs:16) extends only AbstractPort, does NOT implement IDisposable, and has no Dispose method. It never calls _transport.Dispose() anywhere. Close() (lines 110-115) only calls StopPollingAsync + DisconnectAsync.

3. AbstractPort (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication\Ports\AbstractPort.cs) does NOT implement IDisposable — IPort/AbstractPort expose only Open/Close/Read/Write/etc. So there is no inherited disposal path.

4. SerialNfcTransport.DisconnectAsync (SerialNfcTransport.cs:59-69) calls `_pollCts?.Cancel()` and disposes the SerialPort, but does NOT dispose `_pollCts`. The CancellationTokenSource is only disposed in Dispose() (lines 240-250). Confirmed leak of _pollCts if only Disconnect/Close is called.

5. HttpNfcTransport.DisconnectAsync (HttpNfcTransport.cs:58-63) only cancels _pollCts and sets IsConnected=false. The owned HttpClient (_ownsClient when no client injected, line 46-47) and _pollCts are disposed ONLY in Dispose() (lines 165-178). Confirmed leak of HttpClient + _pollCts when Close() is used without Dispose().

6. The constructor (NfcReaderPort.cs:44-45) subscribes to _transport.TagDetected/TagRemoved and never unsubscribes (no Dispose, no removal in Close), keeping the port reachable from the transport's event delegates.

Conclusion: a consumer that constructs and discards NfcReaderPort instances (even calling Close()) leaks SerialPort/HttpClient and CancellationTokenSource resources, because the disposal logic lives only in transport.Dispose() which the port never invokes, and the port itself is not disposable. The event subscription without unsubscription is also confirmed. This is a genuine, actionable resource-leak finding at the cited location.

Minor caveat (does not change the verdict): the transport is constructor-injected, so strict ownership is debatable; but the port clearly takes over the transport's event/lifecycle (subscribes to events, drives Connect/Disconnect/StartPolling/StopPolling), so implementing IDisposable to unsubscribe and dispose the transport is the correct, conventional fix. High severity is justified given native SerialPort handles, HttpClient socket exhaustion, and undisposed CTS.

### CR-H029 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.NFC
- **Title:** HID transport cancellation callback dereferences possibly-null _readTcs and can complete the wrong read
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.NFC\Transports/HidNfcTransport.cs:90`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — ReadTagAsync captures the TCS in a local and registers against it (disposing the registration on return), so a late timer can neither NRE on the nulled field nor complete the next read. Stress test loops short-timeout reads.
- **Detail:** ReadTagAsync registers `cts.Token.Register(() => _readTcs.TrySetResult(null))` capturing the _readTcs field (not the local). After the await completes, line 93 sets `_readTcs = null`. If the linked timeout/cancellation fires after that point (e.g. timer races with the await completion, common during polling), the lambda dereferences a null field -> NullReferenceException on a thread-pool/timer thread. Worse, during StartPollingAsync's tight loop the next iteration assigns a NEW _readTcs before the previous timer callback runs, so a stale timeout can complete the wrong (current) read with null, dropping a tag that was actually fed. This is also a CS8602 nullable-warning (_readTcs is `TaskCompletionSource<string?>?`) under the consumer's Nullable=enable build.
- **Fix:** Capture the TCS in a local and register against it: `var tcs = _readTcs; cts.Token.Register(() => tcs.TrySetResult(null));` Also gate FeedInputAsync against a possibly-null _readTcs (already uses ?.) and consider not nulling the field while a timer may still reference it.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.NFC\Transports\HidNfcTransport.cs. The finding is accurate on all three points.

Line 24 declares `private TaskCompletionSource<string?>? _readTcs;` (nullable field). Line 86 assigns a new TCS, line 90 registers `cts.Token.Register(() => _readTcs.TrySetResult(null))` — the lambda captures the FIELD, not a local. Line 93 then sets `_readTcs = null`. The CancelAfter(timeoutMs) timer (line 89) fires on a threadpool/timer thread.

1. NRE race: When FeedInputAsync completes the read (line 64), the await on line 92 finishes, line 93 nulls the field, and the `using` cts is disposed on method exit. But the CancelAfter timer may already be in-flight on a threadpool thread; if it invokes the lambda after line 93 has run, `_readTcs` is null and `_readTcs.TrySetResult(null)` throws NullReferenceException on a non-awaited thread. Real and possible.

2. Wrong-read completion: StartPollingAsync (lines 109-128) calls ReadTagAsync in a tight loop, each iteration reassigning `_readTcs` (line 86). Because the lambda dereferences the field at invocation time, a late timer from iteration N can call TrySetResult(null) on the NEW TCS instance created in iteration N+1, resolving the current read with null and dropping a tag that was actually fed. This is a genuine correctness bug, and the polling loop makes it likely rather than exotic.

3. CS8602: `_readTcs` is a nullable field dereferenced inside a closure; C# flow analysis does not treat captured fields as non-null in lambdas, so under Nullable=enable (the project's documented "no nullable warnings" convention) this produces CS8602.

The correct fix is to capture the local TCS instance (var tcs = ...; Register(() => tcs.TrySetResult(null))), which resolves all three issues. The cited file, line, severity, and detail are correct.

### CR-H030 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.OAuth
- **Title:** 401 retry resends the same HttpRequestMessage instance
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.OAuth\OAuthDelegatingHandler.cs:44-49`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the body is buffered up front and the 401 retry sends a CloneRequestAsync copy (method/uri/version/headers/options + buffered body), never the already-sent instance. Test uses a strict handler that rejects resending the same instance and asserts the POST body survives.
- **Detail:** On a 401, SendAsync mutates the original `request` (sets a new Authorization header) and calls `base.SendAsync(request, ...)` a second time. An HttpRequestMessage may only be sent once: real handlers (SocketsHttpHandler/HttpClientHandler) mark it as sent and throw InvalidOperationException ('The request message was already sent. Cannot send the same request message multiple times.') on the retry, and for requests with a body the content stream is already consumed/disposed. This works in the unit test only because InspectingHandler bypasses the real send pipeline and never marks the message sent (SendAsync_RetriesOn401WithFreshToken at OAuthDelegatingHandlerTests.cs:53) — so the test gives false confidence. In production this retry path will fail for any non-trivial request.
- **Fix:** Clone the request before the retry (copy Method, RequestUri, Version, Headers, Content, and Options into a new HttpRequestMessage) and send the clone, or buffer the content. A standard CloneHttpRequestMessage helper is the usual fix.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.OAuth\OAuthDelegatingHandler.cs:44-49 reuses the SAME HttpRequestMessage instance on the 401 retry: it mutates request.Headers.Authorization (line 47) and calls base.SendAsync(request, ...) a second time (line 48) after the first send on line 41.

This violates .NET's single-send contract. In .NET Core 3.0+/5+, the concrete transport handlers (SocketsHttpHandler / HttpClientHandler) call MarkAsSent() on the HttpRequestMessage, and a second send throws InvalidOperationException ("The request message was already sent. Cannot send the same request message multiple times."). For requests with a body, the content stream is also already consumed/disposed after the first send. So in production (real InnerHandler), the 401 retry path fails for essentially any request.

The false-confidence claim is also verified. The cited test SendAsync_RetriesOn401WithFreshToken exists (the audit's path was slightly off — it's in the sibling Birko.Communication.OAuth.Tests project, OAuthDelegatingHandlerTests.cs:53) and uses InspectingHandler (lines 108-121), a custom terminal HttpMessageHandler that simply invokes a delegate and never calls MarkAsSent(). Because the message is never marked sent and no real content stream is consumed, sending the same request twice succeeds in the test (callCount reaches 2), masking the production failure.

Severity high is appropriate: the entire 401-retry feature is broken against any real handler. The fix is to clone the request (method, URI, version, headers, content) before the retry instead of resending the original instance.

### CR-H031 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.REST
- **Title:** Static client cache uses a non-thread-safe Dictionary
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.REST\RestClient.cs:18,67-74,321-343`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — _clients is now a ConcurrentDictionary; GetClient uses GetOrAdd, RemoveClient TryRemove, ClearCache snapshots-then-clears. 16-thread concurrent-access regression test added.
- **Detail:** _clients is a plain Dictionary<string,RestClient> mutated by GetClient (Add), ClearCache (Clear) and RemoveClient (Remove) with no locking. GetClient is the canonical entry point for a shared, process-wide client cache, so concurrent calls from multiple threads can corrupt the dictionary's internal state (torn reads/writes, lost entries, or InvalidOperationException). Sibling caches in the framework use ConcurrentDictionary for exactly this reason (GrpcChannelPool, GraphQLClient's static GetClient cache).
- **Fix:** Change _clients to a ConcurrentDictionary<string, RestClient> and use GetOrAdd in GetClient (which also removes the double ContainsKey/indexer lookup). Use TryRemove in RemoveClient and snapshot Values in ClearCache.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.REST\RestClient.cs. The cited lines match exactly:

- Line 18: `_clients` is a plain `Dictionary<string, RestClient>`, NOT a ConcurrentDictionary.
- Lines 67-74 (GetClient): non-atomic check-then-act — `if (!_clients.ContainsKey(baseUri)) { _clients.Add(...); } return _clients[baseUri];` with no lock. Two concurrent threads can both pass the ContainsKey check and then race on Add (one throws ArgumentException on duplicate key), or interleave to corrupt the dictionary's internal buckets.
- Lines 321-328 (ClearCache): iterates `_clients.Values` and calls `_clients.Clear()` — no lock.
- Lines 335-343 (RemoveClient): `TryGetValue` + `_clients.Remove(...)` — no lock.

This is a static, process-wide cache mutated by three methods (Add/Clear/Remove) with concurrent reads, all unsynchronized. System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary is documented as not thread-safe for any mix of reads and writes; concurrent access can cause torn reads/writes, lost entries, or InvalidOperationException. GetClient is documented as the canonical shared-client entry point, so concurrent invocation across threads is realistic. The fix (ConcurrentDictionary, matching the framework's own GrpcChannelPool at GrpcChannelPool.cs:16) is straightforward and actionable.

Minor inaccuracy in the finding (does not affect the verdict): it claims GraphQLClient's static GetClient cache uses ConcurrentDictionary, but GraphQLClient.cs:20 actually also uses a plain Dictionary. So GraphQLClient is a parallel bug, not a positive precedent. GrpcChannelPool, however, does use ConcurrentDictionary exactly as the finding states. The core finding about RestClient is fully accurate and the recommended fix is correct.

### CR-H032 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.REST.Server
- **Title:** RestResponse error factories interpolate unescaped user text into JSON
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.REST.Server\RestServer.cs:578-638`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — all five factories (BadRequest/Unauthorized/Forbidden/NotFound/InternalServerError) now route the message through the shared (now internal) EscapeJson. New Birko.Communication.REST.Server.Tests asserts each produces valid JSON preserving quotes/backslash/newline.
- **Detail:** BadRequest, Unauthorized, Forbidden, NotFound, and InternalServerError all build the body as $"{{\"error\":\"{message}\"}}" with no escaping. SendServerErrorAsync (line 381) correctly routes through EscapeJson, but these factory methods do not. A message containing a double-quote, backslash, or newline (very plausible from exception text via InternalServerError(ex.Message), or attacker-controlled echoed input) produces malformed JSON and is a JSON-injection vector. The Unauthorized factory is also reached from the auth middleware.
- **Fix:** Route all five factories through the existing EscapeJson helper (make it internal/shared), e.g. Content = $"{{\"error\":\"{EscapeJson(message)}\"}}"; or build the object with a serializer.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading RestServer.cs. The five public static factory methods BadRequest (578), Unauthorized (591), Forbidden (604), NotFound (617), and InternalServerError (630) all build their body as $"{{\"error\":\"{message}\"}}" with the message parameter interpolated raw and unescaped. An EscapeJson helper (389-397, escaping backslash/quote/CR/LF/tab) exists and IS used by SendServerErrorAsync (381), proving the codebase knows this JSON-body pattern needs escaping — the factories are an inconsistent gap. RestResponse is a public class with public static factories, so it is consumer-facing API; the natural InternalServerError(ex.Message) usage feeds exception text (containing quotes, Windows-path backslashes, newlines) directly into the unescaped slot, producing malformed JSON / a JSON-injection vector. Unauthorized is also reached from RestAuthenticationMiddleware. The cited file, line range, method list, EscapeJson asymmetry, and middleware reachability are all accurate. Minor caveat: all in-repo callers currently pass static literals, so the defect manifests through consumer code rather than an existing in-repo exploit, and the 'attacker-controlled echoed input' angle is somewhat speculative — but the ex.Message path is highly plausible and the fix (route factories through EscapeJson, as SendServerErrorAsync already does) is clear and actionable.

### CR-H033 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.SOAP
- **Title:** Credentials are silently never applied to outgoing requests
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.SOAP\SoapClient.cs:172-179`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — CreateRequest now applies credentials (parameter overriding the Credentials property) per-request as a Basic Authorization header (the handler is already built). New Birko.Communication.SOAP.Tests verifies param + property + no-credentials cases.
- **Detail:** CreateRequest receives an ICredentials? credentials parameter but never reads it, and the public Credentials property (line 31) is never consulted either. The credentials flow all the way from SendRequest/SendRequestAsync (lines 101/114) into CreateRequest and are then dropped. Every authenticated SOAP call therefore goes out unauthenticated, which will fail silently (or with a 401) even though the API strongly implies auth is wired. The HttpClientHandler created in the constructor (line 77) is also never given the credentials, and because the HttpClient is already built around it, setting them later would be impossible anyway.
- **Fix:** Apply credentials in CreateRequest, e.g. build a Basic/NTLM auth header from (credentials ?? Credentials), or move credentials onto an HttpClientHandler.Credentials at construction and recreate the handler when credentials change. At minimum, if per-request credentials are intended, use them: var creds = credentials ?? Credentials; and translate into request.Headers.Authorization.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.SOAP\SoapClient.cs in full. Every claim holds:

1. CreateRequest (lines 172-179) declares an `ICredentials? credentials` parameter but its body only builds the HttpRequestMessage, sets StringContent, and adds the SOAPAction header — the `credentials` parameter is never read.
2. The public `Credentials` property (line 31, set by the credentials constructor overload at line 91) is never consulted anywhere in the class.
3. Credentials genuinely flow and are dropped: SendRequest (line 101) -> SendRequestAsync (line 114) -> CreateRequest(action, xml, credentials) (line 122), where they are discarded.
4. The HttpClientHandler (line 77) is created with no Credentials/UseDefaultCredentials assignment, is not retained as a field, and the HttpClient (line 78) wraps it; standard per-request auth (handler.Credentials or an Authorization header) is wired nowhere.

Net effect: the constructor overload, the public property, and the per-call parameter form an authentication API that is entirely non-functional — authenticated SOAP calls go out unauthenticated. This is a real, high-severity, actionable bug. The only minor imprecision in the finding's wording is 'fail silently' — the client never throws on non-success status, so a server's 401/403 fault body would be returned to the caller without error, but that does not change the core correctness/security defect.

### CR-H034 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.SSE
- **Title:** Custom internal SemaphoreSlim shadows the real type and never disposes its inner semaphore
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.SSE\Middleware/SseRateLimitMiddleware.cs:85-108`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — deleted the custom SemaphoreSlim shim (uses BCL System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim directly) and made SseRateLimitMiddleware IDisposable, disposing the lock.
- **Detail:** An internal class SemaphoreSlim is declared in namespace Birko.Communication.SSE.Middleware. It wraps System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim but (a) is never Disposed by SseRateLimitMiddleware (which holds one as a field _lock and is not even IDisposable), leaking the underlying semaphore handle, and (b) silently shadows the BCL System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim for any unqualified use inside this namespace. The 'for .NET Standard compatibility' comment is bogus — System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim has existed since .NET Standard 1.0. This is needless indirection that also breaks the IDisposable contract.
- **Fix:** Delete the wrapper class entirely, use System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim directly, add `using System.Threading;`, and make SseRateLimitMiddleware implement IDisposable to dispose _lock.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.SSE\Middleware\SseRateLimitMiddleware.cs. All claims hold:

1. Lines 85-108 declare `internal class SemaphoreSlim` in namespace `Birko.Communication.SSE.Middleware`, wrapping `System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim` (line 87) and exposing only WaitAsync/Release — no Dispose method.
2. The `_lock` field (line 16: `private readonly SemaphoreSlim _lock = new(1, 1);`) uses the unqualified name, which binds to this custom shadowing type, not the BCL type. The inner System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim is never disposed and SseRateLimitMiddleware does not implement IDisposable, so the underlying semaphore is leaked.
3. The custom type shadows the BCL System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim for any unqualified use in this namespace — exactly why line 16 resolves to it.
4. The "for .NET Standard compatibility" comment (line 83) is incorrect: System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim exists since .NET Framework 4.0 / .NET Standard 1.0; this is a shared (.shproj/.projitems) project consumable by any modern target, all of which ship it. The wrapper is needless indirection.

The fix (delete the wrapper, use System.Threading.SemaphoreSlim directly, and either make the middleware IDisposable or accept the singleton lifetime) is clear and actionable.

Minor caveat on severity: SemaphoreSlim only allocates an undisposed OS handle lazily via AvailableWaitHandle, which this code never touches, and the middleware is typically a single long-lived instance — so the real-world handle leak is small. The defect (broken IDisposable contract + BCL type shadowing + bogus comment) is genuine, but "high" is somewhat generous; medium would be defensible. Regardless, the finding itself is real, not a false positive.

### CR-H036 · 🟠 high · Birko.Communication.WebSocket
- **Title:** RemoveReadData with size < 0 throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.WebSocket\Ports/WebSocketPort.cs:171-182`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — RemoveReadData reads+removes atomically under one lock, removing exactly what Read returned (whole buffer for size<0); HasReadData(size<0) returns Count>0. Buffer + concurrent append/drain tests added.
- **Detail:** Read(int size) explicitly supports size < 0 (returns the whole buffer at line 59-62). RemoveReadData calls Read(size) then, if HasReadData(size) is true (Count >= -1 is always true for negative size), executes ReadData.RemoveRange(0, size) with a negative count, which throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException. So the 'read everything' path (size < 0) works for Read but crashes for RemoveReadData. Also the check/read/remove sequence is not atomic: Read locks, then HasReadData reads Count without a lock, then RemoveRange locks separately — another thread (the ReadWorker AddRange) can change Count between the read and the remove, so a different number of bytes is removed than returned.
- **Fix:** Handle size < 0 by removing ReadData.Count (mirror Read). Perform the read+count-check+remove inside a single lock(ReadData) block so the returned bytes and the removed bytes are the same range.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.WebSocket\Ports\WebSocketPort.cs and the base class C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication\Ports\AbstractPort.cs (ReadData is a List<byte>).

PRIMARY CLAIM — REAL and actionable (high severity):
- Read(int size) explicitly supports size < 0: line 59-62 returns the whole buffer (GetRange(0, ReadData.Count)). HasReadData(size) = ReadData.Count >= size (line 168), which is always true for negative size.
- RemoveReadData(size) (lines 171-182) calls Read(size) (works, returns whole buffer), then HasReadData(size) is true for negative size, then executes ReadData.RemoveRange(0, size) at line 178 with a negative count. List<T>.RemoveRange requires count >= 0 and throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException otherwise. So the documented "read everything" path (size < 0) succeeds in Read but crashes in RemoveReadData. This is a genuine asymmetry/bug worth fixing (e.g. clamp size to ReadData.Count when size < 0, mirroring Read's branch).

SECONDARY CLAIM (atomicity) — overstated / largely inaccurate, but does not negate the finding:
- The check/read/remove sequence is indeed not done under a single lock. However, the only concurrent mutation is ReadWorker's ReadData.AddRange (lines 150-153), which only APPENDS to the end. RemoveRange(0, size) removes from the FRONT, which AddRange never touches. So for the normal positive-size case the bytes removed equal exactly the bytes returned (same front size bytes); the claim that "a different number of bytes is removed than returned" does not hold for this append-only writer + front-removal design. (There is a latent correctness concern only if a future writer mutated the front, but as written it is benign.)

Net: the main negative-size crash is a real, reproducible, high-impact defect, so the finding is REAL. The atomicity rationale is partly incorrect but is supplementary.

### CR-H037 · 🟠 high · Birko.Configuration

- **Detail:** The override `public override void LoadFrom(Settings data)` replaces the base `Settings.LoadFrom(Settings)` (which unconditionally copies Location and Name) with a type-guarded path that does nothing unless `data is PasswordSettings`. So calling `new PasswordSettings().LoadFrom(new Settings("loc","name"))` copies NOTHING — Location and Name are silently lost. Before this override existed, the base would have copied them. This is a behavior regression / silent data loss whenever a PasswordSettings is loaded from a less-derived Settings instance via the virtual `LoadFrom(Settings)` slot.
- **Fix:** Always call base.LoadFrom(data) first so Location/Name are copied for any Settings, then conditionally copy the Password when `data is PasswordSettings p`. E.g.: `public override void LoadFrom(Settings data) { base.LoadFrom(data); if (data is PasswordSettings p) Password = p.Password; }`.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Configuration\Settings.cs. PasswordSettings.LoadFrom(Settings) (lines 154-160) is type-guarded `if (data is PasswordSettings passwordData) { LoadFrom(passwordData); }` with NO else branch, so a plain Settings argument copies NOTHING. The base Settings.LoadFrom(Settings) (lines 80-87) unconditionally copies Location and Name, so this override is a genuine behavior regression / silent data loss for the less-derived-argument case via the virtual slot, exactly as described. RemoteSettings.LoadFrom(Settings) (lines 245-251) has the same defect.\n\nThe bug is corroborated as unintentional by the sibling settings classes: SqlSettings (Birko.Data.SQL/Stores/SqlSettings.cs:56-66) and the MSSql/MySql/PostgreSql/SqLite/CosmosDB/RavenDB settings all implement the identical override LoadFrom(Settings) pattern but WITH an `else { base.LoadFrom(data); }` fallthrough that preserves the base copy. PasswordSettings and RemoteSettings omit precisely that else branch, making it an inconsistency/regression rather than a deliberate design. There is no Birko.Configuration.Tests project guarding this. Fix: add `else { base.LoadFrom(data); }` to both PasswordSettings and RemoteSettings overrides.\n\nMinor caveat (does not change the verdict): observed call sites pass same-or-more-derived instances, so the loss path may be latent rather than currently triggered, but it is a real defect in a public virtual API of a base library.

### CR-H039 · 🟠 high · Birko.CQRS
- **Title:** Handler cache keyed only by request type, ignores TResult — InvalidCastException / wrong handler on covariant dispatch
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.CQRS\Mediator/Mediator.cs:16,32,42-46`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — _handlerCache is now keyed on (requestType, resultType), so distinct TResult dispatches get distinct wrappers. Covariant-dispatch regression test asserts a SendAsync<object?> call no longer poisons the cache for a later SendAsync<string?>.
- **Detail:** _handlerCache is a static ConcurrentDictionary<Type, RequestHandlerBase> keyed only on the runtime request type, but CreateHandler<TResult> bakes the call-site TResult into RequestHandlerWrapper<requestType, TResult>. If the same concrete request type is dispatched twice with different TResult arguments, the second call gets the cached wrapper built for the first TResult, then the cast '(RequestHandler<TResult>)handler' on line 33 throws InvalidCastException. Because IRequest<out TResult> is covariant, a query of type IQuery<string> can legally be passed to SendAsync<object>(IRequest<object>); the cache then stores RequestHandlerWrapper<Q, object>, and a later SendAsync<string>(query) hits the cache and fails the cast. Even on the first covariant call, the wrapper resolves IRequestHandler<Q, object> from DI (the handler is registered as IRequestHandler<Q, string>), so GetService returns null and it throws 'No handler registered'. The cache key must incorporate TResult, or the wrapper should resolve the handler/result via the request's actual IRequest<> closed interface rather than the call-site generic.
- **Fix:** Key the cache on a composite of (requestType, typeof(TResult)) — e.g. a (Type,Type) ValueTuple or a struct key — so distinct TResult dispatches get distinct wrappers; or derive TResult from the request's implemented IRequest<> interface instead of the call-site type parameter.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual source at C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.CQRS\Mediator\Mediator.cs and the contracts in C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.CQRS\Core\.

The cited code matches the finding exactly:
- Line 16: `_handlerCache` is `static ConcurrentDictionary<Type, RequestHandlerBase>`.
- Lines 31-32: key is `request.GetType()` (the runtime request type only); `CreateHandler<TResult>` is the value factory.
- Line 33: result is cast `(RequestHandler<TResult>)handler`.
- Lines 42-46: `CreateHandler<TResult>` bakes the call-site `TResult` into `RequestHandlerWrapper<requestType, TResult>`.

Covariance is real: `IRequest<out TResult>` (Core/IRequest.cs:7) and `IQuery<out TResult> : IRequest<TResult>` (Core/IQuery.cs:7), so an `IQuery<string>` is assignable to `IRequest<object>` and can legally be dispatched as `SendAsync<object>(...)`.

Both failure modes hold:
1) InvalidCastException on cache hit: a first `SendAsync<object>(q)` caches `RequestHandlerWrapper<Q, object>` (a `RequestHandler<object>`). A later `SendAsync<string>(q)` for the same runtime type Q returns the cached wrapper; the cast to `RequestHandler<string>` fails because the abstract generic `RequestHandler<TResult>` is invariant. Confirmed.
2) Wrong/missing handler even on the first covariant call: `RequestHandlerWrapper<Q, object>.HandleAsync` resolves `IRequestHandler<Q, object>` (Mediator.cs:61), but the handler is registered as `IRequestHandler<Q, string>`. `IRequestHandler<in TRequest, TResult>` is invariant in TResult (Core/IRequestHandler.cs:12), so GetService returns null and it throws "No handler registered" (line 64). Confirmed.

The constraint `where TRequest : IRequest<TResult>` on the wrapper is satisfied via covariance for `RequestHandlerWrapper<Q, object>`, so MakeGenericType does not fail at construction — the failure is at DI resolution / cast time, exactly as described.

This is legal use of the public API (`SendAsync<TResult>(IRequest<TResult>)` plus covariant IRequest), not exotic. The recommended fix (incorporate TResult into the cache key, or resolve the handler via the request's actual closed IRequest<> interface) is correct. Real, actionable, accurately diagnosed; severity high is reasonable since it manifests as a runtime InvalidCastException / spurious "no handler" with a poisoned static cache shared process-wide.

### CR-H040 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Aggregates
- **Title:** GetCollection/GetSingle cast silently returns null for materialized List<AbstractModel> providers
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Aggregates\Mapping/FlattenResult.cs:47, 57`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — GetCollection now projects with OfType<TChild> (non-null, filters by actual type) instead of a reference cast that returned null for a materialized List<AbstractModel>. Test added for the List<AbstractModel> path.
- **Detail:** GetCollection<TChild> does `collection as IEnumerable<TChild>` and GetSingle does `single as TChild` against the stored IEnumerable<AbstractModel>. This succeeds only when the runtime object is reference-assignable to IEnumerable<TChild> — i.e. the provider stored the original covariant Category[]/List<Category>. A realistic IRelatedDataProvider implementation will commonly project store results to a List<AbstractModel> (e.g. `store.Read(filter).Cast<AbstractModel>().ToList()` or `.Select(x => (AbstractModel)x).ToList()`), whose runtime type is List<AbstractModel> and is NOT assignable to IEnumerable<Category>; `as` then returns null SILENTLY, so consumers get null collections / null singles with no error. The test suite passes only because InMemoryRelatedDataProvider stores the original array reference unchanged (TestResources/InMemoryRelatedDataProvider.cs + AggregateMapperFlattenTests.SetupRelatedData), so the fragile path is never exercised.
- **Fix:** Use a robust projection instead of a reference cast: `return collection.OfType<TChild>();` for GetCollection (still returns non-null, filters by actual type), and `return single as TChild;` is fine for the single case since the element itself IS a TChild. For GetCollection prefer `collection?.OfType<TChild>()` (or `.Cast<TChild>()` if you want a hard failure on mismatch). Add a test where the provider returns a `List<AbstractModel>` (not the concrete array) to lock this in.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code.

CORE ISSUE IS REAL (GetCollection, FlattenResult.cs:47): GetCollection<TChild> does `collection as IEnumerable<TChild>` against the stored `IEnumerable<AbstractModel>` (NestedCollections is typed Dictionary<string, IEnumerable<AbstractModel>>, FlattenResult.cs:27). AggregateMapper.Flatten stores the provider's returned reference unchanged (AggregateMapper.cs:49 `result.NestedCollections[...] = related`). The `as` cast only succeeds when the runtime object is reference-assignable to IEnumerable<TChild>. `IEnumerable<out T>` covariance only allows derived->base element coercion, NOT base->derived: a `List<AbstractModel>` is NOT assignable to `IEnumerable<Category>`, so the cast silently yields null with no error.

The materialization scenario is realistic: IRelatedDataProvider is consumer-implemented (interface only, IRelatedDataProvider.cs) and the README documents it as "queries your SQL stores." A provider wrapping Birko store results would commonly produce `List<AbstractModel>` via `.Cast<AbstractModel>().ToList()` or `.Select(x => (AbstractModel)x).ToList()`, triggering the silent null.

The test masking is confirmed: AggregateMapperFlattenTests.SetupRelatedData (lines 32-46) stores `new Category[]{...}` / `new Image[]{...}`; `Category[]` IS assignable to `IEnumerable<Category>` (array + IEnumerable<out T> covariance), so the fragile path is never exercised. InMemoryRelatedDataProvider stores the reference unchanged (lines 20-23, 30-35).

ONE INACCURACY — the GetSingle claim (line 57) is WRONG: NestedSingles stores `related.FirstOrDefault()` (AggregateMapper.cs:45), i.e. the individual element, whose runtime type is always the concrete entity (e.g. Image), never List<AbstractModel>. So `single as TChild` succeeds regardless of collection materialization. GetSingle is robust; the materialization problem affects collections only. The finding over-broadens by lumping GetSingle in.

Net: high-severity, actionable bug in GetCollection (fix: `collection.Cast<TChild>()` or per-element OfType). The GetSingle half is a false positive, but the finding as a whole identifies a genuine real defect, so isReal=true.

### CR-H041 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Aggregates
- **Title:** ExpandCollection silently drops new child entities that have no Guid yet
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Aggregates\Mapping/AggregateMapper.cs:197-202`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — null-Guid desired children are now emitted as unconditional Inserts; only already-keyed entities go through DiffByKey. Regression test asserts a null-Guid child yields an Insert.
- **Detail:** ExpandCollection diffs via EnumerableHelper.DiffByKey(current, desired, e => e.Guid). DiffByKey excludes any item whose key selector returns null (HasKey filter in EnumerableHelper.cs:66-74). AbstractModel.Guid is `Guid?` and defaults to null. So a desired child entity that has not yet been persisted (Guid == null) is filtered out of `desiredList` before the diff and therefore never appears in `diff.Added` — no Insert SyncOperation is generated for it. For an expand/sync pipeline whose whole purpose is to push new nested children back into relational form, brand-new children are silently skipped.
- **Fix:** Decide and document the contract: either require callers to assign Guids before expand (validate and throw if a desired child has null Guid), or treat null-Guid desired entities as unconditional Inserts (e.g. partition desired into null-Guid => Insert, plus DiffByKey on the rest). DiffByKey (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Helpers\EnumerableHelper.cs:60-84) defines HasKey(e) => keySelector(e) != null (line 66) and filters BOTH lists through it before diffing: desiredList = desired.Where(HasKey).ToList() (lines 72-74). Its own XML doc (line 57) states "Items where this returns null are excluded." diff.Added is computed only from that filtered desiredList (line 79), so any desired child with a null key is gone before Added is built.

AbstractModel.Guid is confirmed `public virtual Guid? Guid { get; set; } = null;` (Birko.Data.Core\Models\AbstractModel.cs:9), so a not-yet-persisted child has Guid == null and is dropped — no Insert SyncOperation is generated for it in ExpandCollection (lines 199-202).

The bug is a real asymmetry: ExpandSingle (lines 170-173) inserts a brand-new OneToOne child with NO Guid check (currentEntity == null && desiredEntity != null => Insert), so the OneToOne path correctly handles null-Guid new children while the collection path silently drops them. The whole stated purpose of Expand is to push desired nested state into relational SyncOperations, so dropping brand-new collection children is a genuine correctness gap.

Existing tests do not catch it: AggregateMapperExpandTests.Expand_NewLineAdded_GeneratesInsert (lines 62-85) pre-assigns Line2Guid to the "new" line, so it passes precisely because the new child already has a Guid; no test exercises a desired child with Guid == null. No Guid-assignment step exists anywhere in the Expand/ExpandAsync pipeline (AggregateMapper.cs:107-160) that would mask the issue.

The finding's file paths, line numbers (197-202 and EnumerableHelper.cs:66-74), and described mechanism are all accurate. The only minor nuance is severity-dependent on caller convention (if entities always get client-generated Guids before expand it won't trigger), but the OneToOne path proves null-Guid new children are an expected input, making the inconsistency real and actionable.

### CR-H042 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.CosmosDB
- **Title:** AsyncCosmosDBStore overrides public ReadAsync(Guid) instead of ReadCoreAsync — bypasses lazy-init
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB\Stores/AsyncCosmosDBStore.cs:181`
- **Category:** convention · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the ReadAsync(Guid) override now runs EnsureInitializedAsync first (keeping the efficient point-read), so a connectionString-constructed store auto-initializes. Tracking-subclass test asserts InitCore runs.
- **Detail:** Convention (CLAUDE.md): concrete stores override the protected *Core methods and let the base public wrapper run EnsureInitializedAsync. The base `ReadAsync(Guid)` delegates to `ReadAsync(filter)` which calls EnsureInitializedAsync (AbstractAsyncStore.cs:84-94). By overriding the public ReadAsync(Guid) directly, this store skips InitCoreAsync: a store constructed via the connectionString ctor (only _cosmosClient set, _container null) and read before an explicit InitAsync returns null silently instead of auto-initializing. The base single-arg path already routes guid lookups through ReadCoreAsync(x => x.Guid == guid).
- **Fix:** Remove the public ReadAsync(Guid) override; rely on the base, or if a native point read is wanted, override the protected single-result ReadCoreAsync only after lazy-init is guaranteed (the base ReadAsync(Guid) builds the filter form). Same fix as the sync store.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the code. AsyncCosmosDBStore.cs:181 declares `public override async Task<T?> ReadAsync(Guid guid, ...)`, overriding the public CRUD method rather than the protected `ReadCoreAsync`. This violates the documented convention (CLAUDE.md: concrete stores override `*Core` methods and let the base wrapper run EnsureInitializedAsync).

Verified base behavior in Birko.Data.Stores/AbstractAsyncStore.cs: the base `ReadAsync(Guid)` (lines 84-87) delegates to `ReadAsync(filter)` which calls `EnsureInitializedAsync` (lines 90-94) before `ReadCoreAsync`. The override bypasses this gate entirely.

Lazy-init bypass is real and observable: the connectionString ctor (lines 67-83) sets `_cosmosClient`/`_databaseName`/`_containerName` but leaves `_container == null`. `_container` is only assigned inside `EnsureDatabaseAndContainerExistAsync` (lines 449-461), reached via `InitCoreAsync`/`EnsureInitializedAsync`. The overridden `ReadAsync(Guid)` opens with `if (_container == null || guid == Guid.Empty) return null;` — so a store constructed via connectionString and read by Guid before any other initialized op returns null silently instead of auto-initializing, exactly as described.

The Cosmos point-read by id (ReadItemAsync) is a legitimate optimization, but it must sit behind the init gate. Correct fix: route guid reads through the protected layer (e.g. override ReadCoreAsync with the point-read, or have the public override call EnsureInitializedAsync first / remove it). Actionable and correctly located.

### CR-H043 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.CosmosDB
- **Title:** CosmosDBStore overrides public Read(Guid) and Read() instead of *Core — bypasses lazy-init
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB\Stores/CosmosDBStore.cs:165,182`
- **Category:** convention · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — Read(Guid) and Read() now call EnsureInitialized first. Tracking-subclass tests assert InitCore runs for both.

Base `Read(Guid)` (AbstractStore.cs:79) and parameterless `Read()` (AbstractBulkStore.cs:43) both route through EnsureInitialized() before hitting ReadCore. Read() also passes allowSynchronousQueryExecution:true and materializes the whole container with no paging — distinct from the intended bulk ReadCore.

CosmosDBStore (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB\Stores\CosmosDBStore.cs) overrides the PUBLIC Read(Guid) at line 165 and public parameterless Read() at line 182, both accessing _container directly with no EnsureInitialized() call. Lazy-init bypass verified against the base classes in the sibling repo:
- AbstractStore.Read(Guid) (AbstractStore.cs:79) delegates to Read(filter) (line 81), which calls EnsureInitialized() (line 69). EnsureInitialized() (lines 24-33) calls InitCore() on first use.
- AbstractBulkStore.Read() (AbstractBulkStore.cs:43) delegates to Read(null,null,null,null) (line 45), which calls EnsureInitialized() (line 33).
The Cosmos overrides skip both paths entirely.

Silent-failure impact verified: the (connectionString, databaseName, containerName) ctor (lines 55-71) sets _cosmosClient/_databaseName/_containerName but NOT _container. _container is only assigned by EnsureDatabaseAndContainerExist() (lines 356-367), called from InitCore() (line 133). So before init, _container == null, and Read(guid) returns null (line 167) / Read() returns Enumerable.Empty (line 184) silently — while every other CRUD method (Create/Update/Delete/Count/filtered Read/bulk ReadCore) auto-initializes. This is a genuine behavioral inconsistency that masks an uninitialized store as 'no data', and it is reachable from a public constructor.

### CR-H044 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.CosmosDB.Views
- **Title:** Aggregate ORDER BY references view-property names against raw container fields
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB.Views\CosmosViewStore.cs:235-240`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — ORDER BY now resolves each view key via ResolveOrderKey: a group key maps to its source field (c.{source}); an aggregate result orders by its SELECT alias. SQL-generation test asserts both.
- **Detail:** In BuildAggregateSql the ORDER BY is emitted as 'c.{f.PropertyName}' where f.PropertyName comes from OrderBy<TView>.Fields — i.e. a VIEW property name (the alias). But the SELECT/GROUP BY produced by CosmosAggregationHelper.BuildAggregateSqlParts use SOURCE property names ('c.{FieldName}') and project them with 'AS {alias}'. Cosmos GROUP BY queries can only ORDER BY a grouped expression, so 'ORDER BY c.{viewProperty}' references a raw document field that either does not exist or is not in the GROUP BY, yielding wrong/empty ordering or a query error. The aggregate aliases and the order key namespace are inconsistent.
- **Fix:** Map each orderBy field back to its source property via the same Fields lookup used by FindViewPropertyForGroupBy (reverse direction: find Field whose ViewProperty == f.PropertyName, emit c.{SourceProperty}). For ordering by an aggregate result, order by the aggregate alias instead. Add a test that orders an aggregate view by a renamed group key and by an aggregate column.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB.Views\CosmosViewStore.cs:235-240 (BuildAggregateSql), ORDER BY is emitted as `c.{f.PropertyName}` where `f` comes from `OrderBy<TView>.Fields`. I verified that `OrderBy<T>` (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Stores\OrderBy.cs) is built from `TView` property expressions, so `f.PropertyName` is the VIEW property name (the alias). Meanwhile `CosmosAggregationHelper.BuildAggregateSqlParts` (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB\Aggregation\CosmosAggregationHelper.cs:41-66) emits GROUP BY using the SOURCE property name (`c.{FieldName}`) and projects SELECT as `c.{source} AS {alias}`. Source and view names are independently specified and can differ — FieldSelector (sourceProperty, viewProperty) and AggregateClause (SourceProperty, ViewProperty) treat them as distinct, and CosmosViewStore even has FindViewPropertyForGroupBy precisely because they differ. So when a view renames a field, ORDER BY references `c.{viewProperty}`, a raw document field that is not the grouped expression (which is `c.{sourceProperty}`) and may not exist; for aggregate-result columns (SUM/AVG) there is no raw `c.{viewProperty}` at all. Result: wrong/empty ordering or a Cosmos query error, since Cosmos GROUP BY queries can only ORDER BY a grouped expression. The bug is real: the ORDER BY namespace (view alias, raw-prefixed) is inconsistent with the SELECT/GROUP BY namespace (source property). Corroborating evidence: the reference SQL views path (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.Views\SqlViewStore.cs TranslateOrderBy + SqlViewTranslator) feeds the view property into a translator that maps it to the proper column/alias, whereas the Cosmos path naively prefixes `c.` with no translation. Caveats keeping this from being trivially fatal in every case: (1) it only manifests when the view renames a grouped field or orders by an aggregate result — in the common case where source name == view name and you order by a grouped field, the emitted SQL happens to be valid; (2) there is no test project (Birko.Data.CosmosDB.Views.Tests does not exist) exercising aggregate ORDER BY, so it went unnoticed. The 'high' severity is slightly generous but defensible since it silently emits broken/incorrect SQL on a supported scenario. Finding is genuine and actionable: the fix is to translate the view property to the grouped source expression / aggregate alias rather than raw-prefixing `c.`.

### CR-H045 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.CosmosDB.Views
- **Title:** Aggregate WHERE clause filters on view-property names, not source fields
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.CosmosDB.Views\CosmosViewStore.cs:219-226, 260-267, 384-397`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — CosmosFilterTranslator.Translate now takes a view->source member mapper (built from _definition.Fields), used by the aggregate + count WHERE paths so a renamed field targets the real source field. Test asserts the generated WHERE uses the source name.
- **Detail:** In the aggregate path, CosmosFilterTranslator.Translate(filter) (and the same call in BuildCountAggregateSql) emits 'c.{member.Member.Name}' where Member.Name is a property of TView (the view). The WHERE runs against the raw container documents (FROM c), whose JSON fields are the SOURCE property names. When a view renames a field (Field.SourceProperty != Field.ViewProperty), the WHERE targets a field that does not exist on the source document, so the predicate silently matches nothing / is wrong. The LINQ (non-aggregate) path is fine because Cosmos maps TView directly, but the SQL aggregate path needs source-name translation.
- **Fix:** Translate filter member names through _definition.Fields (ViewProperty -> SourceProperty) before composing the WHERE clause for aggregate/count SQL, mirroring how group-by source names are used in the SELECT.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. The aggregate path builds a Cosmos SQL query against raw container documents (FROM c). The SELECT/GROUP BY correctly use SOURCE property names: BuildAggregateSql passes g.PropertyName (source) as FieldName and a.SourceProperty for aggregates (CosmosViewStore.cs:210-214), and CosmosAggregationHelper emits c.{FieldName} (CosmosAggregationHelper.cs:48-62); BuildCountAggregateSql GROUP BY also uses g.PropertyName (line 273). However, the WHERE clause comes from CosmosFilterTranslator.Translate(filter) where filter is Expression<Func<TView,bool>>; the translator emits c.{member.Member.Name} (lines 388, 393), and member.Member.Name is a property of TView (the VIEW), not the source. The translator is a static method with no access to _definition.Fields, so there is no source-name mapping anywhere in the filter path. FieldSelector explicitly models SourceProperty != ViewProperty (FieldSelector.cs:13-17), confirming renaming is a supported scenario. Therefore, whenever a view renames a field, the WHERE predicate targets a field absent from the source document, producing a wrong predicate (silently filters nothing in Cosmos). This affects both BuildAggregateSql (lines 219-226) and BuildCountAggregateSql (lines 260-267), with the offending name emission at lines 384-397 — all matching the cited ranges. The fix is to translate view-property member names back to source-property names via _definition.Fields before emitting WHERE. No tests cover this case in the project. The finding is genuine, high severity, and actionable.

### CR-H046 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.ElasticSearch
- **Title:** AsyncElasticSearchStore overrides public ReadAsync(ct) — bypasses lazy-init AND silently truncates to 1000 docs
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.ElasticSearch\Stores/AsyncElasticSearchStore.cs:190`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — deleted the ReadAsync(ct) override; the base now routes read-all through EnsureInitializedAsync + the scrolling ReadCoreAsync (no 1000-doc cap). Tracking-subclass test asserts init runs and ReadCoreAsync is called with null limit/offset.
- **Detail:** The no-arg bulk read `public override async Task<IEnumerable<T>> ReadAsync(CancellationToken ct)` is overridden directly. This violates the framework convention (concrete stores override *Core methods, never public CRUD — base.ReadAsync(ct) in AbstractAsyncBulkStore.cs:72 forwards to ReadAsync(null,...) which calls EnsureInitializedAsync then ReadCoreAsync). The override (a) skips EnsureInitializedAsync (no lazy-init / no cancellation gate), and (b) hard-caps the result at `Math.Min(MaxResultWindow, 1000)` with From=0 and NO scrolling — so `store.ReadAsync()` on a store with >1000 documents silently returns only the first 1000, whereas the streaming ReadCoreAsync(filter,orderBy,limit,offset) path it should have used scrolls the full set. A caller doing an unfiltered read-all gets silently wrong (truncated) data.
- **Fix:** Delete the ReadAsync(ct) override entirely and rely on the base implementation (which routes through ReadCoreAsync -> ReadStreamAsync with scrolling), or if a fast-path is wanted, make it call EnsureInitializedAsync and delegate to the scrolling ReadCoreAsync rather than capping at 1000.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. At C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.ElasticSearch\Stores\AsyncElasticSearchStore.cs:190, the store overrides the public CRUD method `public override async Task<IEnumerable<T>> ReadAsync(CancellationToken ct = default)`, violating the framework convention that concrete stores override only `*Core` methods.

(a) Lazy-init/cancellation bypass: The base implementation (Birko.Data.Stores\AbstractAsyncBulkStore.cs:72-75) forwards `ReadAsync(ct)` to `ReadAsync(null,null,null,null,ct)`, which calls `EnsureInitializedAsync(ct)` (lines 57) then `ReadCoreAsync`. The override does neither — no `EnsureInitializedAsync` and no `ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()` gate; `ct` is only forwarded into the search call. It even returns `Enumerable.Empty<T>()` if `Connector` is null (which init would have set up).

(b) Silent truncation: The override issues a single `SearchAsync` with `Size = Math.Min(MaxResultWindow, 1000)`, `From = 0`, and NO scroll loop. The intended path it replaced — `ReadCoreAsync` (line 213) -> `ReadStreamAsync` (lines 490-592) — detects the unbounded read (`From == null && Size == null`), switches into Scroll mode, and loops via `ScrollAsync` until `count >= end` where `end = searchResponse.Total`, i.e. the full set. So `store.ReadAsync()` on an index with >1000 docs silently returns only the first 1000 instead of all documents.

Additional divergence: the override hard-codes the static `ElasticSearch.MaxResultWindow` rather than the per-type `_settings.IndexSettings...MaxResultWindow` that ReadStreamAsync honors. Both the convention violation and the data-truncation bug are real and actionable; the fix is to delete the public override and let the base route through ReadCoreAsync (which already scrolls).

### CR-H047 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.ElasticSearch.Views
- **Title:** Unparseable filter silently returns ALL documents instead of filtered/erroring
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.ElasticSearch.Views\ElasticSearchViewStore.cs:312-332`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — BuildFilterQuery now throws NotSupportedException when a supplied filter throws OR ParseExpression returns null, instead of widening to MatchAll; only a null filter maps to MatchAll. New test project asserts null->MatchAll, supported->ok, untranslatable->throws.
- **Detail:** BuildFilterQuery has two paths that both fall back to matching every document for a non-null user filter: (1) the try/catch returns MatchAllQuery on any parse exception; (2) more subtly, ElasticSearch.ParseExpression (ElasticSearch.cs:55-68) returns null (no throw) for expression node types it does not support, so BuildFilterQuery returns a null QueryContainer. A null Query on SearchRequest/CountRequest causes ES to match all documents. So a caller who passes a filter the parser cannot translate gets the entire dataset back from QueryAsync/QueryFirstAsync/CountAsync rather than a filtered result or an error. For a count or a 'first matching' call this is a correctness landmine (e.g. an existence/permission check that should match 0 silently matches everything). The XML doc comment downplays this as a 'safety net'.
- **Fix:** Distinguish 'no filter' (filter == null -> MatchAll, correct) from 'filter supplied but untranslatable'. When filter != null and ParseExpression returns null or throws, throw NotSupportedException/InvalidOperationException rather than silently widening to MatchAll. At minimum, log/surface the failure so callers don't get a false full-result set.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.ElasticSearch.Views\ElasticSearchViewStore.cs, BuildFilterQuery (lines 312-332) has two fall-back-to-match-everything paths for a non-null filter:

1. Exception path (lines 326-331): any exception from ParseExpression returns `new MatchAllQuery()`.
2. Silent-null path: line 324 returns `Data.ElasticSearch.ElasticSearch.ParseExpression(filter)`, which is `QueryBase?`. In ElasticSearch.cs:55-68, ParseExpression returns null (no throw) for unsupported expression node types (`_ => null` at line 66, plus numerous other null returns inside the parser, e.g. lines 121, 126). That null flows back through BuildFilterQuery's `QueryContainer` return via NEST's implicit QueryBase->QueryContainer conversion, producing a null/empty Query.

A null Query on NEST SearchRequest/CountRequest means no query is applied, so ES matches ALL documents.

This filterQuery is used directly as the Query on:
- CountRequest (line 82) in CountAsync
- SearchRequest (line 112) in QueryAsync
- QueryFirstAsync (line 68) delegates to QueryAsync with limit 1
- the aggregation path (line 160) also uses it.

So a caller passing a filter the parser cannot translate gets the entire dataset back rather than a filtered/empty result or an error. For Count/First-style existence or permission checks this is a real correctness landmine (a check that should match 0 silently matches everything). The XML doc comment (lines 319-321, 328-329) only frames the exception case as a 'safety net' and does not acknowledge the silent-null path, which isn't even covered by the try/catch.

Every concrete detail in the finding (file, line range, both fall-back paths, the affected methods, the null-Query semantics, the downplaying comment) checks out against the source. The severity rating of high is defensible given the silent existence/permission-check failure mode; the only mitigating factor is that callers using the documented simple operators are unaffected.
