### CR-H049 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.InfluxDB
- **Title:** Wrapped InfluxDBClient (IDisposable) is never disposed — resource leak
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.InfluxDB\Stores/AsyncInfluxDBStore.cs:51 and Stores/InfluxDBStore.cs:48`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — both stores implement IDisposable (dispose the owned client) and SetSettings disposes any existing client before replacing it. Tests assert IDisposable, dispose-clears-client, and double-SetSettings does not throw.
- **Detail:** SetSettings constructs a new Birko.Data.InfluxDB.InfluxDBClient (which wraps InfluxDB.Client.InfluxDBClient holding an HttpClient and implements IDisposable) and assigns it to the Client property. Neither store implements IDisposable, so the underlying client/HttpClient is never disposed. Worse, calling SetSettings twice silently overwrites the previous Client without disposing it, leaking the first connection's HttpClient/sockets each time. The InfluxDbUnitOfWork is careful about disposal but the stores that own the client are not.
- **Fix:** Make both stores implement IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable and dispose Client in Dispose/DestroyAsync; in SetSettings, dispose any existing Client before assigning a new one (Client?.Dispose() first).
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual code. Both stores construct a disposable client in SetSettings and never dispose it, and neither the stores nor their base classes implement IDisposable.

Evidence:
- Stores/InfluxDBStore.cs:48 — SetSettings does `Client = new InfluxDB.InfluxDBClient(settings);`
- Stores/AsyncInfluxDBStore.cs:51 — SetSettings does `Client = new InfluxDB.InfluxDBClient(settings);`
- InfluxDB/InfluxDBClient.cs:9 — the wrapper `public class InfluxDBClient : IDisposable`; its constructor (line 29) creates `new global::InfluxDB.Client.InfluxDBClient(...)` (which holds an HttpClient), and its Dispose() (line 123) calls `Client?.Dispose()`. So the wrapper genuinely owns a disposable resource.
- Grep for `IDisposable|Dispose` across the Stores folder returns no matches — neither InfluxDBStore<T> nor AsyncInfluxDBStore<T> implements IDisposable or exposes any Dispose.
- Base classes AbstractStore<T> (Birko.Data.Stores/AbstractStore.cs:12) and AbstractAsyncStore<T> (AbstractAsyncStore.cs:14) implement only IStore<T>/IAsyncStore<T>; no IDisposable in the hierarchy, so there is no inherited disposal path.

Consequences are exactly as described: the client/HttpClient is never disposed for the lifetime of the store, and calling SetSettings twice overwrites the previous Client (a private-set property) without disposing it, leaking the prior connection's sockets each time. This is a genuine, actionable resource leak; the fix is to implement IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable on the stores and dispose the existing client before reassigning in SetSettings.

Minor inaccuracy in the finding's framing (does not change the verdict): the InfluxDbUnitOfWork is not actually 'careful about disposal' of the client — its Dispose/DisposeAsync only clear the batch context and it does not own/dispose the client either. But the core claim about the stores leaking the client is fully correct.

### CR-H050 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.JSON
- **Title:** JsonSeparateStore/JsonSeparateBulkStore.Destroy has an inverted guard and never deletes when configured
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.JSON\Stores\JsonSeparateStore.cs:56`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — dropped the inverted ! on the Name guard in both sync separate stores so Destroy deletes when configured. Reload-after-Destroy test confirms.
- **Detail:** Destroy returns early when `... || !string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings.Name)` is true. Since a working store always has a non-empty Name, the `!` inverts the intent: the method returns before deleting any files or the directory exactly when the store IS properly configured. The async DestroyAsync (AsyncJsonSeparateStore.cs:60) uses the correct condition `string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings?.Name)`. Same inverted guard exists in JsonSeparateBulkStore.cs:57.
- **Fix:** Drop the `!`: `if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(Path) || !Directory.Exists(Path) || string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings.Name)) return;` in both sync separate stores.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. JsonSeparateStore.cs:56 guards Destroy with `if (string.IsNullOrEmpty(Path) || !Directory.Exists(Path) || !string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings.Name)) return;`. The `!` on the Name check is inverted: a properly configured store always has a non-empty Name, so the method returns early before deleting any files (line 60-67) or the directory (line 68) exactly when the store IS configured. JsonSeparateBulkStore.cs:57 has the identical inverted guard (`|| !string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings.Name)`). The async DestroyAsync (AsyncJsonSeparateStore.cs:60) uses the correct, non-inverted condition `|| string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings?.Name)`. The intended pattern is further corroborated within the same sync file: LoadData (line 93) and SaveData (line 120) both bail out with the correct `string.IsNullOrEmpty(_settings.Name)` (no `!`), proving the two Destroy methods are inverted relative to the rest of the class. Net effect: Destroy/Destroy on the bulk store never deletes files or the directory for any working store, and would only attempt deletion in the broken case of an empty Name (where Directory.GetFiles with an empty search pattern would behave unexpectedly). This is a genuine high-severity functional bug.

### CR-H051 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.JSON
- **Title:** Separate/batch stores save files as "{Name}-{guid}" but reload with search pattern "{Name}" — files never re-match
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.JSON\Stores\AsyncJsonSeparateStore.cs:106`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — added JsonFileNaming.SearchPattern (Name with * -> Name; else {Name}-*) and routed every Directory.GetFiles across all 8 separate/batch stores through it, so saved {Name}-{key} files re-match on reload. Round-trip tests confirm.
- **Detail:** SaveData/SaveDataAsync name files `$"{_settings.Name}-{guid:D}"` when Name has no '*', but LoadData/LoadDataAsync enumerate with `Directory.GetFiles(dir, _settings.Name)` — using the bare Name as the search pattern. A literal pattern "foo.json" will not match files named "foo.json-<guid>", so previously saved entities are not reloaded after a fresh process start. The flow only works if the consumer sets Name to contain a '*' wildcard (e.g. "foo-*.json"), which is undocumented. This mismatch is present in all four separate/batch variants (sync+async, separate+batch).
- **Fix:** Either require/document a '*' in Name, or build the search glob from Name the same way the filename is built (e.g. when Name has no '*', enumerate with $"{Name}-*" / $"{Name}-{{*}}" consistent with the save pattern).
- **Verify reasoning:** CONFIRMED REAL. The save/load filename-pattern mismatch exists exactly as described.

Save side (no-wildcard branch): AsyncJsonSeparateStore.cs:151-153 builds `$"{_settings.Name}-{item.Key:D}"` when Name has no '*'. Same pattern in JsonSeparateStore.cs:136, JsonBatchStore.cs:154, and the async batch variant -> all four separate/batch stores.

Load side: AsyncJsonSeparateStore.cs:106 calls `Directory.GetFiles(pathDirectory, _settings.Name)` using the bare Name as the search pattern (also JsonSeparateStore.cs:99 and JsonBatchStore.cs:80).

I empirically verified the core technical claim on this Windows .NET environment: `Directory.GetFiles(dir, "foo.json")` returns ONLY "foo.json" and does NOT match "foo.json-11111111-...". A `*`-containing pattern like "foo-*.json" is required to match the GUID-suffixed files. So when Name is a literal filename (the conventional/documented value -- README sets `FilePath = "data/customers.json"`, and JsonStore.cs:144 uses Name as a literal file name), saved files named `{Name}-{guid}` are never re-matched by the load pattern `{Name}`.

Impact is correctly scoped: in-process reads still work because the `_files` Guid->path dictionary is held in memory; the failure manifests on a fresh process start / new store instance, where `_files` is empty and LoadData is the only repopulation path -- and its GetFiles call finds nothing. Destroy()/DestroyAsync() use the same bare-Name pattern (line 65 / JsonSeparateStore.cs:60), so they likewise fail to delete the per-entity files.

The '*' workaround is genuinely undocumented (README/docs never mention a wildcard Name), and the test suite (JsonStoreTests.cs, 47 lines) has zero coverage of separate/batch stores or cross-instance reload, so the bug is latent and untested. The save code even branches on `Name.Contains('*')` while the load code never does -- a clear internal inconsistency. High severity is justified: silent data loss on restart for the default configuration.

One small note: the JsonSeparateStore.cs sync variant has a separate latent quirk -- SaveData at line 134 only writes files when `_files.ContainsKey(item.Key)` is already true (inverted vs the async version which writes when NOT present), so first-ever saves there may not even produce files; but that does not weaken the reported finding, it compounds the persistence unreliability.

### CR-H053 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Localization
- **Title:** Bulk wrappers apply translations even on the default culture (missing IsNonDefaultCulture guard)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Localization\Decorators/LocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.cs:279 and Decorators/AsyncLocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.cs:290`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — added the IsNonDefaultCulture guard at the top of ApplyTranslations(Async) in both bulk wrappers, matching the non-bulk ones. Sync + async tests confirm a stray default-culture translation row is no longer applied on a default-culture read.
- **Detail:** ApplyTranslations / ApplyTranslationsAsync in the two bulk wrappers do NOT start with the `if (!IsNonDefaultCulture()) return;` guard that the non-bulk wrappers have (LocalizedStoreWrapper.cs:186, AsyncLocalizedStoreWrapper.cs:180). The singular reads call ApplyTranslations unconditionally even inside the default-culture branch (e.g. AsyncLocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.cs:52-58 and :40-48, LocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.cs:38-46 and :52-57). On the default culture this (a) fires an unnecessary translation-store query per entity for every read, and (b) is an actual correctness bug if a translation row happens to exist whose Culture equals the default culture name: it would overwrite the entity's base field value with the translation. The contract (IEntityLocalizationContext) states translations are not created for the default culture, so reading them back on default culture is wrong.
- **Fix:** Add `if (!IsNonDefaultCulture()) return;` as the first line of ApplyTranslations/ApplyTranslationsAsync in both bulk wrappers, matching the non-bulk wrappers. Then the unconditional calls in the singular reads become safe no-ops on the default culture.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. The bulk wrappers' ApplyTranslations (LocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.cs:279) and ApplyTranslationsAsync (AsyncLocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.cs:290) lack the `if (!IsNonDefaultCulture()) return;` guard that the non-bulk wrappers have (LocalizedStoreWrapper.cs:186, AsyncLocalizedStoreWrapper.cs:180). The singular read paths invoke them even on the default culture: LocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.Read(filter) calls ApplyTranslations at line 55 inside the `!IsNonDefaultCulture()` branch, and Read(Guid) at line 43 has no culture check at all (same for async at AsyncLocalizedBulkStoreWrapper.cs:45 and :57). ApplyTranslations queries the translation store filtered by CurrentCulture.Name (line 286), which on the default branch equals DefaultCulture.Name, so: (a) it fires an unnecessary per-entity translation query on every default-culture singular read (certain inefficiency), and (b) if a translation row with Culture==default exists, line 308 overwrites the base field value (latent correctness bug). IEntityLocalizationContext.cs:18-19 documents that translations are not created for the default culture, so reading them back is contractually wrong, and the asymmetry vs the non-bulk wrappers is a real inconsistency. Caveat: the bulk Read() / Read(filter,orderBy,...) collection overloads ARE correctly guarded; the defect is confined to the singular Read(Guid)/Read(filter) paths the finding cites, and the worst-case data corruption requires a default-culture row that SaveTranslations itself refuses to create (so it'd come from legacy/external data). Even so, the unnecessary query plus the missing guard and inconsistency make this a genuine, actionable issue; the simple fix is to add the IsNonDefaultCulture guard at the top of the bulk ApplyTranslations methods (or before each singular call).

### CR-H054 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations
- **Title:** Async runner methods are sync-over-async; never use the store's real async API
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations\AbstractMigrationRunner.cs:93,126,156`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — InitializeAsync/MigrateAsync/RollbackAsync now await the store's InitializeAsync/GetCurrentVersionAsync and a new overridable ExecuteMigrationsAsync hook (default delegates to the sync path so no provider breaks). Tracking-store tests assert the async store members are used, not the blocking ones.
- **Detail:** InitializeAsync (l.93-97), MigrateAsync (l.126-129) and RollbackAsync (l.156-159) merely wrap the synchronous Initialize/Migrate/Rollback in Task.CompletedTask / Task.FromResult. Those synchronous paths call the BLOCKING store members (Store.Initialize() l.86, Store.GetCurrentVersion() via CurrentVersion l.29/107/138, Store.GetAppliedVersions() l.167/177). IMigrationStore exposes genuine async equivalents (InitializeAsync, GetCurrentVersionAsync, GetAppliedVersionsAsync, RecordMigrationAsync, RemoveMigrationAsync) that the async runner path never invokes. For a provider doing network/DB I/O (SQL, Mongo, Cosmos, etc.) this blocks the caller's thread for the entire migration run -- classic sync-over-async, prone to thread-pool starvation/deadlocks in async hosts. The abstract ExecuteMigrations (l.185) is sync-only, so a derived provider also cannot perform real async execution even if it wanted to.
- **Fix:** Introduce an async execution template: make ExecuteMigrations have an async counterpart (e.g. abstract Task<MigrationResult> ExecuteMigrationsAsync(...)), have MigrateAsync/RollbackAsync/InitializeAsync await the store's *Async members and the async execution path, and have the sync methods delegate to a sync ExecuteMigrations. Avoid wrapping sync I/O in Task.FromResult.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified against the actual code. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations\AbstractMigrationRunner.cs the async methods are pure sync-over-async wrappers at exactly the cited lines: InitializeAsync (l.93-97) calls Initialize() then returns Task.CompletedTask; MigrateAsync (l.126-129) returns Task.FromResult(Migrate(...)); RollbackAsync (l.156-159) returns Task.FromResult(Rollback(...)). The synchronous paths invoke the blocking store members: Store.Initialize() (l.86), CurrentVersion => Store.GetCurrentVersion() (l.29, used at l.107 and l.138), and Store.GetAppliedVersions() (l.167, l.177). The abstract execution hook ExecuteMigrations (l.185) is sync-only with no async counterpart.

IMigrationStore.cs confirms genuine async equivalents exist that the async runner path never calls: InitializeAsync, GetAppliedVersionsAsync, RecordMigrationAsync, RemoveMigrationAsync, GetCurrentVersionAsync. The concrete C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.SQL\SqlMigrationRunner.cs proves the impact: it overrides only sync ExecuteMigrations, opens the DB with connection.Open() (sync, l.45), and records via sync store.RecordMigration/RemoveMigration (l.147/151) — so MigrateAsync runs real SQL network/DB I/O synchronously on the caller's thread. Because ExecuteMigrations is protected abstract and sync-only, a derived provider cannot supply a true async execution path. This is a legitimate, actionable high-severity sync-over-async design flaw with thread-pool-starvation/blocking risk in async hosts. All cited line numbers match exactly.

### CR-H055 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.CosmosDB
- **Title:** Data migrator assumes partition key == document id for arbitrary containers
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.CosmosDB\Context/CosmosDBDataMigrator.cs:43`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the migrator now reads each container's real partition-key path, projects that field, and builds a typed PartitionKey from it (System.Text.Json, matching the store's CosmosGuidIdSerializer convention) — falling back to id only when the PK path is /id. Applies to Update/Delete/Copy/BulkInsert.
- **Detail:** UpdateDocuments, DeleteDocuments, CopyData all do `new PartitionKey(id)` using the document's id as the partition key value (e.g. PatchItemAsync(id, new PartitionKey(id), ...) at line 43, DeleteItemAsync at line 68, UpsertItemAsync at line 103). This is only correct when the target container's partition key path is `/id`. These methods call `_database.GetContainer(collection)` on user-owned data containers whose partition key is almost never `/id` (Cosmos best practice is a high-cardinality business field). When the partition key differs, the point-operation will fail with NotFound/wrong-partition or silently target the wrong logical partition. BulkInsert (line 119-120) has the same assumption when a document has no `id` it generates a Guid and uses it as both id and partition key.
- **Fix:** Query `SELECT * FROM c` (full document) rather than `SELECT c.id`, read the container's partition key path via ReadContainerAsync().Resource.PartitionKeyPath, and extract the partition-key value from the document at that path. Alternatively document this as a hard constraint (only works on `/id`-partitioned containers) — but the schema builder only ever creates `/id` containers, so cross-container data ops on real stores will break.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.CosmosDB\Context\CosmosDBDataMigrator.cs. Every cited point operation hard-codes the document id as the partition key value: PatchItemAsync(id, new PartitionKey(id), ...) at line 43, DeleteItemAsync(id, new PartitionKey(id)) at line 68, UpsertItemAsync(item, new PartitionKey(id)) at line 103, and BulkInsert at lines 119-120 (generates a Guid for a missing id and passes it as both id and PartitionKey via CreateItemAsync). There is no per-collection partition-key configuration anywhere in the migrator or its context — CosmosDBMigrationContext just constructs the migrator with the Database, and IDataMigrator's signatures only take a collection name. This is only correct when the target container's partition key path is /id.

The framework itself proves non-/id partition keys are a supported, expected case: (1) CosmosDBSchemaBuilder.CreateCollection defaults to "/id" but CosmosCollectionBuilder.WithField(isPrimary: true) reassigns _partitionKeyPath to "/{name}", so a migration-created container can legitimately have a business-field partition key; (2) CosmosMigrationStore (the framework's own state container) deliberately uses a dedicated "/partitionKey" path and a configurable MigrationsPartitionKey value, never assuming id == partition key — demonstrating the authors understood the distinction but did not apply it in the data migrator. Against any user-owned container whose partition key is a business field (Cosmos best practice), PatchItemAsync/DeleteItemAsync will hit NotFound (document not present in the id-keyed logical partition) and UpsertItemAsync/CreateItemAsync will silently write to the wrong logical partition.

Real and actionable correctness gap. Note for severity: this is migration tooling (not a runtime hot path), and a fully self-contained workflow that both creates and migrates containers via this framework would default to /id and mostly work; the bug bites when migrating pre-existing/externally-created containers or containers created via the isPrimary override — which is exactly the 'arbitrary user-owned data containers' scenario the finding describes. Appropriate fix: make the partition-key path/value configurable per collection or read the container's partition key definition before issuing point operations.

### CR-H056 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.CosmosDB
- **Title:** RenameField writes a placeholder string instead of preserving the value
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.CosmosDB\Context/CosmosDBSchemaBuilder.cs:112`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — RenameField now SELECTs the old value (and PK field) and copies the real value to the new field (PatchOperation.Set with the actual JsonElement) instead of a debug placeholder; also targets the correct partition.
- **Detail:** RenameField sets the new field to the literal string `"[RESTRICT SCHEMA] renamed from {oldName}"` and then removes the old field. This is data loss: the original value is discarded and replaced with a debug placeholder. A rename must copy the old value to the new key. Because it queries only `SELECT c.id` (line 94) it never reads the old value at all, so it cannot preserve it.
- **Fix:** Query the full document (or at least c.id and c[oldName]), then `PatchOperation.Set($"/{newName}", oldValue)` followed by `PatchOperation.Remove($"/{oldName}")`. Read the old value from the queried document.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.CosmosDB\Context\CosmosDBSchemaBuilder.cs. The RenameField method (lines 88-124) implements a rename via a query + patch loop. The query at line 94 is `SELECT c.id FROM c`, which returns only the document id and never reads the value of the field being renamed. The patch at line 112 is `PatchOperation.Set($"/{newName}", $"[RESTRICT SCHEMA] renamed from {oldName}")`, immediately followed by `PatchOperation.Remove($"/{oldName}")` at line 113. So for every document the new field key is written with a literal debug placeholder string and the old field (with the real value) is deleted. This is genuine data loss: a correct rename must copy the old value into the new key (and the query would need to select the old field, e.g. SELECT *, to even have access to it). There is no alternate/server-side rename path — a project-wide grep shows line 112 is the only RenameField implementation and the only use of the placeholder. The finding's file, line numbers, and description all match the actual code. Real and actionable; the fix is to read the old value (broaden the SELECT) and Set /{newName} to that value instead of the placeholder.

### CR-H058 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.ElasticSearch
- **Title:** Painless script value formatting is unsafe and wrong for non-string types
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.ElasticSearch\Context/ElasticSearchDataMigrator.cs:23-27`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — UpdateDocuments now references each value as a Painless script param (ctx._source.field = params.pN) via .Params(...) so Nest serializes bool/DateTime/decimal/quoted strings correctly instead of hand-formatting into the source; the UpdateByQuery response is validated. Extracted BuildPainlessSource is unit-tested.
- **Detail:** UpdateDocuments builds the Painless `ctx._source` script by wrapping string values in single quotes with no escaping (`$"'{s}'"`) and stringifying everything else via `kvp.Value?.ToString()`. A string value containing a single quote (or newline/backslash) produces a syntactically broken or injectable script. Non-string CLR values render via the invariant-less default ToString(): a DateTime becomes a locale/format-dependent string that is not a valid Painless literal, a bool becomes 'True'/'False' (Painless wants lowercase true/false), and decimals may carry culture-specific separators. The update silently fails (UpdateByQuery response is never checked) or corrupts data.
- **Fix:** Do not hand-build Painless source. Pass values as script params (`.Params(d => d.Add("v0", value))`) and reference `params.v0` in the source, letting Nest serialize them correctly; at minimum escape single quotes/backslashes and format with InvariantCulture. Also check the UpdateByQuery response IsValid and throw on failure (RecordMigration already follows this pattern).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.ElasticSearch\Context\ElasticSearchDataMigrator.cs lines 19-49. The Painless script is built at lines 23-27 exactly as described:

  var valueStr = kvp.Value is string s ? $"'{s}'" : kvp.Value?.ToString() ?? "null";
  return $"ctx._source.{kvp.Key} = {valueStr}";

Every claim holds:
1. String values are wrapped in single quotes with NO escaping ($"'{s}'"). A value containing a single quote (e.g. "O'Brien"), a backslash, or a newline produces a syntactically broken / injectable Painless script (ctx._source.name = 'O'Brien').
2. Non-string values go through the default ToString(): a bool renders as "True"/"False" (Painless requires lowercase true/false → invalid script); a DateTime renders as a culture-dependent bareword that is not a valid Painless literal; decimals/doubles can carry a culture-specific separator. The IDataMigrator contract (IDictionary<string, object> updates) confirms callers legitimately pass raw CLR types (bool, DateTime, decimal), so these are realistic inputs, not hypothetical.
3. The UpdateByQuery<dynamic>(...) call at lines 29-48 discards its response — no .IsValid / .ServerError check — so a script-compilation failure or partial failure is silent.

The correct approach would be to use Painless script params (descriptor.Script(s => s.Source("ctx._source.x = params.x").Params(...))) so NEST/Elasticsearch serializes each value with correct typing instead of string-concatenating literals, plus checking response.IsValid. This is a genuine high-severity correctness + injection bug, not a false positive. The only minor caveat is that exploitability depends on migration authors passing attacker-influenced strings, but the correctness failures (bool/DateTime producing invalid scripts) occur even with fully trusted, ordinary inputs.

### CR-H059 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.ElasticSearch
- **Title:** UpdateByQuery / DeleteByQuery / Bulk / Reindex responses are never validated
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.ElasticSearch\Context/ElasticSearchDataMigrator.cs:29-121`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — each response (UpdateByQuery, DeleteByQuery, ReindexOnServer, Bulk + item-level Errors, Refresh) is now captured and validated via EnsureValid, which throws with DebugInformation/OriginalException (mirroring the store) so a failed data step is no longer recorded as applied.
- **Detail:** UpdateDocuments, DeleteDocuments, CopyData (ReindexOnServer) and BulkInsert (Bulk) fire the request and discard the response. A failed data migration (mapping conflict, version conflict, partial bulk failure, reindex error) is swallowed, so the migration is then recorded as successfully applied by the runner even though the data step did nothing. This breaks the core guarantee of a migration framework.
- **Fix:** Capture each response and throw an InvalidOperationException/MigrationException when !response.IsValid (and for Bulk, when response.Errors), mirroring RecordMigration/RemoveMigration in ElasticSearchMigrationStore.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.ElasticSearch\Context\ElasticSearchDataMigrator.cs. All four data-mutation methods fire-and-forget their NEST responses: UpdateDocuments calls _client.UpdateByQuery<dynamic>(...) (line 29), DeleteDocuments calls _client.DeleteByQuery<dynamic>(...) (line 53), CopyData calls _client.ReindexOnServer(...) (line 89), and BulkInsert calls _client.Bulk(bulkDescriptor) (line 118) — none capture or inspect the returned response. NEST's high-level client does not throw on server/request errors by default; failures (mapping conflicts, version conflicts, partial bulk item failures, reindex errors) are reported only through response.IsValid / ServerError / OriginalException, and for Bulk also response.Errors. Because these are discarded, a failed or partial data step returns normally with no exception, so the migration runner records the migration as successfully applied even though the data work failed or was a no-op — breaking the migration framework's integrity guarantee, consistent with high severity. The finding is further corroborated by the framework's own convention: the sibling ElasticSearchMigrationStore.cs in the same project explicitly checks if (!response.IsValid) and throws InvalidOperationException with response.DebugInformation/OriginalException (lines 115-118, 140-142). The data migrator deviates from this established pattern. Genuine, actionable bug; fix is to capture each response and throw on !IsValid (and check response.Errors for Bulk), mirroring the migration store.

### CR-H060 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.InfluxDB
- **Title:** Batching WriteApi obtained via GetWriteApi() is never disposed (resource leak)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.InfluxDB\InfluxMigrationStore.cs:121-129; Context/InfluxDBDataMigrator.cs:88-120, 123-152`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — replaced the leaked batching GetWriteApi() (IDisposable, background worker, never disposed) with the synchronous GetWriteApiAsync() + WritePointAsync/WritePointsAsync (awaited) across RecordMigration/CopyData/BulkInsert — no background thread, writes committed before return. Mirrors AsyncInfluxDBStore.
- **Detail:** GetWriteApi() returns InfluxDB.Client.WriteApi, a background-batching, IDisposable writer that owns a background worker/timer. The code calls Flush() but never Dispose() (no using block). Flush() does not stop the background writer; the WriteApi remains alive and is leaked on every RecordMigration / CopyData / BulkInsert call. The sibling InfluxDB store (Birko.Data.InfluxDB AsyncInfluxDBStore) deliberately uses GetWriteApiAsync() (the synchronous, no-background-thread variant) for exactly this reason. Records may also not be fully committed before subsequent reads since the batching writer flushes asynchronously.
- **Fix:** Switch to client.GetWriteApiAsync() and await the write (consistent with Birko.Data.InfluxDB), or wrap GetWriteApi() in `using var writeApi = ...` so the writer flushes and disposes deterministically.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. The cited lines match exactly: in InfluxMigrationStore.cs:121-129 (RecordMigration), Context/InfluxDBDataMigrator.cs:88-120 (CopyData), and 127-151 (BulkInsert), the code calls _client.GetWriteApi(), writes points, and only calls Flush() — never Dispose(), and never wraps the writer in a using block. GetWriteApi() returns InfluxDB.Client.WriteApi, the background-batching, IDisposable writer that owns a background worker; Flush() only flushes pending points and does not stop the worker or release the instance, so a new WriteApi is leaked on every call to these methods. The finding is further corroborated by the sibling project Birko.Data.InfluxDB, which uses the correct patterns: the sync InfluxDBStore wraps every GetWriteApi() in `using (var writeApi = Client.GetWriteApi())` (Stores/InfluxDBStore.cs:231,257,382,413), and the async store / UnitOfWork use GetWriteApiAsync() (the non-background-batching WriteApiAsync variant). This proves the framework already knows the correct disposal/variant convention, making the migration code a genuine, actionable inconsistency rather than a stylistic preference or misunderstanding. The fix is simple: wrap each GetWriteApi() in a using block or switch to GetWriteApiAsync().

- **Title:** MongoIndexBuilder.Build() is never invoked — CreateIndex is a silent no-op
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.MongoDB\Context\MongoSchemaBuilder.cs:121-133`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — already resolved by CR-C14: IIndexBuilder now declares a Build() terminal (default no-op) and MongoIndexBuilder.Build() is public and overrides it, executing Indexes.CreateOne (joining the migration session per CR-C09). A CreateIndex(...).WithField(...).Build() chain now creates the index.
- **Detail:** ISchemaBuilder.CreateIndex returns a MongoIndexBuilder whose WithField/Unique/etc. only mutate private state; the actual Indexes.CreateOne call lives in internal void Build() (line 121). Nothing in this project (nor the AbstractMigrationRunner base) ever calls Build() — the IIndexBuilder interface has no Build method and there is no reflection/tracking that calls it. So a migration that does context.Schema.CreateIndex("coll","ix").WithField("x").Unique() compiles and runs but never creates the index. CreateCollection works only because MongoSchemaBuilder.CreateCollection eagerly calls _database.CreateCollection (line 22) before returning its (no-op) builder; CreateIndex has no such eager path, so the index work is entirely lost. (The sibling SqlSchemaBuilder has the same dangling internal Build() pattern, so this may be a framework-wide design gap, but in MongoDB it produces a fully silent functional loss.)
- **Fix:** Make CreateIndex build eagerly (perform Indexes.CreateOne when the terminal configuration is set), or have MongoSchemaBuilder track returned builders and flush them, or add a Build()/Apply() method to the IIndexBuilder contract that the migration framework calls. Mirror whatever fix the framework adopts for the SQL builder.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual source. The finding is accurate on every point.

1. `MongoSchemaBuilder.CreateIndex(collectionName, indexName)` (line 37-40) returns a `MongoIndexBuilder` whose chainable methods (`WithField` L105, `Unique` L111, `Sparse` L117, `WithProperty` L119) only mutate private state and return `this`. The actual `Indexes.CreateOne(model)` call lives solely in `internal void Build()` (lines 121-133).

2. `Build()` is invoked NOWHERE. Grep over the whole project finds `Build` only at its line-121 definition. It is `internal`, so a migration in another assembly cannot even see it.

3. The contract `IIndexBuilder` (Birko.Data.Patterns/Schema/IIndexBuilder.cs) declares only WithField/Unique/Sparse/WithProperty — there is NO Build()/Apply()/completion method. So an interface-typed caller (which is what `ISchemaBuilder.CreateIndex` returns — `IIndexBuilder`) has no way to trigger the index creation. `IMigrationContext` exposes only `Schema`/`Data`/`Raw`, and `AbstractMigrationRunner` has zero schema/index awareness or flush hook. Nothing tracks builders to flush them.

4. The asymmetry the finding cites is real: `CreateCollection` works only because `MongoSchemaBuilder.CreateCollection` eagerly calls `_database.CreateCollection(name)` (line 22) before returning the (no-op) builder. `CreateIndex` has no such eager path, so the index work is entirely lost — a fully silent no-op.

5. The framework-wide claim also checks out: the sibling `SqlSchemaBuilder` has the same dangling `internal void Build()` for both its collection builder (L208) and index builder (L297), neither called anywhere. SQL is actually worse since its `CreateCollection` has no eager fallback either.

Net effect: a migration calling `context.Schema.CreateIndex("coll","ix").WithField("x").Unique()` compiles, runs, reports success, and silently creates no index. Genuine high-severity functional loss, actionable (e.g., make CreateIndex eager, or add a Build/Apply method to IIndexBuilder, or have the builder build on a terminal call).

### CR-H063 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.MongoDB
- **Title:** Failure path can throw ArgumentOutOfRangeException, masking the real migration error
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.MongoDB\MongoMigrationRunner.cs:99`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the catch now indexes migrations[executed.Count] only when executed.Count < migrations.Count (a within-loop failure); a post-loop failure (e.g. CommitTransaction, where the counts are equal) throws the message-only MigrationException instead of indexing out of bounds and masking the real error.
- **Detail:** In the catch block, failedMigration is computed as `executed.Count > 0 ? migrations[executed.Count] : migrations[0]`. The throwing work is not limited to the loop body: session.CommitTransaction() runs after the foreach (line 87). If the commit (or anything after the last migration in the loop) throws, executed.Count == migrations.Count, so migrations[executed.Count] is an out-of-bounds index → ArgumentOutOfRangeException is thrown from the catch handler itself, swallowing the original exception `ex` and producing a confusing stack instead of the wrapped MigrationException. Even within the loop the index is fragile: executed is appended at the end of each iteration, so on a mid-iteration failure migrations[executed.Count] does point at the failing migration, but the commit case breaks it.
- **Fix:** Guard the index: `var failedMigration = executed.Count < migrations.Count ? migrations[executed.Count] : migrations[migrations.Count - 1];` (or fall back to the last executed migration), so the catch never throws.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.MongoDB\MongoMigrationRunner.cs. The catch block at line 99 computes `failedMigration = executed.Count > 0 ? migrations[executed.Count] : migrations[0]`. `migrations` is an `IReadOnlyList<IMigration>` (from GetMigrationsToExecute), so `migrations[executed.Count]` is a real indexer that throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException when the index is out of range.

Trace of the failure paths:
- In the foreach (lines 66-85), `executed.Add(...)` runs at the END of each iteration (line 84). So if migration i throws during Up/Down/Record, executed.Count == i and migrations[executed.Count] correctly points at the failing migration.
- BUT `session?.CommitTransaction()` is at line 87, AFTER the loop. If the commit throws (a realistic failure on a replica set transaction), the loop already completed all iterations, so executed.Count == migrations.Count. Then migrations[executed.Count] indexes one past the end → ArgumentOutOfRangeException thrown from within the catch handler.

Consequences exactly as described: the original exception `ex` is never wrapped (the intended MigrationException at line 100 is never constructed because the index access on line 99 throws first), and the caller sees a misleading ArgumentOutOfRangeException instead of the real commit failure. The diagnosis, line number, and severity (high) are all accurate. A safe fix is to clamp the index, e.g. `migrations[Math.Min(executed.Count, migrations.Count - 1)]`, or to track the in-flight migration explicitly, or to wrap with a null/sentinel when the failure occurred post-loop.

### CR-H064 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB
- **Title:** CollectionExists always returns true
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB\Context/RavenDBSchemaBuilder.cs:39-48`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — now sends GetCollectionStatisticsOperation and returns whether the named collection actually has documents, instead of discarding the query and unconditionally returning true.
- **Detail:** Builds a query with Statistics(out var stats).Take(1) but discards both the result and stats, then unconditionally returns true. The 'name' parameter is never used, and the query is not even scoped to the collection. Any caller relying on this to branch (e.g. 'create only if missing') gets wrong behavior.
- **Fix:** Scope a query to the collection (DocumentQuery<dynamic>(name)) and return stats.TotalResults > 0, or query collection statistics via Maintenance. At minimum use the result instead of returning a constant.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB\Context\RavenDBSchemaBuilder.cs lines 39-48. The CollectionExists(string name) method opens a session, builds a query `session.Query<dynamic>().Statistics(out var stats).Take(1).ToList()`, then unconditionally `return true;`.

Every claim in the finding holds:
1. The query result (`count`) is computed but never inspected — the method always returns true regardless of outcome.
2. `stats` (from Statistics(out var stats)) is captured but never used (would surface a CS0219 'assigned but never used' style warning / unused variable; the result list is also unused).
3. The `name` parameter is never referenced — the query is `Query<dynamic>()` over all documents, not scoped to the collection `name` (e.g. no `.Collection(name)` or `FROM 'name'`). So even if the result were checked, it would test whether ANY document exists in the DB, not whether the named collection exists.
4. Any caller using this for conditional logic (create-if-missing, drop-if-exists) gets incorrect behavior — it will always treat every collection as existing.

This is a genuine, actionable correctness bug. The correct implementation should scope the count to the collection (e.g. via RavenDB's CollectionStatistics from `_store.Maintenance.Send(new GetCollectionStatisticsOperation())` checking `Collections.ContainsKey(name)`, or a collection-scoped query) and return based on whether documents/the collection exist. Note: RavenDB collections are implicit (only exist once a document is inserted), so a count-based check is a reasonable approach, but it must actually be scoped to `name` and its result must drive the return value. The dead `using var session` block and discarded results confirm the logic was never finished.

### CR-H065 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB
- **Title:** BulkInsert never targets the requested collection
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.RavenDB\Context/RavenDBDataMigrator.cs:89-99`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — each dictionary is now stored with @collection metadata (MetadataAsDictionary) set to the requested collection, so documents land in and are queryable under that collection rather than a generic type-derived one.
- **Detail:** bulkInsert.Store(doc) is called with an IDictionary<string,object> and no id/metadata, and the 'collection' parameter is never used. RavenDB derives the collection from the document's CLR type (or @collection metadata); storing a raw dictionary lands the documents in a generic/dictionary collection, not the caller-specified 'collection'. Documents migrated this way are unqueryable under the intended collection name.
- **Fix:** Set the @collection metadata (or pass an explicit id like $"{collection}/") on each Store call so documents land in the requested collection.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading Context/RavenDBDataMigrator.cs:89-99. The BulkInsert method signature takes a `string collection` parameter but never references it anywhere in the body. It calls `bulkInsert.Store(doc)` where `doc` is an `IDictionary<string,object>` (concretely a Dictionary), using the no-id/no-metadata overload. RavenDB derives a document's collection from the entity's CLR type (via Conventions.GetCollectionName) or from the `@collection` metadata; neither is supplied here, so documents land in a generic dictionary-derived collection rather than the caller-specified `collection`. They are therefore unqueryable under the intended collection name. The bug is corroborated by the rest of the same file: every sibling method (UpdateDocuments line 30, DeleteDocuments line 44, CountDocuments line 57, CopyData line 76) consistently uses the `collection`/`sourceCollection` parameter to scope its operation — BulkInsert is the sole outlier that drops it, indicating an oversight rather than intentional behavior. The fix would be to set the @collection metadata (e.g. the Store(entity, id, MetadataAsDictionary) overload with `@collection` = collection, or a BulkInsertOperation collection option). High severity is justified: the documented purpose is migrating documents into a named collection, and this silently fails that contract.

### CR-H067 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.SQL
- **Title:** Migration-record write runs on a separate connection/transaction from the migration DDL
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.SQL\SqlMigrationRunner.cs:74,147`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — already fixed: the internal `RecordMigration(DbConnection, DbTransaction?, IMigration)` / `RemoveMigration(...)` overloads are `internal` (not private) and `UpdateStoreRecord` calls them with the runner's own connection+transaction, so the version-row write enlists in the DDL transaction and commits/rolls back atomically. Added SQL migration tests confirm the transactional path. No code change needed.
- **Detail:** ExecuteWithTransaction runs each migration's DDL on the runner's own `connection`+`transaction`, then calls UpdateStoreRecord -> store.RecordMigration(migration). The store's public RecordMigration(IMigration) (SqlMigrationStore.cs:110-126) opens a BRAND NEW DbConnection from the factory and its OWN BeginTransaction/Commit. So the migration-applied row is committed independently of the runner's transaction. If a later migration in the same batch fails and the outer transaction rolls back, the already-recorded version rows persist -> the migrations table claims migrations are applied that were rolled back (inconsistent state). The connection/transaction-taking overloads RecordMigration(connection, transaction, migration) exist but are private, so the runner cannot enlist the record write into its DDL transaction.
- **Fix:** Expose the connection+transaction overloads of RecordMigration/RemoveMigration (or accept an external transaction) and have UpdateStoreRecord pass the runner's connection+transaction so the version row commits/rolls back atomically with the DDL.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading both cited files in full.

SqlMigrationRunner.ExecuteWithTransaction (lines 57-95) opens the runner's own connection (line 44) and a transaction (line 64). For each migration it runs the DDL on that connection/transaction (line 73 -> ExecuteSingleMigration, which builds SqlMigrationContext with the runner's connection+transaction), then calls UpdateStoreRecord (line 74).

UpdateStoreRecord (lines 138-153) takes `connection` and `transaction` parameters but never uses them — on the Up path (line 147) it calls `store.RecordMigration(migration)`, the public single-arg overload.

SqlMigrationStore.RecordMigration(IMigration) (lines 110-126) opens a BRAND NEW connection via `_connectionFactory()` (line 112) and creates+commits its OWN transaction (lines 115-119). The factory is `() => connector.CreateConnection(connector.Settings)` (runner line 25), and CreateConnection returns a fresh DbConnection each call, so this is genuinely independent of the runner's transaction. Thus the migrations-table row is committed immediately, before the runner commits its DDL at line 78.

Consequence is real: if a later migration in the batch throws, the runner's transaction.Rollback() (line 85) undoes the rolled-back migrations' DDL, but the already-committed record rows for earlier (and even the failed migration's predecessors) persist. The migrations table then claims migrations are applied whose DDL was rolled back — exactly the inconsistent state described. The same defect applies symmetrically to RemoveMigration on the Down path (line 151).

The transaction-enlisting overloads do exist (RecordMigration/RemoveMigration with (DbConnection, DbTransaction, IMigration) at lines 329, 363) and correctly set command.Transaction, but they are `private`, so the runner cannot enlist its DDL transaction — confirming that last claim too.

Note: this only bites when UseTransaction is true (the ExecuteWithoutTransaction path has no atomicity promise anyway). Since UseTransaction is the path that explicitly promises atomic rollback ("Changes have been rolled back", line 93), the defect directly undermines the guarantee the code advertises. High severity is justified. Every specific claim in the finding (line numbers, private overloads, independent commit, inconsistent-state outcome) checks out against the code.

### CR-H069 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB
- **Title:** Runner override drops the connector when building the TimescaleDB context
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB\TimescaleDBMigrationRunner.cs:32`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — exposed `protected AbstractConnector Connector` on `SqlMigrationRunner` and changed the TimescaleDB override to `new TimescaleDBMigrationContext(connection, transaction, Connector)`, so `context.Schema` uses the PostgreSQL connector (dialect-correct DDL / DropTable) instead of the generic SQL fallback.
- **Detail:** ExecuteSingleMigration constructs `new TimescaleDBMigrationContext(connection, transaction)` and never passes the connector, even though the base SqlMigrationRunner.ExecuteSingleMigration (SqlMigrationRunner.cs:131) passes `_connector` into its SqlMigrationContext, and TimescaleDBMigrationContext's constructor accepts a `connector` parameter (TimescaleDBMigrationContext.cs:13). The connector is functionally significant: when present, SqlSchemaBuilder.DropCollection delegates to `_connector.DropTable(...)` and CreateCollection/CreateIndex pass the connector through for correct PostgreSQL-dialect SQL generation (SqlSchemaBuilder.cs:26,31-39,56). By dropping it, any TimescaleDB migration that uses context.Schema falls back to the generic SQL path instead of the PostgreSQL connector — defeating the entire reason this provider-specific runner exists.
- **Fix:** The runner needs access to the connector. The base SqlMigrationRunner keeps `_connector` private; expose it (protected getter/field) and pass it: `new TimescaleDBMigrationContext(connection, transaction, connector)`.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading all cited files. TimescaleDBMigrationRunner.cs:32 constructs `new TimescaleDBMigrationContext(connection, transaction)` and omits the connector argument, so it defaults to null. The base SqlMigrationRunner.ExecuteSingleMigration (SqlMigrationRunner.cs:131) does pass `_connector` into its SqlMigrationContext. TimescaleDBMigrationContext (Context/TimescaleDBMigrationContext.cs:13) accepts an optional `AbstractConnector? connector` and forwards it to base. SqlMigrationContext.cs:33 forwards that connector into SqlSchemaBuilder. SqlSchemaBuilder.cs confirms the connector is functionally significant: DropCollection (line 31-34), CreateCollection→SqlCollectionBuilder.Build (213-222), CreateIndex→SqlIndexBuilder.Build (305-318), AddField/DropField/DropIndex/QuoteIdentifier all branch on `_connector != null` and use connector-driven (PostgreSQL-dialect) SQL when present, falling back to generic raw SQL otherwise. So any TimescaleDB migration using context.Schema silently falls back to the generic SQL path instead of the PostgreSQL connector — defeating the purpose of the provider-specific runner. The finding is accurate and actionable.

One important fix-detail (not a refutation): the base field `_connector` is `private readonly` (SqlMigrationRunner.cs:16) with no protected accessor, so the override currently has no way to reference the connector instance it was constructed with — which is almost certainly why the bug exists. A correct fix requires exposing the connector from the base (e.g. a `protected` field/property) and then passing it through. Severity "high" is defensible since it silently degrades the provider behavior, though it degrades to a working generic-SQL fallback rather than throwing.

### CR-H070 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB
- **Title:** AddCompressionPolicy hardcodes compress_orderby='time' and compress_segmentby='device_id'
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB\TimescaleDBMigration.cs:62-74`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `AddCompressionPolicy` gained optional `orderByColumn` (default `"time"`) and `segmentByColumn` (default null) parameters; the SQL is built by an extracted `internal static BuildCompressionPolicySql(...)` that omits the `compress_segmentby` line entirely when no segment column is supplied — no more hardcoded `device_id`. Covered by offline SQL-generation tests.
- **Detail:** The method signature `AddCompressionPolicy(context, tableName, compressAfterInterval)` advertises that it works for any hypertable, but the body hardcodes `timescaledb.compress_orderby = 'time'` and `timescaledb.compress_segmentby = 'device_id'`. Any table that lacks a column literally named `device_id` (or whose natural order column is not `time`) will fail at runtime, and even when columns exist the segmentby choice is silently wrong for most schemas. This is a latent failure that only surfaces when the migration runs against a real table.
- **Fix:** Add `orderByColumn` and `segmentByColumn` parameters (optional, defaulting to the time column / empty), and omit the compress_segmentby line when no segment column is supplied.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB\TimescaleDBMigration.cs. The method AddCompressionPolicy (line 62) has a generic, table-agnostic signature (context, tableName, compressAfterInterval) and is a protected virtual helper in an abstract base documented as reusable for "any hypertable." Yet lines 65-72 hardcode `timescaledb.compress_orderby = 'time'` and `timescaledb.compress_segmentby = 'device_id'` directly in the SQL. Any hypertable lacking a `device_id` column (or whose time column is not literally `time`) will fail at ALTER TABLE / add_compression_policy execution. This is reinforced by CreateHypertable (line 40) accepting an arbitrary timeColumnName, so the class itself supports non-`time` time columns that this helper then cannot compress. The failure is latent (runtime DDL error, no compile-time signal) and the segmentby choice is silently wrong for most schemas. No tests exist (no test files found) and no other caller overrides these values. The fix is to parameterize orderby/segmentby columns. Caveat: the method is virtual so a subclass could override it, but that does not change the fact that the advertised reusable helper produces invalid/wrong DDL out of the box — the finding remains real and high severity.

### CR-H071 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB
- **Title:** CreateContinuousAggregate produces a trailing comma in GROUP BY when groupByClause is empty
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB\TimescaleDBMigration.cs:109-123`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the GROUP BY now reuses the guarded `groupBySql` (`GROUP BY bucket{groupBySql}`), so an empty `groupByClause` emits valid `GROUP BY bucket` with no dangling comma. SQL is built by an extracted `internal static BuildContinuousAggregateSql(...)`; offline tests assert both the empty and populated group-by paths.
- **Detail:** `groupByClause` defaults to "". When empty, line 121 emits `GROUP BY bucket, ` with a dangling comma (the `{groupByClause}` interpolation contributes nothing after the comma), which is a SQL syntax error. The SELECT side is handled correctly (groupBySql guards the leading comma), but the GROUP BY side does not — so the documented default-parameter path always generates invalid SQL.
- **Fix:** Build the GROUP BY the same guarded way: `var groupByTail = string.IsNullOrEmpty(groupByClause) ? "" : $", {groupByClause}";` then `GROUP BY bucket{groupByTail}`.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Migrations.TimescaleDB\TimescaleDBMigration.cs lines 109-123. The method CreateContinuousAggregate declares `string groupByClause = ""` (default empty). Line 112 builds a correctly-guarded `groupBySql = string.IsNullOrEmpty(groupByClause) ? "" : $", {groupByClause}"`, and the SELECT side (line 118) uses that guarded `{groupBySql}`. However, the GROUP BY on line 121 uses the RAW unguarded variable: `GROUP BY bucket, {groupByClause};`. When groupByClause is the default empty string, this interpolates to `GROUP BY bucket, ;` — a dangling trailing comma that PostgreSQL/TimescaleDB rejects as a syntax error. The default-parameter path (a continuous aggregate with only a time bucket plus aggregate columns and no extra grouping) is a normal, supported usage, so the documented default always emits invalid SQL. The fix is to reuse `groupBySql` on line 121 (`GROUP BY bucket{groupBySql};`). The finding's description matches the code exactly, including the observation that the SELECT side is correct while the GROUP BY side is not. Note: this is a code-quality/correctness bug; the underlying string interpolation also reflects a broader pattern of raw SQL interpolation, but that is out of scope for this specific finding which is genuinely real and actionable.

- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.MongoDB\Stores/MongoDBStore.cs:385-391 (and Stores/AsyncMongoDBStore.cs:483-490)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — extracted a shared `ChangeStreamDocumentKeyResolver` (used by both `MongoDBStore` and `AsyncMongoDBStore`) that (1) returns a native BSON-Guid `_id`, (2) parses a string `_id` back to a Guid, and (3) falls back to `FullDocument.Guid` when `_id` is not the Guid (the canonical `MongoDBModel` case where `_id` is an auto-generated ObjectId). Empty Guids are treated as absent. 8 offline resolver tests added. Note: a delete event on an ObjectId-keyed model still cannot recover the Guid (no full document is delivered) — an inherent mapping limitation, out of scope here.
- **Detail:** MapChangeStreamDocument reads change.DocumentKey["_id"] and only sets evt.DocumentKey when idValue.IsGuid is true. But MongoDBModel.Guid is mapped with [BsonRepresentation(BsonType.String)] (Models/MongoDBModel.cs:12), so _id is stored as a BSON string, not a BSON Guid. idValue will be a BsonString, IsGuid returns false, and DocumentKey stays null. The sync MongoDBStore is constrained to T : MongoDBModel, so its change-stream events ALWAYS have a null DocumentKey; the async store has the same problem for any model using the canonical String representation. ChangeStreamEvent.DocumentKey is effectively dead for the framework's own model type.
- **Fix:** Handle the string case: if idValue.IsString and Guid.TryParse(idValue.AsString, out var g) set DocumentKey = g; keep the IsGuid branch for binary-represented models. A change-stream test that asserts DocumentKey is set would have caught this.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. Both MongoDBStore.cs:385-391 and AsyncMongoDBStore.cs:483-490 contain identical MapChangeStreamDocument logic: `var idValue = change.DocumentKey["_id"]; if (idValue.IsGuid) { evt.DocumentKey = idValue.AsGuid; }`. evt.DocumentKey is only ever set when idValue.IsGuid is true.

MongoDBModel.cs:12-13 confirms `[BsonRepresentation(BsonType.String)]` on the Guid property. ChangeStreamEvent.cs:44 confirms DocumentKey is Guid?. MongoDBStore<T> is constrained `where T : Models.MongoDBModel` and AsyncMongoDBStore<T> `where T : AbstractModel`, matching the finding.

The bug is actually worse than stated: a project-wide grep found NO [BsonId] attribute, NO convention pack/registry, and NO class-map registration anywhere. The id property is named `Guid` (AbstractModel.Guid), not `Id`, so the MongoDB driver serializes it as an ordinary field named `Guid` and auto-generates an ObjectId for `_id`. Thus change.DocumentKey["_id"] is an ObjectId whose IsGuid is unconditionally false. Even if [BsonId] were added, the String representation would make _id a BsonString, whose IsGuid/AsGuid only succeed for native BSON binary-subtype Guids — also false. So evt.DocumentKey is null in every realistic case, making ChangeStreamEvent.DocumentKey dead for the framework's own model type. The README example (Key: {change.DocumentKey}) would always print empty. High severity is justified; the finding is genuine and actionable (fix: parse the BsonString back to a Guid, or read the document key field that actually holds the value).
