### CR-H074 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Patterns
- **Title:** RuleSpecification.IsSatisfiedBy uses `new` not `override`, so interface callers get the wrong evaluator
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Patterns\Specification/RuleSpecification.cs:41`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — made `Specification<T>.IsSatisfiedBy` `virtual` and changed `RuleSpecification<T>.IsSatisfiedBy` from `new` to `override`, so every reference type (ISpecification&lt;T&gt;, Specification&lt;T&gt;, concrete) dispatches to the RuleEvaluator as documented. New `Birko.Data.Patterns.Tests` proves the interface/base references no longer fall through to the compiled-expression path (which NREs on a null member where the evaluator null-guards). Combinator composition remains expression-based by design (out of scope).
- **Detail:** Base Specification<T>.IsSatisfiedBy (Specification.cs:21) is a non-virtual public method that uses the compiled LINQ expression. RuleSpecification declares `public new bool IsSatisfiedBy(T entity)` to use the RuleEvaluator instead (the XML doc says 'Override to use RuleEvaluator ... more accurate than compiled expression for complex types'). Because it is `new`, not an override, the choice is bound at compile time by the static type. Any caller holding an ISpecification<T> or Specification<T> reference (the documented, common case — e.g. specs combined via And/Or/Not, or stored in collections) invokes the BASE compiled-expression path, silently bypassing the rule evaluator. The two paths can disagree (the expression path lacks null-guarding and uses Convert.ChangeType, the evaluator does not), so the same spec yields different results depending on the reference type used to call it.
- **Fix:** Make base Specification<T>.IsSatisfiedBy virtual and change RuleSpecification to `public override bool IsSatisfiedBy(...)`. Then all reference types dispatch to the rule-evaluator implementation as documented.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. Specification.cs:21 declares `public bool IsSatisfiedBy(T entity)` — non-virtual, using the compiled LINQ expression (`ToExpression().Compile()`). RuleSpecification.cs:41 declares `public new bool IsSatisfiedBy(T entity)` (method hiding, NOT override) which uses the RuleEvaluator via ObjectRuleContext. The XML doc on line 38-40 even says "Override to use RuleEvaluator", confirming the author's intent was polymorphic dispatch but `new` does not provide it.

Because the base method is non-virtual and the derived one hides it with `new`, dispatch is bound at compile time by the static reference type. ISpecification<T>.IsSatisfiedBy (interface, line 18) and Specification<T>.IsSatisfiedBy (base) both route any caller holding those reference types to the base compiled-expression path, silently bypassing the evaluator. The combinators reinforce this: AndSpecification stores `ISpecification<T> _left/_right` and composes via `ToExpression()`, so combining a RuleSpecification into And/Or/Not permanently discards the evaluator path. Collections typed as ISpecification<T> (the documented common case) hit the base path too.

The two paths genuinely can disagree: the expression path uses Convert.ChangeType (lines 117, 123-124) and lacks null-guarding, while the evaluator uses a different mechanism — so the same spec object yields different results depending on the reference type used to invoke it. This is a real, classic `new`-vs-`override` correctness bug. Note the cited fix ('use override') would not compile as-is since the base isn't virtual — the proper fix is to make Specification<T>.IsSatisfiedBy virtual and override it — but the finding's diagnosis of the defect and its impact is accurate and high severity is justified.

### CR-H075 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Patterns
- **Title:** AsyncSluggableBulkStoreWrapper.UpdateAsync resolves slugs in parallel against a shared store
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Patterns\Decorators/AsyncSluggableBulkStoreWrapper.cs:42`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — rewrote `UpdateAsync` as a sequential `foreach` with a shared `batchSlugs` set (mirroring `CreateAsync`), materializing the source once. This removes the concurrent `ReadAsync` calls against the shared inner store (unsafe for connection-stateful backends), restores per-batch slug uniqueness, and drops the faulted-antecedent `ContinueWith/Unwrap`. Covered by new `AsyncSluggableBulkStoreWrapperTests` (concurrency probe, duplicate-source batch tracking, single-enumeration).
- **Detail:** UpdateAsync runs `Task.WhenAll(data.Select(async item => await ResolveSlugAsync(item, item.Guid, ct)))`, firing all ResolveSlugAsync calls concurrently. Each ResolveSlugAsync issues `_innerStore.ReadAsync(...)` against the same inner store instance. Most Birko stores (SQL connectors, file-based JSON/XML) are NOT safe for concurrent operations on one instance — this can corrupt connection/reader state or throw 'connection already open'. It also drops the per-batch uniqueness tracking that the sync version and CreateAsync use (no shared batchSlugs HashSet), so two updated rows whose sources normalize to the same base slug can both receive the identical slug. The `.ContinueWith(...).Unwrap()` shape additionally risks running the continuation on a faulted antecedent. Make this a sequential foreach with a shared batchSlugs set, mirroring CreateAsync/Update sync.
- **Fix:** Rewrite as: `var batch = new HashSet<string>(StringComparer.OrdinalIgnoreCase); foreach (var item in data) { await ResolveSlugAsync(item, item.Guid, batch, ct); batch.Add(item.Slug!); } await _innerStore.UpdateAsync(data, storeDelegate, ct);` (and materialize data once — see the enumeration finding).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Patterns\Decorators\AsyncSluggableBulkStoreWrapper.cs and the related files.

CONFIRMED claims:
1. Parallel execution against a shared store (line 42-45): `Task.WhenAll(data.Select(async item => await ResolveSlugAsync(item, item.Guid, ct: ct)))` fires every ResolveSlugAsync concurrently. ResolveSlugAsync (AsyncSluggableStoreWrapper.cs:78) issues `_innerStore.ReadAsync(...)` against the single shared inner store. This wrapper is a transparent decorator placed over arbitrary backends (constraint `TStore : IAsyncBulkStore<T>`), including SQL connectors and file-based JSON/XML stores that are not safe for concurrent operations on one instance. Every other async path in these wrappers (bulk CreateAsync, single CreateAsync/UpdateAsync) uses sequential `await`; this UpdateAsync is the lone parallel outlier. Real, high-severity concern.
2. `.ContinueWith(_ => _innerStore.UpdateAsync(...)).Unwrap()` (line 45) uses no TaskContinuationOptions, so the continuation runs even if the slug-resolution antecedent faulted/cancelled — the inner store update fires regardless and Unwrap surfaces the inner task, obscuring/swallowing the antecedent exception. Genuine antipattern; a plain `await Task.WhenAll(...)` would propagate failures correctly.
3. Missing shared batchSlugs set on update (line 44 passes no batchSlugs, unlike CreateAsync at lines 29-34). The gap is real.

INACCURACY in the finding (does not change the verdict): it claims the fix should mirror "the sync version and CreateAsync" use of batchSlugs, but the SYNC bulk Update (SluggableBulkStoreWrapper.cs:34-39) also does NOT pass batchSlugs — only Create/CreateAsync do. So the batch-tracking omission is not a regression vs. the sync path; both updates lack it. The recommended sequential-foreach-with-shared-set fix is still sound and is the right way to also eliminate the concurrency hazard.

Net: the two core defects (concurrent ReadAsync against one inner store from a transparent decorator, and the faulted-antecedent ContinueWith/Unwrap shape) are real, confirmed, and actionable; high severity is justified because the decorator can wrap connection-stateful backends. Line citation (42) is accurate.

### CR-H076 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Processors
- **Title:** Zip Slip: extracted path built from untrusted entry.FullName
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Processors\Transport/ZipProcessor.cs:129`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `ExtractFirstEntry` now flattens the entry to `Path.GetFileName(entry.FullName)` (neutralizing `../` and rooted paths so the write can only land in `_extractPath`), rejects entries with no file name, and verifies the resolved full path stays under the canonicalized extract directory as defense in depth. New `ZipProcessorZipSlipTests` feed `../pwned.txt` / rooted / normal entry names.
- **Detail:** ExtractFirstEntry does var extractedFile = Path.Combine(_extractPath, entry.FullName); entry.ExtractToFile(extractedFile, overwrite: true);. entry.FullName comes from the (potentially attacker-controlled) ZIP and can contain '../' segments or a rooted/absolute path. Path.Combine with a rooted second argument discards _extractPath entirely, and '../..' segments let the write escape the extract directory. A malicious archive can overwrite arbitrary files (classic Zip Slip). Since the inner file is later opened and processed, this is reachable in the normal flow.
- **Fix:** Resolve the full path and verify it stays under _extractPath, e.g. var destDir = Path.GetFullPath(_extractPath); var full = Path.GetFullPath(Path.Combine(destDir, entry.FullName)); if (!full.StartsWith(destDir + Path.DirectorySeparatorChar, StringComparison.Ordinal)) throw new ProcessorException(...). Prefer extracting to a sanitized flat name (e.g. Path.GetFileName(entry.FullName)).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Processors\Transport\ZipProcessor.cs. Line 128-130 of ExtractFirstEntry does exactly: var entry = archive.Entries[EntryIndex]; var extractedFile = Path.Combine(_extractPath, entry.FullName); entry.ExtractToFile(extractedFile, overwrite: true). entry.FullName is the raw path from the ZIP central directory and is fully attacker-controlled.

Both technical claims hold:
1. Path.Combine with a rooted/absolute second argument discards the first path entirely (documented .NET behavior), so entry.FullName = "C:\\Windows\\System32\\..." would write outside _extractPath.
2. Path.Combine does NOT normalize ".." segments; they are resolved by the filesystem when ExtractToFile opens the path, so entry.FullName containing "../../" escapes the extract directory.

There is no sanitization anywhere in the method: no Path.GetFullPath canonicalization, no StartsWith(_extractPath) containment check, no rejection of rooted paths or ".." segments. overwrite: true means existing files are clobbered. The flow is reachable through Process/ProcessStream/ProcessStreamAsync (all call ExtractFirstEntry), and the extracted file is subsequently opened, so the malicious archive is processed in the normal path.

The only nuance vs a full-extract Zip Slip is that this extracts a single entry (EntryIndex, default 0) rather than iterating all entries, but a single crafted entry name is sufficient to overwrite an arbitrary file. This is a genuine, accurately-located, actionable high-severity Zip Slip vulnerability.

### CR-H077 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.RavenDB
- **Title:** Public Read(Guid)/Read()/ReadAsync(Guid) overrides bypass lazy-init
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.RavenDB\Stores/RavenDBStore.cs:157,171 and Stores/AsyncRavenDBStore.cs:164`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the public `Read(Guid)`, `Read()` (sync) and `ReadAsync(Guid)` (async) overrides now call `EnsureInitialized()` / `await EnsureInitializedAsync(ct)` at the top before the load-by-id/query fast path, so a read as the first operation still runs `InitCore`/`InitCoreAsync` (database creation) and the async path observes an already-cancelled token. The load-by-id optimization is preserved. New `RavenDBStoreLazyInitTests` (offline, InitCore-probe subclasses) confirm all three read paths initialize and the async path throws on cancellation.
- **Detail:** The framework convention is that concrete stores override only the protected *Core methods so the base public CRUD wrappers can run EnsureInitialized/EnsureInitializedAsync first. These stores instead override the PUBLIC methods directly: RavenDBStore.Read(Guid) (157), RavenDBStore.Read() (171), and AsyncRavenDBStore.ReadAsync(Guid) (164). The base implementations route these through Read(filter)/ReadAsync(filter), which call EnsureInitialized(). By overriding the public methods the stores skip that gate, so InitCore/InitCoreAsync (which calls EnsureDatabaseExists() to create the database) never runs when one of these is the first operation invoked on a freshly-constructed-and-SetSettings'd store. Result: a Read against a database that was never created. The async override additionally skips the EnsureInitializedAsync(ct) cancellation gate, so an already-cancelled token is not observed.
- **Fix:** Remove the public overrides. RavenDBStore.Read(Guid) can be expressed by overriding the existing single-result path or by keeping a Guid optimization inside ReadCore. If a Guid fast-path (session.Load by id) is desired, route it through a protected helper invoked after EnsureInitialized, e.g. keep public Read(Guid) calling base then delegating, or override ReadCore to special-case the ModelByGuid filter. Do not override public Read().
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified against actual source in both the RavenDB project and the base Birko.Data.Stores hierarchy.

Cited overrides exist and bypass the init gate:
- RavenDBStore.cs:157 `public override T? Read(Guid guid)` queries `_documentStore.OpenSession()` directly; no EnsureInitialized.
- RavenDBStore.cs:171 `public override IEnumerable<T> Read()` queries directly; no EnsureInitialized.
- AsyncRavenDBStore.cs:164 `public override Task<T?> ReadAsync(Guid guid, ...)` opens an async session directly; no EnsureInitializedAsync and no cancellation check.

Base implementations confirm the convention these overrides defeat:
- AbstractStore.Read(Guid) (line 79-82) delegates to Read(filter), which calls EnsureInitialized() then ReadCore (lines 67-71).
- AbstractBulkStore.Read() (line 43-46) delegates to Read(null,null,null,null), whose body calls EnsureInitialized() (lines 31-35).
- AbstractAsyncStore.ReadAsync(Guid) (line 84-87) delegates to ReadAsync(filter), which awaits EnsureInitializedAsync(ct) (lines 90-92). EnsureInitializedAsync (lines 33-50) calls ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() up front before the _initialized short-circuit.

Consequence is real: InitCore() / InitCoreAsync() call EnsureDatabaseExists(), which issues CreateDatabaseOperation to create the database (RavenDBStore.cs:472-481, AsyncRavenDBStore.cs:574-583). If one of the three overridden methods is the first operation on a freshly-constructed-and-SetSettings'd store with a Database name configured, the database-creation gate never runs, so the read hits a database that was never created. The async override also skips the cancellation gate, so an already-cancelled token is not observed (deviates from the documented 2026-06-15 cancellation convention).

This is a genuine deviation from the documented *Core-override convention with a concrete correctness impact and an actionable fix (route the overrides through EnsureInitialized/EnsureInitializedAsync, e.g. by overriding ReadCore instead, or calling the gate at the top). Severity high is reasonable given the silent missing-database failure. Minor caveat: if no Database name is set, EnsureDatabaseExists is a no-op, so impact is limited to configurations with a named database — but that is the normal case.

### CR-H078 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.RavenDB.Views
- **Title:** Avg aggregate is incorrect under RavenDB re-reduce
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.RavenDB.Views\RavenViewTranslator.cs:200-203`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — implemented the re-reduce-safe average pattern: the map now emits a running `ViewProperty_Sum = value` (alongside the raw field and `ViewProperty_Count = 1`), and the reduce sums `_Sum` and `_Count` separately (both stable under re-reduce) and recomputes `ViewProperty = Sum(_Sum) / Sum(_Count)` each pass — it never re-sums the already-averaged field. Verified against the worked example ([10,20,30]+[5] → 16.25). Covered by new `RavenViewTranslatorTests` (Avg re-reduce shape + no `g.Sum(x => x.Average)`).
- **Detail:** The reduce for Avg computes `ViewProperty = g.Sum(x => x.ViewProperty) / g.Sum(x => x.ViewProperty_Count)`, but the map (line 98) emits the RAW value into `ViewProperty`, not a per-bucket sum. RavenDB map-reduce is tree/incremental: the reduce output is fed back into the reduce again (re-reduce). On the first reduce `ViewProperty` becomes the average; on re-reduce `g.Sum(x => x.ViewProperty)` then sums already-averaged partials and divides by the total count, yielding a wrong number. Count/Sum/Min/Max are re-reduce-safe (sum-of-sums, min-of-mins, max-of-maxes), but Avg is not. The correct pattern is to keep a re-reduce-stable running sum field separate from the exposed average: emit `ViewProperty_Sum = value` and `ViewProperty_Count = 1` in map, reduce both with Sum, and expose the average only as a computed/last-step value (or document Avg as unsupported).
- **Fix:** Carry a `ViewProperty_Sum` (Sum) and `ViewProperty_Count` (Sum) through every reduce pass and compute the ratio in the query projection, not inside the reduce; or drop Avg from the supported set and throw NotSupportedException.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. RavenViewTranslator.cs generates a real RavenDB map-reduce IndexDefinition (RavenViewManager.cs:47-60 builds Maps + Reduce and sends PutIndexesOperation), so RavenDB's incremental tree-based re-reduce semantics apply — the reduce output is fed back into the reduce, requiring the function to be re-reduce-stable.

Map phase: for Avg the map emits the RAW value into ViewProperty (line 98: `ViewProperty = sourceAlias.SourceProperty`) plus a helper `ViewProperty_Count = 1` (line 108).

Reduce phase (lines 200-203): `ViewProperty = g.Sum(x => x.ViewProperty) / g.Sum(x => x.ViewProperty_Count)`. This is correct only on the FIRST reduce, where ViewProperty still holds raw values. On re-reduce, the inputs are prior reduce outputs in which ViewProperty already holds an AVERAGE, not a sum — so summing averages and dividing by total count is wrong.

Worked example: values [10,20,30] reduce to {Avg=20, Count=3}; another value [5] reduces to {Avg=5, Count=1}; re-reduce yields (20+5)/(3+1)=6.25, but the true average of [10,20,30,5] is 65/4=16.25. Wrong.

Count/Sum/Min/Max (lines 195-209) ARE re-reduce safe (sum-of-sums, min-of-mins, max-of-maxes are idempotent); Avg is the unique offender, exactly as the finding states. The proposed fix (keep a re-reduce-stable running sum field like ViewProperty_Sum = value, reduce both Sum and Count with Sum, expose the average as a computed/last-step value) is the standard correct RavenDB map-reduce average pattern.

Minor caveat on visibility (not on validity): the bug only manifests once a group is large enough that RavenDB splits the reduce into a tree and re-reduces; small groups that fit a single reduce page return the correct first-reduce average, which can hide the defect in small-scale tests. But for production-scale grouping it silently produces wrong averages, so the high severity is justified. This is a genuine, actionable correctness bug at RavenViewTranslator.cs:200-203.

- **Status:** done — removed the `DestroyAsync` override entirely; `base.AbstractAsyncRepository.DestroyAsync` already destroys `Store`, and `BulkStore` is the same instance (`Store as IAsyncBulkStore<T>`), so the override destroyed one store twice. - **Detail:** AbstractAsyncBulkRepository.DestroyAsync first calls base.DestroyAsync(ct) (which does `await Store.DestroyAsync(ct)`), then calls `await BulkStore.DestroyAsync(ct)`. BulkStore is just `Store as IAsyncBulkStore<T>` (line 24) — the SAME object instance. IAsyncBulkStore<T> inherits IAsyncStore<T> and DestroyAsync is declared only once (IAsyncStore.cs:25), so this calls DestroyAsync twice on one store. For stores whose DestroyAsync is not idempotent (e.g. disposing a connection/closing a file twice), this can throw ObjectDisposedException or corrupt state.
- **Fix:** Drop the base call and just destroy once: override DestroyAsync to `if (BulkStore == null) { await base.DestroyAsync(ct); return; } await BulkStore.DestroyAsync(ct);` — or simply remove the override entirely, since base.DestroyAsync already destroys the underlying store and BulkStore is the same instance.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual code. AbstractAsyncBulkRepository.DestroyAsync (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Repositories\AbstractAsyncBulkRepository.cs:116-121) calls `await base.DestroyAsync(ct)` then `await BulkStore.DestroyAsync(ct)`. Confirmed each claim:

1. base.DestroyAsync (AbstractAsyncRepository.cs:123-127) does `await Store.DestroyAsync(ct)`.
2. BulkStore is `Store as IAsyncBulkStore<T>` (line 24) — the SAME object reference as Store (or null), never a distinct instance.
3. DestroyAsync is declared exactly once in the store interface hierarchy (Birko.Data.Stores/IAsyncStore.cs:25). IAsyncBulkStore<T> inherits IAsyncStore<T> (IAsyncBulkStore.cs:147) and does NOT redeclare DestroyAsync. So both call sites invoke the identical method on the identical instance.

Net effect: DestroyAsync is invoked twice on a single store instance. This is a genuine defect — the second call is pure redundancy at best, and unsafe for any non-idempotent DestroyAsync (closing a connection / deleting a file / disposing a resource twice → ObjectDisposedException or state corruption).

Corroborating evidence that this is unintended, not a deliberate design: the sync sibling AbstractBulkRepository<T> does NOT override Destroy() at all — it relies on the base AbstractRepository.Destroy() calling Store.Destroy() exactly once. Only the async bulk variant added this extra call, so the asymmetry points to a bug.

Caveat on severity: the finding rates it "high". The framework's own bundled stores happen to be idempotent here (e.g. AsyncJsonStore.DestroyAsync guards with File.Exists; InMemory just clears a dictionary), so the bundled backends would not currently throw. But the IAsyncStore contract does not promise idempotency, and a custom store that closes a connection or disposes a resource in DestroyAsync would break. The bug is real and actionable (the fix is to drop line 119-120, since base already destroys the same store); the realistic severity is closer to medium given the shipped backends, but it is unambiguously a genuine, actionable issue.

### CR-H081 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Repositories
- **Title:** RepositoryLocator reads/mutates a non-concurrent Dictionary outside the lock
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Repositories\RepositoryLocator.cs:49,78,108,123-140`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — moved the final cache read inside the `lock` in all three `GetRepository` overloads, and rewrote `Destroy<TRepository>` to mutate the dictionary under the lock (capturing the repository under the lock and calling its `Destroy()` outside to avoid holding the lock across external code). No more unlocked reads/mutations of the non-concurrent `Dictionary`. New `RepositoryLocatorConcurrencyTests` stress get+destroy across many threads and assert no throw + a single cached instance.
- **Detail:** The class doc claims 'Thread-safe singleton pattern', but all three GetRepository overloads do the final `return (TRepository)_repositories[id][type];` OUTSIDE the lock (lines 49, 78, 108), and Destroy<TRepository> mutates `_repositories` entirely outside the lock (lines 123-140). `_repositories` is a plain Dictionary (line 16), not a ConcurrentDictionary. A concurrent writer holding the lock (Add/resize, or Destroy's Remove) can run while another thread is doing an unlocked read/enumeration of the same Dictionary, which is undefined behavior — it can throw InvalidOperationException, return a torn value, or corrupt the bucket array. Destroy not taking the lock at all means it can race with a creating GetRepository.
- **Fix:** Take the final read inside the same lock block (assign to a local, return after). Wrap the entire body of Destroy<TRepository> in `lock (_lockObject)`. Alternatively switch `_repositories` to nested ConcurrentDictionary.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Repositories\RepositoryLocator.cs in full. Every cited detail is accurate:

- Line 16: `_repositories` is a plain `IDictionary` backed by `new Dictionary<...>()` (lines 38, 66, 97), not a ConcurrentDictionary.
- Lines 49, 78, 108: All three GetRepository overloads close the `lock (_lockObject)` block one line earlier (48/77/107) and then execute `return (TRepository)_repositories[id][type];` OUTSIDE the lock — an unlocked indexer read that walks the dictionary buckets.
- Lines 123-140: Destroy<TRepository> performs ContainsKey reads, indexer reads, two Remove() writes (lines 132, 136), and an Any() enumeration with NO lock whatsoever — concurrent reads AND writes of the shared dictionary outside any synchronization.
- Line 9 doc claims "Thread-safe singleton pattern", contradicting the actual code.

Mechanism is correct: System.Collections.Generic.Dictionary supports concurrent readers only when there are no concurrent writers. A locked GetRepository doing Add/resize can run while another thread does the unlocked return-read, and Destroy mutates with no lock at all and can race a creating GetRepository — classic undefined behavior (InvalidOperationException, torn value, or bucket-array corruption). The unlocked returns at 49/78/108 are exposed specifically to resize of the outer dictionary triggered by a different key's Add; Destroy racing any creator is unconditional and is the most severe instance. Genuine, actionable high-severity thread-safety bug; fix is straightforward (move returns inside the lock, wrap Destroy body in lock).

### CR-H082 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL
- **Title:** isLock serialization is broken for async commands — lock released before work runs
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL\SQL/Connectors/AbstractAsyncConnector.cs:37-44, 55-62`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — replaced the `Task.Run(() => { lock (_lock) { return RunCommandAsync(...); } })` construct (which released the monitor at the first await) with a `SemaphoreSlim(1,1)` held via `await WaitAsync(ct)` / `Release()` across the entire awaited DB operation in both `DoCommandAsync` and `DoCommandWithTransactionAsync`. Verified with a real-SQLite concurrency test (`DoCommandAsync_WithLock_SerializesConcurrentCommands`) that detects no overlap of the awaited work.
- **Detail:** DoCommandAsync/DoCommandWithTransactionAsync implement the isLock=true path as Task.Run(() => { lock(_lock) { return RunCommandAsync(...); } }, ct). RunCommandAsync returns a Task that has only STARTED the async work; the lambda returns that Task immediately, so the lock is exited the instant the synchronous portion (up to the first await) completes — long before the DB command actually executes. The intended mutual-exclusion (used by Insert/Update/Delete which all pass isLock=true) does not hold: concurrent callers can interleave their DB work despite holding the 'lock'. The sync counterpart in AbstractConnector.cs blocks correctly because RunCommand is fully synchronous.
- **Fix:** Make the locked async path actually await inside the critical section, e.g. use a SemaphoreSlim: await _asyncLock.WaitAsync(ct); try { await RunCommandAsync(...); } finally { _asyncLock.Release(); }. A monitor lock cannot span awaits.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL\SQL\Connectors\AbstractAsyncConnector.cs:29-63. Both DoCommandAsync (37-44) and DoCommandWithTransactionAsync (55-62) implement the isLock=true path as Task.Run(() => { lock(_lock) { return RunCommandAsync(...); } }, ct).

The diagnosis is technically correct:
1. RunCommandAsync (97-123) and RunCommandTransactionAsync (65-95) return ExecuteWithRetryAsync(async () => {...}, ct). ExecuteWithRetryAsync (AbstractConnectorBase.cs:76-98) is async and immediately awaits action() (which awaits db.OpenAsync, command execution, and Task.Delay on retry). It therefore returns an INCOMPLETE Task as soon as the first await is reached.
2. Inside the lambda, lock(_lock) wraps only the call that produces this incomplete Task. The lambda returns the Task and the lock block exits immediately — the lock is released at the first await (db.OpenAsync), long before the DB command actually executes. The lock guards only the synchronous prefix (connection construction up to the first await), not the DB work.
3. lock cannot span an await by design, so this construct is fundamentally incapable of serializing the async operation. Task.Run's unwrapping affects only the Task returned to DoCommandAsync's caller; it does not extend the lexical lock scope.
4. The intended mutual exclusion is real: Insert/Update/Delete all pass isLock: true (confirmed positionally — AbstractAsyncConnector_Insert.cs:88, _Update.cs:155, _Delete.cs:39), so concurrent callers can interleave DB work despite the lock.
5. The sync counterpart (AbstractConnector.cs:61-71, 98-108) is correct precisely because RunCommand/RunCommandTransaction are fully synchronous and complete inside the lock.

High-severity, actionable concurrency bug. A correct fix needs SemaphoreSlim.WaitAsync/Release around the awaited work rather than lock + Task.Run.

### CR-H083 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL
- **Title:** CancellationToken not propagated through async reader execution
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL\SQL/Connectors/AbstractAsyncConnector.cs:125-198`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — added `[EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct` to `RunReaderCommandAsync` (passed to `OpenAsync`/`ExecuteReaderAsync`/`ReadAsync`) and threaded an optional `CancellationToken` through every `SelectAsync` overload, `SelectAggregateAsync` (forwards its existing ct), and the `ReadCoreAsync` call sites in `AsyncDataBaseStore`/`AsyncDataBaseBulkStore`. A running streaming query is now cancellable. Verified with `SelectAsync_ObservesCancellation` (real SQLite, pre-cancelled token → `OperationCanceledException`).
- **Detail:** RunReaderCommandAsync takes no CancellationToken; internally it calls db.OpenAsync(), command.ExecuteReaderAsync(), and reader.ReadAsync() all without a token. Every async bulk read funnels through this method — AsyncDataBaseBulkStore.ReadCoreAsync (AsyncConnector.SelectAsync) and SelectAggregateAsync. So although the store/EnsureInitializedAsync gate observes the token before starting, the actual streaming query cannot be cancelled once running. The convention 'Async methods should observe CancellationToken' is violated for the hot read path.
- **Fix:** Thread a CancellationToken through SelectAsync → RunReaderCommandAsync and pass it to OpenAsync(ct), ExecuteReaderAsync(ct), and ReadAsync(ct). SelectAggregateAsync already has [EnumeratorCancellation] ct available to forward.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. RunReaderCommandAsync (AbstractAsyncConnector.cs:125) takes no CancellationToken and calls db.OpenAsync() (133), command.ExecuteReaderAsync() (150), and reader.ReadAsync() (164, 189) all without a token. This is the single chokepoint for every async SQL read.

Most damning: SelectAggregateAsync (AbstractAsyncConnector_Aggregate.cs:15-18) explicitly declares `[EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken ct`, and AsyncDataBaseBulkStore.cs:232 passes ct into it — but at line 26 it calls RunReaderCommandAsync WITHOUT forwarding ct. The token is accepted at the public API and store level, then silently dropped at the reader execution layer. So once the streaming query starts, it cannot be cancelled despite the caller supplying a live token. That is a genuine contract violation, not just a stylistic gap.

The inconsistency is internal to the same file: sibling methods RunCommandAsync (97) and RunCommandTransactionAsync (65) DO accept and propagate ct (OpenAsync(ct), BeginTransactionAsync(ct), ExecuteWithRetryAsync(..., ct)). The reader path is the lone outlier.

The fix is concrete and actionable: add [EnumeratorCancellation] CancellationToken to RunReaderCommandAsync and pass it to OpenAsync/ExecuteReaderAsync/ReadAsync, then thread ct from SelectAggregateAsync (already has it) and from the SelectAsync overloads (which currently don't accept one).

Minor caveat that does not negate the finding: the plain SelectAsync/ReadCoreAsync path never accepts a token anywhere in the chain (ReadCoreAsync:61 calls SelectAsync without ct, and SelectAsync has no ct parameter), so for that path it is 'never threaded' rather than 'dropped after being passed.' But the aggregate path demonstrably accepts-then-drops, and CLAUDE.md's stated convention that async methods observe CancellationToken is violated on the hot read path. Severity high is reasonable given an uncancellable long-running streaming query is exactly the scenario cancellation exists for.

### CR-H086 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql
- **Title:** DbType.DateTime / DbType.Time map to SQL DATE (truncates time component)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql\Database/Connector/MSSqlConnector.cs:127-130`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `MSSqlConnector.ConvertType` now maps `DbType.Date` → `DATE`, `DbType.Time` → `TIME`, and `DbType.DateTime`/`DbType.DateTime2` → `DATETIME2` (SQL Server's full-precision type), so DateTime columns no longer truncate time-of-day. New `Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql.Tests` (offline `ConvertType` mapping tests) pins all four; registered in the solution + workspace.
- **Detail:** ConvertType maps DbType.Time, DbType.Date AND DbType.DateTime all to "DATE". A DateTime field therefore gets a DATE column, which silently discards the time-of-day on write, and a Time field also becomes DATE. The sibling MySQLConnector correctly maps DbType.DateTime/DateTime2 to DATETIME and DbType.Time to TIME. This is a data-loss correctness bug for any timestamped entity (ITimestamped models, audit fields).
- **Fix:** Map DbType.Date -> DATE, DbType.Time -> TIME, DbType.DateTime -> DATETIME2 (SQL Server's full-precision type). Keep DbType.DateTime2 -> DATETIME2.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. MSSqlConnector.ConvertType (MSSqlConnector.cs:127-130) maps DbType.Time, DbType.Date, AND DbType.DateTime all to "DATE". SQL Server's DATE type stores only year/month/day with no time component, so a DateTime column created via this mapping silently truncates time-of-day to midnight, and a Time field also becomes a DATE column (wrong type entirely).

The full chain is verified:
- AbstractField.cs:172-176: every DateTime / DateTime? model property maps to DateTimeField / NullableDateTimeField.
- DateTimeField.cs:12: DateTimeField is constructed with DbType.DateTime.
- ConvertType is used by FieldDefinition (MSSqlConnector.cs:177) which builds CREATE TABLE column definitions, so framework-created MSSql schemas get DATE columns for DateTime properties.

The sibling comparison is also accurate: MySQLConnector.cs:132-138 correctly maps DbType.Time -> TIME, DbType.Date -> DATE, and DbType.DateTime/DateTime2 -> DATETIME, demonstrating both the divergence and the intended correct mapping. MSSql has a proper DATETIME2 (already used for DbType.DateTime2 at line 131-132) that should be the target for DbType.DateTime, plus a TIME type for DbType.Time.

Severity 'high' is justified: DateTimeField is the default mapping for all DateTime model properties including ITimestamped/audit fields, so any timestamped entity persisted to a framework-created MSSql table loses its time-of-day. Actionable fix: split the cases so DbType.DateTime -> DATETIME (or DATETIME2) and DbType.Time -> TIME, leaving only DbType.Date -> DATE.

Minor scoping note (does not negate the finding): the loss occurs at table-creation/write against framework-generated schemas; pre-existing correctly-typed columns are not altered. But for schemas this framework creates, the bug is real and silent.

### CR-H087 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql
- **Title:** DbType.Single (float) maps to TINYINT
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql\Database/Connector/MSSqlConnector.cs:144-147`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — split `DbType.Single` into its own `ConvertType` case returning `REAL` (SQL Server's 4-byte single-precision float), so C# `float` properties no longer generate a TINYINT column. Covered by `Single_MapsTo_Real_NotTinyInt` in `Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql.Tests`.
- **Detail:** DbType.Single is grouped with SByte and Byte and returns "TINYINT". A C# float property would be persisted as a 0-255 integer column, truncating the value and losing the fractional/negative range entirely. The sibling MySQLConnector correctly returns FLOAT for DbType.Single. Also note AbstractConnectorBase.DbTypeToClrType maps DbType.Single -> typeof(float), so BuildDataTable creates a float DataColumn that will then be bulk-copied into a TINYINT column - a runtime conversion failure or truncation.
- **Fix:** Add a separate case DbType.Single: return "REAL"; (SQL Server REAL is 4-byte float).
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual code. MSSqlConnector.cs:144-147 groups `case DbType.Single:` with `DbType.SByte` and `DbType.Byte`, all returning "TINYINT". A C# float (DbType.Single) would thus generate a TINYINT column (0-255 unsigned integer), truncating any fractional part, rejecting negatives, and overflowing values above 255. The correct T-SQL type for a single-precision float is REAL (or FLOAT(24)). This is a genuine, high-severity, actionable type-mapping bug; the fix is to break DbType.Single out into its own case returning "REAL".

CreateConnection (MSSqlConnector.cs:80-104) then receives a plain PasswordSettings that is neither MSSqlSettings nor RemoteSettings, so it falls through to 'throw new Exception("No path provided")'. Passing an MSSqlSettings (which IS a RemoteSettings) to this store cannot produce a working connection. MSSqlStore.SetSettings(RemoteSettings) (Stores/MSSqlStore.cs:29-41) constructs a NEW plain PasswordSettings copying only Location/Name/Password, then calls base.SetSettings(pwSettings). The override SetSettings(PasswordSettings) at lines 47-57 routes any RemoteSettings (which includes MSSqlSettings, since MSSqlSettings : SqlSettings : RemoteSettings — confirmed in MSSqlSettings.cs:12 and CLAUDE.md hierarchy) into this flattening path.

Tracing downstream: DataBaseStore.SetSettings(ISettings) (DataBaseStore.cs:61-67) calls GetConnector<DB>(sets) with that PasswordSettings; DataBase.GetConnector (DataBase.cs:56-66) does Activator.CreateInstance(MSSqlConnector, settings); the connector base stores it verbatim as PasswordSettings _settings (AbstractConnectorBase.cs:19). CreateConnection(_settings) (Database/Connector/MSSqlConnector.cs:80-104) then evaluates: `settings is MSSqlSettings` -> false, `settings is RemoteSettings` -> false (it is a plain PasswordSettings), so it falls through to `throw new Exception("No path provided")` at line 104. The bulk paths also call CreateConnection(_settings) (e.g. BulkInsert line 276), so they break too.

Confirmed the lost data: UserName, Port, UseSecure, and the MSSqlSettings.GetConnectionString() override (MSSqlSettings.cs:30-33) are all dropped. The async store does it correctly via base.SetSettings((ISettings)settings) preserving the runtime type (AsyncMSSqlStore.cs:33-39), so the contrast cited is accurate.

This is a genuine high-severity functional bug: passing any MSSqlSettings to the sync store cannot produce a working connection (every CRUD op throws). It also violates the documented convention 'RemoteSettings should be passed via base.SetSettings(), not constructed inline.' Recommended fix matches the finding: mirror the async store by calling base.SetSettings((ISettings)settings) instead of flattening into a new PasswordSettings.

Minor caveat (does not reduce severity): a caller passing a plain PasswordSettings that is not a RemoteSettings hits the else branch (base.SetSettings(settings)) and is not flattened, but that path lacks credentials anyway; the realistic intended usage path is definitively broken.

### CR-H090 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql.View
- **Title:** CreateIndexedView / DropIndexedView do not invalidate the view-existence cache
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql.View\Database/Connector/MSSqlConnector_View.cs:248,310`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `CreateIndexedView` now calls `InvalidateViewExistsCache(name!)` and `DropIndexedView` calls `InvalidateViewExistsCache(viewName)` after the DDL, mirroring the base `CreateView`/`DropView`, so Auto-mode re-checks existence (uses the newly-created view; stops targeting a dropped one). New `Birko.Data.SQL.MSSql.View.Tests` compile-verifies the fix and the invalidation API; the CREATE/DROP DDL round-trip itself needs a live SQL Server (documented infra gap).
- **Detail:** The base AbstractConnector.CreateView and DropView both call InvalidateViewExistsCache(name) after the DDL runs (AbstractConnector_CreateView.cs:62 and :95), so Auto-mode queries (ShouldUsePersistentView -> _viewExistsCache.GetOrAdd, AbstractConnectorBase_View.cs:43) re-check existence. CreateIndexedView (line 248-292) and DropIndexedView (line 310-322) execute CREATE/DROP VIEW DDL but never call InvalidateViewExistsCache / ClearViewExistsCache. After creating an indexed view, a prior cached 'false' persists so Auto-mode keeps building on-the-fly SELECTs; after dropping one, a cached 'true' persists so Auto-mode keeps targeting a now-missing view and queries fail.
- **Fix:** Call InvalidateViewExistsCache(name!) at the end of CreateIndexedView and InvalidateViewExistsCache(viewName) at the end of DropIndexedView, mirroring the base CreateView/DropView.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code across both projects.

Cache mechanism (Birko.Data.SQL.View/SQL/Connectors/AbstractConnectorBase_View.cs): a single per-connector ConcurrentDictionary<string,bool> _viewExistsCache (line 15). Auto-mode query dispatch uses _viewExistsCache.GetOrAdd(viewName, name => checkViewExists(name)) (line 43), invoked from ShouldUsePersistentView. The query paths AbstractConnector_SelectView.cs:88 and AbstractConnector_SelectViewCount.cs:34 both call ShouldUsePersistentView(view, name => ViewExists(name)). The base CreateView (AbstractConnector_CreateView.cs:62) and DropView (:95) both call InvalidateViewExistsCache(name) after the DDL — establishing the contract that mutating DDL must invalidate the cache so Auto mode re-checks.

The cited methods (MSSqlConnector_View.cs): CreateIndexedView (lines 248-292) executes CREATE OR ALTER VIEW ... WITH SCHEMABINDING + CREATE UNIQUE CLUSTERED INDEX via DoCommandWithTransaction, and DropIndexedView (lines 310-322) executes DROP VIEW IF EXISTS. Neither calls InvalidateViewExistsCache nor ClearViewExistsCache. MSSqlConnector is a partial class on AbstractConnector→AbstractConnectorBase, so it shares the same _viewExistsCache instance, and its ViewExists override queries sys.views (line 30) — which returns true for an indexed view too (an indexed view is a row in sys.views). So a cached entry keyed on the view name applies to indexed views as well.

Consequences are exactly as described: (1) after CreateIndexedView with a prior cached 'false', Auto mode keeps building on-the-fly SELECTs (perf benefit of the indexed view silently lost; data still correct); (2) after DropIndexedView with a cached 'true', Auto mode keeps targeting SELECT ... FROM [view] which now fails — a genuine runtime query failure. The async variants (CreateIndexedViewAsync/DropIndexedViewAsync) just Task.Run the sync methods, so they inherit the bug.

The fix is straightforward and matches the established pattern: add InvalidateViewExistsCache(name!) at the end of CreateIndexedView and InvalidateViewExistsCache(viewName) at the end of DropIndexedView. Real and actionable. The drop-case failure justifies the high severity; the create case is more of a silent perf regression, but the finding's core claim holds.

### CR-H093 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL.SqLite
- **Title:** SqLiteIndexManager.ListAsync uses 'new' instead of 'override' — override is unreachable via IIndexManager and GetInfoAsync
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.SqLite\IndexManagement\SqLiteIndexManager.cs:37`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — made `SqlIndexManager.ListAsync` `virtual` and changed `SqLiteIndexManager.ListAsync` from `new` to `override`, so the inherited `GetInfoAsync` and any `IIndexManager`/`SqlIndexManager`-typed caller dispatch to the SQLite PRAGMA implementation (real column names) instead of the base empty-column query. Verified with real-SQLite tests (`GetInfoAsync`/base-typed `ListAsync` return the actual index column).
- **Detail:** SqLiteIndexManager declares `public new async Task<...> ListAsync(...)`, but the base SqlIndexManager.ListAsync (Birko.Data.SQL\SQL\IndexManagement\SqlIndexManager.cs:99) is NOT virtual and already implements IIndexManager.ListAsync. Because the SQLite method only HIDES (does not override) the base: (1) any caller holding the manager as IIndexManager or SqlIndexManager invokes the BASE ListAsync, which calls ListIndexesSql — a query the SQLite class itself documents as 'Not used' (line 29) and which returns column-name as an empty literal (`SELECT name, '', 0, ...`); (2) the inherited base GetInfoAsync (SqlIndexManager.cs:143) calls the non-virtual base ListAsync, so GetInfoAsync on a SQLite index manager returns IndexInfo objects with blank/wrong field data instead of the correct PRAGMA-derived columns. The PRAGMA-based override only runs when the caller is statically typed as the concrete SqLiteIndexManager.
- **Fix:** Make SqlIndexManager.ListAsync `public virtual` and change SqLiteIndexManager.ListAsync from `new` to `override`. Then GetInfoAsync and interface-typed callers correctly dispatch to the SQLite PRAGMA implementation. Also delete the now-dead ListIndexesSql override (or keep it only if the base ListAsync still uses it for non-SQLite).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading both files directly.

(1) SqLiteIndexManager.cs:37 declares `public new async Task<IReadOnlyList<IndexInfo>> ListAsync(...)` — it HIDES, not overrides.

(2) Base SqlIndexManager.cs:99 declares `public async Task<...> ListAsync(...)` with NO `virtual` modifier; it is marked `/// <inheritdoc />` and is the `IIndexManager.ListAsync` implementation. Grep across Birko.Data.SQL found no `virtual ListAsync` and no real `override ListAsync` — only the SQLite `new` hide.

(3) Because the base method is non-virtual and provides the interface implementation, dispatch via `IIndexManager` or a `SqlIndexManager`-typed reference invokes the BASE method (the `new` member does not participate in interface dispatch or virtual dispatch). The PRAGMA-based SQLite method only runs when the caller is statically typed as the concrete SqLiteIndexManager.

(4) GetInfoAsync (base, SqlIndexManager.cs:141-145) is not overridden in SQLite and calls `await ListAsync(scope, ct)`, which compile-time-binds to the base ListAsync (base-class code cannot see the derived `new` member). So GetInfoAsync on a SQLite manager goes through the base path.

(5) The base path runs SQLite's ListIndexesSql override (SqLiteIndexManager.cs:27-32), which the code itself documents as 'Not used' (line 29) and returns `SELECT name, '', 0, ...` — an empty literal for the column-name field. The base ListAsync (lines 110-134) reads column 1 as the column name, so the resulting IndexInfo.Fields all have blank Name and wrong descending/ordinal data instead of the correct PRAGMA index_info columns.

This is a genuine correctness bug: interface/base-typed consumers and GetInfoAsync silently return wrong index metadata. Fix: make base ListAsync `virtual` and change the SQLite method from `new` to `override`. The cited file/line and all sub-claims match the actual code exactly.

### CR-H094 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL.View
- **Title:** Static _viewCache is a non-thread-safe Dictionary mutated without locking
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.View\SQL/DataBase_View.cs:16,81-94,194,206`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — switched `_viewCache` from a plain static `Dictionary` to an inline-initialized `ConcurrentDictionary<Type, Tables.View>` (matching the sibling `_fieldsCache`), removing the unlocked null-init and eliminating the bucket-corruption race in `LoadView`. Covered by a new concurrency regression (`ViewCacheConcurrencyTests`: 64 parallel `LoadView` calls neither throw nor diverge).
- **Detail:** _viewCache is a plain static Dictionary<Type, Tables.View> that LoadView lazily creates and writes (`_viewCache[type] = view`) from a static method with no lock, while the sibling base cache (_fieldsCache in Birko.Data.SQL/SQL/DataBase_Field.cs:15) is deliberately a ConcurrentDictionary. Connectors are used concurrently across threads/requests; two threads calling LoadView for an uncached type can race on the `if (_viewCache == null)` init and on the dictionary insert, corrupting internal buckets (potential IndexOutOfRange/InvalidOperation) or losing entries. This is exactly the kind of race the framework otherwise avoids by using ConcurrentDictionary.
- **Fix:** Switch _viewCache to ConcurrentDictionary<Type, Tables.View> and use GetOrAdd, matching _fieldsCache. EnsureViewResolverRegistered should also be made idempotent under concurrency (e.g. Interlocked/Lazy).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading both cited files. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.View\SQL\DataBase_View.cs: line 16 declares `private static Dictionary<Type, Tables.View>? _viewCache = null;` — a plain, non-thread-safe Dictionary. LoadView (lines 78-207) is a static method with NO locking that (a) lazily null-initializes it (lines 81-84), (b) reads via ContainsKey (line 85), (c) inserts via `_viewCache[type] = view;` (line 194), and (d) reads via `return _viewCache[type];` (line 206). Two threads hitting LoadView for an uncached type can race on both the null-init and the insert; concurrent mutation of a plain Dictionary can corrupt internal buckets (IndexOutOfRange/InvalidOperationException) or lose entries. The contrast claim is also accurate: the sibling base cache _fieldsCache in C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL\SQL\DataBase_Field.cs:15 is deliberately a ConcurrentDictionary (uses GetOrAdd at line 19), proving the framework's intentional thread-safety convention. Tellingly, DataBase_View.cs line 193 already calls `_fieldsCache.TryAdd(...)` (concurrent-safe) immediately before the unsafe `_viewCache[type] = view;` on line 194 — making the asymmetry an obvious oversight. The finding is genuine, actionable, and the fix (switch _viewCache to ConcurrentDictionary initialized inline) is straightforward and matches existing convention. The 'high' severity is reasonable since connectors/caches are shared static state used across concurrent requests, though in practice many consumers warm the cache during single-threaded startup which can mask the race — hence high severity but the real-world hit rate depends on first-use concurrency.

### CR-H096 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.SQL.Views
- **Title:** Async API is sync-over-async; CancellationToken not honored during DB work
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.Views\SqlViewStore.cs:43-102, SqlViewManager.cs:22-71`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — added genuine async view primitives to `Birko.Data.SQL.View` (`AbstractAsyncConnector.SelectAsync(Tables.View, …, ct)` over the async reader and `SelectCountAsync(Tables.View, …, ct)` over the async command path), then rewrote `SqlViewStore` (QueryAsync/QueryFirstAsync/CountAsync) and `SqlViewManager` (EnsureAsync/DropAsync/ExistsAsync) to detect an `AbstractAsyncConnector` and use those async methods (threading `ct` into the DB call), falling back to the sync path only for a non-async connector. New `Birko.Data.SQL.Views.Tests` exercises the async join-view Query/QueryFirst/Count end-to-end over SQLite. (Also fixed a latent join view-count SQL bug — the count now passes only the left tables, matching the SELECT builder, so a joined view no longer lists the joined tables twice.)
- **Detail:** Every public Task-returning method (QueryAsync, QueryFirstAsync, CountAsync, EnsureAsync, DropAsync, ExistsAsync) calls the SYNCHRONOUS connector methods (_connector.Select, _connector.SelectCount, _connector.ViewExists, _connector.CreateView, _connector.DropView) and wraps the result in Task.FromResult / Task.CompletedTask. The connector hierarchy already exposes genuine async equivalents on AbstractAsyncConnector (SelectAsync, SelectCountAsync, ViewExistsAsync, CreateViewAsync, DropViewAsync, CreateViewIfNotExistsAsync). Because the field is typed as the base AbstractConnector, those async methods are invisible to the store. Result: callers awaiting these methods actually block the calling thread on synchronous DB I/O, and the CancellationToken is only checked once at method entry (ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested()) — it is never threaded into the DB call, so an in-flight query/DDL cannot be cancelled. CLAUDE.md requires async methods to observe the CancellationToken.
- **Fix:** Type the field as AbstractAsyncConnector (or accept it via an overload) and await the *Async connector methods, passing ct through. For QueryAsync, materialize via the async enumerable. For EnsureAsync, prefer CreateViewIfNotExistsAsync to also collapse the check-then-act round-trip.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual code. SqlViewStore.cs:43-102 (QueryAsync, QueryFirstAsync, CountAsync) and SqlViewManager.cs:22-71 (EnsureAsync, DropAsync, ExistsAsync) all invoke the SYNCHRONOUS connector methods (_connector.Select, _connector.SelectCount, _connector.ViewExists, _connector.CreateView, _connector.DropView) and wrap the result in Task.FromResult / Task.CompletedTask. Both classes type the field as the base `AbstractConnector` (SqlViewStore.cs:23, SqlViewManager.cs:15), so the derived async methods are not visible without a cast.\n\nThe genuine async equivalents DO exist and DO thread the token: AbstractAsyncConnector (declared `: AbstractConnector` at AbstractAsyncConnector.cs:17) provides SelectAsync (real ExecuteReaderAsync/ReadAsync, AbstractAsyncConnector_Select.cs), SelectCountAsync with `ct` param (AbstractAsyncConnector_SelectCount.cs), and ViewExistsAsync/CreateViewAsync/DropViewAsync/CreateViewIfNotExistsAsync (AbstractAsyncConnector_CreateView.cs) which pass ct into ExecuteNonQueryAsync(ct)/OpenAsync(ct).\n\nEach public store/manager method calls ct.ThrowIfCancellationRequested() only once at entry, then never passes the token into the DB call, so an in-flight query/DDL cannot be cancelled and the awaiting thread blocks on synchronous DB I/O. This contradicts the project's documented cancellation convention (CLAUDE.md: 'async stores observe cancellation consistently').\n\nMinor caveat that shapes (not invalidates) the fix: the store is constructed with an AbstractConnector, so the connector may not always be an AbstractAsyncConnector; the fix needs a type guard / cast to the async path rather than a blind rewrite. The finding's core claims (sync-over-async, base-type field hiding async methods, token only checked at entry, async equivalents available) are all accurate. High severity is justified for a blocking-I/O + non-cancellable async API.

### CR-H097 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Stores
- **Title:** Time-bucket aggregation mutates the caller's source entities in place
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Stores\AggregateHelper.cs:165-177`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — replaced the mutating `ApplyTimeBucket` (which called `timeProp.SetValue(item, bucketed)` on the caller's own entities) with a non-mutating `BucketTimeOf(item, timeProp, ticks)` computed on-the-fly at group-key and result-row time. A read-only time-bucket aggregation no longer overwrites the source entities' timestamps. New `AggregateHelperTimeBucketTests` assert the source timestamps are unchanged and the bucketing/grouping is still correct.
- **Detail:** ApplyTimeBucket<T> calls timeProp.SetValue(item, bucketed) on each item in the materialized source list. Because the list elements are the caller's own entity instances (e.g. the ConcurrentDictionary values in InMemoryStore, or any IEnumerable<T> the caller passes to LinqAggregate/LinqAggregateAsync), this permanently overwrites the entity's timestamp/time-column with the truncated bucket value as a side effect of merely running an aggregation query. AggregateMath.cs:24-26 explicitly documents the intended contract ('Does not mutate originals — creates shallow copies when bucketing is needed') and even provides a non-mutating AggregateMath.BucketByTime that returns (item, bucketTime) tuples, but AggregateHelper ignores it and mutates instead. A read-only aggregate query should never change stored data.
- **Fix:** Compute the bucketed time without mutating the entity — group/key on AggregateMath.TruncateToBucket((DateTime)timeProp.GetValue(item)) directly (or use the existing BucketByTime helper to carry the bucket alongside the item), and write the bucket value into the result row from that computed value rather than from a mutated property.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified directly against the source. AggregateHelper.cs:165-177 `ApplyTimeBucket<T>` calls `timeProp.SetValue(item, bucketed)` (line 173) on each item, mutating in place. The mutated items are the caller's own entity instances: in `LinqAggregateAsync`, `list` (line 47) is a `ToList()` of the source — a new list but holding the same object references — and line 71 reassigns it via `ApplyTimeBucket(...).ToList()`, which yields back those same mutated references (the generator mutates `item` then `yield return item`). Both InMemory stores pass their live backing store directly: AbstractAsyncInMemoryStore.cs:229 and AbstractInMemoryStore.cs:214 call `LinqAggregate(Async)(_items.Values, ...)`, so a time-bucket aggregation permanently overwrites the time-column of the ConcurrentDictionary's stored entities — a subsequent Read returns the truncated bucket value. AggregateMath.cs confirms the rest: lines 22-26 document a non-mutating contract ("Does not mutate originals — creates shallow copies when bucketing is needed") and lines 27-38 provide `BucketByTime<T>` returning `(T Item, DateTime BucketTime)` tuples without mutation, which AggregateHelper ignores. A read-only aggregate query silently corrupting stored data is a genuine, actionable high-severity bug. The fix is straightforward: use the returned bucket value (as it already does for grouping via the `bucket_time`/key path) rather than writing it back onto the entity, e.g. project to tuples/keys instead of SetValue.

- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync\Internal/SyncProviderBase.cs:348`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `GetUpdatedAt` now matches both `DateTime` and `DateTime?` (`Nullable.GetUnderlyingType(...) == typeof(DateTime)`); the existing `value as DateTime?` cast already handled both. `NewestWins` no longer silently degrades to `LocalWins` for models with a nullable timestamp. New `NewestWinsNullableTimestampTests` (probe subclass exposing the protected method) cover nullable-set/unset and the non-nullable path.
- **Detail:** GetUpdatedAt only reads the property when prop.PropertyType == typeof(DateTime). Any entity whose UpdatedAt is DateTime? (the common case for nullable timestamps) is not matched, so GetUpdatedAt returns null, GetNewest returns the hard-coded "local" default (line 179), and GetNewestConflictResolution returns UseLocal (line 221). The NewestWins policy therefore silently behaves as LocalWins for any model with a nullable timestamp. The bug is masked by the test model, which uses non-nullable DateTime (TestSyncModel.cs:9).
- **Fix:** Match both DateTime and DateTime? (e.g. Nullable.GetUnderlyingType(prop.PropertyType) == typeof(DateTime) || prop.PropertyType == typeof(DateTime)), and read the value accordingly.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code in C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync\Internal\SyncProviderBase.cs.

Line 346-355 GetUpdatedAt: `var prop = typeof(T).GetProperty("UpdatedAt"); if (prop != null && prop.PropertyType == typeof(DateTime)) { ... return value as DateTime?; } return null;`. The guard on line 349 only matches non-nullable DateTime. For an entity whose UpdatedAt is `DateTime?`, `prop.PropertyType` equals `typeof(DateTime?)` (Nullable<DateTime>), which is a distinct Type from `typeof(DateTime)`, so the branch is skipped and the method returns null. (The `value as DateTime?` on line 352 shows the author intended to handle nullables, making the type check a genuine oversight.)

Downstream chain confirmed:
- GetNewest (line 169-180): if either GetUpdatedAt is null, `localUpdatedAt.HasValue && remoteUpdatedAt.HasValue` is false and it returns the hard-coded "local" (line 179).
- GetNewestConflictResolution (line 206-222): same pattern, returns ConflictResolution.UseLocal (line 221).
- ResolveConflict (line 198) and the conflict-resolution switch (line 161) route NewestWins through these methods.

Net effect: ConflictResolutionPolicy.NewestWins silently behaves as LocalWins for any model with a nullable (DateTime?) timestamp — the common case for optional/nullable timestamps. This is a real, actionable high-severity correctness bug in production code.

Minor caveat: the cited TestSyncModel.cs is not present in this checkout (it lives in the separate Birko.Data.Sync.Tests repo), so I could not directly confirm the "masked by the test model" detail. That is incidental color and does not affect the substance of the finding, which I verified directly against the production source. Suggested fix: accept typeof(DateTime?) as well, e.g. via `Nullable.GetUnderlyingType(prop.PropertyType) == typeof(DateTime) || prop.PropertyType == typeof(DateTime)`.

### CR-H099 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Sync
- **Title:** result.Success can be true when there were errors but the token was cancelled
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync\SyncProvider.cs:180 / AsyncSyncProvider.cs:181`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — changed `result.Success = result.Errors.Count == 0 || IsCancellationRequested` to `result.Success = result.Errors.Count == 0` in both `SyncProvider` and `AsyncSyncProvider`, so a run that recorded per-item errors is never reported as successful just because it was cancelled. New `SyncSuccessOnCancellationTests` (a failing-create local store + cancel-on-batch-completed) asserts errors force `Success=false`.
- **Detail:** result.Success = result.Errors.Count == 0 || options.CancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested. The OR means a sync that recorded per-item errors AND was then cancelled reports Success = true, hiding the failures. Cancellation should not flip a failed result to successful. (Separately, treating a cancelled sync as Success at all is questionable, but the error case is the clear bug.)
- **Fix:** Compute success from errors only (result.Success = result.Errors.Count == 0), or track cancellation as a distinct outcome rather than folding it into Success with an OR.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading both cited files. SyncProvider.cs:180 and AsyncSyncProvider.cs:181 both contain exactly: `result.Success = result.Errors.Count == 0 || options.CancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested;`. The OR operator means that when CancellationToken.IsCancellationRequested is true, Success is set to true regardless of how many errors are in result.Errors.

The failure scenario is reachable: the batch loop (lines 135-167 in sync) appends each batch's per-item errors to result.Errors (line 154), then breaks the loop on cancellation (lines 165-166) using cooperative IsCancellationRequested checks rather than ThrowIfCancellationRequested. Because cancellation does not throw here, control flows through to the Success assignment at line 180 (not the catch block). So a sync that recorded item-level errors and was then cancelled reports Success=true, masking the failures — exactly as described. Cancellation should not flip a result that already has errors to successful. The bug is real and actionable; the fix is to AND the cancellation case so errors always force Success=false (e.g. `result.Errors.Count == 0 && !IsCancellationRequested`, or at minimum require Errors.Count == 0 regardless of cancellation).

The sync variant CosmosSyncKnowledgeStore.cs has the identical defect (verified). The tenant intent is real and documented: the core ISyncKnowledgeStore interface describes these as for 'a specific scope and optional tenant' and the parameter is named tenantId, so a caller reasonably believes tenant isolation is enforced when it is not -- a true silent cross-tenant leakage/clobbering risk. ### CR-H101 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Sync.ElasticSearch
- **Title:** Property mapped onto reserved Elasticsearch _id metadata field
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.ElasticSearch\Models/ElasticSyncKnowledgeItem.cs:19-20`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — changed `ElasticSyncKnowledgeItem.Id` from `[Text(Name = "_id")]` to `[Keyword(Name = "docKey")]`, so AutoMap no longer emits a mapping for the reserved `_id` metadata field (which Elasticsearch rejects, breaking index creation). The base store already keys documents off `AbstractModel.Guid`, so this app-level key was never the document identity anyway. New `Birko.Data.Sync.ElasticSearch.Tests` assert no property maps to `_id`, `Id`→`docKey`, and the rendered AutoMap JSON omits `_id`.
- **Detail:** Id is annotated [Text(Name = "_id")]. _id is a reserved Elasticsearch metadata field; AutoMap (used by the base store's InitCoreAsync via cid.Map<T>(m => m.AutoMap())) will try to emit a regular field mapping named "_id", which Elasticsearch rejects (field names beginning with '_' are reserved). This makes index creation throw InvalidOperationException for this index. Separately, the actual document id is keyed off AbstractModel.Guid by the base store (AsyncElasticSearchStore.CreateCoreAsync uses .Id(data.Guid), Update/Delete likewise), so this Id property is never used as the document identity even though CreateKnowledgeItem populates it with GenerateId({EntityGuid}_{Scope}).
- **Fix:** Remove the [Text(Name="_id")] attribute (and likely the Id property + GenerateId helper) since the base store already uses Guid as the ES document id, or if a deterministic application-level key is needed, map it to a non-reserved keyword field name (e.g. "docKey").

1. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.ElasticSearch\Models\ElasticSyncKnowledgeItem.cs:19-20 — `Id` is annotated `[Text(Name = "_id")]`, mapping it onto Elasticsearch's reserved `_id` metadata field name.

2. Base store C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.ElasticSearch\Stores\AsyncElasticSearchStore.cs:93-96 — `InitCoreAsync` calls `InitAsync(cid => cid.Map<T>(m => m.AutoMap()), ct)`. AsyncElasticSyncKnowledgeStore does NOT override InitCoreAsync (verified Stores\AsyncElasticSyncKnowledgeStore.cs), so it inherits the AutoMap path. AutoMap reflects over all mapped properties and will emit a field literally named `_id` in the index `properties` mapping.

3. Elasticsearch rejects index creation when a mapping's `properties` contains a field name beginning with `_` (reserved for internal/metadata use, and `_id` collides with the built-in metadata field) — a mapper_parsing_exception. InitAsync checks `!response.IsValid || response.OriginalException != null` and throws InvalidOperationException (lines 83-88), so the rejection surfaces exactly as the finding describes. Index creation is attempted on first use whenever the index does not yet exist (the normal first-run case), so this is reliably hit by consumers.

4. The `Id` property is functionally dead: every CRUD op keys the ES document id off `data.Guid` — CreateCoreAsync `.Id(data.Guid)` (line 111), UpdateCoreAsync (157), DeleteCoreAsync (174), and BulkAsync `.Id(o.Guid)` (343/347/351). Meanwhile CreateKnowledgeItem populates `Id = GenerateId(...)` (AsyncElasticSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:45) with `{EntityGuid:N}_{Scope}`, which is never used as document identity. This confirms the secondary point that the annotation is both harmful and useless.

The finding is a genuine, actionable bug. Recommended fix: remove the `[Text(Name = "_id")]` annotation (e.g. mark the property not-mapped / `[Ignore]`, or rename the field to a non-reserved name) since it is never the actual document id anyway.
