### CR-H103 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Sync.RavenDB
- **Title:** UpdateKnowledgeAsync creates duplicate documents instead of upserting — stable doc-id helper never used
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.RavenDB\Stores\AsyncRavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:84-90 and RavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs:82-88`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (medium)
- **Status:** done — `ConvertToRavenItem` now derives a **deterministic** Guid from the natural key (`EntityGuid`, `Scope`, `TenantGuid`) when the incoming item has no Guid (instead of `Guid.NewGuid()`), so re-syncing the same key reuses the document identity the base store keys on → an actual upsert rather than a duplicate document each time. The sync variant delegates to the shared async static. New `RavenSyncKnowledgeUpsertTests` assert the same key → same id, different scope → different id, explicit Guid preserved.
- **Detail:** The methods are documented as 'Update or create', but identity is the random record `Guid`. ConvertToRavenItem assigns a brand-new Guid when the incoming item's Guid is null (line 182), so re-syncing the same (EntityGuid, Scope) stores a new document with a new id each time → duplicate knowledge rows. GetKnowledge then de-dups by EntityGuid in ToDictionary, masking the leak but making Max(LastSyncedAt)/counts unreliable. The model defines `GenerateDocumentId(entityGuid, scope)` (RavenSyncKnowledgeItem.cs:72) and `CollectionName` precisely to give a stable idempotent id, but neither is ever referenced.
- **Fix:** Store with a deterministic id derived from GenerateDocumentId(item.EntityGuid, item.Scope) (e.g. StoreAsync(ravenItem, id)) so repeated syncs overwrite the same document, or load-then-update existing docs. Evict-before-store as base UpdateCore does if reusing a session.
- **Verify reasoning:** Core defect confirmed by reading the actual code. In both Stores\AsyncRavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs (UpdateKnowledgeAsync, lines ~78-91) and Stores\RavenSyncKnowledgeStore.cs (lines ~76-89), the "Update or create" methods loop over items and call session.StoreAsync(ConvertToRavenItem(item)). ConvertToRavenItem sets Guid = item.Guid ?? Guid.NewGuid() (line 182 async / 180 sync). The base AsyncRavenDBStore keys RavenDB document identity off the Guid property (ReadAsync does session.LoadAsync<T>(guid.ToString()); CreateCoreAsync does data.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid() then StoreAsync). So storing with a freshly-minted random Guid produces a NEW document id, not an upsert by the natural key (EntityGuid, Scope). Re-syncing the same (EntityGuid, Scope) with null-Guid items genuinely creates duplicate documents. The model's stable-id helpers GenerateDocumentId(entityGuid, scope) (Models\RavenSyncKnowledgeItem.cs:72) and CollectionName (line 66) exist precisely to give an idempotent id; a grep across the project confirms NEITHER is referenced anywhere outside its own definition. So the headline ("stable doc-id helper never used; method creates duplicates instead of upserting") is accurate and actionable. Cited line numbers are slightly off (actual 84-91 / 82-89) but unambiguously point to the right methods.

Two qualifications lower confidence/severity from the stated "high": (1) The detail's claim that "GetKnowledge then de-dups by EntityGuid in ToDictionary, masking the leak" is WRONG about the mechanism — items.ToDictionary(x => x.EntityGuid, ...) (line 59 / 57) THROWS ArgumentException on a duplicate key; it does not silently de-dup. Duplicates would surface as a crash in GetKnowledge, not silent unreliable Max/counts. (2) These non-generic stores appear to be effectively dead code: the real sync engine (Birko.Data.Sync\AsyncSyncProvider.cs / SyncProvider.cs) drives knowledge through the generic IAsyncSyncKnowledgeItemStore<T> (CreateKnowledgeItem + UpdateAsync), not these UpdateKnowledgeAsync methods; no DI wiring or tests reference RavenSyncKnowledgeStore/AsyncRavenSyncKnowledgeStore (the classes don't even declare : ISyncKnowledgeStore, only mention it in doc comments). So real-world blast radius is small. Net: a genuine, fixable correctness bug in the code as written (fix = use GenerateDocumentId / load-or-query by (EntityGuid,Scope) before Store), but with one inaccurate sub-claim and limited actual impact, so high severity is overstated.

### CR-H104 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant
- **Title:** GetVersionHash returns a random GUID when UpdatedAt is absent, breaking change detection
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant\Providers/TenantSyncProvider.cs:834`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `GetVersionHash` now returns the timestamp when present and a **deterministic SHA-256 content hash** of the serialized entity otherwise (instead of `Guid.NewGuid()`), so versions are stable/reproducible across syncs. `GetUpdatedAt` also now matches `DateTime?` (not only `DateTime`). New `Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant.Tests` cover timestamp use (incl. nullable), determinism for equal content, hash-changes-with-content, and that the fallback is not a GUID.
- **Detail:** GetVersionHash does `updatedAt?.ToString("O") ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString()`. For any entity type that has no DateTime UpdatedAt property (GetUpdatedAt returns null), every call produces a fresh, non-deterministic version hash. These hashes are written into TenantSyncKnowledgeItem.LocalVersion/RemoteVersion and into SyncItemPreview, so for such entities the recorded version never matches across syncs and the version data is meaningless. It also makes Preview/Sync results non-reproducible.
- **Fix:** Compute a deterministic hash from the entity's serialized state (or a stable field) instead of Guid.NewGuid(); fall back to a constant/empty marker rather than a random value when no version source is available.
- **Verify reasoning:** The cited line is exactly as quoted. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant\Providers\TenantSyncProvider.cs:834, GetVersionHash does `return updatedAt?.ToString("O") ?? Guid.NewGuid().ToString();`. GetUpdatedAt (line 815-824) returns null when T has no `UpdatedAt` property — and notably only matches a property of exactly `typeof(DateTime)`, so even a nullable `DateTime? UpdatedAt` falls through to the random-GUID branch. For such entities every call produces a fresh, non-deterministic value, which is then stored into SyncItemPreview.LocalVersion/RemoteVersion (lines 212-213) and TenantSyncKnowledgeItem.LocalVersion/RemoteVersion (lines 805-806). So the factual core of the finding is correct: the version field is non-deterministic and meaningless for entities lacking a DateTime UpdatedAt.

HOWEVER, the finding's severity and the "breaking change detection" framing are overstated. I grepped the entire project for any read/comparison of Version/LocalVersion/RemoteVersion — there are NONE. The hashes are write-only. Change detection in AnalyzeItem (lines 231-258) and the real sync path DetermineSyncAction (lines 580-668) is driven exclusively by existence checks (localExists/remoteExists), knowledge-item deletion flags (IsRemoteDeleted/IsLocalDeleted), and GetWinner/conflict policy — never by the version hashes. When both items exist, the action is unconditionally Update; the version strings play no role. So nothing functionally breaks: the version metadata is cosmetic/diagnostic, and sync actions remain correct and reproducible. Only the recorded version strings vary run-to-run.

Verdict: the issue is genuine and actionable (a random GUID is the wrong default for a version hash — a content hash or stable sentinel/null would be correct), so isReal=true. But it is a data-quality/correctness-of-recorded-metadata bug, not the high-severity "breaks change detection / non-reproducible sync" the finding claims. The actionable fix is to replace Guid.NewGuid() with a deterministic value (e.g. a content hash of the entity, or null/constant) and to also handle nullable DateTime UpdatedAt in GetUpdatedAt.

### CR-H105 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant
- **Title:** Knowledge item records IsRemoteDeleted/IsLocalDeleted=true for items merely absent from a directional fetch
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant\Providers/TenantSyncProvider.cs:489`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (medium)
- **Status:** done — `CreateKnowledgeItem` now requires positive evidence to flag a side deleted: `IsLocalDeleted`/`IsRemoteDeleted` are only true when the entity was **previously known** (`hasKnowledge`, already threaded from the loop) AND is now absent on that side. A first-seen one-sided (or fetch-predicate-excluded) item is no longer persisted as "deleted", so it can't later drive a spurious conflict or erroneous delete. New tests cover first-seen-one-sided (not deleted) vs previously-known-now-absent (deleted).
- **Detail:** CreateKnowledgeItem is called for every processed GUID (including Skip actions) and sets IsLocalDeleted = (localItem == null) and IsRemoteDeleted = (remoteItem == null) purely from presence in the fetched dictionaries. During a Download-only or Upload-only sync, or when a fetch predicate excludes an item, an entity that simply wasn't fetched from one side gets persisted as 'deleted' on that side. On the next bidirectional sync DetermineSyncAction reads knowledgeItem.IsRemoteDeleted/IsLocalDeleted and can escalate to a Delete or a false Conflict, causing real data loss / spurious conflicts.
- **Fix:** Only mark a side as deleted when there is positive evidence of deletion (e.g. previously known via knowledge AND now absent in a full sync), not from absence in a single directional/filtered fetch. Consider not writing knowledge for Skip actions.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant\Providers\TenantSyncProvider.cs.

CONFIRMED CORE BUG: CreateKnowledgeItem (called at line 489 for EVERY processed GUID, including Skip — line 473-475 then 489) sets IsLocalDeleted = (localItem == null) and IsRemoteDeleted = (remoteItem == null) purely from presence in the fetched dictionaries (lines 807-808). Items are fetched via GetAllItemsAsync with optional LocalFetchPredicate/RemoteFetchPredicate (lines 560-574). If a fetch predicate excludes a genuinely-existing item from one side's dictionary, but that item exists on the other side (so it enters allGuids at line 389), CreateKnowledgeItem persists that side as deleted. On the NEXT bidirectional sync, DetermineSyncAction reads knowledgeItem.IsRemoteDeleted/IsLocalDeleted (lines 642, 657) and escalates a present-on-one-side item to a spurious Conflict ("Modified locally but deleted remotely"). Under a later Download-only/Upload-only run, the same false flag drives an actual Delete (lines 606-607 / 618-619). So the false-deletion-flag → spurious-conflict / erroneous-delete chain is real and is a genuine data-loss vector. The fetch-predicate vector the finding names is accurate.

INACCURACIES in the finding (why confidence is medium, not high): (1) The "Download-only or Upload-only sync" trigger is wrong — both stores are ALWAYS fully fetched at lines 381-382 regardless of options.Direction; direction only gates the chosen SyncAction, not which store is read, so a directional sync by itself does NOT make an item absent from a dictionary. (2) For the bidirectional re-read the finding cites, the code returns Conflict (line 642-651), not Delete; Delete only occurs on a subsequent directional run. The finding conflates triggers and overstates the Delete escalation.

Net: the central claim (deletion inferred from mere fetch-absence, persisted, then mis-driving DetermineSyncAction) is genuine and actionable via the fetch-predicate path; the surrounding rationale is partly mistaken.

### CR-H106 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant
- **Title:** ApplyConflictResolutionAsync swallows all exceptions with an incorrect comment
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant\Providers/TenantSyncProvider.cs:782`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — removed the swallowing `try/catch` in `ApplyConflictResolutionAsync`, so a failed conflict-resolution write now propagates to the caller's per-item `try/catch` (which records a `SyncError` and increments `progress.Errors`), exactly like the sibling Create/Update/Delete branches. No more silent data loss reported as success. New test asserts a throwing store during `UseRemote` propagates and doesn't bump `UpdatedItems`.
- **Detail:** The catch block swallows every exception with the comment 'Error already handled in calling method'. It is not: the conflict branch in ExecuteSyncAsync calls ApplyConflictResolutionAsync and only its own catch covers exceptions, but those are caught here first and discarded. A failed conflict write (UpdateAsync to local/remote throwing) is silently lost — no SyncError is recorded, progress.UpdatedItems is not incremented, and result.Success stays true. Sync reports success while the conflict resolution did not persist.
- **Fix:** Let the exception propagate to the caller's try/catch (remove the swallowing catch), or record a SyncError here so the failure is surfaced.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code in C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.Sync.Tenant\Providers\TenantSyncProvider.cs.

ApplyConflictResolutionAsync (lines 749-786) wraps its body in try { ... } catch (Exception) { // Error already handled in calling method } (lines 782-785), swallowing every exception with no logging, no rethrow, no error recording.

The comment is false. The only caller is the SyncAction.Conflict branch (lines 477-482), which has no conflict-specific error handling — it simply awaits ApplyConflictResolutionAsync(...) at line 481 inside the shared per-item try (opened at line 409). The per-item catch (lines 491-502) is the only place that records a SyncError and increments progress.Errors, but it never fires for conflict-write failures because the inner catch consumes the exception before it can propagate. So the error is handled nowhere.

Concrete consequences all verified:
- If _remoteStore.UpdateAsync(localItem) (line 764) or _localStore.UpdateAsync(remoteItem) (line 772) throws, the throw is swallowed.
- progress.UpdatedItems++ (lines 765/773) executes only after a successful await, so it is skipped on failure.
- No SyncError is added to result.Errors, so result.Success = result.Errors.Count == 0 (line 533) stays true.
- The sync therefore reports Success=true even though the conflict resolution write was lost.

Notably, the sibling Create/Update/Delete branches (lines 413-471) have NO inner try/catch and correctly let store-write exceptions bubble to the per-item catch at 491, where they become SyncErrors. Only the Conflict path swallows, making the inconsistency a clear defect rather than intentional design. High severity (silent data loss masked as success) and actionable: remove the inner catch (or rethrow / record a SyncError) so conflict-write failures surface like the other branches.

### CR-H109 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.TimescaleDB
- **Title:** TimescaleDBSettings.GetConnectionString() is dead code — custom connection string never used
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.TimescaleDB\Stores\Settings.cs:52`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `TimescaleDBConnector` now overrides `CreateConnection` to return `new NpgsqlConnection(tsSettings.GetConnectionString())` for a `TimescaleDBSettings`, so the configured `CommandTimeout`/`ConnectionTimeout` (and SSL) actually reach the connection. The base `PostgreSQLConnector` only honored `GetConnectionString()` for a `PostgreSqlSettings` (a sibling type), dropping those on the generic branch. New `TimescaleDBConnectorConnectionStringTests` assert the timeouts + SSL mode reach the built `NpgsqlConnection`.

But the connector inherits PostgreSQLConnector.CreateConnection (PostgreSQLConnector.cs:75), which only special-cases 'settings is PostgreSqlSettings' to call GetConnectionString(); a TimescaleDBSettings is NOT a PostgreSqlSettings, so it falls through to the generic RemoteSettings branch that builds a bare 'Host=...;Port=...;Username=...;Password=...;Database=...' string (plus SSL). The result: the configured CommandTimeout/ConnectionTimeout (and the carefully composed connection string) are silently ignored at runtime, and GetConnectionString() is never invoked. The settings appear to work in unit tests (which only read the properties) but have no effect on actual connections.
- **Fix:** Override CreateConnection in TimescaleDBConnector to honor TimescaleDBSettings.GetConnectionString() (return new NpgsqlConnection(tsSettings.GetConnectionString()) when _timescaleSettings is available), or have PostgreSQLConnector.CreateConnection branch on 'settings is SqlSettings sql' and call sql.GetConnectionString() so all SqlSettings subclasses are covered.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual code across three projects.

CHAIN CONFIRMED:
1. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.TimescaleDB\Stores\Settings.cs:10 — `TimescaleDBSettings : SqlSettings` (NOT PostgreSqlSettings). Its GetConnectionString() override (line 52-60) builds a string including `Timeout={ConnectionTimeout};Command Timeout={CommandTimeout};` and optional `SSL Mode=Require;`.
2. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.PostgreSQL\Stores\PostgreSqlSettings.cs:12 — `PostgreSqlSettings : SqlSettings`. So PostgreSqlSettings and TimescaleDBSettings are SIBLINGS; a TimescaleDBSettings is NOT a PostgreSqlSettings.
3. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.TimescaleDB\Database\Connectors\TimescaleDBConnector.cs — `TimescaleDBConnector : PostgreSQLConnector` and does NOT override CreateConnection. Its async paths call inherited CreateConnection(_settings).
4. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL.PostgreSQL\Database\Connectors\PostgreSQLConnector.cs:82 — CreateConnection only calls `pgSettings.GetConnectionString()` when `settings is PostgreSqlSettings`; otherwise (line 87) the `is RemoteSettings` branch builds a bare `Host=...;Port=...;Username=...;Password=...;Database=...` (+SSL) string with NO Timeout/Command Timeout and never calls GetConnectionString(). A TimescaleDBSettings hits this generic branch.
5. C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.SQL\Stores\SqlSettings.cs:35 — GetConnectionString() is virtual; the base throws NotSupportedException and its doc comment explicitly lists TimescaleDBSettings as a provider override the connector is expected to honor — confirming the connector's `is PostgreSqlSettings` check is too narrow (it should accept any SqlSettings / call GetConnectionString()).

RESULT: TimescaleDBSettings.GetConnectionString() is never invoked at runtime; configured CommandTimeout/ConnectionTimeout are silently dropped on real connections (bulk insert/update/delete and CreateHypertableAsync all go through CreateConnection). Reasonable fixes: override CreateConnection in TimescaleDBConnector to handle TimescaleDBSettings, or broaden the PostgreSQLConnector check from `is PostgreSqlSettings` to `is SqlSettings` and call GetConnectionString().

### CR-H110 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.ViewModel
- **Title:** Bulk Create/Update discard the ProcessDataDelegate transform result
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.ViewModel\Repositories/AbstractBulkViewModelRepository.cs:64-69, 79-84`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — bulk `Create`/`Update` in `AbstractBulkViewModelRepository` now capture the transform result (`item = processDelegate?.Invoke(item) ?? item`), matching the single-item path, so a delegate returning a different/wrapped instance is honored instead of discarded. The async bulk repo uses a pass-through `StoreDataDelegate` (no bug). New `Birko.Data.ViewModel.Tests` assert the delegate's returned instance is what gets persisted for bulk create/update.
- **Detail:** ProcessDataDelegate<TModel> is defined as a transform (delegate TModel ProcessDataDelegate<TModel>(TModel data) in IBaseRepository.cs:12) — it returns the possibly-new/possibly-modified model. In bulk Create and Update the code does `TModel item = LoadModelInstance(x); processDelegate?.Invoke(item); return item;` — it invokes the delegate for side effects only and throws the return value away. A delegate that returns a different instance (or a wrapped/cloned model) is silently ignored, so the caller's transformation is lost on the bulk paths. The single-item versions handle this correctly with `x = processDelegate?.Invoke(x) ?? x` (AbstractViewModelRepository.cs:198, 220).
- **Fix:** Capture the result: `var item = LoadModelInstance(x); item = processDelegate?.Invoke(item) ?? item; return item;` in both Create and Update Select lambdas.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. ProcessDataDelegate<TModel> is defined as `public delegate TModel ProcessDataDelegate<TModel>(TModel data)` at Birko.Data.Repositories\IBaseRepository.cs:12 — a transform returning a possibly-different TModel (signature and line number match the finding exactly; the only inaccuracy is the project path — the delegate lives in the sibling Birko.Data.Repositories project, not Birko.Data.ViewModel — but file name + line + signature are correct).

In AbstractBulkViewModelRepository.cs the bulk Create (lines 64-69) and Update (lines 79-84) both do `TModel item = LoadModelInstance(x); processDelegate?.Invoke(item); return item;` — invoking the delegate for side effects only and discarding its return value. A delegate that returns a different/wrapped instance is silently ignored on the bulk paths.

The single-item versions handle it correctly: AbstractViewModelRepository.cs:198 (`x = processDelegate?.Invoke(x) ?? x`) in Create and :220 (same pattern) in Update — line numbers match exactly.

This is a genuine, actionable inconsistency: the delegate contract is a transform, the single-item code honors the return value, and the bulk code ignores it. The bug is latent for in-place-mutating delegates (the common case), but real for any delegate returning a new instance. Fix mirrors the single-item form: `var result = processDelegate?.Invoke(item) ?? item; return result;`.

### CR-H111 · 🟠 high · Birko.Data.XML
- **Title:** File.OpenWrite without truncation can corrupt separate-store files on create
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data.XML\Stores\XmlSeparateStore.cs:146`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `XmlSeparateStore.CreateCore` and `AsyncXmlSeparateStore.CreateCoreAsync` now write the per-entity file with `File.Create` (truncating) instead of `File.OpenWrite` (which opens at offset 0 without truncating), so a shorter payload over a stale/longer `{Name}-{Guid}.xml` no longer leaves trailing bytes that corrupt the XML. New `XmlSeparateAndTruncationTests` plant a long stale file and verify a subsequent shorter create reloads cleanly (sync + async).
- **Detail:** CreateCore opens the per-entity file with File.OpenWrite (also AsyncXmlSeparateStore.cs:159) without first deleting it. File.OpenWrite does NOT truncate — it opens at offset 0 over existing content. If a file with that {Name}-{Guid}.xml name already exists (e.g. a re-create after a crash, or Guid reuse) and the new serialized content is shorter than the old, trailing bytes from the previous content remain, producing malformed XML that then fails to load and is silently skipped by LoadData's catch. UpdateCore correctly deletes first (line 163) but CreateCore does not.
- **Fix:** Use File.Create(filePath) (truncating) or new FileStream(path, FileMode.Create) for the create path, matching UpdateCore's delete-then-write.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the code. XmlSeparateStore.CreateCore (XmlSeparateStore.cs:146) and AsyncXmlSeparateStore.CreateCoreAsync (AsyncXmlSeparateStore.cs:159) both write the per-entity file via `using FileStream fileStream = File.OpenWrite(filePath); WriteToStream(fileStream, data);` with no prior delete and no truncation.

The technical premise is accurate: File.OpenWrite uses FileMode.OpenOrCreate + FileAccess.Write and positions at offset 0 WITHOUT truncating. WriteToStream (AbstractXmlStore.cs:143-146) merely calls `_serializer.Serialize(stream, data)`; it never calls SetLength, so a shorter new payload leaves trailing bytes from a longer pre-existing file -> malformed XML.

The contrast is real and is a clear inconsistency in the same file: UpdateCore (XmlSeparateStore.cs:163) and UpdateCoreAsync (AsyncXmlSeparateStore.cs:179) DO `File.Delete(filePath)` before OpenWrite, so update is safe; CreateCore does not. The corruption is silently swallowed: LoadData (lines 109-124) / LoadDataAsync (lines 112-134) wrap each file read in try/catch and `continue` on failure, so a corrupt file is silently dropped.

Trigger realism: a stale, longer {Name}-{Guid}.xml must pre-exist at create time. Guid is auto-generated when null (collision negligible), but CreateCore honors a caller-supplied data.Guid (`data.Guid ??= Guid.NewGuid()`), so a re-create with a reused Guid across sessions, or a crash/partial-write leaving a longer stale file, can hit it. Within one session `_items.Add` would throw on a duplicate key, so the realistic path is a fresh session where the on-disk file exists but the in-memory dictionary does not (or LoadData skipped a corrupt one). Narrow but legitimate.

Verdict: real, actionable latent data-corruption bug with a trivial fix (delete-first or use File.Create, which truncates) that also removes the Create/Update inconsistency. Affects both the sync and async stores. Severity 'high' is slightly generous given the narrow trigger conditions, but the finding is genuine and correctly diagnosed.

This is the symptom of the missing batch-write implementation: the 'batch' stores behave exactly like separate stores. There is even a secondary read/write mismatch — the batch `LoadData` reads `List<T>` files that the inherited per-entity write path never produces. ### CR-H114 · 🟠 high · Birko.EventBus.MessageQueue
- **Title:** Handler exceptions swallowed, defeating retry and dead-letter delivery
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.EventBus.MessageQueue\DistributedEventBus.cs:176-184`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the delivery callback still runs every handler (error isolation) but now collects handler exceptions and rethrows after the loop (single exception directly, or an `AggregateException`), so the callback Task faults and the transport can retry / dead-letter instead of silently acking a lost event. New `Birko.EventBus.MessageQueue.Tests` (capturing in-memory transport) assert a handler exception faults the callback, all handlers still run when one throws, and successful handlers don't fault.
- **Detail:** In the transport subscription callback, each handler invocation is wrapped in try/catch with an empty catch ('Error isolation: continue to next handler'). Because the message-queue consumer determines redelivery/DLQ by whether the delivery callback throws, swallowing every handler exception means the message is always acked as successful. A handler that fails (e.g. transient DB error) is never retried and never dead-lettered — the event is silently lost. This also directly explains why DistributedEventBusOptions.RetryPolicy and DeadLetterOptions are never wired into the bus: there is no failure path for them to act on.
- **Fix:** Track whether any handler threw and rethrow an aggregated exception after the loop (so the consumer can retry/DLQ), or honor the configured RetryPolicy/DeadLetterOptions explicitly. At minimum, surface the swallowed exception via a logger/error hook rather than discarding it entirely.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. DistributedEventBus.cs:176-184 wraps each handler.HandleAsync call in a try/catch with an empty body and the comment "Error isolation: continue to next handler", exactly as described. The transport delivery callback (Func<QueueMessage, CancellationToken, Task> passed to _messageQueue.Consumer.SubscribeAsync at line 134) signals failure to the queue only by throwing/faulting its Task; the standard MQ ack/redelivery/DLQ model (RejectAsync(requeue), DeliveryCount, x-delivery-count, DeadLetterOptions.GetDeadLetterDestination) is driven by whether the callback throws. Because every handler exception is swallowed, the callback Task always completes successfully, so failed messages are acked and never retried or dead-lettered — the event is silently lost. The finding's secondary claim is also verified: DistributedEventBusOptions declares RetryPolicy (default MaxRetries=3) and DeadLetterOptions (default Enabled=true) at lines 27/32, but a project-wide grep shows they are referenced nowhere in the bus logic — there is no failure path for them to act on, and the empty catch is exactly that missing path. The swallow is also nested inside _pipeline.ExecuteAsync, so even pipeline-level retry behaviors can never observe a handler failure. Only caveat: Birko.MessageQueue is abstractions-only in this checkout, so I could not inspect a concrete consumer literally redelivering on throw; but the RejectAsync/DeliveryCount/DLQ contract makes the throw-drives-redelivery assumption correct and idiomatic. Genuine, high-severity, actionable bug.

### CR-H115 · 🟠 high · Birko.EventBus.Outbox
- **Title:** OutboxOptions.MaxAttempts is never enforced (dead option)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.EventBus.Outbox\Publishing/OutboxProcessor.cs:81 (and Core/OutboxOptions.cs:23, Core/IOutboxStore.cs:35)`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — plumbed the attempt cap through the store contract: `IOutboxStore.MarkFailedAsync` now takes `int maxAttempts`, `OutboxProcessor` passes `_options.MaxAttempts` at all three call sites, and `InMemoryOutboxStore` transitions to `Failed` at `Attempts >= maxAttempts` instead of the hardcoded 5. New `Birko.EventBus.Outbox.Tests` verify the store honors the cap and the processor fails an entry at the configured `MaxAttempts` (2), not 5.
- **Detail:** OutboxOptions.MaxAttempts (default 5) is configurable via AddOutbox(configure => o.MaxAttempts = N) but is read by nothing. OutboxProcessor.ProcessBatchAsync just calls _store.MarkFailedAsync(entry.Id, ex.Message, ct) and leaves the retry-limit decision entirely to the store. The store interface MarkFailedAsync(Guid, string, CancellationToken) does not receive MaxAttempts either, so a custom IOutboxStore implementer has no way to honor it. InMemoryOutboxStore hardcodes '>= 5' (Stores/InMemoryOutboxStore.cs:52), which the project CLAUDE.md even calls out as a known hardcode. Net effect: setting MaxAttempts to anything other than 5 silently does nothing, and a failed event retries forever (or per whatever each store hardcodes).
- **Fix:** Either pass the attempt cap through the store contract (e.g. MarkFailedAsync(Guid entryId, string error, int maxAttempts, CancellationToken)) so the store can transition to Failed, or have OutboxProcessor read entry.Attempts against _options.MaxAttempts and decide Pending-vs-Failed itself. Remove the hardcoded 5 in InMemoryOutboxStore once the cap is plumbed through.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading all cited files plus a full-project grep.

1. OutboxOptions.MaxAttempts exists (Core/OutboxOptions.cs:23, default 5) and is publicly configurable via the options object.

2. It is read by NOTHING in executable code. A project-wide grep for "MaxAttempts" returns only: the definition itself, CLAUDE.md, and README.md (which claims "Failed publishes retried up to MaxAttempts"). A grep for "_options." shows the processor only consumes BatchSize, PollingInterval, and RetentionPeriod — never MaxAttempts.

3. OutboxProcessor.ProcessBatchAsync (Publishing/OutboxProcessor.cs:81) calls _store.MarkFailedAsync(entry.Id, ex.Message, cancellationToken) on failure, delegating the entire retry-limit decision to the store and never passing MaxAttempts.

5. InMemoryOutboxStore.MarkFailedAsync (Stores/InMemoryOutboxStore.cs:52) hardcodes "entry.Attempts >= 5" to decide Failed vs Pending, ignoring the configured MaxAttempts.

The README documenting "retried up to MaxAttempts" makes this a genuine, user-visible contract violation. This is a real, actionable high-severity finding — a dead/unenforced configuration option with a misleading interface contract.

### CR-H116 · 🟠 high · Birko.EventBus.Outbox
- **Title:** OutboxStatus.Publishing is never set — no claim/lock, enabling duplicate publishes
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.EventBus.Outbox\Stores/InMemoryOutboxStore.cs:24-33 (GetPendingAsync), Core/OutboxStatus.cs:16`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `InMemoryOutboxStore.GetPendingAsync` now atomically CLAIMS its batch (Pending → `Publishing`, stamping a new `OutboxEntry.ClaimedAt`) under a lock, so two concurrent processors never return — and publish — the same entries. Stale claims (a crashed processor) are reclaimed to Pending after a configurable `staleClaimTimeout` (default 5 min); `MarkPublished`/`MarkFailed` clear `ClaimedAt`. This implements the previously-dead `OutboxStatus.Publishing` "locked by processor" state. New `OutboxClaimTests` cover claim-on-read, no double-claim (incl. 8-way concurrent), Publishing transition, and stale reclaim.
- **Detail:** OutboxStatus.Publishing is documented as 'Currently being published (locked by processor)', but nothing ever transitions an entry into it. GetPendingAsync returns entries with Status == Pending and leaves them Pending; only MarkPublished/MarkFailed change status afterward. There is no atomic claim step. With more than one processor instance (the normal HA outbox deployment), or any overlap, two processors call GetPendingAsync, both see the same Pending rows, and both publish them — the event bus receives duplicates. The Publishing state and its doc comment describe a guarantee the code does not provide. The IOutboxStore contract also offers no claim primitive, so SQL/Mongo implementers have no hook to do a SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED style claim.
- **Fix:** Add a claim step to the store contract — e.g. GetPendingAsync atomically transitions the returned rows to Publishing (and a real store does it with row locks / conditional updates), with a recovery path to reset stale Publishing rows back to Pending after a timeout. At minimum document that the current design assumes a single processor instance.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified against the actual code in C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.EventBus.Outbox.

1. OutboxStatus.Publishing (Core/OutboxStatus.cs:16) is defined with doc "Currently being published (locked by processor)" but is NEVER assigned anywhere — a project-wide grep for "Publishing" shows only the projitems compile entries, docs, and the enum definition; no code transitions an entry to it. Status assignments only ever set Published (MarkPublishedAsync), Failed/Pending (MarkFailedAsync).

2. InMemoryOutboxStore.GetPendingAsync (Stores/InMemoryOutboxStore.cs:24-33) filters Status == Pending, orders by CreatedAt, takes batchSize, and returns — it does NOT mutate status to Publishing or otherwise claim/lock the rows. They remain Pending until a later MarkPublished/MarkFailed.

3. The IOutboxStore contract (Core/IOutboxStore.cs) exposes only SaveAsync, GetPendingAsync, MarkPublishedAsync, MarkFailedAsync, CleanupAsync — there is no atomic claim/lease primitive, so a SQL/Mongo implementer has no hook for SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED style claiming. Confirmed exactly as the finding states.

4. OutboxProcessor.ProcessBatchAsync (Publishing/OutboxProcessor.cs:42-87) reads pending entries, then in a loop publishes each and only afterward marks published. With two processors (or overlapping batches), both read the same Pending rows and both publish — duplicate delivery, with no claim step between read and publish.

Caveat that does not reduce realness: InMemoryOutboxStore is explicitly documented as test/dev-only (lines 11-12), so the in-memory store itself isn't a production HA target. But the finding's substance is contract/design-level: the documented 'locked by processor' guarantee of OutboxStatus.Publishing is unimplemented, and the IOutboxStore interface offers no claim primitive — so every implementer inherits the duplicate-publish design. For an outbox pattern (whose purpose is reliable delivery), a dead 'Publishing' state plus a contract with no claim hook is a genuine correctness/design gap, accurately and specifically described, with clear remediation (add an atomic claim primitive to IOutboxStore and have GetPending transition to Publishing). High severity is reasonable. Actionable.

### CR-H117 · 🟠 high · Birko.Helpers
- **Title:** PathValidator containment check is vulnerable to sibling-prefix path traversal
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Helpers\PathValidator.cs:50, :101, :184`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — all three containment checks (`ValidatePath`, `CombineAndValidate`, `CombineAndValidateUnchecked`) now delegate to `PathHelper.IsUnderDirectory(normalizedCombinedPath, normalizedBasePath)` instead of the raw `StartsWith`, so a sibling-prefixed path (`C:\data-evil\x` under base `C:\data`) is correctly rejected — the boundary-aware primitive appends the directory separator and allows exact-equality + alt separators. New `PathValidatorTests` regressions cover the sibling-prefix escape (throws), a genuine child (accepted), and the exact-base case (accepted); `Birko.Helpers.Tests` 65 → 68 green.
- **Detail:** ValidatePath, CombineAndValidate, and CombineAndValidateUnchecked all decide containment with normalizedCombinedPath.StartsWith(normalizedBasePath, OrdinalIgnoreCase). This is the exact bug PathHelper.IsUnderDirectory (same project) was written to prevent: with basePath 'C:\data' a resolved path 'C:\data-evil\x' passes StartsWith and is wrongly accepted as 'inside' the base, defeating the traversal guard these methods exist to provide. Because these are the project's security primitives against path traversal, the false-accept is a real escape vector.
- **Fix:** Reuse PathHelper.IsUnderDirectory(normalizedCombinedPath, normalizedBasePath) for the containment test in all three methods instead of raw StartsWith (it appends the directory separator and handles exact-equality + alt separators).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Helpers\PathValidator.cs. Lines 50, 101, and 184 all decide path containment with normalizedCombinedPath.StartsWith(normalizedBasePath, OrdinalIgnoreCase) and no directory-separator boundary. Since Path.GetFullPath strips trailing separators, a base of "C:\data" is a literal string prefix of "C:\data-evil\x" — I empirically verified StartsWith returns True for exactly this case. The finding's claim that the same project already contains the correct primitive is accurate: PathHelper.IsUnderDirectory (Path/PathHelper.cs:74-86) exists specifically to prevent this, with a doc comment stating "Prevents false matches where e.g. 'C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Data' would match 'C:\Source\Birko'", and it correctly checks equality plus base+separator. These are the project's stated path-traversal security primitives. One nuance: CombineAndValidate (101) and CombineAndValidateUnchecked (184) sanitize the user path via SanitizePath (strips leading slashes/drive letters/..) and use Path.Combine, so the combined result is always rooted under base — the sibling-prefix escape is effectively unreachable through those two. But ValidatePath (50) takes a caller-supplied combinedPath with no sanitization and directly false-accepts a sibling-prefixed path, so it is genuinely exploitable. The flawed pattern is present in all three sites and inconsistent with the project's own correct helper, making the fix clear and actionable (delegate to IsUnderDirectory or compare against base+separator). Real, actionable issue; the file path is C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Helpers\PathValidator.cs.

### CR-H118 · 🟠 high · Birko.Localization

The XML doc and the interface (INumberFormatter.cs:14) both promise formatting 'with the specified currency code', but calling FormatCurrency(99.99m, "USD", de-DE) renders '99,99 EUR' (euro), and 'GBP' vs 'USD' under the same culture are indistinguishable. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Localization\Providers\NumberFormatter.cs:24-29, FormatCurrency(decimal, string currencyCode, CultureInfo?) only validates currencyCode via ArgumentException.ThrowIfNullOrWhiteSpace(currencyCode) (line 26) and then returns value.ToString("C", resolved) (line 28) — the currencyCode parameter is never used to affect output. The "C" specifier uses the resolved culture's NumberFormatInfo.CurrencySymbol, so the actual currency code is ignored. The interface contract in Core/INumberFormatter.cs:14 ("Formats a value as currency with the specified currency code") is not honored. A project-wide grep for currencyCode/CurrencySymbol/RegionInfo/ISOCurrencySymbol shows no alternate path consuming the code — there is no other overload or helper that uses it. Thus FormatCurrency(99.99m, "USD", de-DE) renders with the euro symbol, and GBP vs USD under one culture are indistinguishable; the parameter is effectively dead except for the guard. This is a genuine high-severity correctness bug (silently wrong currency output). Caveat: the cited test file NumberFormatterTests.cs:27 does not exist in this repo (tests likely live in a sibling .Tests checkout), so that corroborating detail is unverifiable here, but it does not affect the core finding, which is directly confirmed from the implementation and interface.

### CR-H119 · 🟠 high · Birko.MessageQueue.InMemory
- **Title:** InMemoryChannel and its dispatch loops / CancellationTokenSources are never disposed (resource leak)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.MessageQueue.InMemory\InMemoryMessageQueue.cs:47`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `InMemoryChannel` now implements `IDisposable`: its `Dispose()` iterates every `DestinationState`, cancels + disposes the dispatch loop's `DispatchCts`, completes the channel writer, and clears subscribers/destinations; `InMemoryMessageQueue.Dispose()` now calls `_channel.Dispose()` after disposing Producer/Consumer. `RemoveSubscriber` also disposes (not just cancels+nulls) the CTS when the last subscriber leaves. New `Birko.MessageQueue.InMemory.Tests` (registered in `.slnx` + `.code-workspace`) cover dispatch delivery, disposal stopping delivery, idempotent dispose with an active subscriber, the remove→re-add CTS-recycle path, and queue-level dispose with an open subscription — 7 green. (In-memory backend is test/dev-only, but the leak was real across many queue create/destroy cycles.)
- **Detail:** InMemoryMessageQueue.Dispose() disposes Producer and Consumer but never touches _channel. InMemoryChannel owns one DestinationState per destination, each of which holds a CancellationTokenSource (DispatchCts, an IDisposable) and may have a long-running Task.Run dispatch loop (StartDispatching, InMemoryChannel.cs:111). Disposing the consumer only sets a flag and clears the pending-ack dictionary; it does not call RemoveSubscriber, so the dispatch tasks keep running and the CancellationTokenSources are never cancelled or disposed. Over the lifetime of a process that creates/destroys many queues this leaks tasks and CTS handles. InMemoryChannel has no Dispose method at all.
- **Fix:** Give InMemoryChannel a Dispose() that iterates _destinations, calls DispatchCts?.Cancel()/Dispose(), and completes each Channel.Writer; call it from InMemoryMessageQueue.Dispose(). Also dispose the per-destination DispatchCts inside RemoveSubscriber when it is cancelled+nulled (InMemoryChannel.cs:95-96 cancels but never disposes the old CTS).
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading all four relevant files. The finding is accurate and actionable.

1. InMemoryMessageQueue.Dispose() (InMemoryMessageQueue.cs:47-58) disposes Producer and Consumer but never references _channel.

2. InMemoryChannel (InMemoryChannel.cs) has no Dispose method at all (read the entire file; it does not implement IDisposable).

3. Each DestinationState holds a CancellationTokenSource (DispatchCts, line 142) and a long-running Task.Run dispatch loop (StartDispatching, line 111). The loop only ends when DispatchCts is cancelled (or the channel writer completes), neither of which happens on queue disposal.

4. InMemoryConsumer.Dispose() (InMemoryConsumer.cs:107-111) only sets _disposed = true and clears _pendingAck. It does NOT call RemoveSubscriber, and the consumer never tracks the InMemorySubscription objects it creates (each is returned to the caller and forgotten). So consumer disposal cannot tear down subscriptions or dispatch loops.

5. Cleanup only happens if the caller explicitly invokes InMemorySubscription.UnsubscribeAsync()/Dispose() (InMemorySubscription.cs:25-42), which routes to RemoveSubscriber and cancels the CTS. Disposing the queue alone does none of this.

Therefore, disposing the queue without manually unsubscribing leaves dispatch Task.Run loops running and CancellationTokenSources alive — a genuine leak across many queue create/destroy cycles.

Additional supporting detail (beyond the finding): even on the proper RemoveSubscriber path (line 95) the CTS is Cancel()'d but never Dispose()'d (just set to null), so CTS handles leak even when subscriptions are cleaned up correctly.

Caveat on severity: this is a test/dev-only in-memory backend (per its own XML doc), so "high" is somewhat aggressive in practical impact, but the resource-leak bug, the cited file/line, and every claim in the detail are correct. The proper fix is to make InMemoryChannel IDisposable (cancel + dispose all DispatchCts, complete writers), dispose it from the queue, and ideally Dispose the CTS in RemoveSubscriber.

### CR-H120 · 🟠 high · Birko.MessageQueue.MQTT
- **Title:** Typed SendAsync<T> silently drops Headers and PayloadType on the wire
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.MessageQueue.MQTT\MqttProducer.cs:48-61`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the producer now carries `QueueMessage.PayloadType` and the serialized `Headers` as MQTT5 user properties (`payload_type` / `headers`) on `SendAsync(string, QueueMessage)` (so both the typed and untyped paths benefit), and `MqttConsumer.OnMessageReceivedAsync` reconstructs them from `args.ApplicationMessage.UserProperties` — restoring metadata parity with the Redis/InMemory backends. On an MQTT 3.1.1 connection user properties are unsupported and (as before) not carried; a non-Birko publisher with no user properties keeps defaults. New `Birko.MessageQueue.MQTT.Tests` (registered in `.slnx` + `.code-workspace`; injected `IMqttClient` mocked via Moq) cover producer property emission, a full producer→consumer round-trip (PayloadType + CorrelationId/ReplyTo/GroupId/Custom preserved), typed-subscribe metadata via `MessageContext`, and the no-user-properties defaults case — 4 green.
- **Detail:** SendAsync<T> builds a QueueMessage populating PayloadType (typeof(T).AssemblyQualifiedName) and Headers (ContentType), but the underlying SendAsync(destination, QueueMessage) at line 38-43 only publishes message.Body via WithPayload. The MqttApplicationMessage carries no MQTT user properties / content-type, so PayloadType and all Headers are discarded. On the consume side OnMessageReceivedAsync (MqttConsumer.cs:109-113) reconstructs QueueMessage with only Body and CreatedAt — Headers/PayloadType are always default. A typed publish/subscribe round-trip therefore loses all metadata the producer carefully attached. MQTT 5 user properties (MqttApplicationMessageBuilder.WithUserProperty / WithContentType) should carry these, or the omission should be documented as intentional.
- **Fix:** Map QueueMessage.Headers and PayloadType onto MQTT5 user properties / content-type in the producer, and read them back in OnMessageReceivedAsync; or explicitly document that MQTT transports body only.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading the actual source. The finding is accurate on every cited point:

1. MqttProducer.SendAsync<T> (MqttProducer.cs:48-61) builds a QueueMessage populating PayloadType (typeof(T).AssemblyQualifiedName, line 56) and Headers (ContentType, line 57), then delegates to SendAsync(string, QueueMessage, ...).

2. SendAsync(string, QueueMessage) (MqttProducer.cs:38-43) builds the MqttApplicationMessage with only .WithTopic and .WithPayload(message.Body). It never sets MQTT user properties or content-type. I grep-confirmed there is NO WithUserProperty/WithContentType anywhere in the MQTT project — so PayloadType and all Headers fields (CorrelationId, ReplyTo, ContentType, GroupId, Custom) are discarded on the wire.

3. On the consume side, OnMessageReceivedAsync (MqttConsumer.cs:109-113) reconstructs QueueMessage with only Body and CreatedAt. Headers defaults to a new MessageHeaders() and PayloadType is null. No code reads args.ApplicationMessage user properties.

Impact assessment / corroboration:
- This is a real data-loss bug, not an accepted convention. The peer Redis backend explicitly round-trips this metadata: RedisProducer.cs:45-46 serializes payload_type and headers as wire fields, and RedisConsumer.cs:341/348-351 reconstructs PayloadType and deserializes Headers back. The InMemory backend keeps the same object so metadata survives trivially. MQTT is the deviant one.
- The metadata IS observable to consumers: MessageContext.Message exposes the full QueueMessage (MessageContext.cs:13), and SubscribeAsync<T> hands handlers a MessageContext (MqttConsumer.cs:66). Any handler reading context.Message.Headers.CorrelationId / Custom / ContentType, or Message.PayloadType, silently gets defaults after an MQTT round-trip.

One nuance worth noting (does not reduce realness): the typed deserialization itself still works, because SubscribeAsync<T> deserializes using the static T (DeserializePayload<T>, MqttConsumer.cs:132-139), not the wire PayloadType. So payloads round-trip correctly; it is purely the metadata (PayloadType + all Headers) that is lost. The finding states exactly this. Severity 'high' is defensible since cross-service correlation/reply-to/custom headers and content-type are core message-queue metadata that other backends preserve, and the loss is silent.

The suggested fix is appropriate: MQTT 5 user properties via WithUserProperty/WithContentType on publish, with matching reconstruction from args.ApplicationMessage.UserProperties on receive (or, if MQTT 3.1.1 broker compatibility is required, document the limitation explicitly).

### CR-H121 · 🟠 high · Birko.MessageQueue.Redis
- **Title:** RejectAsync(requeue:true) and ManualAck failures never trigger redelivery
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.MessageQueue.Redis\RedisConsumer.cs:95-103, 127-135`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the consumer-group poll loop now reclaims idle pending entries: after a `">"` read returns empty, it issues **XAUTOCLAIM** (`ReclaimPendingEntriesAsync`) for entries idle ≥ a new `RedisStreamSettings.PendingRetryMilliseconds` (default 30 s; `0` disables) and re-processes them — so ManualAck failures and `RejectAsync(requeue:true)` are actually re-delivered during the subscription lifetime (and entries orphaned by a crashed consumer are reclaimed too). `RejectAsync` now honors `requeue`: `false` **XACK**s the entry (leaves the PEL, not re-delivered); `true` leaves it unacked for the reclaim pass — the old code ignored the flag and only dropped the local tracker (a silent no-op). Per-entry processing (TTL/manual-ack/handler/auto-ack) was factored into a shared `ProcessEntryAsync` used by the live poll, the FromBeginning pass, and reclaim. Added an internal `Func<IDatabase>` test seam; 5 new tests in `Birko.MessageQueue.Redis.Tests` (mocked `IDatabase`): XAUTOCLAIM redelivery + auto-ack end-to-end via the real poll loop, `RejectAsync` requeue-vs-no-requeue XACK semantics, unknown-id no-op, and the settings default — 33 → 38 green.
- **Detail:** In consumer-group mode the poll loop reads with a fixed position of ">" (new messages only) after the optional FromBeginning pass. When a handler throws under ManualAck, or RejectAsync(requeue:true) is called, the entry stays in the Pending Entries List but is never re-read — ">" only returns never-delivered messages, and nothing ever issues XREADGROUP from "0" / XPENDING / XCLAIM again. RejectAsync just removes the pending tracker and returns, so requeue is silently a no-op. The class XML doc and RejectAsync's own comment promise re-delivery via the PEL/XCLAIM, but no code path reclaims those entries during the lifetime of the subscription. Messages that fail processing are effectively lost until a brand-new FromBeginning subscription runs.
- **Fix:** Periodically reclaim pending entries: after the ">" read returns empty, issue a XAUTOCLAIM / XREADGROUP from "0" (or XPENDING + XCLAIM with a min-idle threshold) to re-process unacked entries owned by this consumer. RejectAsync(requeue:true) should leave the entry unacked (already does) but the loop must actually re-read it.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.MessageQueue.Redis\RedisConsumer.cs in full.

The steady-state consumer-group poll loop reads only new messages: the `position` variable (line 127) is `">"` whenever the loop body runs StreamReadGroupAsync (line 145-151). The only `"0"` path is ProcessPendingEntriesAsync, invoked exactly once at startup and only when Options.FromBeginning is true (line 131-135), after which position is forced back to `">"` (line 134). In Redis, XREADGROUP with `>` returns only never-delivered entries; entries already in the Pending Entries List (PEL) require an explicit ID read (`0`), XPENDING, or XCLAIM to retrieve.

Tracing the three failure paths:
1. ManualAck handler throws (line 215-222): removes the tracker, leaves the entry in the PEL with comment "stays in pending entries list for consumer group re-delivery" — but no code ever re-reads `0`/XPENDING/XCLAIM during the subscription lifetime, so it is never re-delivered.
2. RejectAsync(requeue:true) (line 95-103): the `requeue` parameter is entirely ignored. It only calls _pendingAck.TryRemove and returns Task.CompletedTask — no XACK, no XCLAIM, no re-read. requeue:true and requeue:false are identical no-ops. The inline comment (line 99-100) claims Redis re-delivers "via XCLAIM or pending entry list," and grep confirms NO XCLAIM/StreamClaim/StreamPending/XPENDING/XAUTOCLAIM exists anywhere in the project (the only match is that comment).
3. The class XML doc / comments promise PEL+XCLAIM redelivery that no code path implements during a live subscription.

So failed/rejected messages accumulate in the PEL and are only reclaimed if a brand-new FromBeginning subscription is started — exactly as the finding states. The cited line ranges (95-103 for RejectAsync, 127-135 for the position logic) match precisely. One small precision: messages are not strictly "lost" (they persist in PEL and stream and a fresh FromBeginning subscription would reclaim them), but the documented requeue/redelivery contract is silently broken for the normal subscription lifetime. This is a genuine, high-severity correctness bug.

  var normalizedBase = Path.GetFullPath(_basePath);
  if (!fullPath.StartsWith(normalizedBase, StringComparison.OrdinalIgnoreCase)) throw ...

Path.GetFullPath(_basePath) does NOT append a trailing directory separator for a non-root path, so normalizedBase for base 'C:\tpl' is exactly 'C:\tpl'. A prefix-only StartsWith therefore admits any sibling directory whose name begins with the base name.

Reproduced directly: with _basePath = 'C:\tpl' and templateName '../tpl-evil/secret', ResolveFilePath produces fullPath = 'C:\tpl-evil\secret.cshtml', and 'C:\tpl-evil\secret.cshtml'.StartsWith('C:\tpl', OrdinalIgnoreCase) == True. The guard does not throw, so the path escapes the intended base directory into the attacker-controllable sibling 'C:\tpl-evil' — exactly the example in the finding.

The path is reachable: templateName flows from the public GetTemplateAsync with only an IsNullOrWhiteSpace check; '/' and '\' are explicitly normalized and Path.Combine/Path.GetFullPath collapse '../', so '..' traversal segments are resolved before the guard with no earlier sanitization. The stated security intent ('Prevent directory traversal' / 'Template path escapes the base directory') is genuinely not met.

The correct fix is a separator-boundary check, e.g. compare against normalizedBase ending with Path.DirectorySeparatorChar (plus an exact-equality allowance), or use Path.GetRelativePath to confirm containment.

Cited file and line range (102-106) are accurate, and the example is precisely correct. This is a genuine, actionable high-severity directory-traversal weakness.

### CR-H131 · 🟠 high · Birko.Models.Product
- **Title:** ProductList.Filter() combines lambda bodies without rebinding parameters
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Models.Product\Filters/ProductList.cs:30-54`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — replaced the three broken `Expression.Lambda(AndAlso(result.Body, right.Body), …Skip(1)…)` combinations with a shared `AndAlso(left, right)` helper that rebinds `right.Body`'s parameter onto `left`'s single parameter via a `ReplaceParameterVisitor : ExpressionVisitor` before `AndAlso` — so the combined lambda no longer references an unbound parameter and compiles/translates cleanly. New `Birko.Models.Product.Tests` — 6 tests that **compile and execute** the predicate (the operation that used to throw): Search+Category, Search+Tags, Category+Properties, multi-tag AND, single-clause, and no-clause→null.
- **Detail:** Each composed predicate is built as Expression.Lambda<Func<T,bool>>(Expression.AndAlso(result.Body, right.Body), result.Parameters.Concat(right.Parameters.Skip(1)).Distinct()). result.Body and right.Body each reference their OWN distinct ParameterExpression instance (every lambda literal compiles to a fresh 'x'). The combined body therefore references right's 'x', but the lambda's parameter list keeps only result's 'x' (right's is Skip(1)'d away). The resulting expression has a parameter referenced from scope that is not in the lambda's parameter list. This throws InvalidOperationException ("variable 'x' ... referenced from scope ... not defined") on .Compile() or when an ORM/LINQ provider translates it. It only escapes notice when at most ONE clause is active (Search OR Category OR one Tag/Property); the moment two clauses combine (e.g. Search + Category) the filter blows up. The Tags/Properties loops compound it across iterations. A proper ExpressionVisitor that rebinds right.Body's parameter to result.Parameters[0] (or PredicateBuilder.And-style invoke) is required.
- **Fix:** Introduce a parameter-rebinding ExpressionVisitor (replace right's ParameterExpression with the single shared parameter) before AndAlso, or use a shared PredicateBuilder helper. Build the whole predicate against one ParameterExpression created up front. Add tests covering Search+Category, Search+Tags, and Category+Properties combinations.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading Filters/ProductList.cs:25-58 and empirically reproducing the exact pattern. Lines 32, 42, 52 build each composed predicate as Expression.Lambda<Func<T,bool>>(Expression.AndAlso(result.Body, right.Body), result.Parameters.Concat(right.Parameters.Skip(1)).Distinct()). result and right are separate Expression<Func<T,bool>> literals, each with one distinct ParameterExpression (their own 'x'). Because Func<T,bool> always has exactly one parameter, right.Parameters.Skip(1) is always empty, so the lambda's parameter list keeps ONLY result's 'x'. The combined body still references right's 'x', which is therefore unbound. I reproduced the identical construction in a standalone net8.0 program: it throws InvalidOperationException: \"variable 'x' of type 'Foo' referenced from scope '', but it is not defined\" on .Compile(). The bug only manifests when two or more clauses combine (Search+Category, or via the Tags/Properties foreach loops gated by IProductTags/IProductProperties, both of which exist and are reachable); single-clause paths return a bare lambda and work. ToString() of the broken tree even prints plausibly (both params named 'x'), masking the defect on inspection. The finding's mechanism, file/line citation, high severity, and recommended fix (ExpressionVisitor rebinding right.Body's parameter to result.Parameters[0], or PredicateBuilder/Invoke composition) are all accurate.
