- **Detail:** FieldBuilder<T> exposes HasColumnName, HasMaxLength, HasPrecision, HasScale, and HasIndex (IndexName/IndexOrder/IndexDescending) as first-class fluent options, and CLAUDE.md documents ApplyToDatabase() as registering 'table names + field metadata'. But the apply loop only propagates four boolean flags (IsPrimary -> sqlField.IsPrimary, IsUnique -> IsUnique, IsRequired -> IsNotNull, IsAutoIncrement -> IsAutoincrement). FieldDescriptor.ColumnName, MaxLength, Precision, Scale, IndexName/IndexOrder/IndexDescending are never read. A consumer who writes map.Property(x => x.Code).HasColumnName("code").HasMaxLength(256).HasIndex("ix_code") gets a config object that compiles and reads back via GetMap<T>()/GetPropertyMaps(), yet none of it reaches the database schema. This is a correctness mismatch between the advertised/documented API and actual behavior. Note: AbstractField (Birko.Data.SQL) only exposes settable Name and no Precision/MaxLength/index members after LoadTable, so propagating these requires either reconstructing the field or extending AbstractField — the current code can't just assign them. The minimum fix is to make the limitation explicit (throw/log on the unsupported builder calls, or document that they are mapping-metadata-only and not applied), rather than letting them appear to work.
- **Fix:** Either extend ApplyToDatabase to apply ColumnName/MaxLength/Precision/Scale/index settings (requires AbstractField support), or explicitly document/guard the builder methods that have no apply path so callers aren't misled. At minimum, add the gap to CLAUDE.md/README.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified against the actual source. ModelMapRegistry.ApplyToDatabase (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Models.SQL\Mapping\ModelMapRegistry.cs:90-99) propagates only four boolean flags: field.IsPrimary -> sqlField.IsPrimary, IsUnique -> IsUnique, IsRequired -> IsNotNull, IsAutoIncrement -> IsAutoincrement. FieldDescriptor.ColumnName, MaxLength, Precision, Scale, IndexName/IndexOrder/IndexDescending are never read.\n\nFieldBuilder<T> (Mapping/FieldBuilder.cs) does expose all the dropped options as first-class fluent methods: HasColumnName (line 16), HasPrecision (52), HasScale (58), HasMaxLength (64), HasIndex (70) — each writes to the FieldDescriptor, which stores all of them (Birko.Data.Patterns/Schema/FieldDescriptor.cs has ColumnName, MaxLength, Precision, Scale, IndexName, IndexOrder, IndexDescending). So the config compiles and reads back via GetMap/GetPropertyMaps, but none of those facets reach the schema.\n\nDocs confirm the advertised behavior: CLAUDE.md:28 says ApplyToDatabase 'registers table names and field metadata' and README.md:11 says it 'patches field metadata onto the SQL layer'. This is a real mismatch between documented/advertised API and actual behavior.\n\nThe finding's note about AbstractField is also accurate: Birko.Data.SQL/SQL/Fields/AbstractField.cs only has settable Name, IsPrimary, IsUnique, IsNotNull, IsAutoincrement; length/precision/scale are baked into concrete field subtypes (CharField/DecimalField) at construction time in CreateAbstractField, and there is no index member at all — so the post-LoadTable field genuinely cannot accept these via simple assignment. The proposed minimum fix (make the limitation explicit, or document it as mapping-metadata-only) is sound. Severity 'high' is slightly generous for length/precision/scale (DDL-only), but HasColumnName silently dropped is a genuine correctness risk, and the core finding is fully confirmed.

### CR-H133 · 🟠 high · Birko.Random
- **Title:** SnowflakeGenerator.WaitNextMillisecond returns absolute Unix ms, not epoch-relative
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Random\Sequences\SnowflakeGenerator.cs:107-117`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `WaitNextMillisecond` now computes `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds() - _epoch` (epoch-relative, consistent with `Next()`), dropping `static` so it can read `_epoch`. Previously it returned raw absolute Unix ms, so the `while (timestamp <= lastTimestamp)` guard was always false on the first iteration (absolute ≫ relative) and the ~1.7e12 value overflowed the 41-bit timestamp field once the per-ms sequence exhausted. New tests in `Birko.Random.Tests` (113 → 115): a deterministic reflection test asserting `WaitNextMillisecond` returns an epoch-relative value (≈ now − epoch, far below absolute ms), and a 20 000-ID tight-loop test that forces sequence rollover and asserts uniqueness/monotonicity + a sane decoded timestamp.
- **Detail:** Next() works in epoch-relative time: `timestamp = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds() - _epoch` (line 52), and _lastTimestamp stores that relative value. But WaitNextMillisecond returns the raw absolute `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()` (line 113), without subtracting _epoch. When the per-ms sequence (4096 IDs) is exhausted within one millisecond, Next() assigns this absolute value to `timestamp`, stores it in _lastTimestamp, and shifts it into the ID (line 76). The absolute Unix-ms value (~1.7e12) far exceeds the 41-bit timestamp field, so it overflows into the machine-id/sequence bits and the sign bit, corrupting every subsequent ID and breaking ExtractTimestamp/monotonicity. It is latent only because the tests never generate >4096 IDs in a single millisecond.
- **Fix:** Return epoch-relative time from WaitNextMillisecond, e.g. compute `timestamp = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds() - _epoch` in the loop and compare against the (relative) lastTimestamp. Pass/return relative values consistently.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Random\Sequences\SnowflakeGenerator.cs. The mismatch is real:

- Line 52: Next() works in epoch-relative time: `timestamp = DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds() - _epoch`. _lastTimestamp (line 74) therefore stores epoch-relative values.
- Line 60: On sequence exhaustion, `timestamp = WaitNextMillisecond(_lastTimestamp)` passes an epoch-relative argument.
- Lines 107-117: WaitNextMillisecond compares against and returns the raw absolute `DateTimeOffset.UtcNow.ToUnixTimeMilliseconds()` (line 113) WITHOUT subtracting _epoch. It does not even use the relative scale, so the returned value is absolute Unix ms (~1.75e12 in 2026).

Consequences are exactly as described:
1. The loop guard `timestamp <= lastTimestamp` compares absolute (~1.75e12) to epoch-relative (~7.7e10), so it exits immediately on the first iteration and returns an absolute value.
2. Line 76 shifts that absolute value left by TimestampShift = 22 bits. ~1.75e12 occupies ~41 bits; shifting by 22 pushes it to ~63 bits, overflowing into the machine-id/sequence bits and the sign bit (long.MaxValue ~9.2e18 is exceeded once you also account for it landing past bit 62), corrupting the ID and breaking ExtractTimestamp (line 87 expects an epoch-relative shifted value) and monotonicity.
3. _lastTimestamp is then set to the absolute value (line 74). The very next Next() call computes an epoch-relative timestamp (~7.7e10) which is far less than the stored absolute _lastTimestamp, tripping the `timestamp < _lastTimestamp` check (line 68) and throwing "Clock moved backwards" on every subsequent call.

The bug is latent only because triggering it requires exhausting all 4096 sequence values within a single millisecond, which the tests do not do. The fix is to subtract _epoch in WaitNextMillisecond (and make it an instance method, or pass _epoch), so it returns epoch-relative ms consistent with the rest of Next(). Severity "high" is justified. Single definition of the method exists; no compensating logic elsewhere.

### CR-H134 · 🟠 high · Birko.Rules
- **Title:** Disabled child rule fails an AND group (evaluator vs expression-converter inconsistency)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Rules\Evaluation\RuleEvaluator.cs:71-80`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `EvaluateGroup` now skips disabled children (`if (!child.IsEnabled) continue;`) in both the AND and OR branches, mirroring `RuleExpressionConverter.BuildGroupExpression` — so a disabled child no longer fails an AND group. An empty or all-disabled group is documented as `NoMatch` (consistent with the existing empty-group rule), tracked via an `evaluatedAny` flag. New `Birko.Rules.Tests` (130 → 135, shared with CR-H135) assert: disabled child is skipped not failed, the in-memory evaluator and the LINQ converter agree on that tree, an enabled non-matching child still fails, and an all-disabled group is NoMatch. [grouped with CR-H135]
- **Detail:** In EvaluateGroup, an AND group iterates children and calls Evaluate(child). A disabled child (IsEnabled == false) returns RuleResult.NoMatch at RuleEvaluator.cs:13-14, so the AND short-circuits to NoMatch for the whole group. A disabled rule therefore actively fails an AND group instead of being ignored. This directly contradicts the expression-converter path, which skips disabled rules via 'continue' (RuleExpressionConverter.cs:153-154 in BuildGroupExpression, and :48-50/:75-77 in the RuleSet/IEnumerable overloads). The same in-memory vs predicate query over identical rules will produce different results. For OR groups a disabled child is harmlessly skipped, masking the asymmetry. RuleSet evaluation (Evaluate(RuleSet) -> EvaluateMatches) likewise treats top-level disabled rules as non-matches rather than skipping them, but the group case is the clear defect.
- **Fix:** In EvaluateGroup, skip disabled children before deciding match (e.g. 'if (!child.IsEnabled) continue;' for both AND and OR), mirroring BuildGroupExpression. Decide and document the empty/all-disabled group result (currently NoMatch) so both paths agree.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading both files.

RuleEvaluator.cs:
- Evaluate (lines 11-22): a disabled rule returns RuleResult.NoMatch(rule) at lines 13-14.
- EvaluateGroup (lines 66-91), AND branch (lines 71-80): iterates children, calls Evaluate(child); on the first non-match it returns RuleResult.NoMatch(group). Since a disabled child yields NoMatch, a disabled child forces the entire AND group to fail rather than being ignored. The OR branch (lines 81-90) only acts on matches, so a disabled child is harmlessly skipped there — exactly the masking asymmetry the finding describes.

RuleExpressionConverter.cs:
- BuildExpression returns null for a disabled rule (lines 94-95).
- BuildGroupExpression (lines 144-176): for each child it calls BuildExpression and does `if (childExpr is null) continue;` (lines 153-154), so a disabled child is dropped from BOTH the AndAlso and OrElse combination — i.e. truly ignored. The RuleSet overload (lines 47-57, `continue` at 49-50) and the IEnumerable overload (lines 74-83, `continue` at 75-77) apply the same skip.

This is a genuine, actionable semantic divergence: evaluating the same rule tree in-memory (RuleEvaluator) versus as a LINQ predicate (RuleExpressionConverter) produces different results when an AND group contains a disabled child — the converter skips it (so the group can still match on its remaining enabled children), while the evaluator fails the whole group. Cited line numbers are accurate.

The RuleSet top-level claim is slightly weaker but defensible: Evaluate(RuleSet) -> EvaluateMatches filters via Where(r => r.IsMatch), so a disabled top-level rule simply never appears in the matches list — functionally equivalent to skipping at the top level, so no observable divergence there. The finding itself acknowledges the group case is the clear defect, which holds.

Nothing in CLAUDE.md/README documents disabled-child-fails-AND as intended; CLAUDE.md only says the evaluator "respects IsEnabled," which is consistent with treating disabled rules as absent (the converter's behavior), making the evaluator the buggy side. High severity is justified because it silently changes match outcomes between two paths the library presents as equivalent ways to apply the same rules.

### CR-H135 · 🟠 high · Birko.Rules
- **Title:** Static PropertyCache is a non-thread-safe Dictionary
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Rules\Expressions\RuleExpressionConverter.cs:180,185,197,203`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `PropertyCache` is now a `ConcurrentDictionary<(Type,string), PropertyInfo?>` resolved via `GetOrAdd` (matching `ObjectRuleContext.PropertyCache`), eliminating the unsynchronized read/write on a plain `Dictionary` from the static converter's concurrently-callable entry points. New `Birko.Rules.Tests` concurrency test drives 500 parallel `ToExpression` resolutions of the same type/field and asserts no throw + correct predicates. [grouped with CR-H134]
- **Detail:** RuleExpressionConverter is a static class whose methods can be called concurrently, yet PropertyCache is a plain Dictionary<(Type,string), PropertyInfo?> that is both read (TryGetValue) and written (indexer assignment) from ResolveProperty without any synchronization. Concurrent writes/reads on Dictionary<TKey,TValue> can corrupt its internal buckets and throw or return wrong results (IndexOutOfRangeException / infinite loop are documented failure modes). Note ObjectRuleContext.PropertyCache (ObjectRuleContext.cs:13) correctly uses ConcurrentDictionary for the same purpose, so this is an inconsistency as well as a latent race.
- **Fix:** Switch PropertyCache to ConcurrentDictionary<(Type,string), PropertyInfo?> and use GetOrAdd, matching ObjectRuleContext.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Rules\Expressions\RuleExpressionConverter.cs. The class is declared `public static class` (line 15) with public entry points (ToExpression overloads) that can be invoked concurrently. PropertyCache (line 180) is a plain `Dictionary<(Type, string), PropertyInfo?> = []`. ResolveProperty reads via TryGetValue (line 185) and writes via indexer assignment (lines 197 and 203) with zero synchronization (no lock, no ConcurrentDictionary). Concurrent read/write on Dictionary<TKey,TValue> is a documented data-corruption hazard (IndexOutOfRangeException / infinite loop / wrong results). The write path is reachable on every cache miss. The inconsistency claim is also confirmed: Context\ObjectRuleContext.cs:13 uses ConcurrentDictionary for the identical property-cache purpose. The fix is trivial and obviously correct (use ConcurrentDictionary, GetOrAdd). The only inaccuracy in the finding is a wrong folder for the secondary file (it is Context\ObjectRuleContext.cs, not Expressions\), but the line number and content are correct and this does not affect the primary finding. Genuine, high-severity-plausible, actionable latent race.

### CR-H136 · 🟠 high · Birko.Security
- **Title:** AuthenticationService owns a ReaderWriterLockSlim but does not implement IDisposable
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security\Authentication/AuthenticationService.cs:13,254`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `AuthenticationService` now declares `: IDisposable`, so its existing `Dispose()` (releasing the `ReaderWriterLockSlim`) is reachable by DI containers and `using`. Added a `_disposed` double-dispose guard and `GC.SuppressFinalize`. New `Birko.Security.Tests` (registered in `.slnx` + `.code-workspace`) — 3 tests: the service is assignable to `IDisposable`, Dispose is idempotent, and it works in a `using` statement.
- **Detail:** The class holds `private readonly ReaderWriterLockSlim _lock` (an IDisposable) and defines a public `Dispose()` method (line 254), but the class declaration `public class AuthenticationService` does NOT implement IDisposable. As a result, `using` statements won't compile against it, and DI containers (it takes an ILogger<T> constructor injection, so it is clearly DI-registered) will never call Dispose because they only dispose instances registered as IDisposable. The ReaderWriterLockSlim (and its kernel/event handles) leaks for the lifetime of every instance that is created and discarded. The lone `Dispose()` method is effectively dead code today because nothing calls it.
- **Fix:** Declare `public class AuthenticationService : IDisposable`. Optionally guard against double-dispose and suppress finalization. This makes the existing Dispose() reachable by DI and `using`.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security\Authentication\AuthenticationService.cs. Line 13 declares `public class AuthenticationService` with NO base class or interface — it does not implement IDisposable. Line 19 holds `private readonly ReaderWriterLockSlim _lock`, which is IDisposable (and wraps kernel/event handles). Lines 254-257 define a `public void Dispose() { _lock?.Dispose(); }`, but because the class does not implement IDisposable, this method is just an ordinary public method, not part of the disposal contract.

Real consequences, all accurate: (1) `using` statements won't compile against the type since it isn't IDisposable; (2) DI containers only invoke Dispose on instances they recognize as IDisposable, so the ReaderWriterLockSlim leaks for the lifetime of every instance created and discarded; (3) the Dispose() method is effectively dead — a repo-wide grep found no callers of `.Dispose()` on the service and no using-statement usage.

Minor caveat: the finding asserts the class "is clearly DI-registered." That is an inference from the optional ILogger<T> constructor param; no actual AddSingleton/AddScoped registration exists in this repo. But the defect is independent of DI: declaring Dispose() without implementing IDisposable is itself a genuine bug, and the correct, trivial fix is to add `: IDisposable` to the declaration. Severity 'high' is slightly generous (per-instance ReaderWriterLockSlim leak, and the service looks long-lived), but the defect and fix are unambiguous and actionable.

### CR-H137 · 🟠 high · Birko.Security.AzureKeyVault
- **Title:** Timeout set on caller-owned (injected) HttpClient
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.AzureKeyVault\AzureKeyVaultSecretProvider.cs:46-48`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the `Timeout` assignment is now gated on `if (_ownsHttpClient)`, so an injected/shared HttpClient's configuration is respected and never mutated (and can't throw `InvalidOperationException` if it already issued a request). New tests in `Birko.Security.AzureKeyVault.Tests` (19 → 21): an injected client's `Timeout` is unchanged after construction, and constructing with an already-used injected client does not throw.
- **Detail:** The constructor sets `_httpClient.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(_settings.TimeoutSeconds)` unconditionally, even when an HttpClient was injected (`_ownsHttpClient == false`). Mutating a shared/caller-owned HttpClient is a surprising side effect, and HttpClient.Timeout throws InvalidOperationException if the client has already issued a request. A shared HttpClient (the recommended pattern to avoid socket exhaustion) passed to this provider would either have its global timeout silently overwritten or throw at construction.
- **Fix:** Only apply the timeout when the provider owns the client: `if (_ownsHttpClient) _httpClient.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(_settings.TimeoutSeconds);`. For injected clients, respect the caller's configuration (or apply per-request timeouts via a linked CancellationTokenSource).
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.AzureKeyVault\AzureKeyVaultSecretProvider.cs lines 46-48. The constructor computes `_ownsHttpClient = httpClient == null` (line 46), assigns `_httpClient = httpClient ?? new HttpClient()` (line 47), then sets `_httpClient.Timeout = TimeSpan.FromSeconds(_settings.TimeoutSeconds)` UNCONDITIONALLY on line 48, with no guard on `_ownsHttpClient`. So when a caller injects an HttpClient (via the second constructor overload that exists specifically for this), its Timeout is mutated.

The detail's claims hold up: (1) AzureKeyVaultSettings.TimeoutSeconds exists and defaults to 30 (AzureKeyVaultSettings.cs:41), so an injected client's timeout is silently overwritten to 30s by default. (2) BCL HttpClient.Timeout setter calls CheckDisposedOrStarted() and throws InvalidOperationException if the client has already issued a request — a well-documented framework behavior — so passing a shared, already-used HttpClient would throw at construction. (3) A shared/singleton HttpClient is the recommended pattern to avoid socket exhaustion, and this class otherwise respects caller ownership (Dispose at line 157 only disposes when _ownsHttpClient). Mutating the caller's client contradicts that ownership model.

This is a genuine, actionable bug with a clear fix: gate line 48 behind `if (_ownsHttpClient)` (or move it into the owned-client branch). The 'high' severity is mildly debatable since it only affects the injection path and the throw-at-construction case needs an already-used client, but the issue and recommendation are correct.

### CR-H138 · 🟠 high · Birko.Security.BCrypt
- **Title:** No known-answer (reference vector) test — round-trip tests cannot detect a wrong algorithm
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework.Tests\Birko.Security.BCrypt.Tests/BCryptPasswordHasherTests.cs`
- **Category:** test-gap · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — reference-vector coverage now exists: the **CR-C24** critical remediation (2026-07-06) already added `BCryptReferenceVectorTests` asserting `Verify()` against canonical jBCrypt `$2a$06$` vectors (empty / "a" / "abc" / a 33-char special-chars password). This finding is closed by adding `BCryptKnownAnswerTests` extending known-answer coverage to a **second work factor (cost 08)** — an independently-generated canonical vector must `Verify()` true and a wrong password must fail — so a regression in the cost/rounds handling can't hide behind self-consistent hashing. `Birko.Security.BCrypt.Tests` 27 → 29. (While writing this I re-confirmed via the known vectors that the post-CR-C24 implementation is genuinely standard-compatible, including for long passwords.)
- **Detail:** Every functional test hashes with this class and verifies with the same class (Hash_And_Verify_RoundTrip, Verify_WrongPassword, ImplementsIPasswordHasher, etc.). A round-trip passes for ANY deterministic, salt-incorporating function — including a broken or non-standard BCrypt. There is no assertion that a fixed (password, salt) pair produces a specific, externally-known '$2a$' hash string. This is exactly the gap that hides the algorithm deviation in finding #1.
- **Fix:** Add tests with hard-coded reference vectors from the OpenBSD/BCrypt spec, e.g. Verify(knownPassword, knownReferenceHashFromAnotherLibrary) must be true, and Hash(knownPassword) with an injected fixed salt must equal the documented output. Optionally cross-check against BCrypt.Net in the test project only.
- **Verify reasoning:** Verified by reading both the test file and the implementation. CONFIRMED REAL.

Test file (C:\Source\Birko\Framework.Tests\Birko.Security.BCrypt.Tests\BCryptPasswordHasherTests.cs) is the only test file in the project. Every functional test hashes and verifies with the same BCryptPasswordHasher instance (Hash_And_Verify_RoundTrip line 22, Verify_WrongPassword line 34, ImplementsIPasswordHasher line 201, Hash_EmptyPassword_Works line 162, Hash_UnicodePassword_Works line 172, etc.). The format tests only assert structural properties: StartWith("$2a$04$"), HaveLength(60), work-factor prefix. A grep for any full 60-char $2a$/$2b$ reference hash string in the test project returns zero matches, confirming no known-answer/reference-vector test exists.

This matters because BCryptPasswordHasher.cs is a fully hand-rolled BCrypt implementation (from-scratch EksBlowfish + Blowfish, not a wrapper around a vetted library like BCrypt.Net). The implementation even contains non-standard-looking key-schedule logic (e.g. EksBlowfishSetup lines 330-398: the salt-streaming at 349-353 with a keyOffset reset, and per-iteration re-keying with StreamToWord over the salt at 388-396 instead of the standard zero block). A self-consistent round-trip test passes for ANY deterministic, salt-incorporating function — including a BCrypt that is interoperable only with itself and not with the real $2a$ standard. The only way to detect such a deviation is to assert that a fixed (password, salt) pair produces a specific externally-known canonical hash string, which no test does.

The finding's claim is precise and accurate, and the concern is well-founded and actionable for hand-rolled crypto. High confidence.

### CR-H140 · 🟠 high · Birko.Security.Vault
- **Title:** UpdatedAt is read from created_time instead of an update timestamp
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Security.Vault\VaultSecretProvider.cs:246`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `UpdatedAt` no longer copies `created_time`. It now reads a genuine update field (`updated_time`, falling back to `mtime`) and is `null` when none is present — which is the real-Vault KV2 case (version metadata exposes only `created_time`), so `UpdatedAt` stops silently equalling `CreatedAt`. The UpdatedAt branch uses a separate out variable `ut`, but it queries the exact same JSON property, so UpdatedAt always equals CreatedAt and never reflects when the secret was last modified. Vault KV v2 metadata exposes the per-version timestamp under "created_time" only at the version level, but the intent of a distinct UpdatedAt field is clearly to carry a different value; copying created_time into it is a silent logic error. No test asserts CreatedAt/UpdatedAt so it went unnoticed.

As a result UpdatedAt is always identical to CreatedAt and never reflects a last-modification time. UpdatedAt is a real, intentional field on SecretResult (documented in docs/security.md:273 alongside CreatedAt), so the duplication is a genuine silent logic error, not a deliberate design. No test in the project asserts CreatedAt/UpdatedAt (grep over test files found none), corroborating the "went unnoticed" claim. One caveat affecting only severity, not validity: Vault KV v2's data.metadata block on a version read does not actually expose a distinct update timestamp (its fields are created_time, version, deletion_time, destroyed, custom_metadata), so there is no clean "updated_time"/"mtime" source to substitute — the correct fix is likely to drop UpdatedAt from the KV2 parse rather than populate it, which the finding itself acknowledges. The defect (a field promising a different value than it carries) is real and actionable; the "high" severity is arguably overstated since it is non-secret metadata, but the bug is genuine.

### CR-H141 · 🟠 high · Birko.Storage
- **Title:** UploadAsync leaves a partial/orphaned file when the write fails or is cancelled
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Storage\Local\LocalFileStorage.cs:74-85`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `UploadAsync` now writes to a sibling temp file (`<path>.<guid>.tmp`) and `File.Move`s it into place (overwrite honoring `OverwriteExisting`) only after a complete write, inside a try/catch that best-effort-deletes the temp on any failure. So a mid-stream failure (size-limit, cancellation, IO error) no longer leaves an orphaned/partial file, and an existing good file is preserved instead of being truncated up front by `FileMode.Create`. New `LocalFileStorageAtomicUploadTests` in `Birko.Storage.Tests` (39 → 42): a mid-stream IO failure leaves no orphan (and no leftover `.tmp`), a failed overwrite preserves the previous good file, and a cancelled-before-write upload leaves nothing behind.
- **Detail:** The destination file is opened with FileMode.Create (truncating any existing file) before the body is streamed. If CopyWithLimitAsync throws FileTooLargeException mid-stream (line 78/452), or content.CopyToAsync is cancelled via ct (line 82), the using block disposes the FileStream but the partially-written (or zero-length) file remains on disk and no metadata is ever written. Net effects: (1) an orphaned/corrupt file is left behind, and (2) since OverwriteExisting defaults to false, a later retry to the same path throws FileAlreadyExistsException against the corrupt remnant, and (3) for an overwrite of a previously-good file, the old good file has already been destroyed. The .meta.json companion is also now out of sync with the truncated content.
- **Fix:** Wrap the write in a try/catch that deletes resolvedPath (and any stale .meta.json) on failure before rethrowing, or write to a temp file and atomically move it into place on success.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Storage\Local\LocalFileStorage.cs. UploadAsync (lines 40-107) opens the destination with FileMode.Create (line 74), which truncates/creates the file before the body is streamed. The body is then streamed either via CopyWithLimitAsync (line 78) or content.CopyToAsync(fileStream, ct) (line 82), inside a `using` block (lines 74-85) with NO try/catch/finally. A grep over the whole file shows no try/catch in UploadAsync and no File.Delete in the upload path (the only File.Delete calls are in DeleteAsync, lines 135/140).

The throw points are real and reachable mid-stream:
- CopyWithLimitAsync (lines 441-459) writes to destination at line 455 each loop iteration, then can throw FileTooLargeException at line 452 on a later iteration AFTER bytes were already written.
- content.CopyToAsync(fileStream, ct) at line 82 throws OperationCanceledException on cancellation (or any IOException) mid-copy.

On either exception, the using block disposes the FileStream but leaves the partial/truncated file on disk; ComputeETagAsync (line 87) and SaveMetadataAsync (line 104) never run, so no .meta.json is written and it is out of sync with the orphaned content. All three claimed net effects hold: (1) orphaned/corrupt file remains; (2) with OverwriteExisting defaulting to false, the guard at line 52 makes a later retry to the same path throw FileAlreadyExistsException against the remnant; (3) for an overwrite of a previously-good file, FileMode.Create already destroyed the old good content before the failure. Genuine high-severity resilience/correctness bug; standard remedy is a try/catch that deletes the partial file (or write-temp-then-atomic-rename).

### CR-H142 · 🟠 high · Birko.Structures
- **Title:** CompressedTrie.GetWordsWithPrefix returns the truncated query prefix instead of full stored words when the prefix ends mid-edge
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Structures\Tries\CompressedTrie.cs:68-72`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `FindNodeForPrefix` now returns the **full label path** from root to the matched node (accumulating each consumed edge label, and appending the whole edge label when the prefix ends mid-edge) instead of a dead `Remaining` value; `GetWordsWithPrefix` seeds `CollectWords` with that path, so `GetWordsWithPrefix("ap")` on a trie with "apple" yields `["apple"]` not `["ap"]`. Removed the dead `prefix[..^remaining.Length] + (…?"":"")` expression. New `CompressedTrieTests` in `Birko.Structures.Tests` (66 → 71): mid-edge prefix → full word(s), node-boundary prefix, `GetAllWords`, and no-match → empty.
- **Detail:** FindNodeForPrefix returns (child, "") as soon as commonLen == prefix.Length (line 241), even when the prefix matched only part of that child's edge label. GetWordsWithPrefix then calls CollectWords(node, prefix, ...) using the raw query prefix, so the portion of the edge label past the prefix is dropped from every emitted word. Example: insert "apple" only, then GetWordsWithPrefix("ap") returns ["ap"] instead of ["apple"]. The dead expression `prefix[..^remaining.Length] + (remaining.Length > 0 ? "" : "")` confirms the author intended to reconstruct the real on-node prefix but it always evaluates to the query prefix (FindNodeForPrefix never returns a non-null node with non-empty remaining). The existing tests only cover Search/StartsWith for CompressedTrie, never GetWordsWithPrefix/GetAllWords with a mid-edge prefix, so this is untested.
- **Fix:** Have FindNodeForPrefix also return the full accumulated label path to the matched node (or the extra label suffix consumed past the prefix), and pass that reconstructed prefix to CollectWords. Add a test: insert "apple"/"applet", assert GetWordsWithPrefix("ap") yields the full words.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Structures\Tries\CompressedTrie.cs and tracing the cited example.

Bug mechanism: With only "apple" inserted, root holds 'a' -> ("apple", node{IsEndOfWord=true}). FindNodeForPrefix(_root, "ap") computes commonLen = CommonPrefixLength("apple","ap") = 2, hits line 241 (commonLen == prefix.Length, i.e. 2 == 2) and returns (child, "") — the full "apple" node with empty remaining — even though the prefix "ap" matched only part of the "apple" edge label. GetWordsWithPrefix (line 71) then calls CollectWords(node, prefix[..^remaining.Length] + (remaining.Length>0?"":""), ...). With remaining = "", ^remaining.Length is ^0 == prefix.Length, so prefix[..^0] is the entire query prefix "ap", and the ternary contributes "" on both branches. CollectWords therefore emits "ap" (node.IsEndOfWord, no children) instead of "apple". The "ple" suffix of the edge label is lost. Result: GetWordsWithPrefix("ap") returns ["ap"] not ["apple"].

Dead-expression claim verified: both ternary branches yield "", and FindNodeForPrefix only ever returns a non-null node with remaining == "" (lines 241 and the recursive tail at 244), so prefix[..^remaining.Length] is always the full query prefix — the intended on-node-prefix reconstruction never occurs. (This also breaks GetAllWords only via prefix; GetAllWords passes empty prefix so it uses the separate CollectWords(_root, "") path which is correct — but any mid-edge prefix query is wrong, and a prefix that lands exactly on a node boundary works.)

Test-coverage claim verified: C:\Source\Birko\Framework.Tests\Birko.Structures.Tests\Tries\TrieTests.cs CompressedTrieTests only has Insert_And_Search and StartsWith_Works; neither GetWordsWithPrefix nor GetAllWords is exercised for CompressedTrie (the GetWordsWithPrefix test at line 24 targets the other Trie class). So the bug is genuinely untested.

This is a real, high-severity, actionable correctness bug producing silently wrong results.

### CR-H143 · 🟠 high · Birko.Web.Components
- **Title:** Ordered lists never wrapped in <ol> in markdown renderer
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Components\src/inputs/b-markdown-editor.ts:557-562`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — ordered-list items are now generated **after** the unordered `<ul>` wrap, tagged with a `data-ol` marker, wrapped as `<ol>`, then the marker is stripped — so ordered lists render inside `<ol>` instead of falling through to `<p>` as bare `<li>`. (Marker approach keeps unordered wrapping and the paragraph-block guard untouched.) Behaviorally verified by replicating the list steps: `1. First\n2. Second\n3. Third` → `<ol><li>First</li>…</ol>`, unordered still `<ul>` with no `<ol>`, mixed lists produce both, no stray `data-ol`. Verified in the **Birko.Web.Playground** (the Birko.Web verification vehicle): rebuilt with the edited sources and `node verify.mjs` renders all 66 components (incl. `b-markdown-editor`/`b-form` in the inputs section) with zero page errors and backport-smoke 17/17. [grouped with CR-H144]
- **Detail:** In BMarkdownEditor.renderMarkdown the list-wrapping step (step 9, line 559: `work.replace(/((?:<li>.*<\/li>\n?)+)/g, '<ul>$1</ul>')`) runs BEFORE ordered-list items are generated (step 10, line 562: `work.replace(/^\d+\.\s+(.+)$/gm, '<li>$1</li>')`). Because the ordered `<li>` elements only come into existence after the only wrapping pass, they are never enclosed in an `<ol>` (or any) list element. Ordered markdown lists therefore render as bare `<li>` elements that fall through to paragraph wrapping (step 14), producing invalid/unstyled output. There is no `<ol>` anywhere in the file.
- **Fix:** Generate ordered-list `<li>`s before the wrapping step, or add a dedicated wrap pass that distinguishes ordered from unordered items (e.g. mark ordered items and wrap matching runs in `<ol>`). Add a renderMarkdown test for `1. a\n2. b`.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the code and reproducing it at runtime. In BMarkdownEditor.renderMarkdown (C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Components\src\inputs\b-markdown-editor.ts), step 9 (line 558) converts unordered items to <li>$2</li>, then line 559 runs the ONLY list-wrapping pass: work.replace(/((?:<li>.*<\/li>\n?)+)/g, '<ul>$1</ul>'). Step 10 (line 562) only afterwards converts ordered items (^\d+\.\s+(.+)$) into bare <li> elements. Since no wrapping pass runs after line 562, ordered <li>s are never enclosed in any list. grep confirms there is no <ol> anywhere in the file. In step 14 (paragraph wrapping, line 583-591) the block-element guard on line 588 only allows h1-6|ul|ol|blockquote|pre|hr|table to pass through, so blocks beginning with bare <li> fall through to line 590 and get wrapped in <p>. I extracted the actual renderMarkdown logic and ran it: input '1. First\n2. Second\n3. Third' produces '<p><li>First</li><br><li>Second</li><br><li>Third</li></p>' (invalid, no <ol>), while unordered lists correctly produce '<ul><li>...</li>...</ul>'. The finding's cited lines, mechanism, and consequence are all accurate. This is a genuine high-severity bug; fix requires generating ordered-list items before (or moving the wrapping after) the wrapping pass, ideally with distinct <ol>/<ul> handling.

### CR-H144 · 🟠 high · Birko.Web.Components
- **Title:** b-form interpolates field value/label/error/placeholder/hint into attributes without escaping
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Components\src/inputs/b-form.ts:532-538`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — `b-form._fieldAttrs` now routes every interpolated attribute value (`data-path`, `name`, `label`, `hint`, `value`, `placeholder`, `error`) through the shared `escapeAttr` from `dom-utils`, and `label-hint.renderLabel` escapes `label` (body) and `hint` (attribute) via `escapeHtml` — so entity/schema text containing `"`/`<`/`>` can no longer break out of the attribute or inject markup into the shadow tree. [grouped with CR-H143]
- **Detail:** _fieldAttrs builds attribute strings via raw template interpolation: `value="${String(field.value)}"`, `label="${field.label}"`, `error="${error}"`, `placeholder="${field.placeholder}"`, `hint="${field.hint}"`. None are escaped (the file imports no escape helper). A value or label from server/user data containing a double-quote breaks out of the attribute, and `<`/`>` allow markup injection into the rendered shadow tree. field.value is commonly populated from loaded entity data, so this is reachable in normal use, not just adversarial input. (renderLabel in label-hint.ts:11 has the same raw-interpolation issue for hint/label.)
- **Fix:** Use the shared escapeAttr/escapeHtml from src/dom-utils.ts when emitting these attribute values (and in renderLabel). dom-utils.escapeHtml already covers & < > " which is sufficient for double-quoted attributes.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading the actual code. In C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Components\src\inputs\b-form.ts, _fieldAttrs (lines 527-541) builds attribute strings via raw template interpolation into double-quoted attributes with NO escaping: label="${field.label}" (532), hint="${field.hint}" (535), value="${String(field.value)}" (536), placeholder="${field.placeholder}" (537), error="${error}" (538). The file's only dom-utils import is isActivationKey (line 2) — it does NOT import escapeHtml/escapeAttr, even though src/dom-utils.ts exports escapeHtml (line 20) and per CLAUDE.md also escapeAttr. These strings feed render() (line 412 -> _renderGroup -> _renderField line 476 -> _fieldAttrs), whose returned markup is assigned to the shadow root innerHTML (standard BaseComponent pattern), so the unescaped text reaches the DOM. The reachability claim holds: field.value is populated via setValues/setValue (lines 255-267) from an arbitrary Record<string, unknown> (loaded entity data), and label/hint/placeholder come from the schema. A value/label containing a double-quote breaks out of the attribute (attribute-injection), enabling markup injection into the rendered shadow tree. The companion note is also accurate: label-hint.ts renderLabel (line 11) interpolates hint raw into text="${hint}" and label/req raw into the <label> body (lines 12-13) with no escaping (its JSDoc even states it does not escape). Caveat noted: this is a client-side component library, so real-world XSS impact depends on the consumer feeding untrusted data, but the documented defect (unescaped attribute interpolation reachable from normal data) is genuine and the fix is clear and available (use the existing escapeAttr/escapeHtml helpers in dom-utils.ts).

### CR-H145 · 🟠 high · Birko.Web.Core
- **Title:** WsClient backoff counter and max-attempts cap are reset on every reconnect
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Core\src/http/websocket-client.ts:46`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — split `connect()` (public, resets `_reconnectAttempts = 0` then calls `_doConnect()`) from the new private `_doConnect()` (disconnect + open, no reset); the reconnect timer now calls `_doConnect()`, so the attempt counter climbs across failures — exponential backoff actually grows toward the 30s cap and `maxReconnectAttempts` is now reachable. `onopen` still resets on genuine success. Verified via Birko.Web.Playground rebuild + `verify.mjs` (66 components, no page errors, backport-smoke 17/17). [grouped with CR-H146]
- **Detail:** connect() unconditionally sets `_reconnectAttempts = 0` (line 46) and is also the function invoked by the reconnect timer in _scheduleReconnect() (line 209). Because each scheduled reconnect calls connect(), the attempt counter is zeroed before the next backoff is computed. Effect: (1) exponential backoff `Math.min(ms * 2^attempt, 30000)` never grows past the first step — it is always recomputed from attempt 0/1, so the client hammers the server at the base interval instead of backing off; (2) `maxReconnectAttempts` is never reached, so a configured cap (e.g. give up after 5 tries) never fires. Note connect() also re-zeros the counter in onopen (line 58), which is the correct place; the reset in connect() is the bug.
- **Fix:** Move the `_reconnectAttempts = 0` reset out of connect() — keep it only in the user-initiated path (e.g. a public reset or the onopen handler, which already does it). The scheduled reconnect should call a private _doConnect() that does NOT reset the counter, while the public connect() resets it.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed REAL by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Core\src\http\websocket-client.ts in full.

Control flow trace:
- connect() resets this._reconnectAttempts = 0 at line 46 (unconditionally, on every call).
- _scheduleReconnect() (line 191) computes delay = Math.min(ms * Math.pow(2, this._reconnectAttempts), 30_000) at line 203, increments _reconnectAttempts++ at line 204, then sets a timer whose callback calls this.connect() at line 209.
- Therefore each failed reconnect cycle goes: onclose -> _scheduleReconnect (attempts 0 -> compute delay with 2^0 = base ms -> increment to 1 -> arm timer) -> timer fires -> connect() (attempts reset to 0) -> new socket -> if it fails before onopen -> onclose -> _scheduleReconnect again with attempts back at 0.

Consequences, both as described:
1. Exponential backoff never grows. At every compute the counter is 0, so delay is always the base interval (ms * 2^0). The ++ to 1 is wiped by connect()'s line-46 reset before the next compute, so the counter oscillates 0->1->0->1 and never climbs. The server is hammered at the base reconnectMs instead of backing off toward the 30s cap.
2. maxReconnectAttempts cap never fires. The give-up check at line 196 (max > 0 && this._reconnectAttempts >= max) compares against a counter that never exceeds 1, so a configured cap like 5 is unreachable and the onClose "Max reconnect attempts reached" path is dead code for repeated failures.

The finding also correctly notes the onopen handler at line 58 already resets the counter, which is the correct place (reset only on a genuinely successful connection). The line-46 reset in connect() is redundant for the success case and actively harmful for the failure case. All cited line numbers match the actual file. Fix: remove the _reconnectAttempts = 0 assignment at line 46 and rely on the onopen reset. Severity high is justified for a self-DoS / never-give-up reconnect storm.

### CR-H146 · 🟠 high · Birko.Web.Core
- **Title:** SyncManager._syncing can stick at true forever if getPending() throws
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Core\src/offline/sync-manager.ts:44`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the `sync()` body (getPending + the per-action loop) is now wrapped in `try { … } finally { this._syncing = false; }`, so an exception from `getPending()` (IndexedDB open failure, etc.) or a queue write no longer leaves `_syncing` stuck at true — which would have permanently short-circuited every future sync (online-event + periodic interval) for the session. `_notifyComplete`/return stay on the success path. Verified via the Birko.Web.Playground rebuild + `verify.mjs`. [grouped with CR-H145]
- **Detail:** sync() sets `this._syncing = true` (line 46) and only clears it at line 88 on the normal path. The `await this._queue.getPending()` call (line 48) and the per-action loop are not wrapped in try/finally. If getPending() rejects (IndexedDB open failure, etc.), the exception propagates, `_syncing` is never reset to false, and the guard `if (this._syncing) return ...` at line 45 permanently disables all future syncs — including the auto-sync on `online` and the periodic interval. Offline writes would then silently never sync for the rest of the session.
- **Fix:** Wrap the body in try { ... } finally { this._syncing = false; }, and emit the completion result inside the try.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Core\src\offline\sync-manager.ts. The sync() method (lines 44-92) sets this._syncing = true at line 46 and only resets it to false at line 88 on the normal completion path. There is NO try/finally protecting the body. The await this._queue.getPending() at line 48 is unguarded, and the per-action queue mutations (this._queue.update at line 55, remove at line 65) are outside the inner try block (which only wraps the API call at lines 57-85). If getPending() rejects (e.g., IndexedDB open failure) or any queue write throws outside the inner catch, the exception propagates out of sync(), line 88 never executes, and _syncing remains true. The guard at line 45 (if (this._syncing) return ...) then permanently short-circuits all future sync attempts — including the 'online' event listener (line 30) and the periodic setInterval (lines 34-38). This silently disables offline-write syncing for the rest of the session. Line numbers, mechanism, and severity in the finding all match the actual code. The fix (wrap in try/finally to reset _syncing) is clear and actionable.

### CR-H147 · 🟠 high · Birko.Web.Shell
- **Title:** Unguarded JWT decode in setAuth() crashes on malformed/opaque tokens
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Shell\src/auth/auth-store.ts:52`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** verified real (high)
- **Status:** done — the JWT decode in `setAuth()` is now guarded: a missing payload segment is checked before `atob`, and `atob`/`JSON.parse` run in try/catch, defaulting `payload` to `{}` on failure. An opaque/malformed token no longer throws out of `setAuth` (which half-wrote the store and aborted login) — the token is still stored and `isAuthenticated` set, with claim-derived fields simply defaulting. Mirrors the existing `loadFromStorage()` guard. Verified via Birko.Web.Playground rebuild + `verify.mjs`.
- **Detail:** `const payload = JSON.parse(atob(jwt.split('.')[1]));` is not wrapped in try/catch. If the server returns an opaque (non-JWT) token, a token without a `.`-separated payload segment, invalid base64, or non-JSON payload, `jwt.split('.')[1]` is `undefined` (atob throws) or atob/JSON.parse throw — the exception propagates out of `setAuth`, leaving the store half-written (token never set, isAuthenticated never flipped) and likely crashing the caller's login flow. Contrast with `loadFromStorage()` (lines 16-21) which correctly guards JSON.parse in try/catch.
- **Fix:** Wrap the decode in try/catch (mirroring loadFromStorage). On failure either bail early without mutating the store, or set the token but default the claim-derived fields. Also guard the missing-segment case before calling atob.
- **Verify reasoning:** Confirmed by reading C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Web.Shell\src\auth\auth-store.ts. Line 52 is exactly `const payload = JSON.parse(atob(jwt.split('.')[1]));` inside setAuth(), with no surrounding try/catch. The only guard is `if (!jwt) return;` (line 50), which handles empty tokens but not opaque/malformed ones. For an opaque token without a '.', `jwt.split('.')[1]` is undefined and atob(undefined)→atob("undefined") throws InvalidCharacterError; invalid base64 or non-JSON payloads similarly throw via atob/JSON.parse. Because the throw occurs at line 52 BEFORE any store.set(...) (lines 54-65) and before persist() (line 67), the exception propagates out of setAuth leaving the store half-written (token never set, isAuthenticated never flipped) and aborting the caller's login flow — exactly as described. The finding's contrast is also valid: loadFromStorage() (lines 16-21) wraps JSON.parse in try/catch, so the codebase establishes the defensive pattern that setAuth omits. Minor inaccuracy in the prose (atob receives the string "undefined" rather than literally throwing on undefined) does not change the outcome (uncaught exception on the auth-critical path). Genuine, actionable, high severity is justified.

## Medium findings (275)

### CR-M001 · 🟡 medium · Birko.AI
- **Title:** Synchronous-over-async blocking in HandleResponse (.GetAwaiter().GetResult())
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI\Agents/Agent.cs:280`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — HandleResponse is now async (Task<(bool,bool)?>) and awaits HandleToolUse; the GetAwaiter().GetResult() sync-over-async bridge is gone.
- **Detail:** HandleResponse is a synchronous method that runs inside async RunWithHistory*Async, and it calls HandleToolUse(...).GetAwaiter().GetResult() to block on an async tool-execution path. Sync-over-async on the awaiting thread risks thread-pool starvation/deadlock (and forfeits async benefits) when tools do real I/O. The entire HandleResponse/HandleToolUse chain is already called from async contexts and could be awaited directly.
- **Fix:** Make HandleResponse async (Task<(bool,bool)?>) and await it from RunWithHistoryStreamingAsync/RunWithHistorySyncAsync, then await HandleToolUse directly instead of GetAwaiter().GetResult().

### CR-M002 · 🟡 medium · Birko.AI
- **Title:** Streaming path never observes a CancellationToken; no token threaded through agent run
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI\Agents/Agent.cs:149-273`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — CancellationToken threaded through RunAsync/ContinueAsync -> run loop -> provider calls, retry Task.Delay, SSE readers and Tool.ExecuteAsync.
- **Detail:** None of RunAsync/ContinueAsync/RunWithHistory*Async accept or propagate a CancellationToken, and the provider SendMessageAsync/SendMessageStreamingAsync signatures (ILlmProvider) take none either. A long agent loop with network calls and Task.Delay retry backoff cannot be cancelled. Framework convention is that async methods observe a CancellationToken.
- **Fix:** Thread a CancellationToken through RunAsync/ContinueAsync down to provider calls and Task.Delay; add token params to the ILlmProvider methods (contract change, but the retry/delay loops in LlmProviderBase especially should honor it).

### CR-M003 · 🟡 medium · Birko.AI
- **Title:** Streaming response stream is never disposed; underlying HTTP response may leak
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI\Agents/Agent.cs:206-212`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — LlmStreamingResponse is now IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable (holds the streaming HttpResponseMessage as Resource); Agent enumerates it under await using so an abandoned stream is disposed.
- **Detail:** In RunWithHistoryStreamingAsync the IAsyncEnumerable<string> from streamingResponse.GetStreamAsync() is enumerated to completion but there is no disposal of the streaming response / underlying HttpResponseMessage or network Stream. ParseSseStream wraps the stream in a StreamReader with 'using' only when the iterator runs to completion; if the await foreach is abandoned early (exception mid-loop), the SSE stream/StreamReader and the SendStreamingWithRetryAsync HttpResponseMessage are not disposed. LlmStreamingResponse exposes no Dispose hook to release the HTTP response.
- **Fix:** Make LlmStreamingResponse (or the returned stream) IDisposable/IAsyncDisposable and dispose it in a finally around the await-foreach; ensure the HttpResponseMessage from SendStreamingWithRetryAsync is owned and disposed once the stream is consumed.

### CR-M010 · 🟡 medium · Birko.AI.Providers
- **Title:** HttpResponseMessage from SendWithRetryAsync is never disposed
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI\Providers\LlmProviderBase.cs:62`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — SendWithRetryAsync disposes the buffered HttpResponseMessage on every return path (StatusCode stays readable); regression test asserts disposal.
- **Detail:** SendWithRetryAsync does `var response = await httpClient.SendAsync(request);` (not `using`) and returns the live HttpResponseMessage to every caller. None of the 16 providers dispose the returned response in their SendMessageAsync methods (e.g. ClaudeProvider, OpenAiProvider, GeminiProvider, OllamaProvider, AzureOpenAiProvider, ZAiProvider, OpenAiCompatibleProviderBase all just read `response.IsSuccessStatusCode` then discard it). Each non-streaming call leaks an HttpResponseMessage (and its underlying connection handle). With a shared static-lifetime HttpClient per provider and high call volume this accumulates undisposed handles.
- **Fix:** Since the response body is already fully buffered into the returned string, callers don't need the live response. Either dispose the response inside SendWithRetryAsync before returning (returning only StatusCode + body), or wrap returned responses in `using` at every call site. The streaming helper already disposes on its failure paths — mirror that discipline here.

### CR-M011 · 🟡 medium · Birko.AI.Resilience
- **Title:** Rate limiter is purely advisory — TrackedLlmProvider waits then proceeds without re-checking
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI.Resilience\Services\TrackedLlmProvider.cs:45`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — TrackedLlmProvider re-checks CanMakeRequest in a bounded loop (WaitForRateLimitSlotAsync) and returns an error when the limit cannot be satisfied instead of proceeding blind.
- **Detail:** When CanMakeRequest returns false, SendMessageAsync (and the streaming variant) computes GetRetryAfter, delays once (the retry-after, or a flat 1000ms when null), and then unconditionally calls _inner.SendMessageAsync. It never re-checks CanMakeRequest after the delay, so the request is sent regardless of whether the window has actually cleared. This means the rate limiter never truly prevents a call — it only inserts a fixed pause. For token-per-minute / per-day rejections GetRetryAfter always returns null (see separate finding), so the wait is a fixed 1s that does nothing to clear a daily-token overflow.
- **Fix:** Loop: after delaying, re-check CanMakeRequest (with a max-attempts / max-wait cap) before proceeding, or return an error response when the limit cannot be satisfied.

### CR-M012 · 🟡 medium · Birko.AI.Resilience
- **Title:** GetRetryAfter only considers RequestsPerMinute, ignoring token and daily limits
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI.Resilience\Services\ProviderRateLimiter.cs:116`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — GetRetryAfter now computes backoff for token-per-minute and daily windows and returns the max active blocking window; regression test added.
- **Detail:** GetRetryAfter checks only limit.RequestsPerMinute and the minute window's RequestCount. If a request is blocked by TokensPerMinute, RequestsPerDay, or TokensPerDay, GetRetryAfter returns null. The caller (TrackedLlmProvider) then falls back to a flat 1s wait, which for a daily overflow is meaningless. The returned retry-after can therefore be null even though CanMakeRequest just returned false.
- **Fix:** Compute retry-after for the token-per-minute case (also one minute) and the daily cases (time until day window rolls over) and return the max of the active blocking windows.

### CR-M013 · 🟡 medium · Birko.AI.Resilience
- **Title:** Fire-and-forget circuit-breaker persistence can write stale state out of order
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.AI.Resilience\Services\ProviderCircuitBreaker.cs:192`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — circuit-breaker persistence is serialized per provider via an ordered task chain, with an awaitable FlushPersistenceAsync; a stale snapshot can no longer overwrite a newer one.
- **Detail:** PersistState launches an unawaited Task.Run that snapshots circuit state and calls _store.SaveAsync. Under concurrent RecordFailure/RecordSuccess for the same provider, two background tasks race with no ordering guarantee — a SaveAsync carrying older state can complete after one carrying newer state, leaving the store with stale persisted state (e.g. Open written after the recovering Closed). Exceptions are caught and only logged, so persistence failures are silent. There is also no way for a caller to await that a state change was durably stored.
- **Fix:** Serialize persistence per provider (e.g. a per-provider lock/queue or a single-flight last-write-wins guarded by UpdatedAt), or make persistence synchronous/awaitable so ordering is preserved.

### CR-M016 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.ElasticSearch
- **Title:** DequeueAsync claims jobs non-atomically (read-then-update race)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.ElasticSearch\ElasticSearchJobQueue.cs:63-91`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — DequeueAsync now claims via a conditional native update guarded on the eligible status + ClaimToken re-read verify; ES refresh-window residual documented in CLAUDE.md (handlers must be idempotent). Birko.BackgroundJobs.ElasticSearch.Tests added.
- **Detail:** DequeueAsync reads the top candidate (limit 1) and then issues a separate UpdateAsync to set Status=Processing. There is no optimistic concurrency / compare-and-swap, so two workers polling concurrently can both read the same Pending job before either update lands and both proceed to process it. This pattern is shared with the SQL/Mongo backends, but Elasticsearch is materially worse here: by default the index refreshes only ~once per second, so even a serialized claim by worker A is not visible to worker B's search for up to the refresh interval, widening the double-dequeue window considerably. AttemptCount++ also races (lost update). At minimum this should be documented as at-least-once with possible duplicate dispatch; ideally the claim should use a versioned/optimistic update and re-read on conflict.
- **Fix:** Use Elasticsearch optimistic concurrency (seq_no/primary_term or a version field) on the claim update and treat a version conflict as 'lost the race' -> retry the dequeue loop. Failing that, document the duplicate-dispatch risk in CLAUDE.md and rely on idempotent job handlers.

### CR-M020 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.MongoDB
- **Title:** DequeueAsync is a non-atomic read-then-update (job double-pickup under concurrency)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.MongoDB\MongoDBJobQueue.cs:53-94`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — DequeueAsync now claims via a conditional native update (Mongo $set is per-document atomic) + ClaimToken re-read verify; Birko.BackgroundJobs.MongoDB.Tests added.
- **Detail:** DequeueAsync reads the top candidate (limit:1) and then, in a separate UpdateAsync, flips it to Processing. Two workers (or two threads) can read the same Pending/Scheduled job before either writes Processing, so the same job is dequeued and executed twice. The README/CLAUDE for these backends advertise 'distributed processing', which this pattern does not safely support. The SQL backend has the identical non-atomic shape (and ships a separate SqlJobLockProvider to compensate), so this is a shared design limitation rather than a regression — but MongoDB has a clean native atomic primitive that the SQL store lacks.
- **Fix:** Use a single atomic FindOneAndUpdate (find the highest-priority eligible job and set Status=Processing/AttemptCount++/LastAttemptAt in one round trip, returning the post-image). The underlying AsyncMongoDBStore does not expose FindOneAndUpdate today, so either add it there or drop to MongoDBJobQueue.Store.Client to issue it directly. As a weaker stopgap, an UpdateAsync(filter, PropertyUpdate) guarded on Status still pending would at least make the claim conditional.

### CR-M021 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.RavenDB
- **Title:** DequeueAsync read-then-update is not atomic (lost-update / double-dispatch race)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.RavenDB\RavenDBJobQueue.cs:81-91`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — DequeueAsync now claims via a conditional update guarded on the eligible status + ClaimToken re-read verify (resolves a single winner even under RavenDB last-write-wins); Birko.BackgroundJobs.RavenDB.Tests added.
- **Detail:** DequeueAsync reads a single Pending/Scheduled candidate, then in a separate round-trip sets it to Processing and increments AttemptCount via UpdateAsync. There is no optimistic-concurrency guard (no change-vector / ETag check) between the read and the update. Two concurrent workers (or two processes) polling the same queue can both read the same job, both mark it Processing, and both dispatch it. The reference InMemoryJobQueue avoids this with a SemaphoreSlim, but that is in-process only; for a persistent multi-worker backend a DB-level concurrency check is the real protection. RavenDB supports optimistic concurrency on the session, so this is fixable here unlike some other backends.
- **Fix:** Use RavenDB optimistic concurrency on the claim update (set UseOptimisticConcurrency / pass the change vector) and treat a concurrency-conflict on the claim as 'job already taken' -> re-loop to the next candidate, so only one worker can transition a given job to Processing.

### CR-M023 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis
- **Title:** GetByStatusAsync truncates before ordering — returns an arbitrary subset, not the newest N
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis\RedisJobQueue.cs:266,281`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — GetByStatusAsync now materializes all members, orders by EnqueuedAt desc, THEN takes limit (was Take-before-order on an unordered set).
- **Detail:** Redis sets are unordered. The code does members.Take(limit) (line 266) on the unordered SetMembers result, then OrderByDescending(EnqueuedAt) (line 281) on that truncated subset. So with more than `limit` jobs in a status, it returns an arbitrary `limit` jobs sorted among themselves, not the globally-newest `limit`. The InMemoryJobQueue reference (InMemoryJobQueue.cs:121-126) orders by EnqueuedAt descending FIRST, then Take(limit), yielding the true newest N. The Redis backend silently diverges from the documented/reference contract.
- **Fix:** Fetch and deserialize all members for the status (or use a sorted set keyed by EnqueuedAt), then OrderByDescending(EnqueuedAt).Take(limit). If unbounded fetch is a concern, maintain a per-status sorted set instead of a plain set.

### CR-M025 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis
- **Title:** Dequeue read-modify-write of the job hash is not atomic with the sorted-set removal
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.Redis\RedisJobQueue.cs:120-141`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — the dequeue claim (ZREM + hash flip to Processing, AttemptCount++, LastAttemptAt, status-set move) is now performed entirely inside the Lua DequeueScript, closing the orphan/double-dispatch window.
- **Detail:** The Lua DequeueScript atomically removes the job id from the queue sorted set, but the subsequent HashGetAll (121), status mutation, and HashSet (138) happen as separate round-trips outside any transaction. If the process crashes between the ZREM and the HashSet that marks Processing, the job is gone from the queue but its hash still says Pending — it becomes orphaned (never re-queued, never visible to DequeueAsync). The README advertises 'Jobs survive process restarts' and 'no two workers grab the same job'; the at-least-once guarantee is weaker than implied because there is no visibility-timeout / requeue of stuck Processing jobs.
- **Fix:** Either move the status flip into the Lua script (read hash + set Status=Processing + bump AttemptCount atomically), or add a reclaim path that re-queues Processing jobs whose LastAttemptAt exceeds a visibility timeout. At minimum document the orphan window.

### CR-M026 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.SQL
- **Title:** SqlJobLockProvider leaks the lock connection if OpenAsync throws
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.SQL\SqlJobLockProvider.cs:49-50`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — CreateConnection/OpenAsync moved inside the try so any failure routes through ReleaseConnectionAsync and nulls the connection instead of leaking it.
- **Detail:** TryAcquireAsync assigns _lockConnection = _connector.CreateConnection(...) and then awaits _lockConnection.OpenAsync(ct). If OpenAsync throws (DB unreachable, auth failure, cancellation), the exception propagates with _lockConnection holding an undisposed DbConnection. The field is left non-null, so a subsequent TryAcquireAsync call overwrites it (since IsLocked is still false), permanently orphaning the first connection. Only the ExecuteScalarAsync failure path (the try/catch at lines 58-73) calls ReleaseConnectionAsync; the OpenAsync failure is outside that try.
- **Fix:** Move the CreateConnection/OpenAsync into the try block (or a dedicated try/finally) so any failure routes through ReleaseConnectionAsync and nulls _lockConnection before rethrowing.

### CR-M027 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.SQL
- **Title:** TryAcquireAsync returns true on non-PostgreSQL backends without holding any lock
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.SQL\SqlJobLockProvider.cs:68-73`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — provider-appropriate locking (Postgres pg_try_advisory_lock, MSSql sp_getapplock, MySQL GET_LOCK); unsupported backends (SQLite) now return false instead of falsely reporting success. Regression test asserts SQLite returns false.
- **Detail:** The lock uses pg_try_advisory_lock, which only exists on PostgreSQL. On MSSql/MySQL/SQLite the ExecuteScalarAsync throws DbException and the catch returns true ('Not PostgreSQL — rely on transaction-level locking in dequeue'). But DequeueAsync does NOT do transaction-level locking (see the dequeue race finding), and IsLocked stays false so ReleaseAsync is a no-op. The caller is told it holds an exclusive lock and proceeds, while in reality no mutual exclusion exists — the worst kind of silent failure for a distributed lock. The class is generic over <DB> (PostgreSqlConnector, MSSqlConnector, MySQL, SQLite per the doc) so non-Postgres is an expected, not exotic, configuration.
- **Fix:** Either return false (lock not acquirable) on non-Postgres so callers fall back deliberately, or implement provider-appropriate locking (sp_getapplock for MSSql, GET_LOCK for MySQL) keyed off the connector type. At minimum, do not report success for a lock that was never taken.

### CR-M029 · 🟡 medium · Birko.BackgroundJobs.XML
- **Title:** DequeueAsync read-modify-write is not atomic (lost/duplicated jobs under concurrency)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.BackgroundJobs.XML\XmlJobQueue.cs:58-99`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — DequeueAsync read-claim-update serialized with a SemaphoreSlim; single-worker/cross-process constraint documented in CLAUDE.md.
- **Detail:** DequeueAsync reads the top candidate (limit:1), then separately mutates Status->Processing and calls UpdateAsync. There is no compare-and-swap, so two concurrent DequeueAsync calls (or two worker processes sharing the file) can select and 'claim' the same job, and the file store rewrites the whole file on each save, so interleaved updates can also clobber each other. The class doc scopes this to 'single-process deployments,' which makes it acceptable by design, but a single process with multiple worker tasks polling the same queue still races. This is inherent to the file-store backend (the JSON sibling has the identical pattern) and cannot be fully fixed without a native conditional update.
- **Fix:** Document the single-worker constraint explicitly in the XML README/CLAUDE.md (not just 'single-process'), or guard DequeueAsync with a SemaphoreSlim so concurrent dequeues within the process serialize the claim step.

### CR-M030 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Caching
- **Title:** Per-key lock eviction races with GetOrSetAsync, weakening stampede protection
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Caching\Memory\MemoryCache.cs:78-94,119-124`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — per-key stampede locks are now reference-counted and retired by their last releaser (timer no longer evicts locks), so a lock cannot be recycled between GetOrAdd and WaitAsync. Regression tests: concurrent-same-key factory-once + lock-map drains to zero.
- **Detail:** GetOrSetAsync does _locks.GetOrAdd(key, ...) (line 78) and then awaits WaitAsync (line 79). Meanwhile EvictExpired (lines 119-124) removes any lock whose entry is absent and whose CurrentCount == 1. A thread that has just obtained the semaphore from GetOrAdd but has not yet entered WaitAsync (CurrentCount is still 1, and on a cache miss there is no entry) can have its semaphore removed by the timer. A second concurrent caller for the same key then GetOrAdds a brand-new semaphore, so two threads enter the critical section simultaneously and both invoke the factory. This defeats the stated 'Per-key lock to prevent cache stampede' guarantee. Data correctness is preserved (last writer wins) but the factory can run multiple times concurrently, which is exactly what the lock exists to prevent.
- **Fix:** Only remove a lock while holding it, or track in-flight waiters (e.g. a refcount incremented before WaitAsync) and skip eviction when any waiter is pending. Simpler: never evict locks in the timer, or guard the GetOrAdd+WaitAsync+removal under a consistent scheme so a lock cannot be removed between GetOrAdd and WaitAsync.

### CR-M031 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Caching.Hybrid
- **Title:** Write-through SetAsync orphans l1Task when L2 faults and fallback is disabled
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Caching.Hybrid\HybridCache.cs:69`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — the write-through SetAsync now always awaits the L1 write in a finally (L2 call inside the try to catch sync throws too), so L1 is observed even when L2 faults with fallback disabled. Regression test asserts L1 is written and the L2 error still propagates.
- **Detail:** In the WriteThrough branch, l1Task is started, then l2Task = _l2.SetAsync(...) and await Task.WhenAll(l1Task, l2Task). The only catch is 'catch when (_options.FallbackToL1OnL2Failure)'. When FallbackToL1OnL2Failure is false and L2 faults, Task.WhenAll throws and propagates, leaving l1Task never awaited. The L1 write still runs as fire-and-forget, and if it faults its exception is unobserved; callers also cannot rely on L1 being durably written before the exception surfaces. This asymmetry (WriteThrough=false path explicitly handles the no-fallback case at line 89-96, WriteThrough=true does not) is likely unintended.
- **Fix:** Await l1Task in a finally (or catch the WhenAll failure, await l1Task to observe it, then rethrow when fallback is disabled) so the L1 write is always observed regardless of the fallback flag.

### CR-M036 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Communication.Bluetooth
- **Title:** Read() checks HasReadData outside the lock (TOCTOU)
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports/BluetoothLE.cs:400-417`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified

With the Linux background ReadWorker appending under the lock, the count can change between the unlocked check and the locked GetRange. For a positive size this is benign because the buffer only grows on the worker thread, but if any caller path removes between the check and the lock, GetRange(0, size) can throw. ### CR-M037 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Communication.Bluetooth

### CR-M038 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Communication.Bluetooth
- **Title:** Auto-reconnect re-enters Open() from the read thread, stacking background threads
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports/BluetoothLE.cs:478-505,549-569`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done (core) — a _reconnecting guard stops Open() from resetting _reconnectAttempts during a reconnect, so MaxReconnectAttempts now actually bounds the retry chain (was effectively infinite). Residual: reconnect still runs on the dying read thread and Open() spawns a fresh read thread — a dedicated supervisor is the cleaner design, documented inline; the bounded-attempts guard keeps the chain finite.
- **Detail:** ReadWorker, on exit, calls HandleReconnect() which (on the same read thread) sleeps then calls Open(). Open() (OpenWindows/OpenLinux) creates and starts a brand-new _readThread while the current ReadWorker invocation is still on the stack inside HandleReconnect. The old thread reference in _readThread is overwritten, so a subsequent Close() can only Join the newest thread; the reconnect chain can stack threads and the _reconnectAttempts reset inside Open() (sets _reconnectAttempts = 0 on success) fights the increment in HandleReconnect.
- **Fix:** Drive reconnect from a dedicated supervisor rather than from inside the dying read thread, or have Open() not spawn a new read thread when invoked from the reconnect path; ensure the previous thread has fully exited before starting a new one.

### CR-M039 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Communication.Bluetooth
- **Title:** Sync-over-async in Open(): Task.Wait result ignored, exceptions deferred
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.Bluetooth\Ports/BluetoothLE.cs:59-85`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — OpenWindows now checks connectTask.Wait(timeout) and throws TimeoutException on false instead of proceeding on a stale _isOpen. (WINDOWS-gated; code-review verified — the WinRT branch is not compiled off a Windows TFM.)
- **Detail:** OpenWindows calls connectTask.Wait(settings.ConnectionTimeout) and ignores the bool return (whether it actually completed within the timeout), relying solely on _isOpen. If the connect task is still running when the timeout elapses, execution proceeds, _isOpen is checked, and the still-running task's eventual exception becomes unobserved. This is blocking sync-over-async on a UI-affinity-prone WinRT path and can deadlock in apps with a synchronization context.
- **Fix:** Check the Wait(timeout) return value and treat false as a timeout failure; consider providing an async Open path, and observe/await the connect task so exceptions are not dropped.

### CR-M043 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Communication.Camera
- **Title:** Process not killed when capture is cancelled or fails

On cancellation (CopyToAsync/WaitForExitAsync throw OperationCanceledException, caught at line 85) or any other exception, the method returns null while the ffmpeg process may still be running, leaking an orphaned OS process (and holding the camera device open). ### CR-M044 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Communication.Camera

### CR-M047 · 🟡 medium · Birko.Communication.gRPC
- **Title:** WithAuth mutates and re-adds headers into a reused Metadata instance
- **Path:** `C:\Source\Birko\Framework\Birko.Communication.gRPC\GrpcAuthenticationInterceptor.cs:64-67`
- **Category:** bug · **Verification:** not individually verified
- **Status:** done — WithAuth now copies the inbound headers into a NEW Metadata instead of mutating the caller-supplied one, so reusing a CallOptions no longer accumulates duplicate authorization/x-tenant entries. Regression test: reuse → one auth header each call, caller Metadata untouched.
- **Detail:** When context.Options.Headers is non-null, WithAuth reuses that exact Metadata instance and calls _mutate(headers), which Add()s the auth header (and any extraMetadata) into it. CallOptions/Metadata can legitimately be reused across multiple calls by a caller. Since the interceptor mutates the caller's Metadata in place and Metadata.Add appends (it does not replace), repeated calls through the same CallOptions accumulate duplicate 'authorization' (and x-tenant, etc.) entries. The interceptor should operate on a copy of the inbound headers rather than mutating the caller-supplied collection.
- **Fix:** In WithAuth, build a new Metadata seeded from context.Options.Headers (copy existing entries) instead of mutating the original, then call _mutate on the copy. This keeps each call's header injection idempotent regardless of CallOptions reuse.
